 \_ chrome --type=renderer      # tab 2 unaffected

Threading models

ModelMapping
1:1 (kernel threads)each user thread = one kernel thread. True parallelism, kernel schedules them. Linux/Windows default.
N:1 (user threads / green)many user threads on one kernel thread. Fast switching, but one blocking syscall stalls all, no multicore.
M:N (hybrid)M user threads over N kernel threads. Best of both, complex; Go's goroutines, old Solaris.
// 1:1  -- pthread_create makes a real kernel thread (clone(CLONE_VM|CLONE_THREAD))
pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, arg);   // visible as an LWP: `ps -eLf`

// M:N -- Go multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a few OS threads (GOMAXPROCS)
for i := 0; i < 100000; i++ {
    go handle(conn[i])                // ~2 KB each; the runtime scheduler parks/resumes them
}

When to use threads

CPU-bound parallel work on shared data (parallel matrix ops), or keeping a UI/event loop responsive while background work runs. For pure I/O concurrency, async/event loops often beat thread-per-connection. For isolation or scaling across machines, use processes.

# CPU-bound: threads give real speedup (split the array across cores)
$ ./sum_parallel --threads=8        # 8x on an 8-core box

# I/O-bound: 10k idle connections -> one async event loop beats 10k threads
#   10k threads * ~1 MB stack = ~10 GB;  epoll loop = a few MB

# untrusted / must-not-share-a-crash: separate processes
$ firejail --seccomp ./plugin      # sandboxed child process, own address space
Cheat Sheet
  • Threads share: address space, heap, globals, fds, PID. Threads own: stack, registers, TLS, errno.
  • Thread pros: cheap create/switch, shared-memory comms. Cons: no isolation — one thread's crash/corruption kills all.
  • Process pros: fault isolation, security boundary. Cons: heavier, IPC needed.
  • Models: 1:1 (kernel threads, real parallelism, Linux/Windows), N:1 (user/green, no multicore, blocks all), M:N (hybrid, e.g. Go).
  • Context switch: thread→thread in same process is cheaper (no page-table/TLB swap) than process→process.
  • Use threads for CPU-parallel shared-data work; processes for isolation; async loops for I/O concurrency.
Q&A
What do threads in a process share, and what is private?
Shared: the address space (code, heap, globals), file descriptors, PID, signal handlers. Private: each thread's stack, register set/PC, thread-local storage, and errno.
Why is a thread context switch cheaper than a process one?
Threads of the same process share the page tables, so switching between them doesn't require loading a new address space or flushing the TLB — just saving/restoring registers and the stack pointer.
1:1 vs M:N threading?
1:1 maps each user thread to a kernel thread — simple, true multicore, but creation and switching go through the kernel. M:N multiplexes many user threads over fewer kernel threads — ultra-cheap user-level switching and huge thread counts, at the cost of a complex runtime scheduler that must handle blocking syscalls (Go's runtime does this for goroutines).
When would you choose multiple processes over multiple threads?
When you need fault isolation (a crash shouldn't kill everything), a security boundary (sandboxing untrusted code — browser tabs, plugins), or to scale beyond one machine. Also when the language/runtime has a global lock (CPython's GIL) that limits threaded CPU parallelism.
Does creating a thread give you a new address space?
No — it runs in the same address space as its process. Only fork()/a new process gets a separate address space.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Do two threads in one process share the heap?
Yes. They also share globals and file descriptors. Each has its own stack.
If one thread segfaults, what happens to the others?
The whole process is killed — there's no isolation between threads.
Which threading model gives true multicore parallelism for CPU-bound work?
1:1 (kernel-level threads). Pure N:1 user threads can't use more than one core.

Intermediate core

Your Python program uses threads for CPU-heavy number crunching and sees no speedup on 8 cores. Why?
CPython's Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound threads run serially. Use multiprocessing (separate processes, separate GILs), a C extension / numpy that releases the GIL, or the no-GIL builds. Threads still help Python for I/O-bound work (the GIL is released during blocking I/O).
Why do web browsers use a process per site/tab rather than threads?
Isolation and security. A crash or a memory-corruption exploit in one tab's renderer is contained — it can't read another site's data or bring down the browser. The OS process boundary + sandboxing (seccomp, restricted tokens) enforces the same-origin trust boundary. The cost is higher memory (per-process overhead), which browsers manage by consolidating tabs from the same site and limiting process count on low-memory devices.

Advanced deep

How does an M:N runtime (e.g. Go) keep a blocking syscall in one goroutine from stalling the others?
The runtime has P (logical processors, = GOMAXPROCS), M (OS threads), and G (goroutines). Normally each M runs goroutines from a P's run queue. When a goroutine is about to make a blocking syscall, the runtime detaches the P from that M (hands it off to a spare or new M) so other goroutines keep running on other cores while this M is parked in the kernel. When the syscall returns, the M tries to reacquire a P; if none is free, its goroutine is put back on a global queue and the M sleeps. For non-blocking I/O the runtime uses an integrated network poller (epoll/kqueue): the goroutine is parked, the M moves on, and the poller reschedules the goroutine when the fd is ready. Plus a preemption mechanism (async signals / safepoints) stops a CPU-bound goroutine from monopolising its M. This is why you can have a million goroutines with a handful of OS threads.
What is clone() on Linux and how does it unify threads and processes?
Linux doesn't have separate "create process" and "create thread" primitives at the lowest level — both are clone() with a set of flags controlling exactly what the new task shares with its creator: CLONE_VM (share address space), CLONE_FILES (share fd table), CLONE_FS (share cwd/root/umask), CLONE_SIGHAND/CLONE_THREAD (share signal handling and appear in the same thread group / PID), CLONE_NEWNS/NEWPID/NEWNET… (new namespaces — the basis of containers). A POSIX thread is clone() with VM+FILES+FS+SIGHAND+THREAD; a plain fork() is clone() with almost nothing shared (COW address space). Containers are clone() with the namespace flags. So "process vs thread" is really just a point on a spectrum of what a task shares.

CPU Scheduling Algorithms

Deciding which ready process runs next — and what metric you're optimising.

Notes

Metrics

  • Throughput — jobs completed per unit time.
  • Turnaround — completion time − arrival time.
  • Waiting time — time spent in the ready queue.
  • Response time — arrival to first CPU (matters for interactivity).
  • Fairness / no starvation.

You can't maximise all at once — batch systems favour throughput/turnaround, interactive systems favour response time.

# jobs: A(burst 6), B(burst 8), C(burst 7), D(burst 3), all arrive at t=0
# FCFS order A,B,C,D:
#   finish: A=6  B=14  C=21  D=24
#   waiting: A=0 B=6  C=14 D=21   -> avg wait = 41/4 = 10.25
# SJF order D,A,C,B:
#   waiting: D=0 A=3  C=9  B=16   -> avg wait = 28/4 = 7.0   (provably minimal)

The classic algorithms

AlgorithmRuleNote
FCFSrun in arrival order, non-preemptivesimple; convoy effect — one long job delays everyone
SJFshortest next CPU burst firstprovably minimum average waiting time; needs burst prediction; can starve long jobs
SRTFpreemptive SJFeven better average wait; more context switches
Round Robineach gets a time quantum, then rotatefair, good response time; quantum too small = switch overhead, too big = FCFS
Priorityhighest priority firststarvation of low priority → fix with ageing
MLFQmultiple RR queues; jobs demoted for using full quantum, promoted if I/O-boundapproximates SJF without knowing burst lengths; what real OSes use
# MLFQ: 3 priority queues, quanta 10/20/40 ms
#   new job -> Q0 (highest)
#   used its whole quantum without blocking -> demote (CPU hog -> lower priority)
#   yielded early for I/O           -> stay (interactive -> keep it responsive)
#   every ~1 s: boost ALL jobs back to Q0  (prevents starvation)
job = dequeue(highest_nonempty_queue())
run(job, quantum[job.level])
job.level = min(job.level + used_full_quantum, MAX_LEVEL)

Real schedulers

Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler): tracks per-task "virtual runtime", always runs the task with the least vruntime — approximates giving every task an equal share, weighted by nice. Its successor EEVDF (2023) adds latency-sensitivity. Also: real-time classes (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR) that preempt normal tasks.

$ chrt -f 50 ./low_latency_audio     # SCHED_FIFO prio 50 -> preempts every normal task
$ nice -n 19 ./batch_job             # lowest CFS weight -> runs only when nothing else wants the CPU
$ cat /proc/<pid>/sched | grep vruntime
se.vruntime : 918273.451               # CFS always dispatches the task with the SMALLEST vruntime

Preemptive vs cooperative

Preemptive: the OS can interrupt a running task (timer interrupt) — needed for responsiveness and to contain runaway tasks. Cooperative: tasks must yield voluntarily — simpler, but one bad task freezes the system (old Windows/Mac, some coroutine runtimes).

# PREEMPTIVE (OS threads): the timer interrupt fires ~every 4-10 ms, kernel may switch
while (1) { }                   // a runaway thread: annoying, but the machine stays usable

# COOPERATIVE (asyncio, old Windows): control only moves at an explicit yield point
async def handler():
    result = heavy_cpu_work()      # NO await inside -> blocks the entire event loop
    await db.save(result)          # only HERE can another task run
Cheat Sheet
  • Metrics: throughput, turnaround, waiting, response time, fairness/no starvation — trade-offs, can't win all.
  • FCFS: arrival order, non-preemptive, convoy effect.
  • SJF/SRTF: shortest burst (preemptive = SRTF); optimal average wait; starves long jobs; needs prediction.
  • Round Robin: fixed quantum, fair, good response; tune the quantum.
  • Priority: highest first; add ageing to avoid starvation.
  • MLFQ: multi-level feedback queues, demote CPU hogs / favour I/O-bound — approximates SJF without knowing bursts.
  • Linux CFS: least virtual-runtime task runs; nice weights the share. EEVDF adds latency targets.
  • Preemptive (timer-driven) beats cooperative for responsiveness and containing runaway tasks.
Q&A
What is the convoy effect?
Under FCFS, a long CPU-bound job at the head of the queue makes all the short jobs behind it wait, tanking average waiting/turnaround time even though the short jobs would finish almost instantly.
Why is SJF optimal, and why can't we just use it?
Running the shortest job first provably minimises average waiting time. The catch: the OS doesn't know future burst lengths. It's approximated by predicting from history (exponential average) or by MLFQ, which lets behaviour reveal the burst pattern.
How does round-robin's quantum size matter?
Too small → the scheduler spends a large fraction of time context-switching (overhead). Too large → it degenerates toward FCFS and response time suffers. A typical quantum is 10–100 ms — a few times the context-switch cost.
How do you stop low-priority processes from starving?
Ageing: gradually raise the priority of processes that have waited a long time, so they eventually run. MLFQ also periodically boosts all jobs back to the top queue.
What does Linux's CFS actually equalise?
Virtual runtime — CPU time each task has received, scaled by its weight (from nice). It always picks the task with the smallest vruntime, so over time every task gets a fair, weight-proportional share.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which algorithm minimises average waiting time in theory?
Shortest Job First (and its preemptive form, SRTF).
What problem does ageing solve?
Starvation of low-priority processes under priority scheduling — their priority is boosted the longer they wait.
Preemptive vs non-preemptive scheduling — one-line difference?
Preemptive: the OS can forcibly take the CPU from a running task. Non-preemptive: the task keeps the CPU until it blocks or exits.

Intermediate core

Compute average waiting time for FCFS with bursts arriving at t=0: P1=24, P2=3, P3=3.
P1 waits 0, P2 waits 24, P3 waits 27 → average (0+24+27)/3 = 17. In SJF order (P2, P3, P1): 0 + 3 + 6 = 9/3 = 3. Same jobs, the convoy effect costs ~14 units of average wait.
How does MLFQ approximate SJF without knowing burst lengths?
New jobs start in the highest-priority (shortest-quantum) queue. A job that uses its entire quantum is likely CPU-bound / long, so it's demoted to a lower queue with a longer quantum. A job that yields early (I/O-bound, interactive) stays high. So short/interactive jobs run first with low latency, long jobs sink and run in the background — the SJF ordering emerges from observed behaviour. Periodic priority boosts prevent long jobs starving forever and adapt to phase changes.

Advanced deep

What is priority inversion and how do real-time schedulers handle it? (Mars Pathfinder)
A high-priority task H blocks waiting for a lock held by a low-priority task L; a medium-priority task M preempts L (it doesn't need the lock), so L never runs to release it, and H is indirectly blocked by M — the priority ordering is inverted. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder rover kept resetting because of exactly this. Fixes: priority inheritance — while L holds a lock that H wants, L temporarily runs at H's priority so it finishes and releases quickly; or priority ceiling — a lock has a priority equal to the highest of any task that can acquire it, and a task holding it runs at that ceiling. Pathfinder was fixed by enabling priority inheritance on the mutex (a flag that shipped disabled).
How does multicore scheduling differ from single-core, and what are the key concerns?
Now you're placing tasks across N run queues (usually per-CPU, to avoid a global lock). Concerns: load balancing — periodically migrate tasks from busy to idle CPUs, but not too eagerly. Cache affinity — a task rebuilds its L1/L2 working set after migrating, so schedulers prefer to keep a task on its last CPU ("sticky"); Linux tracks this per-domain. NUMA — migrating a task away from the node holding its memory makes every access a remote (slower) access; the scheduler and memory allocator cooperate to keep tasks near their pages. Power — consolidating work onto fewer cores lets others enter deep sleep (race-to-idle), but hurts latency and thermals; big.LITTLE / P+E cores add "which kind of core" to the decision. Scalability — per-CPU queues + work stealing / periodic balancing rather than one contended global queue.

Context Switches & Mode Switches

The cost of multitasking, and the two different "switches" people conflate.

Notes

Mode switch vs context switch

  • Mode switch: user mode ↔ kernel mode, same process (a syscall, an interrupt handler, a page fault). Save/restore a few registers; no scheduler involved. Cheap (~tens–hundreds of ns).
  • Context switch: the scheduler swaps one thread/process off the CPU and another on. Includes a mode switch plus saving/restoring the full register set into the PCB/TCB and (for a different process) switching the address space.
# MODE switch only: getpid() enters/leaves the kernel, same process, no scheduler
$ strace -c ./tight_syscall_loop
  % time   calls  syscall
  99.1   1000000  getpid          # ~100 ns each -- just the user/kernel boundary

# CONTEXT switches: yield between two processes hammering a pipe
$ pidstat -w 1
   UID   PID   cswch/s  nvcswch/s  Command
  1000  7010    48210        3     pingpong     # voluntary (blocked) vs involuntary (preempted)

What a context switch costs

  1. Save the outgoing task's registers (GP, PC, SP, FP/SIMD state — sometimes lazily) into its control block.
  2. Run the scheduler to pick the next task.
  3. Restore the incoming task's registers.
  4. If it's a different process: load the new page-table base register → the TLB is flushed (or partially, with tagged TLBs / PCIDs). Subsequent memory accesses miss the TLB and must walk page tables — the real hidden cost.
  5. Cache pollution: the new task evicts the old task's cache lines; both suffer misses afterward.

Direct cost ~1–5 µs; indirect (TLB + cache refill) can be much more for cache-heavy workloads. Thread→thread within a process skips step 4 (shared address space) — noticeably cheaper.

$ perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations,dTLB-load-misses ./app
     41,882   context-switches
        612   cpu-migrations
  9,203,551   dTLB-load-misses      # the "hidden cost": cold TLB after each cross-process switch

# mitigations:
$ taskset -c 2 ./app        # pin to one core -> fewer migrations, warmer cache
$ ./server --threads=$(nproc)   # ~1 runnable thread per core -> fewer preemptions

What triggers one

  • Time-slice expiry (timer interrupt).
  • The running task blocks (I/O, lock, sleep).
  • A higher-priority task becomes runnable (preemption).
  • Voluntary yield(); process exit.
read(fd, buf, n);        // data not ready -> task BLOCKS -> scheduler switches away (voluntary)
sched_yield();           // explicit "let someone else run"
while (1) work();         // never yields -> switched out only by the TIMER interrupt (involuntary)
// a just-woken SCHED_FIFO task -> immediate preemption of the current task

Traps vs interrupts

Trap / exception: synchronous, caused by the current instruction (syscall via a trap/syscall instruction, divide-by-zero, page fault). Interrupt: asynchronous, from hardware (timer, NIC, disk). Both enter the kernel via a vectored handler; both are mode switches, and either may lead to a context switch.

// TRAP (synchronous -- THIS instruction caused it):
int x = a / 0;            // -> #DE fault -> SIGFPE
syscall(SYS_write, ...);   // -> `syscall` instruction traps into the kernel deliberately
*(int*)0 = 1;             // -> page fault trap -> SIGSEGV

// INTERRUPT (asynchronous -- unrelated to what the CPU was doing):
$ cat /proc/interrupts
           CPU0
 LOC:   9182734   Local timer interrupts     # timer -> drives preemption
  24:    442119   eth0                        # NIC -> packet arrived
Cheat Sheet
  • Mode switch = user↔kernel, same task (syscall/interrupt/fault). Cheap. No scheduler.
  • Context switch = scheduler swaps tasks: mode switch + full register save/restore + (cross-process) address-space swap.
  • Cross-process switch flushes the TLB (unless PCID/ASID tags it) → page-table walks afterward = the big hidden cost.
  • Also pollutes caches; new task starts cold.
  • Thread→thread in the same process is cheaper (shared page tables, no TLB flush).
  • Triggers: quantum expiry, blocking, preemption by higher priority, yield, exit.
  • Trap = synchronous (syscall, fault); interrupt = asynchronous (hardware). Both enter kernel via a handler.
  • Reduce switches: bigger quanta, batching syscalls, async I/O, pinning threads, fewer runnable threads than cores.
Q&A
Mode switch vs context switch?
A mode switch changes privilege level (user↔kernel) within the same process — e.g. entering the kernel for a syscall. A context switch changes which task is on the CPU and involves the scheduler, saving/restoring full state, and (across processes) swapping the address space.
Why is switching between processes more expensive than between threads of one process?
Different processes have different page tables, so the switch loads a new page-table base and flushes the TLB; memory accesses then miss and require page-table walks. Threads share the address space, so that whole step is skipped.
What's the "hidden" cost of a context switch beyond saving registers?
TLB flush (on cross-process switches) and cache pollution — the incoming task runs with a cold TLB and cold caches, causing a burst of misses that can dwarf the direct save/restore cost.
Is a page fault a context switch?
Not by itself — it's a trap (mode switch into the kernel's fault handler). If the fault requires disk I/O (a major fault), the faulting process blocks and the scheduler then does a context switch to something else.
Trap vs interrupt?
A trap is synchronous, produced by executing an instruction (syscall, divide-by-zero, invalid memory access). An interrupt is asynchronous, raised by hardware independent of the current instruction (timer tick, packet arrival, key press).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Does a system call require a context switch?
No — only a mode switch (user → kernel) in the same process. A context switch happens only if the syscall blocks or the scheduler decides to run something else.
Name two events that cause a context switch.
Time-slice expiry, the task blocking on I/O, preemption by a higher-priority task, voluntary yield, process exit — any two.
Where is a task's register state saved during a context switch?
In its PCB / thread control block (kernel memory).

Intermediate core

A latency-sensitive service degrades when co-located with many other processes. Scheduling-level fixes?
Pin (affinity) its threads to dedicated CPUs and isolcps those cores from the general scheduler so nothing else runs there (no context-switch/cache eviction). Raise its scheduling class (SCHED_FIFO/chrt) so it preempts noise. Reduce the number of runnable threads it has to below the core count. Disable deep C-states / frequency scaling on those cores. Use NUMA-local memory. Together these cut both the direct switch cost and the cache/TLB pollution from neighbours.
How do PCIDs / ASIDs reduce context-switch cost?
They tag each TLB entry with an address-space identifier. On a process switch the CPU just changes the "current ASID" instead of flushing the whole TLB, so entries for the previous process stay cached and are still valid when you switch back. This makes frequent switching between a small set of processes much cheaper. (The Meltdown mitigation KPTI reintroduced some flush cost by splitting user/kernel page tables, partly offset by PCID.)

Advanced deep

Why did async / event-loop servers (nginx, Node) win over thread-per-connection, in context-switch terms?
Thread-per-connection at 10k+ connections means 10k threads, most blocked; every time a socket becomes ready the kernel wakes a thread → a context switch, with register save/restore, possible cache/TLB disturbance, and scheduler work — and threads' stacks (often 1–8 MB each) blow the cache and RAM. An event loop runs a handful of threads (ideally one per core), stays on-CPU processing many ready fds returned by a single epoll_wait, and only context-switches when it genuinely has nothing to do. It trades kernel-managed blocking for user-space state machines, amortising one syscall over many connections and keeping the working set hot. The cost is code complexity (callbacks/async) and that one slow CPU-bound handler stalls everything on that loop — hence hybrid designs (event loop + a small worker thread pool for blocking/CPU work).
Estimate the throughput ceiling imposed by context-switch overhead. Show the reasoning.
Suppose a context switch (direct + amortised indirect: TLB refill, cache misses) effectively costs ~5 µs of otherwise-usable CPU. If a workload forces a switch every 50 µs of real work (e.g. tiny time slices, or every request blocks immediately), you lose 5/(50+5) ≈ 9% of the CPU to switching. Push the quantum / work-between-switches to 500 µs and the loss drops to ~1%. Conversely, a pathological pattern — two threads ping-ponging a lock, each doing 1 µs of work then switching — spends 5/6 ≈ 83% of CPU on switching, so effective throughput collapses to ~1/6. This is why "reduce lock ping-pong", "batch work between yields", and "fewer runnable threads than cores" matter: the ceiling is roughly work_per_slice / (work_per_slice + switch_cost).

Virtual Memory & Address Translation

Every process thinks it owns a huge, private, contiguous memory. The MMU keeps up the illusion.

Notes

Why virtual memory

  • Isolation — a process can't name another's memory.
  • Illusion of abundance — a 64-bit address space far larger than RAM; unused pages cost nothing.
  • Simple layout — each process sees the same predictable map (code low, stack high) regardless of where its pages physically sit.
  • Enables demand paging, copy-on-write, memory-mapped files, shared libraries.
$ ./a.out & ./a.out          # two runs of the SAME binary
$ grep '\[stack\]' /proc/$(pgrep -n a.out)/maps
7ffe1c2a1000-7ffe1c2c2000 rw-p ... [stack]   # both see the "same" virtual layout...
# ...mapped to different physical frames; neither can address the other's memory

$ ./huge_alloc                # malloc(100 GB) on a 16 GB box:
$ grep VmSize /proc/$!/status   # VmSize: 100 GB (virtual)
$ grep VmRSS  /proc/$!/status   # VmRSS: 4 MB   (physical -- only touched pages cost RAM)

Paging & translation

Memory is divided into fixed pages (typically 4 KB) and physical frames. A page table per process maps virtual page → physical frame + permission bits (present, writable, user/kernel, dirty, accessed, no-execute). The MMU does the lookup on every access; on x86-64 it's a 4- or 5-level radix tree walk (a "page walk").

# a 48-bit virtual address splits into 4 x 9-bit table indices + 12-bit offset:
#   [ PML4 : 9 ][ PDPT : 9 ][ PD : 9 ][ PT : 9 ][ offset : 12 ]
frame = walk(cr3):
    l1 = mem[cr3        + va.pml4 * 8]     # 4 dependent memory loads on a TLB MISS
    l2 = mem[l1.frame   + va.pdpt * 8]
    l3 = mem[l2.frame   + va.pd   * 8]
    pte = mem[l3.frame  + va.pt   * 8]
    if not pte.present: raise page_fault
# physical addr = pte.frame << 12 | va.offset       (offset copied through unchanged)

The TLB

A small associative cache of recent virtual→physical translations. A hit avoids the multi-level page walk. TLB miss → hardware (or OS) walks the page table and fills the TLB. A process switch that isn't tagged (no PCID) flushes it. Huge pages (2 MB/1 GB) cover more memory per TLB entry — big win for large-heap, memory-bound apps.

$ perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses,dTLB-loads ./app
   1,204,882  dTLB-load-misses   #  3.1% of all dTLB loads   # each miss = a page walk

# 4 KB pages: one TLB entry covers 4 KB.  A 512-entry TLB reaches 2 MB.
# 2 MB huge pages: one entry covers 2 MB.  Same TLB reaches 1 GB.
$ ./app --huge-pages          # or: madvise(p, len, MADV_HUGEPAGE)  -> far fewer misses on a big heap

Segmentation

An older/alternate scheme: variable-length segments (code, data, stack) each with a base+limit. Gives logical structure and protection but suffers external fragmentation. Modern x86-64 mostly retired it (flat model); the concept survives in "segmentation fault" (an access outside any valid region).

$ ./crash
Segmentation fault (core dumped)

$ gdb -q ./crash core
(gdb) bt
#0  0x0000... in main () at crash.c:4
4       *(int*)0 = 1;             # virtual address 0 is in NO mapping -> MMU fault -> SIGSEGV
(gdb) info proc mappings         # address 0 falls below the lowest mapped region

mmap

Maps a file (or anonymous memory) into the address space. File reads become page faults that pull in file pages on demand; writes go to the page cache and back to disk lazily. malloc uses anonymous mmap for large allocations; shared libraries and executables are file-backed shared mappings.

int fd = open("big.bin", O_RDONLY);
struct stat st; fstat(fd, &st);
char *p = mmap(NULL, st.st_size, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
// NO read() -- touching p[offset] triggers a page fault that pulls that page from the page cache
char c = p[4 * 1024 * 1024];   // only THIS 4 KB page is loaded, not the whole file
munmap(p, st.st_size);
Cheat Sheet
  • Virtual memory: per-process private address space, translated to physical by the MMU via page tables.
  • Page (4 KB) ↔ frame; page-table entry = frame number + present/writable/user/dirty/accessed/NX bits.
  • x86-64: 4–5 level page-table walk on a TLB miss.
  • TLB = translation cache; hit avoids the walk; untagged process switch flushes it; huge pages stretch its reach.
  • Benefits: isolation, over-commit, COW, mmap'd files, shared libs, ASLR.
  • Segmentation = base+limit variable regions (mostly historical on x86-64); "segfault" = access outside any mapping.
  • mmap: file-backed (demand-load pages) or anonymous (used by malloc for big blocks).
  • Page-table memory itself is per-process; multi-level tables keep it sparse.
Q&A
What does the MMU do on every memory access?
Translates the virtual address to a physical one using the TLB (fast path) or a page-table walk (slow path), and checks the permission bits — raising a fault if the page isn't present or the access violates permissions.
What is the TLB and why does it matter?
A cache of recent virtual→physical translations. Without it, every load/store would need a multi-level page walk (several extra memory accesses). TLB hit rate is a major performance factor for memory-heavy code; huge pages and good locality improve it.
Why does a multi-level page table use less memory than a single flat one?
A flat table needs an entry for every possible virtual page whether used or not (huge for 64-bit). A multi-level tree only allocates lower-level tables for regions of the address space that are actually mapped, so the sparse, mostly-empty address space costs little.
What causes a "segmentation fault"?
Accessing a virtual address that isn't in any valid mapping, or violating a mapping's permissions (writing read-only memory, executing non-executable memory) — the MMU raises a fault the kernel turns into SIGSEGV.
How does mmap'ing a file avoid explicit read() calls?
The mapping is lazy: the file's pages aren't loaded until you touch them, at which point a page fault pulls the needed page from the page cache (or disk). You just dereference pointers into the mapped region.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Typical page size?
4 KB (with optional huge pages of 2 MB or 1 GB).
What hardware performs virtual-to-physical translation?
The MMU (Memory Management Unit), accelerated by the TLB.
Two processes both have a valid pointer with value 0x400000. Do they point to the same physical memory?
Not necessarily — that's a virtual address, and each process's page table can map it to a different physical frame (or the same one, if shared).

Intermediate core

A memory-bound program speeds up 20% after enabling transparent huge pages. Why?
Each TLB entry now covers 2 MB instead of 4 KB, so the same TLB reaches 512× more memory — far fewer TLB misses and page-table walks for a large working set. Page-table depth is also shorter. Downsides that sometimes bite: internal fragmentation, higher latency on COW/fault of a 2 MB page, and allocation stalls from THP compaction (some workloads disable THP for latency predictability).
How does copy-on-write use the page-table permission bits?
After fork(), parent and child page tables both point at the same physical frames, marked read-only (even for originally writable pages). A write triggers a protection fault; the kernel allocates a fresh frame, copies the page, updates the faulting process's PTE to point at the copy with write permission, and resumes. Pages neither side writes are never duplicated.

Advanced deep

Explain the page-table walk on x86-64 and why 5-level paging was added.
A 48-bit virtual address is split into four 9-bit indices plus a 12-bit page offset. The CPU reads CR3 (physical address of the top-level table, PML4), indexes it with bits 47–39 to get the PDPT base, indexes that with bits 38–30, then the PD with 29–21, then the PT with 20–12; the PT entry gives the physical frame, combined with the 12-bit offset. So a TLB miss costs up to 4 dependent memory reads (mitigated by a page-walk cache). 4-level paging caps usable virtual address space at 2^48 = 256 TB and physical at ~64 TB. 5-level paging (Intel Ice Lake+, opt-in) adds a PML5 level, extending virtual to 2^57 = 128 PB and physical to 4 PB — needed by huge in-memory databases, large NUMA machines, and to give more room for ASLR / sandboxing. Cost: one extra walk level on a TLB miss, so it's enabled only when the memory size justifies it.
What is memory over-commit and the OOM killer, and how do you reason about it?
Linux by default lets processes malloc/mmap more virtual memory than physical RAM + swap, betting that not all of it will be touched (sparse allocations, forked COW pages, large arenas). Backing is allocated lazily on first write (page fault). If actual usage does exceed RAM+swap, the kernel can't fault in a page and invokes the OOM killer, which picks a victim by an oom_score (roughly proportional to RSS, adjustable via oom_score_adj) and SIGKILLs it — abrupt, no cleanup. Implications: a successful malloc is not a guarantee you can use the memory; long-tail latency spikes from reclaim/swap thrash precede the kill; and one leaky process can get an innocent bystander killed. Controls: vm.overcommit_memory (2 = strict accounting, refuse over-commit at allocation time — safer for servers, but breaks fork-heavy and sparse-allocation software), cgroup memory limits (contain the blast radius, trigger per-cgroup OOM), disabling swap for predictability, and setting oom_score_adj to protect critical processes.

Paging, Page Faults & Replacement

Loading pages only when touched — and deciding what to evict when RAM is full.

Notes

Demand paging

Pages aren't loaded until first accessed. Starting a program maps its executable but faults in code pages as execution reaches them — fast startup, only the working set is resident.

$ /usr/bin/time -v ./app
    Major (requiring I/O) page faults: 12       # pages fetched from disk
    Minor (reclaiming a frame)  faults: 48213   # pages already in RAM, just mapped in
    Maximum resident set size (kbytes): 20480   # RSS << VmSize -- only touched pages loaded
# a 200 MB binary starts fast: only the code pages actually executed get faulted in

Page fault types

TypeCauseCost
Minor (soft)page is in RAM (page cache, COW, zero page) but not in this PTE yetµs — just fix the mapping
Major (hard)page must be read from disk / swapms — the process blocks; scheduler switches away
Invalidaddress in no mapping / bad permissionSIGSEGV
$ ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,cmd -p $(pgrep -n app)
 MINFL MAJFL CMD
 91233    18 ./app          # mostly minor (cheap); 18 major = 18 disk reads (~ms each)

$ perf stat -e minor-faults,major-faults ./batch
      41,003  minor-faults    # COW after fork, first-touch of fresh malloc'd pages, page-cache hits
       2,551  major-faults    # swap-in / cold file pages -- the ones that hurt

Replacement algorithms

AlgoEvictsNote
OPTpage used furthest in the futureoptimal but unimplementable (needs the future); a benchmark
FIFOoldest loadedsimple; suffers Belady's anomaly (more frames → more faults)
LRUleast recently usedgood approximation of OPT; true LRU is too costly (per-access bookkeeping)
Clock / Second-chancescan a circular list; skip pages with the "accessed" bit set (clearing it)cheap LRU approximation — what real kernels use

Linux uses active/inactive LRU lists with reference bits, plus aging and per-cgroup reclaim.

# Clock / second-chance: cheap LRU approximation using the hardware "accessed" bit
while need_a_frame:
    pte = frames[hand]
    if pte.accessed:
        pte.accessed = 0          # give it a second chance, move on
        hand = (hand + 1) % N
    else:
        evict(pte); return frames[hand]   # untouched since last sweep -> evict

# reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 under FIFO:
#   3 frames -> 9 faults ;  4 frames -> 10 faults  (Belady's anomaly -- LRU never does this)

Thrashing & the working set

If the sum of processes' working sets (pages actively used in a recent window) exceeds RAM, the system spends nearly all its time paging in/out — CPU utilisation collapses, disk saturates. Fixes: reduce multiprogramming level (suspend/swap out whole processes), add RAM, use working-set / page-fault-frequency control to give each process enough frames.

$ vmstat 1
 r  b   swpd   free   si   so    us sy id wa
 8 12 2039488  10240 41233 38901  3  9  0 88   # si/so = pages swapped in/out per sec (huge)
                                              # wa 88%: CPU idle, everyone blocked on the disk = THRASHING

# fixes: cgroup memory limit to cap a hog, add RAM, or reduce concurrency
$ systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=2G ./hungry_job
Cheat Sheet
  • Demand paging: load a page on first access → fast start, only working set resident.
  • Minor fault = page in RAM, fix PTE (µs). Major fault = fetch from disk/swap (ms, process blocks). Invalid = SIGSEGV.
  • Replacement: OPT (ideal, needs future), FIFO (simple, Belady's anomaly), LRU (good, expensive exact), Clock/second-chance (cheap LRU approx — used in practice).
  • Belady's anomaly: FIFO can fault more with more frames; stack algorithms (LRU, OPT) never do.
  • Working set = pages used in a recent time window. Σ working sets > RAM → thrashing.
  • Thrashing fix: lower multiprogramming (swap out processes), add RAM, PFF/working-set frame allocation.
  • Dirty pages must be written back before eviction; clean pages just dropped.
Q&A
Minor vs major page fault?
Minor: the page is already in physical memory (page cache, a shared/COW page, the zero page) and the kernel just needs to add the mapping — microseconds. Major: the page must be read from disk or swap — milliseconds, and the process blocks meanwhile.
What is Belady's anomaly?
With FIFO replacement, giving a process more frames can sometimes increase the page-fault count — counterintuitive. "Stack" algorithms like LRU and OPT are provably immune.
Why isn't true LRU used?
It would require updating a timestamp or moving a list node on every memory access — far too expensive in hardware/software. Clock (second-chance) approximates it using just the hardware "accessed" bit, scanned periodically.
What is thrashing?
When the combined working sets of running processes exceed physical memory, so the system is constantly evicting a page it will need again immediately. Page-in/out I/O saturates, CPU sits idle waiting, throughput collapses.
How does the working-set model prevent thrashing?
The OS estimates each process's working set (pages referenced in the last Δ time) and only admits a process to run if enough free frames exist to hold its working set. If not, it suspends a process to free frames.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is demand paging?
Loading a page into RAM only when it's first accessed (via a page fault), rather than loading the whole program up front.
Which replacement algorithm is optimal but impossible to implement?
OPT / MIN — it evicts the page that won't be used for the longest time, which requires knowing the future.
What real algorithm approximates LRU cheaply?
Clock (second-chance), using the hardware reference/accessed bit.

Intermediate core

Trace FIFO with 3 frames on the reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5. Count faults, then try 4 frames.
3 frames: faults on 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,3,4 = 9 faults (hits on the second 1,2 after 5 is loaded... actually 9). 4 frames: 1,2,3,4 (4 faults), 1,2 hit, 5 evicts 1 (fault), 1 evicts 2 (fault), 2 evicts 3 (fault), 3 evicts 4 (fault), 4 evicts 5 (fault), 5 evicts 1 (fault) = 10 faults. More frames, more faults — Belady's anomaly.
Server latency spikes badly under memory pressure though CPU is low. Diagnosis?
Likely thrashing / heavy swap: major page faults are serialising on disk, so processes block for milliseconds each, CPU idles waiting on I/O. Check vmstat (si/so swap columns), /proc/PID/stat majflt, pgmajfault. Fixes: add RAM, reduce per-process footprint or concurrency, set cgroup memory limits to contain the offender, tune vm.swappiness, or disable swap and let the OOM killer act decisively rather than degrade everything.

Advanced deep

Why does Linux keep two LRU lists (active/inactive) per memory zone instead of one?
A single LRU list is vulnerable to scan resistance failure: a one-time sequential read of a huge file (a backup, a grep over a big log) would touch every page once, pushing the genuinely hot working set out of the list — "cache pollution". The two-list scheme requires a page to be referenced while on the inactive list before it's promoted to the active list; pages that are touched once and never again stay on inactive and are reclaimed first. Reclaim pulls from the tail of inactive; the kernel also periodically ages the active list (moving unreferenced pages to inactive) to keep roughly a balanced ratio. Anonymous and file-backed pages have separate list pairs so the kernel can bias reclaim (vm.swappiness) toward dropping clean file pages vs swapping anon pages. This gives approximate LRU-2 behaviour cheaply and resists streaming workloads trashing the cache.
Compare page-fault-frequency (PFF) control with the working-set model for allocating frames.
Both aim to give each process "enough" frames to avoid thrashing without wasting memory. Working-set model: define a window Δ; a process's working set W(t, Δ) is the distinct pages referenced in the last Δ; allocate that many frames, and only run the process if Σ|W| ≤ total frames. Accurate in principle but needs per-reference tracking (approximated with periodic reference-bit sampling), and picking Δ is workload-dependent. PFF: measure the process's page-fault rate. If it's above an upper threshold, give the process more frames; if below a lower threshold, take some away. It's a simple feedback loop using an easily-measured signal (fault count) and self-tunes to the phase behaviour of the program. PFF is closer to what real systems do (it's essentially what per-cgroup memory reclaim + pressure stall information implement); the working-set model is the cleaner theoretical framework that explains why it works and predicts thrashing onset.

Synchronization Primitives

Mutex, semaphore, condition variable, spinlock — what each is for.

Notes

The critical section problem

When threads share mutable state, concurrent access must be serialised. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion (one at a time), progress (no unnecessary blocking), and bounded waiting (no starvation).

int counter = 0;

// RACE: counter++ is load, add, store -- two threads interleave and lose an increment
void *bump(void *_) { for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) counter++; return NULL; }
// 4 threads -> final counter is ~1.4M, not 4M

// FIX: serialise the critical section
pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
void *bump_ok(void *_) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; i++) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&m); counter++; pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);   // exactly 4M
    }
    return NULL;
}

The primitives

PrimitiveUse
MutexMutual exclusion for a critical section. Has an owner; only the locker unlocks. Blocks (sleeps) if contended.
SpinlockBusy-waits instead of sleeping. Only worthwhile when the critical section is very short and you can't sleep (interrupt context). Wastes CPU under contention.
SemaphoreA counter with wait(P, decrement/block) and signal(V, increment). Counting semaphore = "N units of a resource"; binary semaphore ≈ mutex (but no ownership).
Condition variableWait for a predicate to become true. Always used with a mutex: wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps; signal/broadcast wakes waiters. Re-check the predicate in a while loop (spurious wakeups).
MonitorLanguage construct bundling a mutex + condition variables with the data (Java synchronized + wait/notify).
RW lockMany readers or one writer. Helps read-heavy data; risk of writer starvation.
// condition variable: wait for a PREDICATE, always with a mutex, always in a while-loop
pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
while (queue_empty())                     // re-check: spurious wakeups + other consumers
    pthread_cond_wait(&not_empty, &m);    // atomically unlocks m + sleeps; relocks on wake
item = dequeue();
pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);

// spinlock: busy-wait, no sleep -- only for <1us sections / interrupt context
while (atomic_flag_test_and_set(&lock)) { /* spin, burning CPU */ }
/* very short critical section */
atomic_flag_clear(&lock);

Mutex vs semaphore

A mutex is for locking (ownership, released by the same thread). A semaphore is for signalling / counting resources (any thread can post). Using a binary semaphore as a lock loses ownership checks and priority-inheritance support.

// MUTEX: same thread locks and unlocks -- it's a "who's in the room" token
pthread_mutex_lock(&m);   /* critical section */   pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);

// SEMAPHORE: a counter -- ANY thread can post(); great for "N permits" or signalling
sem_t db_conns;
sem_init(&db_conns, 0, 5);       // pool of 5 connections
sem_wait(&db_conns);            // take one (blocks if all 5 are out)
/* use a connection */
sem_post(&db_conns);            // return it -- a DIFFERENT thread may have taken it
// using a binary semaphore as a lock loses ownership checks + priority inheritance

The producer–consumer pattern

mutex m; condvar not_full, not_empty; queue q; int cap;
produce(x): lock(m); while q.size==cap: wait(not_full, m); q.push(x); signal(not_empty); unlock(m)
consume():  lock(m); while q.empty():   wait(not_empty, m); x=q.pop();  signal(not_full);  unlock(m); return x
Cheat Sheet
  • Correct critical section = mutual exclusion + progress + bounded waiting.
  • Mutex: owned lock, sleeps on contention, unlock by locker. Default choice.
  • Spinlock: busy-wait; only for ultra-short sections / interrupt context / uniprocessor-with-preempt-off. Burns CPU otherwise.
  • Semaphore: counter, wait/signal, no ownership; counting = resource pool, binary ≈ mutex/signal.
  • Condition variable: wait for a predicate; pair with a mutex; wait releases+sleeps atomically; always re-check in a while (spurious wakeups).
  • Mutex = lock (ownership). Semaphore = signal/count (no ownership).
  • RW lock for read-heavy shared data (watch writer starvation).
  • Prefer higher-level constructs (channels, concurrent collections, atomic) over hand-rolled locking.
Q&A
Mutex vs binary semaphore?
Both allow one holder, but a mutex has an owner (only the locking thread may unlock, enabling priority inheritance and error checking), while a semaphore is just a counter any thread can post to. Use a mutex for protecting a critical section; a semaphore for signalling between threads or limiting a resource count.
Why must a condition-variable wait be inside a while loop?
Because of spurious wakeups (the thread can wake without a signal) and because another thread may have changed the state back between the signal and this thread reacquiring the mutex. Re-checking the predicate makes it robust.
When is a spinlock the right choice?
When the critical section is only a handful of instructions, contention is rare, and you cannot sleep (e.g. holding it in an interrupt handler), on a multiprocessor. On a single CPU with preemption, spinning is pointless — the holder can't run to release it.
What does a condition variable's wait do atomically?
Releases the associated mutex and puts the thread to sleep as a single atomic step, so it can't miss a signal that happens between "check predicate" and "go to sleep". On wakeup it reacquires the mutex before returning.
What's a monitor?
A synchronisation construct that encapsulates shared data together with a mutex and condition variables, so all access is automatically mutually exclusive. Java's synchronized methods + wait()/notify() are a monitor.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which primitive would you use to limit access to a pool of 5 database connections?
A counting semaphore initialised to 5.
What must a condition variable always be paired with?
A mutex.
Does a spinlock put the waiting thread to sleep?
No — it busy-waits (spins), repeatedly checking the lock.

Intermediate core

Implement a bounded blocking queue with a mutex and condition variables.
One mutex, two condition variables (notFull, notEmpty). put: lock; while (size == capacity) notFull.wait(lock); enqueue; notEmpty.signal(); unlock. take: lock; while (size == 0) notEmpty.wait(lock); dequeue; notFull.signal(); unlock; return. The while loops handle spurious wakeups and multiple waiters; signalling the other condition after each operation wakes a blocked counterpart.
Why can notify() (signal one) instead of notifyAll() cause a deadlock in some designs?
If threads wait on the same condition variable for different predicates (e.g. a bounded buffer where producers and consumers share one condvar), notify() might wake a thread whose predicate is still false; it re-checks, goes back to sleep, and the thread that could have proceeded was never woken — the system stalls with work available. Fixes: use separate condition variables per predicate, or always notifyAll() (correct but can cause a thundering herd).

Advanced deep

How does a futex-based mutex avoid a syscall in the uncontended case?
The lock is a plain integer in shared user memory. Lock: atomically CAS it from 0→1 in userspace; if that succeeds (uncontended), you're done — no kernel involvement at all. Only if the CAS fails (someone holds it) does the thread call futex(FUTEX_WAIT), passing the address and expected value; the kernel double-checks the value (avoiding a lost-wakeup race) and, if it still matches, sleeps the thread on a kernel wait queue keyed by that address. Unlock: atomically set to 0; if the old value indicated waiters, call futex(FUTEX_WAKE) to wake one. So the fast path (the overwhelmingly common case) is a single atomic instruction, and the kernel is touched only under real contention. glibc's mutex uses a 3-state variant (0 free, 1 locked-no-waiters, 2 locked-with-waiters) so the unlock fast path also skips the syscall when there are no waiters.
Compare lock-based synchronisation with RCU (read-copy-update) for a read-mostly data structure.
A reader/writer lock still has readers taking and releasing the lock (atomic ops, cache-line bouncing on the lock word across cores) and can starve writers or readers. RCU: readers take no lock and pay essentially nothing — they just mark a lightweight "read-side critical section" (on Linux, often just disabling preemption) and dereference the pointer. Writers make a copy of the node, modify the copy, then atomically swap the pointer; old readers keep using the old version. The writer then waits for a grace period — until every CPU has passed through a quiescent state (context switch / idle / user mode), guaranteeing no reader still holds the old pointer — before freeing the old node. Wins: near-zero reader overhead, perfect reader scalability, no reader/writer contention. Costs: writers are more expensive and serialised among themselves (still need a lock), reclamation is deferred (memory lingers for a grace period), and it only suits structures where readers can tolerate seeing a slightly stale but consistent version (linked lists, routing tables, config). It's heavily used in the Linux kernel.

Deadlock: Conditions, Prevention, Avoidance

When everyone is waiting for everyone else — the four conditions and the four responses.

Notes

The four Coffman conditions (all needed for deadlock)

  1. Mutual exclusion — a resource is held by at most one process.
  2. Hold and wait — a process holds resources while waiting for more.
  3. No preemption — a resource can't be forcibly taken; only released voluntarily.
  4. Circular wait — a cycle of processes each waiting for a resource the next holds.

Break any one and deadlock is impossible.

// all four conditions present -> classic deadlock
// T1:                              T2:
pthread_mutex_lock(&A);   //        pthread_mutex_lock(&B);   -- mutual exclusion
/* ...work... */                 //        /* ...work... */          -- hold and wait
pthread_mutex_lock(&B);   //        pthread_mutex_lock(&A);   -- circular wait, no preemption
// T1 holds A waits B, T2 holds B waits A -> both blocked forever

The four strategies

StrategyHow
PreventionStructurally negate a condition: acquire all resources at once (no hold-and-wait); impose a global lock order (no circular wait); allow preemption / rollback.
AvoidanceGrant a request only if the resulting state is "safe" (there exists an order in which all processes can finish). Banker's algorithm — needs max-claims up front.
Detection & recoveryLet deadlocks happen; periodically look for a cycle in the wait-for graph; recover by killing a victim or rolling back.
OstrichIgnore it — deadlocks are rare, and the cost of prevention isn't worth it. What general-purpose OSes (and most apps) actually do.
// PREVENTION by lock ordering: always take the lower-addressed lock first
void transfer(Account *a, Account *b, long amt) {
    Account *first  = a < b ? a : b;
    Account *second = a < b ? b : a;
    pthread_mutex_lock(&first->m);
    pthread_mutex_lock(&second->m);      // every thread agrees on the order -> no cycle
    a->bal -= amt; b->bal += amt;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&second->m);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&first->m);
}

// PREVENTION by try_lock + backoff: don't hold-and-wait
while (1) {
    lock(&A);
    if (try_lock(&B) == 0) break;   // got both
    unlock(&A); usleep(rand() % 100);  // release everything, retry
}

In practice

The overwhelmingly common real-world fix is consistent lock ordering: number your locks and always acquire them in increasing order. Also: keep critical sections short, use try_lock with backoff, avoid calling out to unknown code while holding a lock, and use a single coarse lock where the concurrency isn't worth the risk. Databases use detection (wait-for graph) + victim abort.

# the DB does detection + victim abort for you:
mysql> SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
*** (1) WAITING FOR ... lock on `accounts` ...
*** (2) HOLDS THE LOCK(S) ...
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)          # app gets error 1213 -> just retry the txn

Livelock & starvation

Livelock: processes keep changing state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a corridor). Starvation: a process is perpetually denied a resource (always lower priority, or unlucky in lock acquisition).

// LIVELOCK: both retry forever in lockstep (no deadlock -- they're "busy")
while (1) {
    lock(&A);
    if (try_lock(&B)) break;
    unlock(&A);                 // both threads back off at the exact same time, repeat
}
// fix: RANDOMISED backoff (usleep(rand()...)) so they desynchronise

// STARVATION: a writer never runs because readers keep arriving on an RW lock
//   fix: writer-preferring rwlock, or FIFO ticket lock
Cheat Sheet
  • Coffman conditions (need all 4): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
  • Prevention = negate one structurally (all-at-once acquisition; global lock ordering; allow preemption).
  • Avoidance = only grant if the new state is safe; Banker's algorithm (needs max claims).
  • Detection = find a cycle in the wait-for graph, then kill/roll back a victim (databases do this).
  • Ostrich = ignore; what general-purpose OSes do.
  • Practical fix: consistent global lock order; short critical sections; try_lock + backoff; don't call unknown code under a lock.
  • Livelock = active but no progress. Starvation = perpetually denied (fix with ageing/fair locks).
Q&A
List the four conditions necessary for deadlock.
Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four must hold simultaneously.
What's the simplest practical way to prevent deadlock among multiple locks?
Impose a total order on the locks and always acquire them in that order everywhere. A cycle in the wait-for graph then becomes impossible, so circular wait is broken.
Deadlock avoidance vs prevention?
Prevention removes the possibility by design (negating a Coffman condition). Avoidance allows the conditions but checks each allocation request at runtime and only grants it if the system stays in a "safe" state where all processes can still complete (Banker's algorithm).
What does the "ostrich algorithm" mean and why is it common?
Ignoring deadlocks entirely. Prevention/avoidance impose real costs (resource under-utilisation, up-front declarations, overhead), and deadlocks in practice are rare and often recoverable by killing a process. So most general-purpose OSes just don't handle it.
Livelock vs deadlock?
In deadlock, processes are blocked and doing nothing. In livelock, they're actively running and changing state in response to each other but never making forward progress — e.g. two threads that both back off and retry in lockstep forever.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which Coffman condition does "acquire all locks at once, or none" eliminate?
Hold-and-wait.
What does the Banker's algorithm require processes to declare?
Their maximum possible resource needs, up front.
How do databases typically deal with deadlock?
Detection — they build a wait-for graph, find cycles, and abort a victim transaction (which is then retried).

Intermediate core

Two threads: T1 locks A then B; T2 locks B then A. Show the deadlock and two fixes.
Interleaving: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, T1 waits for B (held by T2), T2 waits for A (held by T1) — circular wait, both stuck. Fix 1: consistent order — make T2 also lock A then B. Fix 2: try_lock B after locking A; if it fails, release A, back off a random interval, retry (breaks "no preemption"). Fix 3: a single lock covering both A and B if the extra concurrency isn't needed.
Why is deadlock avoidance rarely used in real systems?
It needs every process's maximum resource claim declared in advance, which is often unknown or wildly conservative; the safety check runs on every allocation (overhead); and it under-utilises resources by refusing requests that would probably be fine. It fits constrained, well-characterised systems (some embedded/real-time), not general-purpose ones.

Advanced deep

Explain "lock ordering" enforcement tools like Linux's lockdep.
Lockdep builds, at runtime, a graph of observed lock-acquisition orders: whenever lock B is taken while lock A is held, it records an edge A→B for the lock classes (not instances — e.g. "inode→mutex" as a class). If it ever sees the reverse order (B held, A taken) it reports a potential deadlock immediately, even if the actual timing that triggers it never occurs in this run — because the two orderings existing anywhere in the codebase means an interleaving can deadlock. It also validates rules like "no sleeping lock taken in IRQ context", recursive locking, and irq-safe/irq-unsafe consistency. This shifts deadlock discovery from rare production hangs to CI/testing. The cost is significant runtime overhead (it's a debug-kernel feature), and it needs correct "lock class" annotations to avoid false positives/negatives when the same code path legitimately locks two instances of the same class in a defined order (handled with nesting subclasses).
Dining philosophers: give a solution that is deadlock-free and starvation-free, and explain why each property holds.
One clean solution: a central "waiter"/arbitrator (a mutex or semaphore initialised to N−1) that limits the number of philosophers simultaneously trying to eat to N−1. Deadlock-free: with at most N−1 philosophers contending for N forks, at least one philosopher can always get both forks (pigeonhole) — circular wait is broken because the cycle can't fully form. Starvation-free if the arbitrator and the fork mutexes use FIFO / fair queuing, so every philosopher's request is eventually served. Alternative: asymmetric ordering — odd philosophers pick up the left fork first, even philosophers the right first; this breaks the uniform circular wait (deadlock-free) but needs fair mutexes to also be starvation-free. The resource-hierarchy solution (number the forks, always pick up the lower-numbered first) is deadlock-free but the highest-numbered philosopher can be starved without additional fairness.

Inter-Process Communication

Isolated processes need channels — and each channel makes a different speed/scope trade.

Notes

The mechanisms

MechanismShapeNotes
Pipe (anonymous)unidirectional byte streamrelated processes only (shared fd via fork); the shell's |
Named pipe / FIFObyte stream via a filesystem pathunrelated processes on the same host
Message queuediscrete messages, optionally prioritisedpreserves boundaries; POSIX (mq_*) or SysV
Shared memorya region mapped into multiple processesfastest (no copy through the kernel); needs your own synchronisation (semaphore/mutex)
Unix domain socketstream or datagram, bidirectionallocal, fast, supports passing fds and credentials; same API as network sockets
Signala single async notification (number)no payload (bar sigqueue); for events/termination, not data
Memory-mapped fileshared memory backed by a filepersistent, and OS syncs to disk
eventfd / futex / pidfdlightweight kernel-assisted signallingmodern Linux building blocks
// anonymous pipe: parent -> child stream (the shell's `|`)
int fds[2]; pipe(fds);
if (fork() == 0) { close(fds[1]); read(fds[0], buf, n); }   // child reads
else              { close(fds[0]); write(fds[1], msg, n); }  // parent writes

// shared memory: the fastest -- no kernel copy, but YOU add the lock
int shm = shm_open("/ring", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0600);
ftruncate(shm, SZ);
void *p = mmap(NULL, SZ, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, shm, 0);
// both processes see *p; guard it with a sem_t in the shared region

Choosing

  • Need max throughput / big data → shared memory (+ a lock or lock-free ring).
  • Need message boundaries and simple flow → message queue or datagram socket.
  • Local RPC, fd passing, auth → Unix domain socket.
  • Simple parent→child stream → pipe.
  • Across machines → TCP/UDP sockets (only option).
  • Just "wake up" / "please stop" → signal / eventfd.
# local RPC + fd passing + peer credentials -> Unix domain socket
srv = socket(AF_UNIX, SOCK_STREAM, 0); bind(srv, "/run/app.sock"); listen(srv, 8);
# pass an open fd to another process via SCM_RIGHTS; check SO_PEERCRED for uid/pid

# big streaming data, same host -> shared-memory ring beats a socket (no copy)
# cross-machine -> you have no choice: TCP/UDP
# "reload your config" -> a signal:  kill -HUP $(pidof app)

Gotchas

Pipes have limited buffer (default 64 KB) — a full pipe blocks the writer; a reader closing early makes the writer get SIGPIPE/EPIPE. Shared memory has no built-in synchronisation — races are on you. SysV IPC objects leak if not removed (ipcrm).

$ yes | head -1              # head exits -> `yes` gets SIGPIPE and dies (that's intended here)

$ ipcs -m                    # SysV shared memory segments -- these LEAK past process exit
key        shmid  owner  bytes   nattch
0x00000000 98304  leo    4194304 0        # nattch 0 and still here -> orphaned
$ ipcrm -m 98304             # must clean up manually (POSIX shm_unlink is friendlier)
Cheat Sheet
  • Pipe: unidirectional stream, related processes (shell |). FIFO: same via a pathname, unrelated processes.
  • Message queue: discrete, boundary-preserving, prioritised messages.
  • Shared memory: fastest (zero-copy); you provide the synchronisation.
  • Unix domain socket: local, bidirectional, fast, can pass fds + peer credentials.
  • Signal: async notification, essentially no payload; for events/termination.
  • mmap'd file: shared memory that persists and syncs to disk.
  • Cross-machine → network sockets only.
  • Watch: pipe buffer full → writer blocks; reader gone → SIGPIPE; SysV objects persist until ipcrm.
Q&A
Why is shared memory the fastest IPC?
Data isn't copied into and out of the kernel — both processes map the same physical pages and read/write directly. Other mechanisms copy through kernel buffers (at least once, often twice).
What's the catch with shared memory?
It provides no synchronisation. Concurrent access is a data race unless you add your own mutex/semaphore (often placed in the shared region) or use a lock-free structure.
Anonymous pipe vs named pipe (FIFO)?
An anonymous pipe exists only as file descriptors shared via fork() — only related processes can use it. A FIFO has a name in the filesystem, so any process that can open that path can connect, related or not.
What can a Unix domain socket do that a TCP socket to localhost can't?
Pass open file descriptors between processes (SCM_RIGHTS) and the peer's verified credentials (SO_PEERCRED), with lower overhead (no TCP/IP stack, checksums, or loopback routing).
Can you send data with a signal?
Barely — a plain signal carries only its number. sigqueue() with a real-time signal can attach one integer/pointer value. Signals are for notification ("child exited", "please reload config", "terminate"), not data transfer.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What IPC mechanism does the shell's | use?
An anonymous pipe.
Which IPC needs you to add your own locking?
Shared memory.
Which IPC works across different machines?
Network sockets (TCP/UDP). The others are host-local.

Intermediate core

Two processes exchange millions of small records per second on one host. Design the IPC.
A shared-memory ring buffer (SPSC: single-producer, single-consumer) with atomic head/tail indices and acquire/release ordering — no locks, no per-message syscall. Use a semaphore or eventfd only for "wake the consumer when it was idle" (with a batched/coalesced signal) to avoid busy-waiting. Pad head and tail to separate cache lines to prevent false sharing. Fall back to a Unix domain socket if you need boundary framing and flow control without writing the ring yourself.
A writer process hangs when its pipe reader is slow. Why, and options?
The pipe's kernel buffer (default 64 KB) filled up, so write() blocks until the reader drains it — this is backpressure, often desirable. Options: make the writer's pipe fd non-blocking and handle EAGAIN (drop or buffer in userspace); increase the pipe capacity with fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ); use a larger-buffered mechanism (socket with a big SO_SNDBUF, or a message queue); or fix the real problem — the slow reader.

Advanced deep

How does passing a file descriptor over a Unix socket actually work, and why is it useful?
You send a normal message with sendmsg() that carries an ancillary data block of type SCM_RIGHTS containing one or more fd numbers. The kernel intercepts this: on the receiving side it installs new fd entries in the receiver's fd table that refer to the same underlying open-file description (same offset, same file, incremented refcount) — the numeric fd value differs, but it's the "same handle". This lets a privileged process open a resource the unprivileged one can't (a low port, a device, a file outside a sandbox) and hand it over; lets a listener process accept connections and distribute the connected sockets to worker processes (systemd socket activation, some load balancers); and underpins privilege-separation designs where one tiny trusted process owns all the dangerous opens. The security model: the receiver gets exactly the access the sender had on that description, nothing more.
Compare the copy costs of pipe, Unix socket, and shared memory for a 1 MB transfer, and how zero-copy techniques change it.
Pipe / Unix socket: write() copies from the sender's buffer into a kernel buffer (copy 1); read() copies from the kernel buffer into the receiver's buffer (copy 2) — ~2 MB of memory traffic plus two syscalls, for 1 MB of payload. Shared memory: the sender writes 1 MB into the shared region (copy 1, unavoidable unless it produced the data there directly), the receiver reads it in place (copy 0) — ~1 MB traffic, no per-transfer syscall. Zero-copy paths: splice()/vmsplice() move pages between a pipe and a file/socket by reference (page "stealing"), avoiding the userspace bounce; sendfile() streams a file to a socket entirely in the kernel; MSG_ZEROCOPY lets the kernel DMA directly from user pages for large socket sends (with an async completion notification, since the buffer must stay stable). For local bulk transfer the winning designs are: put the producer's output directly in shared memory (true zero-copy), or use memfd + fd-passing so the receiver mmaps the sender's buffer.

System Calls & the Kernel Boundary

How user code asks the kernel for something — and why crossing that line costs.

Notes

User space vs kernel space

The CPU runs at a privilege level. User mode can't touch hardware, other processes' memory, or privileged instructions. Kernel mode can. A system call is the controlled doorway: user code executes a special instruction (syscall on x86-64, svc on ARM) that traps into a fixed kernel entry point.

// user code CANNOT do this directly -- it must ask the kernel
*(volatile uint8_t*)0xB8000 = 'A';   // write to VGA memory -> SIGSEGV in user mode
outb(0x3F8, 'A');                    // privileged I/O instruction -> #GP fault

// the sanctioned doorway: a syscall
write(1, "A", 1);                    // libc wrapper -> `syscall` instruction -> kernel does the I/O

What happens on a syscall

  1. libc wrapper puts the syscall number in a register and arguments in others, executes syscall.
  2. CPU switches to kernel mode, jumps to the kernel's entry handler, switches to the kernel stack.
  3. Handler validates the number, copies/validates user pointers (copy_from_user — never trust a user address), dispatches via the syscall table.
  4. Does the work (maybe blocking → scheduler runs something else).
  5. Puts the return value / -errno in a register, switches back to user mode.

Cost: ~100–500 ns direct, more with mitigations (Spectre/Meltdown page-table isolation). Not free — hence batching (readv, io_uring, sendmmsg) and the vDSO.

$ strace -T -e trace=write ./app
write(1, "hi\n", 3)  = 3 <0.000004>      # <time> = ~4 us here incl. the terminal

# x86-64 calling convention: nr in rax, args in rdi,rsi,rdx,r10,r8,r9
mov  rax, 1          # __NR_write
mov  rdi, 1          # fd
mov  rsi, msg
mov  rdx, 3          # len
syscall             # trap; kernel returns result (or -errno) in rax

vDSO

A small shared library the kernel maps into every process so hot, read-only calls like gettimeofday()/clock_gettime() can be served in user space from a kernel-updated memory page — no mode switch at all.

$ cat /proc/self/maps | grep vdso
7ffe...000-7ffe...000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0   [vdso]   # kernel-mapped code page

# clock_gettime() reads a kernel-updated timestamp page in USER mode -> no syscall
$ strace -e trace=clock_gettime ./ts_loop     # prints (almost) nothing: the calls never trap
$ ltrace ./ts_loop                            # but ltrace still sees the libc call

Kernel architectures

MonolithicMicrokernel
In-kernelscheduler, MM, drivers, filesystems, network stackonly scheduler, MM, IPC; drivers/FS are user-space servers
Speedfast (direct calls)slower (IPC between servers)
Reliabilitya driver bug can crash the kernela driver crash is a restartable service
ExamplesLinux, *BSD (modular monolithic)QNX, seL4, MINIX 3; macOS/Windows are hybrids
# Linux monolithic-but-modular: a driver is a function call away, and can panic the box
$ lsmod | head -3
Module        Size  Used by
nvme         57344  3
ext4        901120  1
$ sudo rmmod nvme        # unload a driver from the running kernel (no reboot)

# microkernel (QNX/seL4): that same nvme driver is a user process;
# if it crashes, a supervisor restarts it and the kernel never notices
Cheat Sheet
  • User mode = restricted; kernel mode = privileged. Syscall = the guarded transition (a trap instruction).
  • Flow: set syscall number + args → syscall/svc traps → kernel entry, validate, copy_from_user → dispatch via syscall table → return value/-errno → back to user mode.
  • Cost ~100–500 ns (+ KPTI overhead) → batch calls (io_uring, readv/writev, sendmmsg).
  • vDSO serves clock_gettime/getpid-class calls in user space — no mode switch.
  • Kernel must never trust user pointers — always validate + copy.
  • Monolithic (Linux): everything in kernel, fast, driver bug = crash. Microkernel: minimal core + user-space servers, robust, IPC overhead.
  • Interrupts/exceptions also enter kernel mode but aren't syscalls.
Q&A
Why can't user code just call kernel functions directly?
They run at different privilege levels in separate address spaces. The only way in is a trap instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed, validated entry point — so the kernel controls exactly what user code can trigger and can check every argument.
What is the vDSO and why does it exist?
A kernel-provided shared object mapped into every process. It lets frequently-called, safe, read-only operations (getting the time, the PID) run entirely in user space against a kernel-maintained data page — eliminating the mode-switch cost for the hottest "syscalls".
Why must the kernel copy user-supplied buffers with copy_from_user?
A user pointer might be invalid, unmapped, point into kernel memory, or be concurrently unmapped by another thread. copy_from_user checks the address range is legitimately user memory and handles faults gracefully, preventing a malicious or buggy program from making the kernel read/write arbitrary memory.
Monolithic vs microkernel — core trade-off?
Monolithic keeps drivers, filesystems, and the network stack in kernel space: fast (plain function calls) but a bug anywhere can take down the whole system. Microkernel runs those as isolated user-space servers: a crash is contained and restartable, at the cost of IPC overhead on every cross-component interaction.
How does io_uring reduce syscall overhead?
It sets up shared submission and completion ring buffers between user space and the kernel. The app writes many I/O requests into the submission ring and can process many completions from the completion ring, amortising or eliminating per-operation syscalls (with SQPOLL, a kernel thread polls the ring so the app makes no syscall at all).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What CPU state change does a system call cause?
A switch from user mode to kernel (privileged) mode, via a trap, and back on return.
Is printf a system call?
No — it's a libc function that may eventually invoke the write system call (after formatting and buffering).
Where do device drivers live in a microkernel?
In user space, as separate server processes; the kernel only mediates IPC and basic scheduling/memory.

Intermediate core

A program reading a file byte-by-byte with read(fd, &c, 1) is extremely slow. Why and fix?
Every byte is a full syscall (mode switch + kernel work) — hundreds of ns each, millions of times. Fix: read in large blocks (read(fd, buf, 65536)) and parse from the buffer, or use buffered stdio (fread/getc over a FILE*, which does big read()s under the hood), or mmap the file and access it as memory.
Why did Meltdown/Spectre mitigations make syscalls measurably slower?
Kernel Page-Table Isolation (KPTI) gives user mode and kernel mode separate page tables, so a syscall/interrupt must switch CR3 on entry and exit — adding TLB flushes (partly mitigated by PCID) and page-table reloads that a syscall previously didn't need. Retpolines / IBRS for Spectre add indirect-branch overhead in the kernel. Net effect: syscall-heavy workloads (databases, high-connection servers) saw single-digit to ~30% regressions depending on call rate, which is why syscall batching (io_uring) got more important.

Advanced deep

Trace a write(fd, buf, n) from the instruction to the return, including the security checks.
The libc wrapper loads the syscall number for write into rax, fd→rdi, buf→rsi, n→rdx, and executes syscall. The CPU saves the user rip/rflags, switches to ring 0, and jumps to the address in the LSTAR MSR — the kernel's entry stub. The stub switches to the kernel stack for this thread, saves the full user register set, (with KPTI) switches to the kernel page tables, and runs any entry-time mitigations. It bounds-checks rax against the syscall table size and calls sys_write. That resolves fd through the process's fd table to a struct file (returns -EBADF if invalid or not opened for writing), checks the file's write permission and any LSM (SELinux/AppArmor) hook, then calls the file's write operation. For a regular file that means copy_from_user(kernel_page, buf, n) — which verifies [buf, buf+n) lies in user address range and handles a fault by returning -EFAULT rather than oopsing — then copies into the page cache, marks pages dirty, updates the file offset, and returns the byte count. Back in the stub: the return value goes in rax, mitigations run, page tables/stack switch back, registers restore, sysret returns to just after the syscall instruction in user mode. libc checks for a negative value in [-4095, -1], and if so sets errno = -rax and returns -1.
Why are hybrid kernels (macOS XNU, Windows NT) neither purely monolithic nor microkernel, and what did they keep from each?
Both started with microkernel ambitions (XNU wraps the Mach microkernel; NT was influenced by microkernel design) but found the IPC cost of running performance-critical subsystems — the filesystem, network stack, and especially the graphics/window server — as separate user-space servers unacceptable for a desktop OS. So they pulled those back into kernel space for speed, while keeping microkernel-style structure and interfaces internally: XNU keeps Mach's message-passing, ports, and memory-object abstractions and layers a BSD "personality" (POSIX syscalls, sockets, VFS) on top, all in one kernel address space; NT keeps a layered "executive" of subsystems communicating through well-defined interfaces, with the microkernel-ish core ("kernel layer") handling scheduling and synchronisation, but drivers and file systems run in kernel mode. The result: the modularity, portability, and clean internal APIs of a microkernel, with the in-address-space call performance of a monolith — and the monolith's downside that a bad kernel-mode driver can still crash the system (hence Windows' driver signing and, later, moving some drivers back to user mode via UMDF).

Races & the Critical Section

Why count++ from two threads loses increments — and the vocabulary for it.

Notes

The classic bug

// two threads run this; count starts at 0, ends at... maybe 1, not 2
count = count + 1;
//   load count -> reg      (both read 0)
//   add 1                  (both compute 1)
//   store reg -> count     (both write 1)  -- one increment lost

The read-modify-write isn't atomic; a thread switch between the load and the store loses an update. This is a data race: two threads access the same location, at least one writes, with no synchronisation and no defined ordering — undefined behaviour in C/C++/Java's model.

Data race vs race condition

  • Data race — the concrete "unsynchronised concurrent access" defect above. Tools (TSan) detect these.
  • Race condition — a broader logic bug where correctness depends on timing/ordering, even with each individual operation synchronised (e.g. check-then-act on shared state).
// DATA RACE (TSan flags it): two threads, no sync, one writes
int total;
void *w(void*_) { total += 1; return NULL; }   // $ clang -fsanitize=thread

// RACE CONDITION with NO data race: each op is atomic, the SEQUENCE is wrong
if (map.contains_key(k))          // thread A passes...
    v = map.get(k);               // ...thread B removes k here -> A gets null / throws
// fix: map.get_or_default(k), or hold the lock across check+use

Critical section

A region of code that accesses shared state and must run atomically with respect to other threads — only one thread inside at a time. Protect it with a lock (or make the operation a single atomic instruction, or avoid sharing).

void deposit(Account *a, long amt) {
