$ gdb -p 4201 -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt' 2>/dev/null | grep -A4 'pthread_mutex_lock'

# "can't find file" -> strace names it:
$ strace -f ./prog 2>&1 | grep ENOENT
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/app/config.yml", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
Cheat Sheet
  • Build with -g; keep -O0 while debugging (else "optimized out").
  • gdb: break/run/bt/next/step/finish/print/watch; thread apply all bt for hangs; -p PID to attach; prog core post-mortem.
  • Enable core dumps: ulimit -c unlimited, check kernel.core_pattern, use coredumpctl gdb.
  • strace: what it asks the kernel — -f follow forks, -e trace= filter, -T/-tt timing, -c summary, -p attach.
  • ltrace: library/API calls and their arguments.
  • strace/ltrace slow the target a lot — diagnostic, not production monitoring.
  • Nondeterministic bug → rr record/replay for time-travel debugging.
Q&A
gdb vs strace — when each?
gdb for source-level state: where did it crash, what's in this variable, why did this branch run. strace for the process/kernel interface: which files/sockets it touches, which syscall it's blocked in, why an operation returns an error.
How do you get a backtrace from a program that already crashed?
Ensure core dumps are enabled, reproduce the crash, then gdb ./prog core and run bt (bt full for locals). With systemd, coredumpctl gdb <PID or exe> does it in one step.
Your program prints "No such file or directory" but you can't tell which file. Tool?
strace -e trace=openat,stat ./prog — you'll see the exact path it tried and the ENOENT return, plus whether it was searching a wrong directory.
How do you diagnose a hung process without restarting it?
Attach: gdb -p PID then thread apply all bt to see every thread's stack (spot the lock cycle or the blocking call). Or strace -p PID to see if it's stuck in a syscall (futex, read, poll). Or cat /proc/PID/stack for the kernel stack.
Why does gdb say a variable is "<optimized out>"?
The compiler (at -O1+) kept it only in a register that's since been reused, or eliminated it entirely, so there's no memory location to read. Rebuild the relevant file with -O0 -g, or use -Og which optimises but preserves debuggability.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What compiler flag adds debug symbols?
-g.
gdb command to print the call stack?
bt (backtrace); bt full also shows local variables.
Which tool shows every system call a process makes?
strace.

Intermediate core

A service is slow. strace -c -p PID shows 80% of time in futex. What does that suggest?
Heavy lock contention: threads are repeatedly blocking/waking on a mutex (futex is the syscall behind a contended pthread mutex/condvar). Follow up with perf lock / a profiler to find which lock, then reduce critical-section size, shard the lock, or switch to a lock-free / read-mostly structure. (Lots of futex with ETIMEDOUT can also just be idle condvar waits — check the args.)
Set a gdb breakpoint that only fires on the 500th call or when a condition holds.
Conditional: break process_item if item->id == target. Ignore count: break func then ignore 1 499 (skip 499 hits, stop on the 500th). Also useful: commands to auto-run gdb commands at a breakpoint (e.g. bt 3; continue) for logging without stopping.

Advanced deep

How does rr achieve deterministic replay of a nondeterministic bug, and what are its limits?
rr records a program's execution by intercepting every source of nondeterminism at the syscall boundary: it serialises threads onto a single core (so there's one deterministic interleaving), logs the results and any injected data of every syscall, records signal delivery points (by instruction count via hardware performance counters), and captures scheduling decisions. Replay re-runs the exact same instruction stream, feeding back the recorded syscall results instead of really executing them, and delivering signals at the identical points — so a heisenbug that reproduces 1-in-1000 becomes 100% reproducible, and you can run gdb backwards (reverse-continue, reverse-step, hardware watchpoints going back in time) to walk from the crash to the corruption. Limits: single-core recording means it can't reproduce true-parallel data races that only manifest on multiple cores (it finds the ones that occur under some interleaving, which is most but not all); ~1.2–2× slowdown while recording; needs specific CPU perf-counter support (works best on Intel, limited on some AMD/ARM/VMs); can't record programs that use certain hardware features (RDTSC without patching, some GPU/DMA paths), CPUID-dependent code paths, or extremely large memory footprints efficiently. For the bugs it does cover, it collapses days of "add a print, rebuild, wait for it to recur" into minutes.
Compare strace's ptrace-based tracing with perf trace / eBPF-based syscall tracing for production use.
strace uses ptrace: the tracer is stopped-and-resumed around every syscall of the tracee (two context switches per syscall, plus data copies to format arguments). Overhead is often 10–100× for syscall-heavy programs, and it serialises the tracee — enough to change timing, mask races, and cause user-visible latency. Fine for a dev box or a quick look; dangerous on a hot production service. eBPF-based tools (perf trace, bpftrace, execsnoop/opensnoop from bcc) attach small verified programs to syscall tracepoints in the kernel; they aggregate or filter in kernel space and only copy out what you asked for, with per-event overhead in the tens-to-hundreds of nanoseconds. You can run "show me every openat that returns ENOENT, system-wide" or "histogram of read latency for PID X" on a live server with negligible impact, and detach cleanly. Trade-offs: eBPF needs a recent kernel and (often) root/CAP_BPF, the tooling is less turnkey for "just show me this one process's exact syscall sequence with decoded structs", and the verifier constrains what you can express. Rule: reach for strace to understand one process in dev; reach for eBPF to observe production without perturbing it.

Profiling: perf, valgrind & friends

Finding where the time and the memory actually go — sampling vs instrumentation.

Notes

Two philosophies

  • Sampling (perf): interrupt the program N times/sec, record the stack. Low overhead (~1–5%), safe on production, statistical — shows where time is spent proportionally.
  • Instrumentation (Valgrind, gprof): rewrite/observe every operation. Exact counts, but 10–50× slower — dev only, and it changes timing.
# SAMPLING: safe on a live server, ~2% overhead, statistical
$ perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pgrep app) -- sleep 30   # 99 Hz for 30 s
$ perf report --stdio | head
  38.2%  app  [.] parse_row          # proportional -- "38% of samples were here"

# INSTRUMENTATION: exact, but 20-50x slower -- dev box only
$ valgrind --tool=callgrind ./app    # every instruction counted
$ callgrind_annotate callgrind.out.* | head   # exact call counts per line

perf

perf stat ./prog                 # cycles, instructions, IPC, cache misses, branch misses
perf record -g ./prog            # sample with call graphs
perf report                      # interactive hot-function view
perf top                         # live system-wide hotspots
perf record -e cache-misses ...  # sample on a specific hardware event

Pipe perf script into Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph for the classic width-is-time visualisation. Key metrics: low IPC (<1) → stalled on memory/branches; high cache-miss rate → poor locality; high branch-miss rate → unpredictable branches.

Valgrind

ToolFinds
Memcheck (default)invalid reads/writes, use-after-free, leaks, uninitialised values, bad free
Cachegrind / Callgrindcache miss + branch simulation, per-line/function; call graph (view in KCachegrind)
Massifheap profiler over time (what's allocating, when peak is)
Helgrind / DRDdata races and lock-order errors
$ valgrind --leak-check=full --track-origins=yes ./app
==1234== Invalid write of size 4
==1234==    at 0x1091AB: main (bug.c:12)
==1234==  Address 0x4a8b04c is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd   // off-by-one
==1234== LEAK SUMMARY:
==1234==    definitely lost: 40 bytes in 1 blocks               // with the alloc stack

$ valgrind --tool=massif ./app && ms_print massif.out.*   # heap-over-time graph, finds the peak

Sanitizers (compile-time, faster than Valgrind)

-fsanitize=address (ASan — memory errors + leaks, ~2×), =undefined (UBSan), =thread (TSan — races), =memory (MSan — uninitialised reads). Run your test suite under them in CI.

$ clang -fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1 app.c -o app && ./app
==5678==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000000010
    #0 0x... in use_it app.c:20
    freed by thread T0 here:  #1 0x... in main app.c:18
    # exact line, both stacks, ~2x slowdown (vs Valgrind's 20-50x) -> run it in CI

$ CFLAGS="-fsanitize=address" make check     # the usual CI wiring

Method

Measure first (perf stat) → find the hot spot (perf record/flame graph) → understand why it's hot (IPC, cache misses, a bad algorithm) → fix → re-measure. Don't optimise by guessing.

$ perf stat ./app
     12,400,000,000  instructions   #  0.41  insn per cycle    // IPC < 1 -> stalled
        910,000,000  cache-misses   #  38.1% of all cache refs  // -> poor locality, not CPU-bound

# 1. measure  2. perf record -g + flamegraph -> parse_row is 38%
# 3. why? cache-misses high -> it chases pointers per row
# 4. fix: struct-of-arrays layout   5. perf stat again -> IPC 2.1, misses 4%
Cheat Sheet
  • Sampling (perf): low overhead, production-safe, statistical. Instrumentation (Valgrind): exact, 10–50× slower, dev-only.
  • perf stat for the summary (IPC, cache/branch misses); perf record -g + perf report / flame graph for hotspots; perf top live.
  • IPC < 1 → memory/branch stalls. High cache-miss % → locality problem. High branch-miss % → unpredictable branches.
  • Valgrind Memcheck: leaks + invalid memory access. Massif: heap over time. Callgrind: call graph. Helgrind: races.
  • Sanitizers (-fsanitize=address/undefined/thread/memory): faster than Valgrind, run in CI.
  • Always: measure → locate → explain → fix → re-measure. No guessing.
  • Frame pointers or DWARF unwinding needed for good perf call graphs (-fno-omit-frame-pointer).
Q&A
Sampling profiler vs instrumenting profiler?
A sampling profiler (perf) periodically snapshots the call stack — low overhead, statistical, safe in production. An instrumenting profiler (Valgrind/Callgrind, gprof) observes every call/instruction — exact counts but 10–50× slowdown and altered timing, so dev-only.
What does a low IPC (instructions per cycle) in perf stat tell you?
The CPU is stalling rather than retiring instructions — usually waiting on memory (cache misses, TLB misses) or mispredicted branches. It points you toward data-locality or branch-prediction fixes rather than "do less work".
Which Valgrind tool finds memory leaks, and what does it cost?
Memcheck (the default). It also catches invalid reads/writes, use-after-free, and uninitialised-value use. Cost: roughly 10–30× slower and higher memory use.
What's a flame graph and how do you read it?
A stacked visualisation of sampled stacks: the x-axis is proportion of samples (not time order), the y-axis is stack depth. Wide frames = where the CPU spends its time; you look for the widest boxes and their callers. Generated from perf script output.
ASan vs Valgrind Memcheck?
Both find memory errors. ASan is a compile-time instrumentation, ~2× slowdown, catches out-of-bounds and use-after-free with precise reports, and integrates into CI easily. Memcheck needs no recompile, also catches uninitialised-value reads (which ASan doesn't — that's MSan), but is much slower. Use ASan routinely, Valgrind for the cases ASan misses or when you can't rebuild.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which is production-safe: perf record or valgrind?
perf record — sampling, ~1–5% overhead. Valgrind is 10–50× slower.
What does perf stat give you?
Aggregate hardware counters for the run: cycles, instructions, IPC, cache misses, branch misses, context switches, etc.
Compiler flag for the AddressSanitizer?
-fsanitize=address.

Intermediate core

A loop over a large 2-D array is slow. perf stat shows a very high cache-miss rate. Likely fix?
You're probably iterating column-major over a row-major array (a[j][i] in the inner loop), so each access jumps a whole row and misses cache. Swap the loop order to march contiguously (a[i][j]), or block/tile the loops so a working set fits in L1/L2. Confirm with a re-run of perf stat — cache-miss rate should drop and IPC rise.
Your flame graph is a flat forest of tiny frames with no obvious wide box. What does that mean?
No single hotspot — the cost is spread across many functions ("death by a thousand cuts"). Possibilities: an inefficiency in something called everywhere (allocation, logging, a lock, string formatting) — look at inverted/"hot leaf" views; or the profile is dominated by framework/runtime overhead; or you're missing symbols (frames collapsed as [unknown]). Also check whether it's actually CPU-bound at all — if wall-time >> CPU-time, profile off-CPU (blocking) with perf sched / off-CPU flame graphs instead.

Advanced deep

Explain "off-CPU" profiling and why on-CPU flame graphs can be misleading for a slow service.
An on-CPU sampling profiler only records what's running on a CPU when the timer fires. If your service's latency comes from waiting — blocked on a lock, a disk read, a downstream RPC, a condition variable, being descheduled — those threads are off-CPU and invisible to perf record; the flame graph shows only the small fraction of time spent computing, so you "optimise" a function that isn't the bottleneck. Off-CPU profiling instead measures where threads block: it hooks the scheduler (kernel sched:sched_switch tracepoint via eBPF, or perf sched) to record, for each thread that goes off-CPU, the stack at the moment it blocked and how long it stayed blocked, then aggregates into an off-CPU flame graph (width = time blocked). Combined ("wall-clock") flame graphs merge both. Workflow for a latency problem: first compare CPU-time to wall-time; if wall >> CPU, the answer is in off-CPU analysis — which lock, which syscall, which RPC — not in tightening a hot loop. Brendan Gregg's bcc offcputime / wakeuptime are the standard tools; the catch is that very short, frequent blocking events generate huge trace volume, so you filter by minimum block duration.
What is the "skid" problem in hardware-event sampling and how do PEBS / precise events address it?
When a performance counter overflows (e.g. every 100,000 cache misses) it raises an interrupt, but by the time the CPU takes the interrupt and the kernel reads the instruction pointer, the pipeline has moved on — several to dozens of instructions past the one that actually caused the event. This "skid" means perf attributes the cache miss / branch miss to the wrong instruction (and sometimes the wrong basic block or function), which is maddening when you're trying to pin down exactly which load is missing. PEBS (Precise Event-Based Sampling, Intel; IBS on AMD, SPE on ARM) fixes this: the CPU hardware itself captures a record — the precise instruction pointer, registers, and for memory events the data address and which cache level was hit — into a buffer at the moment the event retires, and only interrupts when the buffer fills. So perf record -e mem_load_retired.l3_miss:pp (the :pp/:ppp suffix requests precise) gives you the actual missing load and even the address, enabling data-oriented analysis (perf c2c for false-sharing detection, perf mem for per-address miss breakdown). Limitations: only a subset of events support precise mode, PEBS records add some overhead and buffer management, and virtualised environments often don't expose it.

Number Representation & Endianness

Two's complement, IEEE-754, and which byte comes first.

Notes

Two's complement

The near-universal signed-integer format. To negate: invert all bits and add 1. Properties:

  • One representation of zero; range for N bits is -2^(N-1) to 2^(N-1)-1 (asymmetric — no positive counterpart to INT_MIN).
  • Addition/subtraction hardware is identical for signed and unsigned — the bits are the same, only interpretation differs.
  • The top bit is the sign bit; sign-extension replicates it when widening.
int8_t x = 5;                 // bits 0000 0101
int8_t negx = ~x + 1;          // invert -> 1111 1010 ; +1 -> 1111 1011 == -5

// same ADD hardware, different interpretation:
uint8_t u = 200 + 100;          // bits 1 0010 1100 -> keep 8 -> 44 (wraps, DEFINED)
int8_t  s = (int8_t)(100 + 100);  // bits 1100 1000 -> read as signed -> -56

int32_t w = (int32_t)(int8_t)0xFB;  // sign-extend: 0xFFFFFFFB == -5, not 251

Overflow

  • Unsigned: wraps modulo 2^N — defined behaviour.
  • Signed: overflow is undefined behaviour in C/C++ (the compiler assumes it can't happen); at the hardware level it wraps and sets the overflow flag.
  • INT_MIN / -1 and -INT_MIN overflow (the asymmetry).
uint32_t a = 0xFFFFFFFF; a + 1;   // 0  -- defined wraparound

int b = INT_MAX; b + 1;           // UB: compiler may assume b+1 > b is always true
// safe: detect it before doing it
if (__builtin_add_overflow(b, 1, &b)) handle_overflow();

int m = INT_MIN;
m / -1;                          // UB + SIGFPE on x86: |INT_MIN| doesn't fit in int

IEEE-754 floating point

[sign | exponent | mantissa] — 32-bit: 1+8+23; 64-bit: 1+11+52. Value = (-1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exp-bias).

  • Not all decimals are representable (0.1 isn't) → never compare floats with ==; use a tolerance.
  • Special values: ±0, ±∞, NaN (NaN ≠ everything, including itself), subnormals (gradual underflow, often slow).
  • Precision decreases as magnitude grows; adding a small number to a large one can be a no-op. Sum small-to-large, or use Kahan summation.
printf("%.17f\n", 0.1 + 0.2);   // 0.30000000000000004  -- NOT 0.3
if (fabs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9) { }  // compare with a tolerance

double nan = 0.0 / 0.0;
nan == nan;                     // false! use isnan(nan)

float big = 1e20f;
big + 1.0f == big;              // true -- 1.0 is below the ULP at 1e20 (lost)

Endianness

Little-endianBig-endian
Byte order of 0x1234567878 56 34 12 (LSB first)12 34 56 78 (MSB first)
Used byx86, ARM (default), RISC-Vnetwork byte order, older MIPS/SPARC/PowerPC

Matters when reading binary formats, casting between int and char[], or sending data over the network. Use htonl/ntohl (or explicit shift-and-mask) — never memcpy a multi-byte integer to the wire without converting.

uint32_t v = 0x12345678;
uint8_t *b = (uint8_t*)&v;
b[0];                            // 0x78 on x86 (little-endian), 0x12 on a big-endian box

// wire protocols are big-endian ("network byte order") -- always convert:
uint32_t on_wire = htonl(v);    // send this
uint32_t host    = ntohl(on_wire);   // receive this
// send(sock, &v, 4, 0)  WITHOUT htonl -> corrupt on any peer with different endianness
Cheat Sheet
  • Two's complement: negate = invert + 1; one zero; range -2^(N-1)…2^(N-1)-1; same add/sub HW for signed/unsigned.
  • Unsigned overflow wraps (defined). Signed overflow = UB in C/C++.
  • Sign-extend when widening signed; zero-extend unsigned.
  • IEEE-754: sign/exp/mantissa; 0.1 not exact; never == floats; NaN ≠ NaN.
  • Float precision drops with magnitude; sum smallest-first or use Kahan.
  • Little-endian (x86/ARM) = LSB first; big-endian = network byte order.
  • Wire/binary I/O: convert with htonl/ntohl or explicit byte assembly; don't rely on host layout.
Q&A
Why is two's complement preferred over sign-magnitude?
It has a single representation of zero, and addition/subtraction use the exact same circuitry as unsigned arithmetic — no special-casing the sign. Sign-magnitude and one's complement have two zeros and need correction steps.
Is x + 1 > x always true for int x?
Mathematically no (fails at INT_MAX), but a C compiler may assume it's always true because signed overflow is UB — and optimise the check away. For unsigned, it genuinely wraps and the check is false at the max.
Why shouldn't you compare floats with ==?
Most decimal fractions aren't exactly representable in binary floating point, and rounding in intermediate operations accumulates, so two computations that "should" be equal often differ in the last bits. Compare with an absolute/relative epsilon appropriate to the magnitude.
What is endianness and when does it bite you?
The order in which a multi-byte value's bytes are stored in memory. It matters when you reinterpret bytes as integers (parsing binary files, network packets, casting char* to int*) — the same bytes mean different numbers on little- vs big-endian machines.
What's special about NaN?
It's not equal to anything, including itself — x != x is a NaN test. It propagates through arithmetic. It's produced by 0.0/0.0, sqrt(-1), ∞ - ∞, etc.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How do you negate a number in two's complement?
Invert all the bits and add 1.
What is "network byte order"?
Big-endian — most significant byte first.
How do you test for NaN?
x != x (true only for NaN), or isnan(x).

Intermediate core

Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 return false?
None of 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 is exactly representable in binary double. 0.1 and 0.2 each round to the nearest double, their sum rounds again, and the result differs from the double nearest 0.3 by one ULP (0.30000000000000004). Compare with a tolerance, or use decimal/fixed-point for money.
You memcpy a uint32_t into a network packet and it's garbled on the other end. Fix?
The sender and receiver differ in endianness (or you're relying on host order). Convert to a defined wire order: uint32_t net = htonl(host); before sending, uint32_t host = ntohl(net); after receiving — or serialise byte-by-byte with explicit shifts so it's endianness-independent.

Advanced deep

Explain catastrophic cancellation and a technique to avoid it.
When you subtract two nearly-equal floating-point numbers, the leading significant digits cancel and the result is dominated by the rounding error that was already present in the inputs — you can lose most or all of your significant figures in one operation. Classic example: the quadratic formula (-b + sqrt(b² - 4ac)) / 2a when b² >> 4ac: sqrt(b²-4ac) ≈ |b|, so one root subtracts two almost-equal values. Fix: compute the "safe" root x₁ = (-b - sign(b)·sqrt(disc)) / 2a (an addition, no cancellation), then get the other from the identity x₁·x₂ = c/a. General techniques: algebraically rearrange to replace the subtraction (rationalise, use log1p/expm1 for log(1+x)/eˣ-1 near 0), use higher precision for the intermediate, or compensated arithmetic (Kahan/two-sum) to carry the lost bits.
Why are subnormal (denormal) floating-point numbers sometimes a performance problem, and what's "flush to zero"?
Subnormals fill the gap between the smallest normal number and zero by giving up the implicit leading 1 and reducing precision as the value shrinks (gradual underflow) — important for numerical stability near zero. But many CPUs handle them in microcode or take a fault-and-fixup path rather than the fast hardware path, so an operation that produces or consumes a subnormal can be 10–100× slower than the same operation on normals. Audio DSP, physics simulations with decaying values, and recursive filters are notorious for drifting into the subnormal range and suddenly dropping to a fraction of expected throughput. Mitigations: enable FTZ (flush-to-zero: results that would be subnormal become ±0) and DAZ (denormals-are-zero: subnormal inputs are treated as ±0) via the CPU's floating-point control register (_MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE / -ffast-math sets these), or add a tiny "dither"/DC offset to keep signals out of the subnormal region. The trade-off is a small loss of accuracy near zero, which is acceptable for most real-time media and games but not for high-accuracy scientific code.

The Memory Hierarchy & Caches

Why "memory is slow" is the single most important performance fact.

Notes

The latency ladder (rough, modern desktop)

LevelLatencySize
Register0 cycles~1 KB
L1 cache~4 cycles (~1 ns)32–64 KB per core
L2 cache~12 cycles (~4 ns)256 KB–2 MB per core
L3 cache~40 cycles (~15 ns)8–64 MB shared
Main RAM~200–300 cycles (~80 ns)GBs
NVMe SSD~50–100 µsTBs
Network / spinning diskms—

Each level down is ~3–10× slower and ~10× bigger. A last-level-cache miss to RAM costs hundreds of instructions' worth of time — the CPU may stall entirely.

$ lscpu | grep -i cache
L1d cache:  384 KiB (12 instances)     # 32 KiB per core
L2 cache:   12 MiB  (12 instances)
L3 cache:   30 MiB  (1 instance)       # shared

// working set that fits vs spills a level:
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += a[i % SIZE];   // SIZE=8K -> L1 (~1ns/access)
                                            // SIZE=8M -> RAM (~80ns) -> 80x slower, same code

Why caches work

Locality: programs reuse recently-touched data (temporal) and touch nearby data soon (spatial). Caches exploit both — keep recent data, and fetch a whole 64-byte cache line on a miss so neighbours are already present.

// SPATIAL: one miss on a[i] pulls in a[i..i+15] (16 ints = 64 B line) for free
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += a[i];      // ~1 miss per 16 elements

// same data, stride 16 -> touch one element per line -> 16x the misses
for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 16) total += a[i];

// TEMPORAL: the loop counter + `total` stay hot in registers/L1 the whole time

The mental model that matters

  • Modern CPUs are so fast that most non-trivial code is memory-bound, not compute-bound.
  • "Big-O" ignores constants, but a cache-friendly O(n²) can beat a pointer-chasing O(n log n) for realistic sizes.
  • Reducing memory traffic and improving locality is often a bigger win than reducing instruction count.
// sum a million ints: contiguous vector vs pointer-chased linked list
std::vector<int> v(1'000'000);   // ~0.3 ms  -- prefetcher streams it, ~all L1/L2 hits
std::list<int>   l(v.begin(), v.end());  // ~6 ms   -- a cache miss per node, 20x slower
// identical O(n), identical instruction count -- the difference is 100% memory layout

Inclusive vs exclusive, write policies

  • Inclusive (Intel historically): L3 contains everything in L1/L2 — simplifies coherence, wastes some capacity. Exclusive (AMD): a line lives in only one level.
  • Write-back (normal): writes update the cache, main memory later. Write-through: every write also hits the next level (simpler, more traffic).
// write-back: this loop touches RAM roughly once per 64 B line, not once per store
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = 0;   // stores coalesce in the L1 line, flush later

// non-temporal store: bypass the cache for data you won't re-read (big memset/memcpy)
_mm_stream_si128((__m128i*)&a[i], zero);   // write straight to RAM, don't pollute L1/L2
// MMIO regions are effectively write-through: every store goes to the device now
Cheat Sheet
  • Rough latencies: L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~4 ns, L3 ~15 ns, RAM ~80 ns, SSD ~50 µs, disk/net ~ms. Each level ~10× bigger, several× slower.
  • An LLC miss = hundreds of cycles — the CPU can stall completely.
  • Cache line = 64 bytes; a miss fetches the whole line (spatial locality payoff).
  • Caches exploit temporal + spatial locality.
  • Most real code is memory-bound; improving locality often beats reducing instructions.
  • Write-back (default): cache updated now, RAM later. Write-through: both, more traffic.
  • Inclusive L3 (some Intel) vs exclusive (AMD) — affects effective capacity + coherence.
Q&A
Roughly how much slower is a main-memory access than an L1 hit?
About 50–100× (a few cycles vs a couple hundred). In wall time, ~1 ns vs ~80 ns.
Why does the CPU fetch a whole 64-byte line on a cache miss, not just the word you asked for?
Spatial locality — programs very often access nearby addresses soon after (the next array element, another struct field). Bringing the whole line amortises the expensive memory transaction over several likely-future accesses.
What does "memory-bound" mean?
The program's speed is limited by how fast data can be moved from memory into the CPU, not by how fast the CPU can compute. Adding more arithmetic is free; adding cache misses is expensive.
Temporal vs spatial locality?
Temporal: if you accessed an address recently, you'll likely access it again soon (loop counters, hot objects). Spatial: if you accessed an address, you'll likely access nearby ones soon (array traversal, struct fields).
Write-back vs write-through cache?
Write-back keeps the modified line in cache and only writes it to the next level when it's evicted — less memory traffic. Write-through writes to cache and the next level on every store — simpler coherence, more bandwidth used.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How big is a typical cache line?
64 bytes on x86 and most ARM.
Which is bigger and slower: L1 or L3?
L3 — megabytes and ~10× the latency of L1's tens of kilobytes.
Two properties caches exploit?
Temporal locality and spatial locality.

Intermediate core

An array-of-structs traversal that only reads one field is slow. Why, and the fix?
Each struct is, say, 64 bytes but you only use 4 — so every cache line brought in is ~94% wasted, and you touch far more memory than necessary. Fix: structure-of-arrays (SoA) — store that field in its own contiguous array, so a traversal reads only what it needs and every cache line is fully used. Trade-off: worse locality when you do need multiple fields of one element together.
Why can a linked list be dramatically slower than a vector for the same O(n) traversal?
Vector elements are contiguous, so the hardware prefetcher streams them in and each cache line holds many elements — near-zero miss rate. List nodes are scattered heap allocations; each node = node->next is a dependent load to an unpredictable address, likely a cache miss (~80 ns), and you can't prefetch what you haven't loaded the pointer for. So the list traversal is a chain of full memory latencies; the vector's is bandwidth-limited streaming.

Advanced deep

Estimate the performance ceiling of a data-parallel loop using the roofline model.
The roofline model plots attainable GFLOP/s against arithmetic intensity (FLOPs performed per byte of memory traffic), with two ceilings: a horizontal line at the machine's peak compute rate, and a diagonal line = (memory bandwidth) × (arithmetic intensity). Your kernel's ceiling is the lower of the two at its intensity. Example: a loop doing c[i] = a[i] + b[i] over doubles reads 16 bytes, writes 8 (24 bytes, or 16 if c is write-allocate-avoided), does 1 FLOP → intensity ≈ 1/24 ≈ 0.04 FLOP/byte. On a machine with 50 GB/s bandwidth that caps you at ~2 GFLOP/s regardless of a 500 GFLOP/s compute peak — you are firmly memory-bound and the only wins are reducing traffic (fuse loops so intermediates stay in registers/cache, use lower precision, avoid the write-allocate read of c with non-temporal stores) or raising intensity (do more math per element loaded, e.g. a stencil that reuses neighbours). A matrix multiply, by contrast, has intensity O(n) with blocking and sits under the compute roof — there SIMD/FMA and instruction scheduling matter. The model tells you which optimisation category can possibly help before you spend time on it.
What is a hardware prefetcher, what patterns does it catch, and how can it hurt?
Prefetchers are dedicated units that watch the stream of cache misses/accesses and speculatively fetch lines they predict you'll need, hiding memory latency behind current work. Common types: next-line (fetch line N+1 on access to N), stride (detect constant-stride access like a[i], a[i+8], a[i+16] and run ahead), stream (multiple concurrent sequential streams), and per-core adjacent-line and L2 stream prefetchers. They make linear array traversal essentially free of visible latency. They fail on pointer-chasing (address isn't known until the previous load completes — no pattern), random access, and indirect access (a[idx[i]]). They can hurt by: (1) wasting bandwidth and evicting useful lines when the predicted pattern doesn't continue (e.g. at array boundaries, or a stride that changes); (2) "prefetcher thrashing" when too many streams compete; (3) polluting the cache in latency-sensitive code where the extra bandwidth contention delays demand misses; (4) crossing a page boundary conservatively stops most prefetchers (they don't do the TLB walk speculatively), so 4 KB-granular access patterns lose the benefit — huge pages help. Some workloads disable specific prefetchers via MSRs, and software prefetch intrinsics (_mm_prefetch) are used for the irregular patterns hardware can't predict, though modern hardware prefetchers have made explicit software prefetch rarely worthwhile.

Cache Lines, Associativity & Misses

How a cache decides where a line can live, and the three reasons it isn't there.

Notes

Organisation

A cache is an array of 64-byte lines. An address is split into [ tag | set index | line offset ]. The set index picks a set; the line can go in any way of that set (an N-way set-associative cache has N ways per set).

// 32 KiB, 8-way, 64 B lines -> 32768 / (8 * 64) = 64 sets
//   address bits: [ tag : rest ][ set index : 6 ][ line offset : 6 ]
uint64_t addr;
size_t offset = addr & 63;              // which byte in the 64 B line
size_t set    = (addr >> 6) & 63;       // which of the 64 sets
// the line may sit in any of that set's 8 ways; a hit compares 8 tags in parallel
TypePlacement
Direct-mapped (1-way)each line has exactly one possible slot — fast, but two hot addresses mapping to the same set thrash
N-way set-associativeN candidate slots per set; a replacement policy (pseudo-LRU) picks the victim. The common design (L1 8-way, L3 12–16-way)
Fully associativea line can go anywhere — no conflict misses, but expensive to search (used for small TLBs)

The 3 C's of cache misses

  • Compulsory (cold) — first-ever access to a line. Unavoidable except by prefetching.
  • Capacity — the working set is bigger than the cache; lines are evicted and re-fetched. Fix: shrink the working set (blocking/tiling, smaller data types).
  • Conflict — too many active addresses map to the same set, so they evict each other even though the cache isn't full. Fix: change data layout/strides, add padding, or (hardware) more associativity.

(Multicore adds a 4th: coherence misses — a line invalidated because another core wrote it. See False Sharing.)

# COMPULSORY: hint the prefetcher / warm the line early
__builtin_prefetch(&a[i + 64]);

# CAPACITY: matrix multiply -- tile so a block of each operand fits in L1
for (ii = 0; ii < n; ii += BS)          // BS chosen so 3*BS*BS*sizeof(float) < L1
  for (jj = 0; jj < n; jj += BS)
    for (kk = 0; kk < n; kk += BS)
      /* multiply the BS x BS sub-blocks -- data reused before eviction */ ;

Pathological strides

Accessing an array with a stride that's a large power of two (e.g. walking column-major through a 1024×1024 float matrix) makes every access map to the same handful of sets → conflict misses on every access despite tiny data volume. Padding the row to a non-power-of-two length breaks the pattern.

// column walk of a 1024x1024 float matrix: stride 4096 B
float m[1024][1024];
for (int r = 0; r < 1024; r++) sum += m[r][col];   // every access -> same few sets -> conflict miss

// FIX: pad the row so the stride isn't a power of two
float m2[1024][1024 + 8];                        // stride 4128 B -> spreads across sets
// or just iterate row-major (m[r][c]) so consecutive accesses share a line
Cheat Sheet
  • Address = tag | set index | 6-bit line offset (64-byte line). Set index selects a set; line goes in one of N ways.
  • Direct-mapped (1 slot, thrash-prone) < N-way set-associative (typical) < fully associative (TLBs only).
  • 3 C's: compulsory (cold, first touch), capacity (working set > cache), conflict (same-set collisions though cache isn't full).
  • + coherence misses on multicore (another core wrote the line).
  • Fix capacity misses: blocking/tiling, smaller types, fewer fields.
  • Fix conflict misses: avoid power-of-two strides; pad array rows; interleave/transpose.
  • perf stat -e L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-load-misses to measure.
Q&A
What are the three types of cache miss?
Compulsory (first access to a line, nothing could be cached yet), capacity (the working set exceeds the cache size, so needed lines get evicted), and conflict (multiple hot addresses map to the same set and evict each other even though the cache has free space elsewhere).
What does "8-way set-associative" mean?
Each set has 8 slots (ways). A given memory line maps to exactly one set (by its set-index bits) but can occupy any of that set's 8 ways; the hardware picks which one to evict on a miss.
Why can walking a matrix column-by-column be catastrophically slow even though the matrix is small?
Column stride equals the row length; if that's a power of two, consecutive column accesses have addresses differing by a large power of two, so they all index the same cache set — conflict misses on nearly every access. The data would fit in cache, but the mapping defeats it. Padding the row length breaks the alignment.
Which miss type does loop blocking (tiling) reduce?
Capacity misses — by processing the data in blocks small enough that each block's working set fits in cache and is fully reused before moving on.
Can a direct-mapped cache have conflict misses even when mostly empty?
Yes — that's its defining weakness. Two frequently-used addresses that happen to map to the same single slot will evict each other repeatedly regardless of how much of the cache is unused.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many bytes does the line-offset field of an address cover for a 64-byte line?
6 bits (2^6 = 64).
Which cache-miss type is unavoidable for data you've never touched?
Compulsory (cold) misses — short of prefetching.
Fully associative caches eliminate which miss type?
Conflict misses (a line can go anywhere).

Intermediate core

You process a 2048×2048 float array and see a huge L1 miss rate; changing the array to 2049 columns fixes it. Explain.
2048 floats = 8192 bytes = a power of two that's a multiple of (L1 size / associativity), so accessing a[i][j] and a[i+1][j] (stride 8192) lands in the same L1 set. A column walk or a stencil touching several rows thrashes that one set (conflict misses) despite low data volume. Making the row 2049 floats adds a 4-byte skew per row, so successive rows' same-column elements map to different sets — the conflicts disappear. This "array padding" trick is standard in HPC.
How would you distinguish a capacity-miss problem from a conflict-miss problem?
Shrink the working set (or use a machine with a bigger cache) — if misses drop roughly in proportion, it's capacity. Change only the layout/stride (pad rows, transpose, add offset) while keeping total data the same — if misses drop, it was conflict. Cache simulators (Cachegrind) and perf c2c / associativity-aware tools can also attribute misses.

Advanced deep

Modern L1 caches are "virtually indexed, physically tagged" (VIPT). Why that combination, and what constraint does it impose?
On every load the CPU must both (a) select the cache set and (b) verify the tag, and it wants to overlap these with the TLB lookup that translates virtual→physical. If the cache were physically indexed, you'd have to finish the TLB translation before you could even pick the set — serial, slow. If it were virtually indexed and tagged, you'd have aliasing problems (two virtual addresses mapping to one physical address occupying two different cache locations, so a write via one isn't seen via the other) and you'd have to flush on context switch. VIPT is the compromise: use the virtual address bits for the set index (available immediately, in parallel with the TLB) but the physical address for the tag (from the TLB result, ready by the time you compare). The constraint: the set-index bits must come entirely from the page offset (the bits that don't change during translation) — otherwise two virtual addresses for the same physical page could index different sets and you're back to aliasing. That caps the indexable size at page_size × associativity: with 4 KB pages, an 8-way L1 can be at most 32 KB, a 16-way at most 64 KB. This is precisely why L1 caches have been stuck around 32–48 KB for two decades despite transistor budgets exploding — growing L1 means growing associativity (costly, power-hungry) or larger pages. Apple's M-series uses 16 KB pages partly to allow larger VIPT L1 caches.
What is a "way-predictor" and why do L1 caches use one despite being set-associative?
A traditional set-associative lookup reads the tags from all N ways of the selected set in parallel, compares them to the address tag, and muxes out the matching way's data — fast but it powers up N tag arrays and N data arrays every access (energy) and the N-way comparison + mux is on the critical path (latency). A way-predictor is a small table (indexed by a hash of the address, or by PC + stride history) that guesses which way will hit; the cache then speculatively reads only that one way's data, checks its tag, and if the prediction was right (typically 90–95%) you got direct-mapped-like latency and energy from a set-associative cache. On a mispredict it falls back to the full parallel lookup, costing an extra cycle. This is how L1 caches hit in ~4 cycles despite being 8-way. Downsides: the extra cycle on mispredict, the predictor table's area, and — discovered later — way-predictor state is a microarchitectural side channel (the "Take A Way" / AMD way-predictor attacks) that can leak which way an address hit, usable for cache-based covert channels and ASLR breaking.

Locality & Cache-Friendly Code

Concrete transformations that turn a memory-bound loop into a fast one.

Notes

Traverse in memory order

// C is row-major: a[i][j] and a[i][j+1] are adjacent
for (i) for (j) sum += a[i][j];   // GOOD: sequential, prefetcher-friendly
for (j) for (i) sum += a[i][j];   // BAD: stride = row length, a miss per access

Fortran/MATLAB are column-major — the loop order flips.

AoS vs SoA

  • Array of Structs: struct P{float x,y,z; int id;} p[N]; — good when you use most fields of one element together.
  • Struct of Arrays: float x[N], y[N], z[N]; int id[N]; — good when a pass touches one field across all elements (SIMD-friendly, no wasted bytes per line).
// "sum all x" -- AoS drags y,z,id through cache too
struct P { float x, y, z; int id; } aos[N];   // 16 B/elem -> 1 useful float per 16 B
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sx += aos[i].x;    // 4 elements per 64 B line

// SoA -- x[] is dense: 16 floats per line, and the loop vectorises
struct { float x[N], y[N], z[N]; int id[N]; } soa;
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sx += soa.x[i];      // 4x fewer misses, SIMD-friendly

Loop blocking / tiling

Process the data in cache-sized blocks so each block is fully reused before eviction. Matrix multiply goes from cache-thrashing to compute-bound this way — the classic example.

// naive: for a big n, the row of A and column of B are evicted before reuse
for (i) for (j) for (k) C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];

// tiled: each BxB block of A and B stays hot across the inner triple loop
for (i0 = 0; i0 < n; i0 += B)
 for (j0 = 0; j0 < n; j0 += B)
  for (k0 = 0; k0 < n; k0 += B)
   for (i = i0; i < i0+B; i++)
    for (j = j0; j < j0+B; j++)
     for (k = k0; k < k0+B; k++)
      C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];      // same work, ~3-10x faster for large n

Other wins

  • Shrink the data: int16_t instead of int, bitfields, indices instead of pointers, deduplicate.
  • Hot/cold splitting: put rarely-used fields in a separate struct so the hot struct is smaller and more per line.
  • Pack the working set: keep the data a loop touches contiguous (arena allocation, sorting by access order).
  • Avoid pointer chasing: flat arrays over linked structures; if you must chase, prefetch the next node.
  • Software prefetch (__builtin_prefetch) for irregular-but-predictable access (e.g. a[idx[i+8]]) — rarely needed for regular patterns.
// hot/cold split: the hot loop only needs price -> pack prices densely
struct Order   { double price; OrderCold *cold; };   // 16 B -> 4 per line
struct OrderCold{ String notes, address; Timestamp ts; };  // touched rarely

// gather with a known-ahead index -> prefetch 8 iterations early
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    __builtin_prefetch(&table[idx[i + 8]]);      // hide the miss latency
    acc += table[idx[i]];
}
Cheat Sheet
  • Iterate in storage order: C = row-major (for i for j a[i][j]); column-major langs flip it.
  • AoS for "use many fields of one element"; SoA for "use one field across all elements" (also SIMD-friendly).
  • Blocking/tiling: work in cache-sized chunks → reuse before eviction (matmul, stencils, transpose).
  • Shrink data: smaller types, indices vs pointers, hot/cold field splitting, dedup.
  • Keep the working set contiguous (arena alloc, sort by access order).
  • Prefer flat arrays to linked structures; prefetch the next node if you must chase pointers.
  • __builtin_prefetch only for irregular-but-predictable access; hardware handles regular strides.
  • Measure with perf stat (miss rate, IPC) before and after.
Q&A
In C, which loop order sums a 2-D array fastest and why?
for (i) for (j) a[i][j] — row-major storage means a[i][0..cols-1] is contiguous, so you stream through memory sequentially and the prefetcher keeps ahead. The transposed order strides by a full row each step, missing cache almost every access.
When is Struct-of-Arrays better than Array-of-Structs?
When a given pass reads only one or two fields across all elements. SoA puts those fields contiguously, so every cache line is fully used and the loop vectorises cleanly. AoS wins when you need most fields of one element together (better temporal locality per element).
What does loop tiling achieve?
It restructures nested loops to operate on sub-blocks that fit in cache, so each loaded block is fully reused before being evicted — converting capacity misses into cache hits. Essential for matrix multiply, image convolution, and transposition.
Why prefer array indices over pointers in a hot data structure?
Indices are smaller (often 4 bytes vs 8), so more elements fit per cache line; the backing array is contiguous so traversal prefetches well; and there's no per-node allocation overhead. You trade a base-plus-offset computation for far fewer cache misses.
Is software prefetching usually worth it?
Rarely for regular strided access — the hardware prefetcher already handles that. It can help for irregular-but-computable patterns (hash probes, a[index[i]]) where you can prefetch several iterations ahead. Get the distance wrong and it hurts (evictions, bandwidth). Measure.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is C row-major or column-major?
Row-major — a[i][j] and a[i][j+1] are adjacent in memory.
What layout is best for SIMD over one field of many elements?
Struct-of-Arrays (SoA).
What optimisation makes matrix multiply cache-efficient?
Loop blocking / tiling.

Intermediate core

A game's particle update reads position only but stores particles as 128-byte structs. How do you speed it up 10×?
Split to SoA: a contiguous vec3 positions[N] array (plus separate arrays for velocity, colour, etc.). The position pass now reads 12 useful bytes per 64-byte line instead of 12 out of 128, cutting memory traffic ~10× and letting the loop vectorise. If some passes need position+velocity together, keep those two interleaved and the rest separate ("AoSoA" / hybrid).
You transpose a large matrix and it's slow. Approach?
Naive transpose has one operand strided (a miss per element). Tile it: transpose in small blocks (e.g. 16×16 or 32×32) that fit in cache, so each block is read once and written once with good locality. Optionally use non-temporal stores for the output (you won't re-read it), and pad the array to avoid conflict misses on the strided side.

Advanced deep

Derive the optimal tile size for blocked matrix multiplication.
For C += A×B with a tile size b, the inner blocked loops work on a b×b tile of A, a b×b tile of B, and a b×b tile of C. To keep all three resident so each is loaded from memory only n/b times (instead of n times), you need 3b² × sizeof(elem) ≤ cache_size — solve for b ≤ sqrt(cache_size / (3·elem_size)). For a 32 KB L1 and 8-byte doubles: b ≤ sqrt(32768/24) ≈ 36, so tiles around 32 are typical for L1, with an outer level of tiling sized to L2/L3 for a multi-level blocked kernel. In practice you tune empirically around this estimate because associativity, TLB coverage (want the tile within a few pages), register-blocking of the innermost micro-kernel, and prefetch all shift the sweet spot — which is why libraries like OpenBLAS ship hand-tuned, architecture-specific block sizes and micro-kernels rather than a formula.
What is the difference between "cache-aware" and "cache-oblivious" algorithms, and why does the latter matter?
A cache-aware (or "cache-conscious") algorithm has the cache/block size as a parameter — blocked matmul with a tuned tile size, a B-tree with node size = page size. It's optimal when tuned but must be re-tuned per machine and per cache level, and picking one block size can't be optimal for L1 and L2 and L3 simultaneously. A cache-oblivious algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal cache complexity without knowing the block size, typically via recursive divide-and-conquer that keeps halving the problem until subproblems fit in whatever cache level — e.g. recursive matrix multiply (split into 8 half-size products), recursive/Z-order matrix transpose, funnelsort, van Emde Boas tree layout. Because the recursion naturally passes through every "granularity", it's simultaneously good for L1, L2, L3, TLB, and even disk, and it needs no tuning or platform detection. It matters for portable library code and for deep hierarchies (a single tiled algorithm can't block for 4 levels at once), though hand-tuned cache-aware kernels still win the last ~10–30% on a specific machine because they also control register blocking, prefetch, and instruction scheduling that the oblivious recursion leaves to the compiler.

The CPU Pipeline & Hazards

Overlapping instruction execution — and the three things that stall it.

Notes

Pipelining

An instruction goes through stages — classic 5-stage RISC: Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback. Instead of finishing one before starting the next, the CPU overlaps them: while instr 1 executes, instr 2 decodes, instr 3 fetches. Ideal throughput: one instruction retired per cycle even though each takes 5 cycles end-to-end. Real CPUs have 14–20 stages.

# 5-stage pipeline, no hazards -> 1 instr retired per cycle after fill
#          c1  c2  c3  c4  c5  c6  c7
#   i1:    F   D   E   M   W
#   i2:        F   D   E   M   W
#   i3:            F   D   E   M   W
# each instr: 5 cycles latency ; throughput: 1/cycle (5x over run-to-completion)

Hazards (things that break the overlap)

HazardCauseMitigation
Structuraltwo instructions need the same hardware unitduplicate units, more ports
Datainstr N needs a result instr N−1 hasn't written yetforwarding/bypassing (route the result straight from execute), else stall ("bubble")
Controla branch — the CPU doesn't know which instructions to fetch next until the branch resolvesbranch prediction + speculative execution; a misprediction flushes the pipeline
# DATA hazard: i2 needs i1's rax result
add  rax, rbx        # i1 produces rax in E (c3)
mov  rcx, rax        # i2 wants rax in D (c3) -> forwarded from i1's E, no stall

# CONTROL hazard: which way does this branch go?
cmp  rax, 0
jne  label          # CPU speculates one path; wrong guess -> flush ~15-20 in-flight instrs

Costs

  • A data-hazard stall the compiler/scheduler couldn't hide: 1–a few cycles.
  • A load that misses cache: hundreds of cycles — the pipeline drains or the CPU finds other work (out-of-order).
  • A branch misprediction: flush everything fetched speculatively and refill — ~15–20 cycles on a deep pipeline.
$ perf stat -e cycles,instructions,stalled-cycles-frontend,branch-misses ./app
   9,900,000,000  cycles
   4,100,000,000  instructions              #  0.41  IPC          # badly stalled
   3,200,000,000  stalled-cycles-frontend   #  32.3% frontend cycles idle
      82,000,000  branch-misses             #  ~18 cycles each -> ~1.5B cycles wasted

Why deeper pipelines are a trade-off

More stages → shorter stage → higher clock frequency — but each hazard/misprediction wastes more cycles, and it takes longer to refill. The Pentium 4's 31-stage pipeline chased GHz and lost to shorter, wider designs. Modern CPUs are moderately deep and very wide (see ILP topic).

# deeper pipeline: higher GHz, but a mispredict costs MORE cycles to refill
#   Pentium 4 (31 stages, ~3.8 GHz): mispredict penalty ~20-30 cycles
#   Core 2      (14 stages, ~3.0 GHz): ~15 cycles, and won on real workloads
# modern: ~16-19 stages + issue 4-6 instrs/cycle (width beats depth)
Cheat Sheet
  • Pipeline: overlap Fetch/Decode/Execute/Mem/Writeback → ~1 instr/cycle throughput despite multi-cycle latency.
  • Structural hazard: resource conflict → more units/ports.
  • Data hazard: need a not-yet-written result → forwarding/bypassing hides most; else a bubble.
  • Control hazard: branch → predict + speculate; mispredict = full flush (~15–20 cycles).
  • Cache-missing load = hundreds of cycles; OoO execution finds other work meanwhile.
  • Deeper pipeline → higher clock but costlier mispredicts/refills; modern = moderate depth, very wide.
  • Write branch-predictable code and expose independent work to keep the pipeline full.
Q&A
What does pipelining buy you?
Throughput. Each instruction still takes several cycles start-to-finish, but by overlapping the stages the CPU can retire (up to) one instruction per cycle instead of one every N cycles.
What is a data hazard and how do CPUs usually avoid stalling on it?
An instruction needs a value that a recent prior instruction is still computing/writing. Forwarding (bypassing) routes the result directly from the execute stage's output to the dependent instruction's input, so it doesn't have to wait for the writeback. Only unhidable dependencies cause a stall (bubble).
Why is a branch a "control hazard"?
Until the branch condition resolves in the execute stage, the front end doesn't know whether to fetch the fall-through or the target instructions. Rather than stall, it predicts and speculatively executes down the predicted path; a wrong guess means discarding that work.
Roughly what does a branch misprediction cost?
On a modern deep pipeline, ~15–20 cycles — the entire speculative pipeline is flushed and refilled from the correct address.
Why aren't pipelines just made very deep for a high clock?
Deeper means each hazard and misprediction wastes more cycles and the pipeline takes longer to refill, so per-instruction penalties grow. Past a point the clock gains don't offset the stall losses — the Pentium 4 is the cautionary tale.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the classic 5 pipeline stages.
Fetch, Decode, Execute, Memory, Writeback.
What hardware technique hides most data hazards?
Forwarding / bypassing.
What kind of hazard does a conditional jump create?
A control hazard.

Intermediate core

Why can a tight loop with a hard-to-predict branch inside it run several times slower than the same loop with the branch removed?
Each mispredict flushes ~15–20 cycles of speculative work. If the branch is ~50% predictable and the loop body is only ~10 cycles of real work, you're paying roughly a full extra flush per iteration — effectively 2–3× the work. Removing the branch (branchless cmov/arithmetic/masking, or sorting the data so the branch becomes predictable) recovers the pipeline throughput.
A dependent chain x = f(x) repeated N times runs at 1/latency, but N independent y[i] = f(y[i]) run much faster on the same CPU. Why?
The dependent chain is limited by the latency of f — each iteration must wait for the previous result, so the pipeline can't overlap them; throughput = 1 / latency. The independent operations have no data dependency between them, so the out-of-order engine issues several in flight at once, and throughput is limited by the execution unit's throughput (issue rate), which is much higher than its latency. This is why unrolling with multiple accumulators speeds up reductions.

Advanced deep

What is the front-end vs back-end bottleneck distinction, and how do you tell which you're hitting?
A modern core has a front end (fetch, branch prediction, decode, µop cache, delivering µops into the queue) and a back end (rename, schedule, execute, retire). "Top-down" analysis (Intel's methodology, exposed via perf as topdown-* events / toplev) attributes every pipeline slot to one of four buckets: Retiring (useful work), Bad Speculation (mispredicts — slots filled then flushed), Front-End Bound (back end was ready but the front end couldn't deliver µops — i-cache/iTLB misses, decode bottlenecks, too many branches, µop-cache misses), and Back-End Bound (front end delivered but the back end couldn't accept — further split into Core Bound: execution-port contention, long dependency chains, divides; and Memory Bound: L1/L2/L3/DRAM stalls, store-buffer full). You measure the percentages and drill into the dominant one: Front-End Bound → reduce code size, align hot loops, cut indirect branches, use PGO/LTO; Memory Bound → the locality work from the cache topics; Core Bound → break dependency chains, reduce expensive ops, add ILP; Bad Speculation → make branches predictable or branchless. Guessing which one it is without top-down metrics is the classic way to waste optimisation effort.
What is the µop cache (DSB / loop stream detector) and why does hot-loop alignment matter?
x86 instructions are variable-length and expensive to decode (find boundaries, crack into µops). To avoid re-decoding hot code, the CPU caches the decoded µops in a µop cache (Intel's DSB, ~1.5–4K µops, organised in lines tied to 32- or 64-byte code regions) and, for very short loops, a loop stream detector that replays µops straight from the queue with the fetch/decode stages powered down. Delivering from the µop cache is higher bandwidth (e.g. 6+ µops/cycle vs 4–5 from legacy decode) and lower power. The catch: the µop cache is filled and indexed in aligned code chunks, and there are microarchitectural rules about how many µops/branches fit per chunk and per way. If a hot loop straddles a 32-byte boundary awkwardly, or has too many branches in one window, parts of it can't be cached and fall back to legacy decode — a sudden throughput cliff. Compilers therefore pad/align loop entry points (-falign-loops, .p2align), and the infamous Intel "JCC erratum" microcode fix (which disables µop-cache lines where a jump ends on a 32-byte boundary) made alignment even more consequential — assemblers added mitigation padding, and some codebases saw multi-percent regressions purely from instruction-address shifts. It's why "I added a log line and an unrelated loop got slower" is a real phenomenon.

Branch Prediction & Speculation

Guessing the future to keep the pipeline full — and the security fallout.

Notes

Why predict

On a deep pipeline, waiting for each branch to resolve before fetching would waste 15–20 cycles every branch (~1 in 5 instructions). So the CPU predicts the outcome and direction, speculatively executes down that path, and commits the results only if the guess was right. A mispredict flushes and refills.

// ~1 in 5 instructions is a branch; without prediction, 20-cycle bubble EACH
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)     // the loop-back branch: taken n times, not-taken once
    work(a[i]);                // predictor learns "taken" -> ~100% accurate -> free

Predictor mechanics (roughly)

  • Branch Target Buffer (BTB) — caches "this branch address jumps to that target".
  • Direction predictors — from simple 2-bit saturating counters ("mostly taken/not-taken") to sophisticated TAGE-style predictors that use long global history to recognise patterns (loop trip counts, correlated branches).
  • Return Address Stack for ret; indirect branch predictors for switch/vtables/function pointers.
  • Accuracy on typical code: 95–99%. Data-dependent branches on random data: ~50% (worst case).
// 2-bit saturating counter: needs TWO wrong guesses to flip prediction
//   states: STRONG_NT - WEAK_NT - WEAK_T - STRONG_T
//   -> one anomalous iteration in a loop doesn't derail the predictor

// INDIRECT branch (vtable call): target varies -> harder to predict
shape->area();     // call [rax] -- BTB caches the last target; polymorphic call sites mispredict

Writing predictable code

  • Loops with fixed iteration counts predict perfectly.
  • Sorting data before a threshold-branch makes the branch a long run of one outcome (the famous "why is processing a sorted array faster" result).
  • Branchless techniques for genuinely unpredictable branches: cmov, arithmetic/bit-mask select, table lookup, min/max intrinsics. Trade a predictable data dependency for an unpredictable control dependency.
  • [[likely]]/[[unlikely]], PGO (profile-guided optimisation) let the compiler lay out the hot path fall-through.
// unpredictable on RANDOM data (~50% mispredict) -> slow
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    if (a[i] >= 128) sum += a[i];      // sort a[] first -> one long run each way -> ~6x faster

// BRANCHLESS: no misprediction possible (cmov / mask select)
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int mask = -(a[i] >= 128);          // 0xFFFFFFFF or 0
    sum += a[i] & mask;                // data dependency, but NO branch
}

Speculation & security

Spectre / Meltdown (2018): speculatively executed instructions — even ones later discarded — leave microarchitectural traces (cache-line residency), which an attacker reads via timing to exfiltrate data across security boundaries. Mitigations (retpolines, IBRS, KPTI, lfence barriers) cost real performance. Speculation is fundamental to modern performance, so this is an ongoing tension.

// Spectre v1 gadget: the bounds check is speculated PAST
if (idx < array1_len)              // predicted true even when idx is out of bounds
    y = array2[array1[idx] * 4096];  // speculative load leaves a cache footprint...
// ...attacker times array2[] accesses to recover the secret byte array1[idx]

// mitigation: a speculation barrier between the check and the use
if (idx < array1_len) { _mm_lfence(); y = array2[array1[idx] * 4096]; }
$ cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/spectre_v1   # Mitigation: usercopy/swapgs barriers
Cheat Sheet
  • Predict branch direction + target → speculate → commit if right, flush ~15–20 cycles if wrong.
  • Hardware: BTB (targets), direction predictor (2-bit → TAGE with global history), Return Address Stack, indirect predictor.
  • Typical accuracy 95–99%; random data-dependent branch ≈ 50% (worst case).
  • Predictable: fixed-count loops; sorting data before a threshold branch; the hot path as fall-through.
  • Unpredictable branch in a hot loop → go branchless (cmov, masks, table lookup, min/max).
  • Branchless trades a control dependency for a (predictable) data dependency — not always a win; measure.
  • Spectre/Meltdown: speculation leaves cache traces → timing side channel across boundaries; mitigations cost perf.
Q&A
What does a branch predictor predict, and what happens when it's wrong?
The direction (taken/not-taken) and the target address of a branch, so the front end can keep fetching and the pipeline stays full. A wrong prediction means every speculatively executed instruction after the branch is discarded and the pipeline refills from the correct address — a ~15–20 cycle penalty.
Why is iterating a sorted array with a value-threshold branch faster than an unsorted one?
When sorted, the branch (if (a[i] > threshold)) is not-taken for a long run then taken for the rest — the predictor nails it. On random data it's ~50/50, so nearly every iteration mispredicts and pays the flush.
When should you make code branchless?
Only when the branch is genuinely unpredictable (data-dependent on random-ish input) and in a hot loop. You replace the control dependency with a data dependency (a cmov or arithmetic select), which is unconditional. If the branch is actually predictable, branchless code is often slower because it always does both sides' work.
What's the connection between speculation and Spectre?
The CPU speculatively executes instructions past a branch/bounds-check before it's confirmed. Even though wrong-path results are architecturally discarded, side effects like which cache lines got loaded persist. An attacker trains the predictor to mis-speculate into code that touches secret-dependent addresses, then times cache accesses to recover the secret.
Does adding [[likely]] change the branch predictor's behaviour?
No — the hardware predictor learns at runtime regardless. [[likely]]/[[unlikely]] and PGO influence the compiler: code layout (hot path as straight-line fall-through, cold path out-of-line), which improves i-cache/µop-cache density and makes the static "not-taken" default correct before the predictor has warmed up.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a branch misprediction cost, roughly?
~15–20 cycles on a modern pipeline (full flush + refill).
How predictable is a fixed-count for loop's back-edge branch?
Essentially perfectly — taken every iteration except the last.
What x86 instruction does a compiler use for a branchless conditional select?
cmov (conditional move).

Intermediate core

Turn if (x < 0) x = 0; (clamp) into branchless code, and say when it helps.
x = x & ~(x >> 31); (arithmetic shift makes a 0 or all-ones mask), or x = max(x, 0) which compiles to a maxss/cmov. It helps when x's sign is unpredictable and this is a hot loop — you remove the mispredicts. If x is almost always non-negative, the branch predicts well and the branchy version is fine (or faster, since it skips the work).
A switch over an enum in a hot interpreter loop mispredicts constantly. Options?
The single indirect jump for the switch is hard to predict when opcodes are effectively random. Computed goto / threaded code: each opcode handler ends with its own indirect jump to the next handler (goto *dispatch[next_op]), spreading the indirect branch across many sites so each gets its own predictor entry correlated with the current opcode — historically 20–30% faster for interpreters. Other options: a jump table the compiler already emits (helps target prediction a bit), replicating the dispatch, or in extreme cases a JIT that removes the dispatch entirely.

Advanced deep

Explain how a TAGE-style predictor recognises correlated and history-dependent branches that a 2-bit counter can't.
A per-branch 2-bit saturating counter only captures "this branch is usually taken/not-taken" — it fails on branches whose outcome depends on recent history (e.g. if (i % 3 == 0) in a loop, or branch B that's taken iff branch A was taken). TAGE (TAgged GEometric history length) keeps several tables indexed by a hash of the branch PC and the global branch-history register, where each table uses a different history length forming a geometric series (e.g. 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 bits). A short history captures local patterns; a long history captures long-range correlations and loop periods. On a lookup, all tables are probed; the matching entry (tag hit) using the longest history wins, on the theory that a longer matching context is more specific. Entries are tagged (partial hash of PC+history) to detect aliasing, and there's a usefulness bit + a base bimodal predictor as fallback. Allocation on mispredict adds an entry in a table with a slightly longer history than the one that failed. This lets TAGE learn things like "branch X is taken on iterations 3, 7, 11, ... of this loop" or "taken only when the previous two branches went not-taken, taken". Real predictors (e.g. in recent Intel/AMD/Apple cores) are TAGE variants plus a perceptron/statistical-corrector component and dedicated loop and indirect predictors, reaching 99%+ accuracy on SPEC. The cost is significant area/power and warm-up time — a cold predictor (after a context switch or into new code) mispredicts a lot until the history tables fill.
Why did Spectre variant 1 (bounds-check bypass) prove so hard to fix in hardware, and what's the software mitigation?
Variant 1 is: if (i < array_len) x = array2[array1[i] * 64]; — the CPU speculatively executes the body while the bounds check is still resolving (the length might be a cache miss), using an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds i; array1[i] reads a secret byte, and array2[secret*64] pulls a secret-dependent cache line in; the results are squashed when the check fails, but the cache line stays, and the attacker times array2 to recover the byte. It's hard to fix in hardware because speculating past a not-yet-resolved conditional is the entire point of branch prediction — you can't disable it without crippling performance, and the leak is through the cache (and dozens of other microarchitectural structures: TLBs, ports, the predictor itself), so plugging one channel leaves others. There's no clean architectural boundary being crossed the way Meltdown crossed user/kernel — it's an in-bounds program speculating on its own data. The practical software mitigation is a speculation barrier on the specific gadget: after the bounds check, insert lfence (x86) / csdb (ARM), which stalls speculation until the branch resolves — but you must find every vulnerable pattern (compilers and static analysers help: -mspeculative-load-hardening / MSVC /Qspectre insert masks or fences), and it only matters where untrusted code shares an address space with secrets (JS engines, kernels, sandboxes). Data masking (i &= (i < len) ? ~0 : 0 so an out-of-bounds index becomes 0 even on the speculative path) is cheaper than lfence and is what SLH and hand-hardened crypto use.

ILP & Out-of-Order Execution

Why a modern core runs 3–6 instructions per cycle — and why latency ≠ throughput.

Notes

Superscalar + out-of-order

A modern core has multiple execution units (several ALUs, load/store units, FP/SIMD units) and issues several instructions per cycle (superscalar). It doesn't run them in program order — it runs whatever is ready (operands available, unit free), then commits results in order for correctness.

// these 3 are independent -> a 3+ wide core issues them in ONE cycle
add  rax, rbx        # ALU port 0
mul  rcx, rdx        # ALU port 1
mov  r8, [rsi]       # load port -- all three retire together

# out-of-order: a slow load doesn't block later independent work
mov  rax, [slow]     # cache miss, ~200 cycles
add  rbx, rcx        # runs NOW, doesn't wait for rax

The machinery

  • Register renaming — maps architectural registers to a large pool of physical registers, removing false ("write-after-read", "write-after-write") dependencies so more instructions can run in parallel.
  • Reservation stations / scheduler — hold decoded instructions until their operands are ready, then dispatch to a free unit.
  • Reorder Buffer (ROB) — tracks all in-flight instructions so results retire in program order and exceptions/mispredicts can roll back. Its size (hundreds of entries) sets the "window" the CPU can look ahead.
  • Load/store queue — lets loads execute early and store-to-load forwarding happen.
// WITHOUT renaming these two "reuse rax" -> a false dependency
mov  rax, [a]        # write rax
add  rbx, rax        # read rax
mov  rax, [b]        # write rax again -- renamed to a DIFFERENT physical reg -> runs in parallel
add  rcx, rax

# ROB ~500 entries -> the core can have ~500 instrs in flight,
# hiding a couple of L2 misses' worth of latency behind independent work

Latency vs throughput

  • Latency — cycles from an instruction's inputs ready to its output ready (e.g. FP multiply ~4, division ~20+, dependent chain).
  • Throughput — how often you can start a new one (e.g. 2 FP multiplies/cycle).
  • A dependent chain runs at 1/latency. Independent operations run at the unit's throughput. Hence: unroll reductions with multiple accumulators, avoid long dependency chains, interleave independent work.
// dependent chain: each add waits for the last -> runs at 1 add / LATENCY
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];             // ~n * add-latency

// 4 independent accumulators -> runs at the ALU's THROUGHPUT (~4x faster)
double s0=0, s1=0, s2=0, s3=0;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 4) {
    s0 += a[i]; s1 += a[i+1]; s2 += a[i+2]; s3 += a[i+3];   // 4 in flight, no chain
}
double sum = (s0 + s1) + (s2 + s3);

What limits ILP

True data dependencies, branch mispredictions (window flushed), cache misses that don't fill the ROB fast enough to hide, and running out of a resource (physical registers, ROB entries, load queue). Real code averages ~1–3 IPC despite 4–8-wide hardware.

$ perf stat ./app
   instructions       #  1.8  insn per cycle    # 4-6 wide HW, but real code averages 1-3

# pointer chasing pins IPC near the floor: each load address DEPENDS on the last load
while (node) node = node->next;     # 1 dependent load per ~cache-miss-latency -> IPC ~0.05
Cheat Sheet
  • Superscalar: multiple execution units, several instrs issued/cycle. Out-of-order: run what's ready, retire in order.
  • Register renaming removes false (WAR/WAW) deps → more parallelism. Real deps (RAW) still serialise.
  • ROB size = look-ahead window; scheduler dispatches ready instrs to free units; load/store queue enables early loads + forwarding.
  • Latency = input-ready to output-ready. Throughput = issue rate. They differ a lot (mul: ~4 lat, 2/cycle tput).
  • Dependent chain runs at 1/latency; independent ops at throughput → use multiple accumulators, unroll, interleave.
  • ILP limited by true deps, mispredicts, cache misses, and resource limits. Typical IPC ~1–3.
  • To speed up: shorten dependency chains, expose independent work, reduce mispredicts and misses.
Q&A
What does out-of-order execution do?
It executes instructions as soon as their operands and an execution unit are available, rather than strictly in program order, then retires (commits) results in order so the architectural state stays correct. This lets it work around stalls (e.g. keep going during a cache-missing load).
What is register renaming for?
To eliminate false dependencies. If two independent instructions both write architectural register rax, they'd appear dependent; renaming gives each its own physical register so they can execute in parallel. Only genuine read-after-write dependencies remain.
Latency vs throughput of an instruction — why does the distinction matter?
Latency is how long one result takes; throughput is how many you can start per cycle. A chain of dependent operations is bottlenecked by latency (each waits for the last). Independent operations run at throughput, which is much higher. Restructuring code to have independent work (multiple accumulators) exploits this.
Why does a sum reduction speed up when you unroll it with 4 partial sums?
A single accumulator makes every sum += a[i] depend on the previous one — the loop runs at the FP-add latency. Four independent partial sums break the chain into 4 parallel chains, so the out-of-order engine keeps 4 adds in flight and you hit the adder's throughput. Combine the 4 at the end.
Why is real-world IPC only ~1–3 on 4–8-wide cores?
True data dependencies serialise work, branch mispredicts periodically flush the window, cache misses stall dependent instructions faster than the ROB can hide, and code often can't be reordered enough to keep all units busy. The wide hardware is there for the bursts where ILP is available.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does "superscalar" mean?
The core can issue and execute more than one instruction per clock cycle.
In what order are results made architecturally visible in an OoO core?
In program order — via the reorder buffer — even though execution was out of order.
A dependent chain of operations runs at roughly what rate?
1 / (operation latency) — each step waits for the previous result.

Intermediate core

You have a hot loop for i: acc = acc*31 + s[i]; (string hash). It's latency-bound. Speed it up.
The acc chain serialises on the multiply-add latency. Split into independent sub-hashes: process 4 (or 8) input positions in parallel with 4 accumulators using precomputed powers of 31 (acc0 = acc0*31^4 + ...), so 4 independent dependency chains run concurrently at the FMA throughput, then combine. Or use a hash with more ILP (a tree/parallel-friendly mixing function). This is the same trick as multi-accumulator reductions and is how fast hash/CRC implementations work.
Why doesn't out-of-order execution hide a chain of dependent cache-missing loads (pointer chasing)?
Each load's address depends on the previous load's result, so the CPU can't issue load N+1 until load N returns — hundreds of cycles later. The ROB fills up with the dependent instructions waiting on load N and stalls; there's no independent work to overlap. This is why linked-list / tree traversal is latency-bound at full memory latency per node, and why converting to arrays (parallel prefetchable loads) or prefetching several nodes ahead is the only real fix.

Advanced deep

What is "memory-level parallelism" (MLP) and how do you increase it?
MLP is the number of independent cache-miss/memory requests a core keeps outstanding at once. The memory subsystem can service many concurrent misses (limited by MSHRs — Miss Status Holding Registers, ~10–20 per L1/L2 — and DRAM bank parallelism), so if your code has 12 independent misses in flight, total time ≈ one memory latency, not twelve. Pointer chasing has MLP = 1 (serial dependent misses) → worst case. To raise MLP: (1) make misses independent — iterate an array of pointers rather than following next links; batch-process K items so their loads are unrelated. (2) Prefetch several iterations ahead so the requests are issued before they're needed. (3) Restructure algorithms to a "gather then process" phase (issue all the loads, then use the results) rather than interleaved load-use. (4) Larger OoO window / more MSHRs on newer cores helps automatically. A concrete example: a hash join probing a hash table one row at a time is MLP-1; software-pipelining the probe (compute hash for row i+8, prefetch bucket, while processing row i) can be 2–4× faster purely from overlapping the misses. Tools: perf can estimate it as (L1 miss count × miss latency) / (stall cycles) — a ratio well below 1 means you're serialising misses.
How do modern cores handle the fact that a store's value or address may not be known when a later load executes?
The core wants to execute loads as early as possible (they're often on the critical path), but a load might alias an earlier, still-pending store to the same address — executing it early with stale data would be wrong. Structures involved: the store buffer / store queue holds in-flight stores (address + data) not yet committed to cache; the load queue tracks in-flight loads. On a load, the core checks the store queue for an older store to the same address: if found with data ready, it does store-to-load forwarding (get the value directly, no cache access); if found but data not ready, the load waits; if no match, the load goes to cache. The hard case is when an older store's address isn't computed yet — the core doesn't know if the load aliases.
