Options: conservative (wait for all older store addresses — safe, slow) or speculative memory disambiguation: predict (via a predictor keyed on the load's PC) that the load doesn't alias, execute it early, and if a later store address turns out to match, squash and re-execute the load and everything after it (a "memory-order violation", visible in perf as machine_clears.memory_ordering). Getting this wrong repeatedly — e.g. a real store-load dependency the predictor keeps mispredicting — causes a nasty performance cliff, which is why some code deliberately separates producer/consumer accesses or pads to avoid 4K-aliasing (loads and stores whose addresses match in the low 12 bits are conservatively treated as possibly aliasing on some Intel cores).

Alignment & Struct Layout

Where the padding comes from, why it matters, and how to control it.

Notes

Natural alignment

Each scalar type prefers an address that's a multiple of its size: int at 4, double / pointer at 8, a 32-byte SIMD vector at 32. Hardware reads are fast when aligned; misaligned access is slower on x86 (may span two cache lines → two accesses) and faults on some ARM/SPARC configs and for some SIMD instructions.

_Static_assert(_Alignof(double) == 8, "");   // double wants an 8-aligned address

// misaligned load from a packed buffer: works on x86 (slow), FAULTS on strict ARM / with _mm256
char buf[64];
double d = *(double*)(buf + 3);         // UB in C; memcpy(&d, buf+3, 8) is the portable way

__m256d v = _mm256_load_pd(p);         // #GP if p is not 32-byte aligned; use _mm256_loadu_pd for unaligned

Struct padding

struct Bad { char a; double b; char c; };
//  a[1]  pad[7]  b[8]  c[1]  pad[7]   = 24 bytes
struct Good { double b; char a; char c; };
//  b[8]  a[1]  c[1]  pad[6]           = 16 bytes
  • The compiler inserts padding between members so each is naturally aligned, and at the end so arrays keep every element aligned.
  • Struct alignment = the largest member's alignment; struct size is rounded up to a multiple of it.
  • Order members largest to smallest to minimise padding.

Controlling it

  • alignof(T) / offsetof(T, m) to inspect; alignas(N) to over-align (e.g. cache-line-align a hot struct).
  • #pragma pack(1) / __attribute__((packed)) removes all padding — needed for exact wire/hardware layouts, but then members may be misaligned (slow / faulting; don't take pointers to them).
  • Cache-line awareness: pad a per-thread struct to 64 bytes so two threads' structs don't share a line (false sharing — see next topic).
// exact wire layout: no padding, must not take pointers to members
struct __attribute__((packed)) EthHdr {
    uint8_t  dst[6], src[6];
    uint16_t ethertype;            // at offset 12 -- would be padded to 14 without `packed`
};
_Static_assert(sizeof(struct EthHdr) == 14, "");

// over-align a hot per-thread counter to its own cache line
struct alignas(64) Counter { std::atomic<long> n; char pad[56]; };
Counter counters[NUM_THREADS];      // no two threads' counters share a 64 B line

Cache-line straddling

A 16-byte value at offset 56 of a 64-byte line spans two lines → two cache accesses per read. Align hot, frequently-accessed fields to line boundaries or keep them within one line.

// a 16 B struct whose base is at offset 56 -> bytes 56..63 in line A, 64..71 in line B
struct Vec4 { float x, y, z, w; };      // 16 B
struct Row { char tag[56]; Vec4 v; };       // v straddles two cache lines -> 2 accesses per read

// fix: put the hot field first, or pad `tag` to 64
struct RowFixed { Vec4 v; char tag[56]; };   // v fully inside line A
Cheat Sheet
  • Natural alignment: type at an address multiple of its size (int@4, double/ptr@8, SIMD@16/32/64).
  • Misaligned access: slow on x86 (may split a cache line), faults on some ARM / SIMD.
  • Compiler pads between members (align each) and at the end (align array elements).
  • Struct alignment = max member alignment; size rounded up to that.
  • Order members big→small to cut padding.
  • alignof/offsetof inspect; alignas(N) over-align; packed/#pragma pack remove padding (then don't take member pointers).
  • Cache-line-align (64) hot/per-thread structs to prevent false sharing and line straddling.
Q&A
Why does the compiler add padding to structs?
So each member sits at a naturally aligned address (fast, and required by some hardware), and so that in an array of the struct, every element's members stay aligned — hence trailing padding to make the size a multiple of the struct's alignment.
How do you minimise a struct's size?
Declare members from largest alignment to smallest, so padding is only ever needed for trailing alignment. Also consider using smaller types, bitfields, or splitting rarely-used fields into a separate struct.
What does __attribute__((packed)) do and what's the risk?
Removes all padding so the layout exactly matches, e.g. a network packet or hardware register block. The risk: members are now potentially misaligned, so accessing them (especially taking a pointer and dereferencing) can be slow on x86 and fault on stricter architectures. Access via memcpy or the compiler's packed-aware member access.
What is the alignment of a struct?
Equal to the strictest (largest) alignment requirement among its members. Its total size is padded up to a multiple of that.
Why cache-line-align a per-thread counter struct?
To prevent false sharing: if thread A's counter and thread B's counter are in the same 64-byte line, every write by A invalidates that line in B's cache and vice versa, serialising them. Padding each to its own line removes the contention.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What alignment does a double normally require?
8 bytes.
How do you get a struct member's byte offset?
offsetof(struct T, member).
Best member order to minimise padding?
Largest/strictest-aligned members first, down to smallest.

Intermediate core

struct { char c; int i; short s; }; — give its size and layout on a typical 64-bit system.
c at 0, 3 bytes pad, i at 4, s at 8, 2 bytes trailing pad (struct alignment 4) → total 12 bytes. Reordered { int i; short s; char c; }: 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 pad = 8 bytes.
You memcpy received bytes into a struct Packet * pointer and read a uint32_t field; it works on x86 but crashes on an ARM device. Why?
The received buffer isn't 4-byte aligned (or the field is at an odd offset in a packed struct), so the uint32_t load is misaligned. x86 tolerates misaligned loads (with a penalty); many ARM configurations fault (SIGBUS) on misaligned word access, and NEON aligned loads always do. Fix: parse field-by-field with memcpy into an aligned local, or use __attribute__((aligned)) on the buffer and don't pack, or use byte-wise assembly.

Advanced deep

How does over-aligning a heap allocation work, and why can't plain malloc guarantee 64-byte alignment?
malloc guarantees alignment suitable for any standard type — alignof(max_align_t), which is 8 or 16 bytes on mainstream ABIs (enough for long double / __int128). It has no way to know you want a 64-byte-aligned buffer for AVX-512 or cache-line isolation, and internally it packs chunks with 8/16-byte granularity headers, so a returned pointer is generally not 64-aligned. To get stronger alignment: C11 aligned_alloc(64, size) (size must be a multiple of the alignment), POSIX posix_memalign(&p, 64, size), C++17 operator new(size, std::align_val_t{64}) / alignas(64) on the type (which routes to the aligned new), or Windows _aligned_malloc. Under the hood these typically over-allocate by alignment + sizeof(void*), round the address up to the alignment boundary, and stash the original pointer just before the returned block so the matching free can recover it — which is why you must pair _aligned_malloc/_aligned_free and not mix aligned allocation with plain free on some platforms (C11 aligned_alloc and posix_memalign results can use plain free). For arrays of hot structs, alignas(64) struct Foo makes both stack and (properly routed) heap allocations line-aligned automatically.
What is the "empty base optimization" and how does [[no_unique_address]] generalise it for layout?
An empty class (no data members, e.g. a stateless allocator, comparator, or deleter) still has sizeof ≥ 1 so distinct objects have distinct addresses. As a member, that 1 byte plus its alignment padding is pure waste — a std::vector storing an empty allocator by value would grow. The empty base optimization (EBO): if you make the empty class a base instead of a member, the standard allows it to occupy zero bytes as long as it doesn't collide with a base of the same type. So library types historically inherited from their empty policy classes (or used a helper like boost::compressed_pair) to avoid the overhead — ugly, and it exposes the base's interface. C++20 [[no_unique_address]] generalises this to members: [[no_unique_address]] Alloc alloc_; tells the compiler the member may share address space with other members (or occupy no space if empty), so unique_ptr's deleter, vector's allocator, and small function wrappers can carry a stateless policy for free without the inheritance trick. Caveats: two [[no_unique_address]] members of the same type still need distinct addresses (so they can't both be zero-size), and MSVC needed a separate spelling ([[msvc::no_unique_address]]) for ABI reasons.

The Hardware Memory Model & Barriers

Store buffers, why x86 and ARM disagree, and what a fence actually does.

Notes

Why order isn't preserved

  • Store buffer: a write goes into a per-core FIFO and completes to cache later. The writing core sees its own store immediately (store-to-load forwarding); other cores don't see it until it drains.
  • The core may also let a later load execute before an earlier store drains (store→load reordering) — the most common relaxation.
  • Compilers separately reorder independent memory ops.
// x=y=0. Even on x86, r1==r2==0 is a legal outcome (store buffers):
// core A            core B
x = 1;      //      y = 1;      -- each store sits in the local buffer
r1 = y;     //      r2 = x;     -- each load runs before the OTHER core's store drains

// the compiler ALSO reorders on its own -- prove it:
$ gcc -O2 -S f.c    # the two independent stores may be emitted in either order

x86-TSO vs ARM/POWER

x86 (TSO)ARM / POWER (weak)
load–load, load–store, store–storepreservedcan all be reordered
store–loadcan reorder (store buffer)can reorder
atomic storeplain mov (has release semantics)needs explicit barrier / stlr

Consequence: lock-free / racy code that "works" on x86 frequently breaks on ARM — x86 is accidentally forgiving.

# std::atomic<int> x; x.store(1, std::memory_order_release);

# x86-64:
mov  DWORD PTR x[rip], 1     # a plain store -- x86 already gives release ordering

# AArch64:
stlr w1, [x0]               # "store-release" instruction -- explicit ordering needed
# drop the release on x86 and the bug hides; drop it on ARM and it breaks in the field

Barriers / fences

  • Full barrier (x86 mfence, ARM dmb ish) — no memory op crosses it in either direction; drains the store buffer.
  • Acquire — no later load/store moves before it (used after taking a lock / after a flag load).
  • Release — no earlier load/store moves after it (used before releasing a lock / before a flag store).
  • Compilers emit these from std::atomic operations with the given memory_order; atomic_thread_fence is a standalone barrier.
// fix the r1==r2==0 bug: a full fence between each store and load, drains the store buffer
x.store(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_seq_cst);   // -> mfence on x86
r1 = y.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);

// the workhorse: release publishes, acquire observes -- no full fence needed
flag.store(true, std::memory_order_release);   // nothing above moves below
if (flag.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) use(data);  // nothing below moves above

volatile is not a barrier

C/C++ volatile stops the compiler from eliding/reordering accesses to that one variable. It emits no CPU fence, gives no atomicity, and doesn't order other memory. For cross-thread communication use std::atomic (which is volatile-like plus the right barriers). Java's volatile is different — it does imply acquire/release.

// WRONG: volatile keeps the flag re-read, but `data` writes can still float PAST the flag store
volatile bool ready = false;
data = compute(); ready = true;      // no CPU fence -> other core may see ready before data

// RIGHT: std::atomic emits the release fence
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
data = compute();
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
// volatile's real job stays MMIO: volatile uint32_t *reg = ...;
Cheat Sheet
  • Store buffer → your own stores are visible to you instantly, to others only after drain; store→load reorder is the common relaxation.
  • x86-TSO: keeps LL/LS/SS order, allows SL reorder, atomic store = plain mov. ARM/POWER: reorders everything, needs explicit barriers.
  • Racy code that passes on x86 often fails on ARM — test on weak-memory hardware.
  • Fences: full (mfence/dmb), acquire (nothing after moves before), release (nothing before moves after).
  • Release store publishes prior writes; a paired acquire load that sees it observes them all.
  • C/C++ volatile = compiler-only, no fence, no atomicity → use std::atomic. (Java volatile = acquire/release.)
  • Let the compiler emit barriers via std::atomic + memory_order; hand-written asm fences are a last resort.
Q&A
What is a store buffer and how does it cause reordering?
A per-core queue that holds stores before they reach cache. The core continues past the store without waiting, and can execute a later load before the buffered store is globally visible — so another core can observe the load's effect before the store's (store–load reordering).
Why does racy code often work on x86 but fail on ARM?
x86's TSO model only permits store–load reordering and gives atomic stores release semantics for free. ARM's weak model reorders load–load, load–store, and store–store as well, so missing barriers that x86 tolerated now manifest as real bugs.
What does an acquire barrier guarantee?
No memory operation after the acquire (in program order) can be reordered to before it. Combined with a matching release on another thread, if your acquire-load sees the released value, you also see every write the other thread did before its release.
Is volatile (C/C++) enough to communicate a flag between threads?
No. It prevents the compiler from optimising away or reordering accesses to that variable, but emits no CPU memory barrier, provides no atomicity, and doesn't order other data. Use std::atomic with an appropriate memory order.
When do you need a full barrier (mfence) rather than acquire/release?
For patterns needing store–load ordering — e.g. Dekker/Peterson-style mutual exclusion where each thread stores its "want" flag then loads the other's; without a full fence the store can sit in the buffer while the load proceeds, and both threads enter. A seq_cst operation or an explicit full fence between the store and the load fixes it.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which reordering does x86 allow?
Store–load (a later load can be observed before an earlier store completes). It preserves the other three orderings.
Does C/C++ volatile emit a CPU memory fence?
No. It's a compiler directive only.
A release store pairs with which barrier on the reader?
An acquire load.

Intermediate core

Producer: buf = data; ready = 1; Consumer: while (!ready); use(buf); — make it correct on ARM.
Both variables must be std::atomic. Producer: write buf, then ready.store(1, memory_order_release) — the release ensures the buf write is visible before ready becomes 1. Consumer: while (ready.load(memory_order_acquire) == 0) ; then read buf — the acquire ensures that once it sees ready == 1, the buf write is visible. On x86 the barriers are nearly free (plain movs); on ARM the compiler emits stlr/ldar or a dmb.
Why is the double-checked-locking singleton bug fundamentally a memory-ordering problem?
The publishing store instance = new Foo() is really: allocate, construct the object's fields, then store the pointer. Without a release barrier on that pointer store (and an acquire on the reader's load), another thread can observe the non-null pointer before the field writes are visible — it dereferences a half-constructed object. The fix is to make instance an atomic with release on publish / acquire on read (or use a language-level guaranteed-once init like a function-local static in C++11, or an eager/holder idiom).

Advanced deep

Explain "multi-copy atomicity" and how x86, ARMv8, and POWER differ on it.
A memory system is multi-copy atomic if, whenever any core other than the writer can observe a store, all other cores can observe it (a store becomes visible to everyone at once). x86-TSO is multi-copy atomic: the only relaxation is a core seeing its own buffered store early via forwarding; once a store leaves the store buffer it's visible to all other cores simultaneously. This is why the IRIW litmus test (two readers disagreeing on the order of two independent writes) is forbidden on x86. Classic POWER (and older ARM) are non-multi-copy-atomic: a store can propagate to different cores at different times (cache-coherence protocol + write-through-shared-buffers), so two reader cores genuinely can observe two independent writes in opposite orders — IRIW is allowed, and you need heavyweight sync/dmb ish (not just lwsync) plus, on POWER, cumulative barriers to recover a total order. ARMv8 was revised to be "other-multi-copy atomic": a core may see its own stores early, but any store visible to one other core is visible to all other cores — a middle ground that still forbids IRIW-without-fences but is weaker than TSO on the single-thread orderings. Practical impact: an algorithm proven correct only under multi-copy atomicity (some seqlock and RCU variants, certain lock-free constructs) is safe on x86 and ARMv8 but needs extra full barriers on classic POWER; and seq_cst in C++ is the portable way to get a single total order everywhere without reasoning about which model you're on.
Why is seq_cst more expensive than acquire/release, and where does the cost actually land on x86 vs ARM?
acquire/release give you pairwise ordering: a release store synchronises-with an acquire load of the same variable, and transitively publishes prior writes. But two seq_cst operations on different variables must also appear in one global total order that all threads agree on — a much stronger, non-local guarantee (it's what makes Dekker's algorithm and IRIW-free reasoning work). To enforce it the compiler must prevent store–load reordering across the operation, which the cheap fences don't. On x86: a seq_cst load is a plain mov (loads already have acquire, and TSO forbids the other reorderings), but a seq_cst store must drain the store buffer — emitted as xchg (which is a locked, fencing operation) or mov+mfence, costing ~20–40 cycles because the core stalls until pending stores are globally visible. So on x86 the cost is entirely on seq_cst stores/RMWs. On ARMv8: seq_cst maps to ldar/stlr (acquire/release variants that are also mutually ordered), which are cheaper than a full dmb but still more than a relaxed load/store, and both loads and stores pay. The upshot: prefer acquire/release for producer/consumer, refcounts, and flags; reserve seq_cst (the default) for the rare cases that genuinely need a single global order across multiple locations, and don't sprinkle it "to be safe" — on a hot atomic it's a measurable throughput hit.

SIMD, False Sharing & Measuring

Doing 8 operations per instruction, the multicore trap that silently kills scaling, and how to benchmark honestly.

Notes

SIMD (vectorization)

  • One instruction operates on a vector of values: SSE 128-bit (4×float), AVX2 256-bit (8×float), AVX-512 512-bit (16×float), ARM NEON 128-bit, SVE variable.
  • Auto-vectorization: the compiler vectorises simple loops at -O2/-O3 if there are no loop-carried dependencies, the trip count is knowable, memory access is unit-stride, and there's no aliasing (use restrict / __restrict). Check with -fopt-info-vec.
  • Intrinsics (<immintrin.h>) for control the compiler won't find: shuffles, horizontal ops, gather/scatter, masked ops. Portable wrappers: std::simd (C++26/experimental), Highway, xsimd, ISPC.
  • Needs SoA layout, alignment, and independent iterations to pay off.
// auto-vectorises at -O3 IF `a` and `b` can't alias -> tell the compiler
void axpy(int n, float k, float *restrict a, const float *restrict b) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] += k * b[i];   // 8 floats/iter with AVX2
}
$ gcc -O3 -march=native -fopt-info-vec axpy.c
axpy.c:3: optimized: loop vectorized using 32 byte vectors

// explicit AVX2 when the compiler won't: process 8 floats per instruction
__m256 vk = _mm256_set1_ps(k);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 8) {
    __m256 va = _mm256_loadu_ps(&a[i]);
    va = _mm256_fmadd_ps(vk, _mm256_loadu_ps(&b[i]), va);
    _mm256_storeu_ps(&a[i], va);
}

False sharing

Two threads write two different variables that happen to sit in the same 64-byte cache line. The coherence protocol treats the line as one unit: each write invalidates the other core's copy, so the line ping-pongs between cores and the two "independent" writes serialise — often a 5–50× slowdown that scales negatively with core count.

struct Counters { long a; long b; };          // a and b share a line -> false sharing
struct Counters { alignas(64) long a; alignas(64) long b; }; // each on its own line

Fix: pad/align per-thread data to a cache line; keep read-only and written-by-different-threads data apart.

Benchmarking pitfalls

  • Dead-code elimination — the compiler deletes work whose result is unused. Consume the result (DoNotOptimize, print a checksum).
  • Cold caches / warm-up — discard the first iterations; report a distribution, not one number.
  • Frequency scaling / turbo / thermal — pin the CPU frequency, disable turbo, pin the thread (taskset).
  • Measuring the wrong thing — wall time vs CPU time; include the setup you didn't mean to; too-small input fits in L1 and hides the real behaviour.
  • Use a real harness (Google Benchmark, nanobench, Criterion) and perf stat for counters.
// BROKEN benchmark: result unused -> the whole loop is deleted -> "0 ns"
for (auto _ : state) { long s = 0; for (int i=0;i<n;i++) s += a[i]; }

// FIXED: consume it + stop optimisation, warm up, pin the core & frequency
for (auto _ : state) {
    long s = 0; for (int i=0;i<n;i++) s += a[i];
    benchmark::DoNotOptimize(s);
}
$ sudo cpupower frequency-set -g performance
$ taskset -c 3 ./bench --benchmark_min_time=2s
Cheat Sheet
  • SIMD: 1 instr, N lanes (SSE 4×f32, AVX2 8×f32, AVX-512 16×f32, NEON 4×f32).
  • Auto-vec needs: no loop-carried deps, unit stride, known trip count, no aliasing (restrict), often SoA + alignment. Verify with -fopt-info-vec.
  • Intrinsics/libraries (Highway, xsimd, ISPC) for shuffles, gather, masks the compiler won't emit.
  • False sharing: different vars, same 64-byte line, different threads writing → line ping-pongs → huge slowdown, negative scaling. Fix: alignas(64) / pad per-thread data.
  • Benchmark: prevent dead-code elimination (DoNotOptimize), warm up, pin freq + core (no turbo), report a distribution, use inputs bigger than L1.
  • Tools: Google Benchmark / nanobench + perf stat.
Q&A
What conditions let a loop auto-vectorize?
No loop-carried dependency (iteration i+1 doesn't need iteration i's result), a trip count the compiler can determine, unit-stride (contiguous) memory access, no possible pointer aliasing between input and output (add restrict), and the target ISA enabled (-march=native or specific -mavx2).
What is false sharing?
Two threads writing to distinct variables that reside in the same cache line. Cache coherence works at line granularity, so each write invalidates the line in the other core's cache; the line bounces back and forth and the writes serialise despite being logically independent.
How do you fix false sharing?
Separate the contended data onto different cache lines — alignas(64) on per-thread structs, or padding fields, so no two threads' hot writes share a line. Also group read-mostly data away from write-heavy data.
Why might a micro-benchmark show a function taking "0 ns"?
The compiler saw the result was unused and deleted the whole computation (dead-code elimination). You must consume the result — write it to a volatile, pass it to benchmark::DoNotOptimize, or accumulate a checksum you print.
Why can a benchmark with a tiny input mislead you?
If the working set fits in L1, you measure L1-hit behaviour and instruction throughput, hiding the cache-miss and memory-bandwidth costs that dominate at production data sizes. Benchmark with realistic input sizes, including ones that exceed each cache level.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many 32-bit floats fit in an AVX2 (256-bit) register?
8.
What cache-line-related bug silently kills multithreaded scaling?
False sharing.
One thing every micro-benchmark must do to its result?
Consume it so the compiler can't eliminate the work (e.g. DoNotOptimize).

Intermediate core

A parallel histogram (each thread increments counts[bucket] in a shared array) scales worse than single-threaded. Why and fix?
Adjacent counts[] entries share cache lines, and different threads hitting nearby buckets cause constant line invalidation (false sharing), plus the increments themselves race (need atomics or per-thread copies). Fix: give each thread its own private counts[] array (padded so they don't overlap lines), accumulate locally, then sum the per-thread arrays once at the end. Now the hot path is contention-free.
Your loop won't auto-vectorize; -fopt-info-vec-missed says "possible aliasing". Fix?
The compiler can't prove the output pointer doesn't overlap the input pointers, so vectorising could produce wrong results. Add restrict (__restrict in C++) to the pointer parameters to promise no aliasing, or use #pragma omp simd / #pragma GCC ivdep to assert independence, or copy to local non-overlapping buffers. Verify the vectorised code is actually correct for your call sites (you're making a promise the compiler will trust).

Advanced deep

Why can enabling AVX-512 make a program slower overall?
Several effects: (1) Frequency throttling — on many Intel server chips, executing 512-bit (and heavy 256-bit) instructions drops the core (and sometimes package) clock by 10–40% for a licence-based period, because those execution units draw more power; if only a small fraction of your code is vectorised, the whole program runs at the lower clock and the scalar majority loses more than the vector minority gains. (2) Warm-up / transition penalty — the first AVX-512 (or dirty-upper-state AVX↔SSE transition) instructions after a gap incur a stall of tens to hundreds of cycles while the wide datapath powers up / state is saved. (3) Larger register save area — context switches and signal handling save 512-bit state (2 KB+ with AVX-512), raising syscall/switch cost. (4) Code bloat / i-cache pressure from wider unrolled loops. (5) On some microarchitectures only one AVX-512 FMA port is enabled, so peak throughput isn't double AVX2. Guidance: measure end-to-end, not the kernel in isolation; use AVX-512 where the vectorised region is large and hot enough to dominate; consider staying at AVX2 for mixed workloads; and check whether your CPU has the frequency penalty (later Intel client chips and AMD Zen4/5 largely removed it, so "AVX-512 is always slower" is now often outdated).
Design a rigorous latency micro-benchmark for a single function. What must you control?
Compiler: prevent dead-code elimination (feed the result to DoNotOptimize/an asm volatile sink) and prevent hoisting the call out of the loop (make an input depend on the previous output, or use ClobberMemory). Compile with the exact flags you'll ship. Measurement: use a monotonic high-resolution clock or rdtscp with a serialising fence; measure many iterations and divide, but also record the distribution (min is often the "true" cost with least noise; median and p99 show variance) — never a single mean. System: pin the thread to one core (taskset/pthread_setaffinity), pin the CPU frequency and disable turbo and deep C-states (or the first calls run at a different clock), isolate the core from the scheduler and IRQs if possible, run at elevated priority, and quiesce the machine (no builds/browsers). Data: choose input sizes that reflect production and that don't all fit in L1 unless that's the real case; randomise access patterns you can't predict; if the function has data-dependent branches, feed a realistic mix. Warm-up: run and discard iterations until timings stabilise (caches, branch predictors, frequency, page faults settled). Cross-check: run under perf stat to see whether cycles/instructions/misses match your model — if the counters don't explain the number, the benchmark is measuring something you didn't intend. Use an established harness (Google Benchmark, nanobench, Criterion.rs) that bakes in most of this rather than hand-rolling.

The C/C++ Compilation Pipeline

Four stages from .c to executable — and what you can inspect at each.

Notes

The four stages

StageToolIn → OutSee it with
Preprocesscpp.c + headers → expanded .i (one translation unit)gcc -E
Compilecc1 / clang.i → assembly .sgcc -S
Assembleas.s → object file .o (machine code + symbol table + relocations)gcc -c
Linkld / lld / gold.o files + libraries → executable or shared librarygcc (default final step)
$ gcc -save-temps -c hello.c       # keeps hello.i, hello.s, hello.o
$ gcc -E hello.c | wc -l           # ~750 lines after <stdio.h> is pasted in
$ gcc -S hello.c && head -3 hello.s
$ gcc -c hello.c && nm hello.o
0000000000000000 T main
                 U puts             # U = undefined -> the linker must resolve it
$ gcc hello.o -o hello             # link: resolves puts against libc

What each stage does

  • Preprocess: #include file inclusion, #define macro expansion, #if conditional compilation, comment removal, line markers. No knowledge of C syntax.
  • Compile: parse, type-check, optimise, generate target assembly for this TU only. Errors like "undeclared identifier", type mismatches, most warnings.
  • Assemble: encode instructions to bytes; build a symbol table (what this .o defines and needs) and relocation entries (addresses to patch later).
  • Link: resolve every undefined symbol against another .o or library, lay out sections, apply relocations, produce the final binary. Errors like "undefined reference", "multiple definition".
// which stage catches which error:
#include "nope.h"          // PREPROCESS: fatal error: nope.h: No such file or directory
int x = "str";             // COMPILE:   error: initialization of 'int' from 'char*'
extern void missing();
int main(){ missing(); }   // LINK:      undefined reference to `missing'

Separate compilation

Each .c compiles independently to a .o; only changed files (and dependents via headers) recompile, then a fast relink. This is why the preprocessor + a stable header interface matter for build times, and why LTO (optimising across TUs at link time) is a separate opt-in that costs link time.

$ gcc -c a.c b.c c.c              # three independent compiles -> a.o b.o c.o
$ touch b.c && make              # only b.c recompiles, then a fast relink

$ gcc -flto a.o b.o c.o -o app   # LTO: optimise ACROSS TUs at link time (inlines a.c calls into b.c)
                                 # -> smaller/faster binary, but the link now does real optimisation work
Cheat Sheet
  • Preprocess (-E) → Compile (-S) → Assemble (-c) → Link (default).
  • Preprocessor: #include/#define/#if, text only, no C awareness.
  • Compiler: parse + type-check + optimise + emit asm, per translation unit; "undeclared", type errors, warnings.
  • Assembler: asm → machine code + symbol table + relocations in a .o.
  • Linker: resolve undefined symbols, place sections, apply relocations; "undefined reference", "multiple definition".
  • Separate compilation: recompile only changed TUs, then relink — fast incremental builds.
  • LTO defers optimisation to link time for cross-TU inlining, at the cost of link time.
Q&A
Name the four stages of building a C program.
Preprocessing, compilation (to assembly), assembly (to an object file), and linking (to an executable or library).
Which stage produces an "undefined reference" error?
Linking — the compiler happily accepts a call to a function it has only a declaration for; the linker fails when no object file or library defines that symbol.
What does gcc -c file.c produce and stop at?
It preprocesses, compiles, and assembles file.c into file.o, but does not link. You link the .o files together in a separate step.
Does the preprocessor understand C syntax?
No — it operates purely on tokens/text: inclusion, macro substitution, conditional compilation. It doesn't know types, scopes, or expressions.
Why does changing one header trigger recompiling many source files?
Every .c that #includes that header (directly or transitively) has a different preprocessed translation unit now, so its .o is stale and must be rebuilt. This is why minimising header dependencies (forward declarations, PImpl) speeds up builds.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Flag to see preprocessor output only?
gcc -E file.c.
What's inside a .o file besides machine code?
A symbol table (defined and undefined symbols) and relocation entries (places to patch with final addresses).
Which tool resolves symbols across object files?
The linker (ld / lld / gold).

Intermediate core

You get "undefined reference to `foo`" but the header declaring foo is included. What's wrong?
A declaration isn't a definition. The header tells the compiler foo exists; you still need to link the object file or library that defines it — you forgot to add foo.o / -lfoo to the link line, or it's after the thing that uses it (link order), or it's a C function being called from C++ without extern "C" (name mangling mismatch).
Your build is slow. How does understanding the pipeline guide fixes?
Profile which stage dominates. Preprocessing/parsing heavy → cut header bloat (forward declares, PImpl, precompiled headers / modules, include-what-you-use). Compile (optimisation) heavy → lower -O for dev builds, split huge TUs, use -ftime-trace (Clang) to find expensive templates. Link heavy → use a fast linker (lld/mold), disable LTO for dev, dynamic instead of static linking locally. Whole rebuilds → ccache, better dependency tracking, unity/jumbo builds cautiously.

Advanced deep

What is Link-Time Optimization (LTO) actually doing, and what are its costs?
Without LTO, the compiler optimises each translation unit in isolation — it can't inline a function defined in another .c, can't propagate constants across the boundary, can't devirtualise based on whole-program knowledge, and can't remove a function that's unused program-wide (only unused within its TU). LTO defers final code generation: each .o stores the compiler's intermediate representation (GIMPLE / LLVM bitcode) instead of (or alongside) machine code; at link time a plugin in the linker hands all the IR back to the compiler, which now optimises with a whole-program view — cross-module inlining, interprocedural constant propagation, aggressive dead-code and dead-data elimination, better devirtualization, and (with PGO) hot/cold splitting across modules. Typical wins: 5–20% runtime, and meaningful binary-size reduction from dead-stripping. Costs: link time explodes (the "link" step is now a whole-program compile — minutes for large binaries; ThinLTO mitigates this with a lightweight summary phase + parallel per-module backend optimisation, trading some cross-module optimisation quality for near-parallel-compile link times); memory (monolithic LTO can need many GB); debuggability suffers (inlining and reordering across modules); incremental builds lose their benefit since a change can force re-optimising the whole program (ThinLTO's caching helps); and it can expose latent UB/ODR violations that per-TU compilation accidentally hid. Practice: LTO (usually ThinLTO) for release/CI builds, off for local dev.
How do C++20 modules change the pipeline compared to headers?
Headers are a textual mechanism: every #include pastes the file's tokens into the TU, so a widely-included header is preprocessed and parsed once per TU that includes it — the same 50k lines of standard-library headers re-parsed for every .cpp, which is why C++ builds are slow and why include order and macro leakage cause bugs. Modules add a real compilation artifact: a module interface unit (export module foo;) is compiled once into a BMI/CMI (Binary Module Interface — a serialised, already-parsed AST + exported symbol table), and every TU that says import foo; just loads that binary form — no re-parsing, no preprocessor exposure (macros defined in the module don't leak to importers), and import order doesn't matter. This restructures the build graph: the compiler now needs the BMIs of a TU's imports built before it, so the build system must discover the module dependency graph (a new "scan" phase) and schedule interface units first — a significant change for Make/CMake/Ninja, and the main reason adoption has been slow despite the compilers supporting it. Payoffs when it works: large drops in build time for module-heavy code, genuine encapsulation (only exported names are visible), and the death of include guards / the ODR-via-textual-inclusion footguns. Costs: BMIs are compiler- and flag-specific (not portable, must be rebuilt on flag changes), tooling (IDEs, static analysers, ccache) is still catching up, and mixed header/module codebases have subtle visibility rules.

Translation Units & the Preprocessor

What "one file compiles independently" really means, and the One Definition Rule.

Notes

Translation unit

A single .c/.cpp plus every header it #includes (recursively), after preprocessing. The compiler sees exactly this and nothing else — it has no knowledge of other .cpp files. Each TU becomes one .o.

$ gcc -E -H main.c 2>&1 | grep '^\.'   # the header tree pulled into ONE TU
. /usr/include/stdio.h
.. /usr/include/features.h
.. /usr/include/bits/types.h
. ./widget.h

$ echo 'inline int helper(){ return foo(); }' > bad.h
$ gcc -c a.c b.c        # a.c and b.c both #include bad.h -> compiled separately,
                        # neither knows the other exists; the linker joins the .o files

Headers & include guards

// widget.h
#ifndef WIDGET_H
#define WIDGET_H
/* declarations only */
#endif

A header can be pulled in multiple times through different paths in one TU; the guard (or #pragma once) makes the second and later inclusions no-ops so you don't get duplicate declarations. Headers should contain declarations, inline/constexpr definitions, templates, and type definitions — not non-inline function or variable definitions.

The One Definition Rule (ODR)

  • Each entity (non-inline function, variable) may be defined once across the whole program.
  • Types, templates, inline functions may be defined in every TU — but every definition must be token-for-token identical (same tokens, same meaning of names).
  • Violating the "identical" clause is ODR-UB: it usually links fine (the linker keeps one copy) but behaves unpredictably. Caused by: a header compiled with different macros/flags in different TUs, a struct with different members in two files, inconsistent packing.
// point.h -- struct layout depends on a macro
struct Point { int x, y;
#ifdef WITH_Z
    int z;
#endif
};

$ gcc -c a.c              # sizeof(Point) == 8
$ gcc -c b.c -DWITH_Z     # sizeof(Point) == 12   -- SAME type, two layouts
$ gcc a.o b.o -o app      # LINKS FINE. Then a.c writes p.y where b.c expects p.z -> corruption

Reducing TU coupling

  • Forward declarations instead of includes where only a pointer/reference is used.
  • PImpl (pointer to implementation): the header exposes only an opaque pointer; the real members live in the .cpp, so changing them doesn't recompile clients.
  • Put implementation details in the .cpp; keep headers minimal.
// widget.h -- clients never see Impl's fields, so changing them doesn't recompile them
class Widget {
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> p_;      // opaque pointer
public:
    Widget(); ~Widget();
    void draw();
};

// forward-declare instead of #include when only a reference is used:
class Renderer;                    // not #include "renderer.h"
void paint(Renderer& r);
Cheat Sheet
  • TU = one .c/.cpp + its includes, after preprocessing → one .o. The compiler sees only this.
  • Include guard / #pragma once makes repeated inclusion in one TU harmless.
  • Headers: declarations, type defs, templates, inline/constexpr defs. Not plain function/variable definitions.
  • ODR: define a non-inline function/variable exactly once program-wide; define types/templates/inline funcs once per TU but identically.
  • ODR "not identical" (different macros/flags/members across TUs) = silent UB — often links, then misbehaves.
  • Cut recompiles: forward declare, PImpl, keep headers light, avoid heavy transitive includes.
Q&A
What is a translation unit?
The single source file plus everything it includes, after the preprocessor runs. It's the unit of compilation — the compiler processes one TU at a time and emits one object file, with no visibility into other TUs.
Why do headers need include guards?
Within one translation unit a header can be reached via multiple include paths (A includes B and C, both of which include D). Without a guard, D's declarations appear multiple times — a redefinition error for types. The guard skips all but the first inclusion.
State the One Definition Rule.
A non-inline function or variable must have exactly one definition in the entire program. Types, templates, and inline functions may be defined in multiple TUs, but every definition must be identical token-for-token with the same name lookups.
What's a subtle ODR violation that still links?
A struct defined with an extra member (or different packing) in one .cpp than another — e.g. because a config macro differs between the two compilations. The linker picks one layout; code compiled against the other reads/writes wrong offsets. It builds and runs, then corrupts memory nondeterministically.
How does PImpl reduce build times?
The public header only declares a class holding a pointer to an undefined Impl; all real data members and includes live in the .cpp. Changing the implementation's members or its includes doesn't change the header, so client TUs don't recompile — only the one .cpp does.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many object files does one translation unit produce?
One.
Where do you put a non-inline function's definition — header or source?
Source file (.cpp). The header gets only the declaration.
What can you use instead of #include when you only need a pointer to a type?
A forward declaration: class Foo;.

Intermediate core

You define const int MAX = 100; in a header included by several .cpp files. C or C++ — what happens?
In C: file-scope const has external linkage, so each TU defines the same symbol → multiple-definition link error. In C++: a const at namespace scope has internal linkage by default, so each TU gets its own private copy — it links, but there are N copies (fine for an int, wasteful for large objects, and their addresses differ). Cleanest: inline constexpr int MAX = 100; (C++17) for one shared entity, or constexpr/enum.
A program links fine but crashes only in release builds. You suspect an ODR issue. How do you find it?
Look for a type/inline function whose definition depends on a macro, optimisation level, or flag that differs between TUs — grep for #ifdef around struct members, check that all files use the same -Ds, packing pragmas, and standard version. Build with -Wodr (GCC, needs LTO) or -flto which often diagnoses mismatched definitions. Clang's -fsanitize=cfi or the "gold"/lld ODR checks help. Also check for a header that's compiled once as C and once as C++, or two libraries each carrying a differently-built copy of the same header-only type.

Advanced deep

Why is the ODR "same tokens, same lookups" wording necessary — give a case where identical-looking definitions still violate it.
Two TUs can contain byte-identical text for an inline function or template yet have it mean different things because unqualified names resolve differently in each context. Example: a header-only template<class T> void log(const T& x){ write(x); } — in TU A, write finds a void write(int) visible at the point of definition; in TU B, a different write (a local overload, a different namespace brought in by a using, or a macro) is in scope. Both instantiations compile; the linker merges them (COMDAT) keeping one; now half the program calls the wrong write. Same with a definition that references a static/anonymous-namespace entity (different object per TU), an inline function whose body calls another inline function with a TU-specific definition, or a class with a member whose type is a macro expanding differently. That's why the rule isn't "same source" but "same sequence of tokens and each name refers to the same entity in every definition". Practically: header-only code must not depend on what's visible at the include site — fully qualify names, avoid ADL surprises, don't reference internal-linkage symbols from inline/template definitions.
How do inline functions and templates avoid multiple-definition link errors despite being defined in every TU that uses them?
The standard grants them an explicit ODR exemption (multiple definitions allowed, provided they're identical), and the toolchain implements it with COMDAT sections / weak symbols. When the compiler emits an out-of-line copy of an inline function or a template instantiation, it places it in its own section marked as a "COMDAT group" keyed by the mangled name (e.g. .text._Z3fooIiEvv), and marks the symbol weak or linkonce. The linker, seeing the same COMDAT key from multiple object files, keeps one and discards the rest (rather than erroring on the duplicate the way it would for a strong symbol). This is also how the same std::string methods end up defined in hundreds of .os but the final binary has one copy each. The catch: the linker assumes the copies are equivalent and just picks one (often the first, or the largest) — if they actually differ (ODR violation), you silently get whichever copy won, with no diagnostic. It's also why an inline function's address is consistent across the program (one surviving copy) and why removing inline from a header function definition breaks the build with "multiple definition" (now it's a strong symbol).

Object Files, Symbols & Relocations

What's inside a .o, and the vocabulary linker errors use.

Notes

ELF sections

SectionHolds
.textmachine code (read + execute)
.rodatastring literals, const data
.datainitialised globals/statics (non-zero)
.bsszero/uninitialised globals/statics — just a size, no file bytes
.symtab / .strtabsymbol table + names
.rela.text etc.relocation entries
.debug_*DWARF debug info (from -g)
// int g = 7;  int z;  const char *s = "hi";
$ size -A obj.o | grep -E '\.text|\.data|\.bss|\.rodata'
.text     124
.data       8      # g and the pointer s (non-zero init)
.bss        4      # z (zero) -- size only, no bytes in the file
.rodata     3      # the literal "hi\0"
$ readelf -SW obj.o | head    # full section headers

Symbols

  • Defined (this .o provides it) vs undefined (needs it from elsewhere — shows as U in nm).
  • Global (external linkage, visible to the linker) vs local (static, lowercase in nm).
  • Weak (W): a global that a strong definition overrides; multiple weaks are allowed. Used for inline functions, __attribute__((weak)) optional hooks.
  • Common (C): a tentative definition (int x; in C) — merged by the linker. Modern default (-fno-common) makes these normal definitions so duplicates error.
$ nm util.o
0000000000000000 T api            # T: global text definition
0000000000000010 t helper         # t: local (static) -> invisible to other .o
                 U printf          # U: undefined -> resolved at link
0000000000000000 W inline_fn       # W: weak -> a strong def elsewhere wins
0000000000000004 D shared          # D: initialised global data

$ __attribute__((weak)) void on_start(void);   // optional hook: null if nobody defines it

Relocations

The assembler doesn't know final addresses, so it emits placeholders plus relocation entries saying "patch the 4 bytes at offset X to point at symbol foo (+ addend), using this formula". The linker (and, for shared libs, the dynamic loader) applies them. PC-relative relocations enable position-independent code.

$ objdump -dr obj.o
  11:   e8 00 00 00 00   call   16 <main+0x16>
                12: R_X86_64_PLT32   puts-0x4      # "patch bytes at 0x12 to reach `puts`"
  1d:   48 8d 05 00 00 00 00   lea    0x0(%rip),%rax
                20: R_X86_64_PC32   .rodata        # PC-relative -> position-independent
# the 00 00 00 00 placeholders get filled in by the linker once addresses are known

Inspection tools

nm file.o            # symbols: T=text def, D=data def, U=undefined, W=weak, t/d=local
nm -C ...            # demangle C++ names
objdump -d file.o    # disassemble
objdump -r file.o    # relocations
readelf -a file.o    # full ELF structure
c++filt _Z3fooi      # demangle one name
size file.o          # .text/.data/.bss sizes
strings file         # printable strings
Cheat Sheet
  • ELF sections: .text (code), .rodata (const), .data (init non-zero), .bss (zero, no file bytes), .symtab, .rela.*, .debug_*.
  • Symbol states: defined vs undefined (U); global vs local (static); weak (W, overridable); common (C, tentative — killed by -fno-common).
  • Relocations = "patch bytes here to reference symbol S" — applied by the linker / dynamic loader.
  • nm letters: T/t text, D/d data, B/b bss, U undefined, W weak. Uppercase = global.
  • Tools: nm -C, objdump -d/-r, readelf -a, c++filt, size, strings, ldd.
  • Strip debug/symbols with strip (or ship a separate .debug via objcopy --only-keep-debug).
Q&A
What does U mean in nm output?
An undefined symbol — the object file references it but doesn't define it, so the linker must find it in another object or library.
Why does .bss take no space in the object file but .data does?
.bss is zero-initialised, so only its size needs recording; the loader zero-fills that region at startup. .data holds non-zero initial values, which must be stored byte-for-byte in the file.
What is a weak symbol?
A global definition that yields to a strong (normal) definition of the same name if one exists, and doesn't conflict with other weak definitions. Compilers emit weak symbols for inline functions and template instantiations; you can mark optional hook functions __attribute__((weak)).
What is a relocation?
An instruction to the linker/loader: "the value at this offset in this section needs to be computed from the final address of symbol S (plus an addend), using this relocation type". It exists because the assembler can't know final addresses.
How do you see the symbols a shared library exports?
nm -D --defined-only libfoo.so (dynamic symbol table), or readelf --dyn-syms, or objdump -T.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which section holds string literals?
.rodata.
Command to demangle a C++ symbol name?
c++filt, or nm -C / objdump -C.
What kind of symbol does a static function produce?
A local symbol (lowercase t in nm) — not visible to the linker outside its object file.

Intermediate core

Two libraries both define int global_config; at file scope. Historically it linked; now it errors. Why?
Old default (-fcommon): an uninitialised file-scope variable became a "common" symbol, and the linker merged same-named commons into one — silently. GCC 10 / modern Clang default to -fno-common, making each a normal (tentative-then-emitted) definition, so two of them is a "multiple definition" error. The correct fix: define it once in one .c, and put extern int global_config; in a shared header.
Your binary is huge. How do you find out what's taking the space?
size -A binary for per-section sizes; nm --size-sort -C binary | tail for the biggest symbols; bloaty (Google) for a hierarchical breakdown by section, symbol, compile unit, and even diffing two binaries. Common culprits: unstripped debug info (strip or split it), template instantiation bloat, statically linked libraries, no -ffunction-sections -Wl,--gc-sections to drop unused code, RTTI/exception tables, embedded resources.

Advanced deep

Explain -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections + --gc-sections and its limits.
Normally the compiler puts all functions from a TU into one .text section and all data into .data/.bss; the linker's unit of inclusion is the whole section, so if you reference any symbol from an object file, you pull in all its code (for a static lib, at least the whole member .o). -ffunction-sections/-fdata-sections tells the compiler to emit each function and each data object into its own section (.text.foo, .data.bar). Then the linker's --gc-sections does a mark-and-sweep from the entry point (and other roots: exported symbols, KEEP() sections, init/fini arrays) and discards any section nothing references — dead-code elimination at link granularity. Big wins for embedded firmware and for trimming statically-linked libraries. Limits and gotchas: (1) it's conservative — anything reachable via a function pointer, a vtable, an exception-handling table, RTTI, or a relocation from a kept section is retained, so C++ with polymorphism/exceptions keeps more than you'd hope. (2) Sections referenced only from the symbol table or by name (interrupt vector tables, linker-script-placed data, plugin entry points) must be protected with KEEP() in the linker script or __attribute__((used)), or they vanish. (3) It slightly increases .o size and link time (many more sections). (4) It doesn't cross into shared libraries. LTO does a better job (whole-program reachability on the IR, including devirtualization to prove a virtual isn't called) but at much higher link cost; --gc-sections is the cheap, always-on baseline.
What are the common relocation types (R_X86_64_PC32, _PLT32, _GOTPCREL, _64) and when is each used?
R_X86_64_64: patch a full 64-bit absolute address of the symbol — used for pointer-sized data that must hold a real address (a global pointer initialised to &foo, vtable entries in non-PIE). Requires the target to be at a known address, so in PIE/PIC these become dynamic relocations resolved at load time. R_X86_64_PC32: 32-bit PC-relative — "displacement from the next instruction to the symbol". Used for direct calls/jumps and RIP-relative data access within the same module, where the distance fits in ±2GB. Position-independent (only relative), no dynamic reloc needed if the symbol is defined locally. R_X86_64_PLT32: like PC32 but the target is allowed to be a PLT stub — emitted for calls to functions that might be in another shared library; if the symbol turns out local the linker relaxes it to a plain PC32 direct call, otherwise it points at the Procedure Linkage Table entry that does the lazy dynamic resolve. R_X86_64_GOTPCREL: PC-relative reference to the symbol's slot in the Global Offset Table — used to access a global variable that may be defined in another shared object; the code loads the address from the GOT (which the dynamic loader filled in), adding one indirection. So roughly: intra-module code → PC32; inter-module (or maybe-inter-module) calls → PLT32; inter-module data → GOTPCREL; absolute pointers in data → 64 (becoming a load-time dynamic reloc under ASLR/PIE). Reading objdump -dr and seeing which of these appear tells you how position-independent and how "library-boundary-crossing" the code is.

The Linker: Resolution & Ordering

Why link order matters, and how "undefined reference" and "multiple definition" happen.

Notes

What the linker does

  1. Symbol resolution: for every undefined symbol, find exactly one definition among the inputs.
  2. Section placement: merge same-named sections, assign addresses (per a linker script).
  3. Relocation: patch every reference with the now-known address.
  4. Write the executable / shared object (headers, program segments, dynamic info).
$ ld --verbose | grep -A2 '\.text'      # the default linker script: where .text lands
  .text : { *(.text .text.*) }          # merge every input's .text into one

$ gcc -Wl,-Map=app.map a.o b.o -o app   # -> app.map: every symbol's final address + which .o it came from
$ readelf -l app | grep LOAD           # the PT_LOAD segments the kernel will mmap

Link order (the classic gotcha)

The traditional Unix linker processes inputs left to right, keeping a set of "currently undefined" symbols. When it reaches a static library (.a), it pulls in only the member objects that satisfy a currently-undefined symbol. So a library must come after the objects that use it:

gcc main.o -lfoo         # OK: main.o needs foo, then -lfoo provides it
gcc -lfoo main.o         # FAIL: at -lfoo nothing is undefined yet, so it's skipped;
                         #       then main.o needs foo -> "undefined reference"

Circular dependencies between static libs: repeat them, or wrap in -Wl,--start-group ... --end-group. Object files (.o) are always fully included regardless of order.

Common errors

  • undefined reference to X: no input defines X (missing .o/library, wrong link order, C/C++ mangling mismatch, wrong library version).
  • multiple definition of X: two strong definitions (a real function/variable definition in a header included twice, missing inline/static, two libs with the same symbol).
  • DSO missing from command line: an indirect dependency you now must name explicitly.
// C++ calling a C function without extern "C" -> name mangling mismatch
// C: defines   sqrt_impl
// C++: expects _Z9sqrt_impld   -> "undefined reference to `sqrt_impl(double)'"
extern "C" double sqrt_impl(double);   // FIX in the C++ header

// header with a real definition, included by 2 TUs -> "multiple definition of `k'"
// int k = 3;               // in a header -> BAD
inline int k = 3;                     // C++17: OK in a header
// extern int k;  in header + one `int k = 3;` in a .c  -> also OK

Optimisations at link

--gc-sections (drop unused sections), --icf (identical code folding — merge byte-identical functions), -flto (whole-program optimisation), -s (strip). Fast linkers: lld, mold, gold — large wins over classic ld for big binaries.

$ gcc -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wl,--gc-sections a.c -o app
                                 # unreferenced functions/data dropped from the binary
$ gcc -flto -O2 *.o -o app       # cross-TU inlining + dead-code removal at link
$ strip app                      # or link with -s : remove the symbol table
$ gcc -fuse-ld=mold ...          # swap in a fast linker: 5-10x quicker link for big binaries
Cheat Sheet
  • Linker: resolve every undefined symbol to exactly one definition → place sections → apply relocations → emit binary.
  • Static libs (.a) are scanned left-to-right; only members that resolve a currently-undefined symbol are pulled in → put libraries after the code that uses them.
  • Circular static-lib deps: list them twice, or -Wl,--start-group ... --end-group.
  • Plain .o files are always fully linked, order-independent.
  • "undefined reference" = missing/mis-ordered lib, mangling mismatch, wrong version.
  • "multiple definition" = two strong defs (def in header, missing inline/static, duplicate lib symbol).
  • Link-time: --gc-sections, --icf, -flto, -s (strip). Use lld/mold for speed.
Q&A
Why does gcc -lm main.o fail but gcc main.o -lm work?
The linker scans left to right tracking undefined symbols. At -lm (first) nothing is undefined yet, so no members of libm are pulled in. Then main.o introduces undefined math symbols, but libm has already been passed. Put libraries after the objects/libraries that depend on them.
How do you resolve a circular dependency between two static libraries?
List them more than once (-la -lb -la), or group them: -Wl,--start-group -la -lb -Wl,--end-group, which makes the linker re-scan the group until no new symbols are resolved.
What causes "multiple definition of `foo`"?
Two strong definitions of the same symbol in the link — commonly a non-inline function or a variable defined in a header that's included by two .cpp files, or forgetting static/inline, or linking two libraries that each carry the symbol.
Are object files order-sensitive on the link line?
No — every .o is included in full regardless of position. Only static libraries (.a) are order-sensitive because the linker pulls members from them selectively.
What does the linker's identical-code-folding (ICF) do?
Detects functions whose compiled machine code is byte-for-byte identical (very common with templates instantiated for different-but-layout-compatible types) and keeps just one copy, redirecting all callers to it — shrinking the binary. "Safe" ICF avoids folding functions whose address is taken and compared.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Where on the link line do libraries go relative to the objects that use them?
After — to the right of the objects/libraries that reference their symbols.
Which input type is order-independent: .o or .a?
.o object files (always fully linked). .a archives are order-sensitive.
Two error strings a linker produces?
"undefined reference to X" and "multiple definition of X".

Intermediate core

A C library function called from C++ gives "undefined reference" even though you linked the library. Why?
Name mangling: the C++ compiler mangled the call to _Z3fooi (or similar), but the C library exports the plain symbol foo. The C header must wrap its declarations in extern "C" { ... } (usually guarded by #ifdef __cplusplus) so the C++ compiler emits an unmangled reference. If you can't edit the header, wrap the include yourself.
Your app pulls in a huge static library but uses two functions from it. Binary is bloated. Options?
Ensure the library was built with -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections and link with -Wl,--gc-sections so unused members' sections are discarded (a static lib's member object is the minimum inclusion unit otherwise, so one used symbol drags in its whole .o). Or use a shared library so the code isn't copied in at all. Or LTO, which can dead-strip across the whole program. Or find a smaller/modular alternative.

Advanced deep

Explain how the linker resolves a symbol when it appears in an executable, one shared library it links directly, and another it doesn't — and what "symbol interposition" means.
At static link time, the linker only needs to know that some shared object on the link line (or a transitive DT_NEEDED) exports the symbol — it records an undefined dynamic symbol and a dependency, and defers actual binding to runtime. At load time, the dynamic loader builds a single global symbol namespace by processing objects in a defined order (executable first, then its DT_NEEDED libraries breadth-first). The first definition found for a given name wins for everyone — this is symbol interposition: because the executable is searched before the libraries, a function the executable defines with the same name as one in a library will be the one the library itself calls (unless the library was built to prevent it). This is the mechanism behind LD_PRELOAD (inject a library that gets searched first, so your malloc/open replaces the real one everywhere), and behind the classic bug where an app accidentally defines read or _init and breaks libc. The cost: to preserve the possibility of interposition, position-independent code in a shared library must call even its own global functions through the PLT/GOT (an indirection) rather than a direct call, and access its own globals via the GOT — measurable overhead. Mitigations that opt out of interposition for speed: -fvisibility=hidden + explicit __attribute__((visibility("default"))) on the real API (non-exported symbols get direct calls), -Bsymbolic / -Bsymbolic-functions (bind references to definitions within the same DSO at link time), and protected visibility. These make the library faster and more self-consistent but mean LD_PRELOAD can no longer override its internal calls.
Why can link order between two static libraries that mutually depend still fail even with a single pass, and how does --start-group actually work?
Single-pass left-to-right resolution keeps a running "undefined set". Say liba.a has a_func (which calls b_func) and libb.a has b_func (which calls a_helper from liba.a). Link line main.o -la -lb: main.o leaves a_func undefined → at -la, pull in the member with a_func, which adds b_func to undefined → at -lb, pull in the member with b_func, which adds a_helper to undefined → but -la is already behind us, so a_helper stays undefined → error. -Wl,--start-group -la -lb -Wl,--end-group tells the linker to treat the enclosed archives as a unit and iterate: scan the group, and if the pass resolved any new symbols (i.e. pulled in new members that introduced new undefineds satisfiable within the group), scan it again — repeat until a full pass adds nothing. So the second pass over the group finds a_helper in liba.a. The cost is O(passes × group size) link time, which is why you scope the group tightly rather than wrapping the whole link line. The cleaner fix is to break the cycle (merge the libraries, or move the shared helper into a third base library that both depend on), or use a linker like lld/gold which effectively does whole-archive symbol resolution and is far less order-sensitive. -Wl,--whole-archive (force all members in, order-independent) is the sledgehammer — correct but bloats the binary.

Static vs Dynamic Libraries

Copy the code in at build time, or load it at run time — and everything that follows.

Notes

The two models

Static (.a / .lib)Dynamic (.so / .dll / .dylib)
When linkedbuild time — needed members copied into the binaryload time (or later via dlopen)
Binary sizelarger (code baked in)smaller
Memoryeach process has its own copyone copy of the code shared across processes
Deploymentself-contained, no external depsmust ship / have the right .so versions present
Updatesrelink to pick up a library fixdrop-in a new .so (if ABI-compatible)
Startupfastloader must find, map, and relocate each library
# build both from the same object
$ gcc -c -fPIC util.c
$ ar rcs libutil.a util.o                    # static archive = just a bag of .o files
$ gcc -shared -Wl,-soname,libutil.so.1 -o libutil.so.1 util.o

$ gcc app.c -static -L. -lutil -o app_s      # ~900 KB, `ldd` -> "not a dynamic executable"
$ gcc app.c        -L. -lutil -o app_d       # ~16 KB, `ldd` -> libutil.so.1 => ./libutil.so.1

Position-independent code

Shared libraries are built with -fPIC so they work at any load address (ASLR). References to globals and cross-library functions go through the GOT (Global Offset Table) and PLT (Procedure Linkage Table), filled in by the dynamic loader — a small indirection cost. Executables use -fPIE (PIC for the main program) — now the default for ASLR.

$ gcc -shared util.c -o libutil.so
/usr/bin/ld: util.o: relocation R_X86_64_32 ... recompile with -fPIC   # forgot -fPIC

$ gcc -c -fPIC util.c && gcc -shared util.o -o libutil.so   # fixed
$ objdump -d app | grep '@plt'
  call  1050 <printf@plt>     # cross-.so calls jump through the PLT; GOT gets patched on first call
$ readelf -d app | grep PIE   # FLAGS_1  ...  PIE   -> main program is position-independent too

Runtime loading

  • The loader (ld.so) reads the executable's DT_NEEDED list, searches RUNPATH/LD_LIBRARY_PATH//etc/ld.so.cache/system dirs, maps each library, and applies relocations. ldd binary shows the resolved list.
  • Lazy binding: a function's address is resolved on first call (via the PLT). LD_BIND_NOW forces eager resolution.
  • dlopen/dlsym/dlclose for plugins loaded explicitly at runtime.
$ ldd app
    libfoo.so.1 => not found          # DT_NEEDED not on the search path
$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=./libs ldd app     # or: gcc ... -Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN/libs'
$ LD_DEBUG=libs,bindings ./app       # trace every search + symbol bind

// runtime plugin:
void *h = dlopen("./plugin.so", RTLD_NOW);
int (*run)(void) = dlsym(h, "run");
run(); dlclose(h);

Versioning

SONAME (libfoo.so.2) encodes the ABI major version; a compatible update bumps only the minor (libfoo.so.2.3 → 2.4) and keeps the same SONAME so existing binaries keep working. Symbol versioning (libc.so.6 with GLIBC_2.34 tags) lets one .so serve old and new callers. Break the ABI → bump the SONAME.

$ ls -l /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libssl*
libssl.so       -> libssl.so.3       # dev symlink (link with -lssl)
libssl.so.3     -> libssl.so.3.0.2   # SONAME -- what binaries record in DT_NEEDED
libssl.so.3.0.2                       # the real file; a 3.0.x fix keeps SONAME libssl.so.3

$ objdump -T /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | grep 'GLIBC_2.34' | head
# one libc.so.6 exposes memcpy@GLIBC_2.14 AND memcpy@GLIBC_2.34 -> old binaries still run
Cheat Sheet
  • Static (.a): linked at build, code copied in → bigger binary, per-process copy, self-contained, fast start, relink to update.
  • Dynamic (.so/.dll): linked at load (or dlopen) → smaller binary, code shared across processes, external dependency, slower start.
  • .so built with -fPIC; calls/globals go via PLT/GOT (loader fills them, small indirection). Executables use -fPIE.
  • Loader: DT_NEEDED + search path (RUNPATH > LD_LIBRARY_PATH > ld.so.cache > defaults); lazy binding by default; ldd to inspect.
  • SONAME = ABI major version; compatible updates keep it, incompatible ones bump it. Symbol versioning serves old + new callers from one .so.
  • dlopen/dlsym for runtime plugins.
  • Static for reproducible single-file deploys / containers-from-scratch; dynamic for shared system libs and hot-patchable updates.
Q&A
Static vs dynamic linking — the core trade-off?
Static: the library code is copied into your binary at build time — self-contained, no runtime dependency, faster startup, but bigger and you must relink to get library fixes. Dynamic: the library is a separate file loaded at run time — smaller binaries, one shared copy in memory across processes, drop-in updates, but you depend on the right version being present and pay startup/indirection cost.
Why must shared libraries be compiled with -fPIC?
They can be loaded at any address (different per process under ASLR, and different libraries can't all claim the same fixed address). Position-independent code uses PC-relative addressing and indirection tables (GOT/PLT) so it works regardless of load address, without the loader having to rewrite every instruction.
What is a SONAME and why does it matter?
An embedded name like libssl.so.3 that captures the ABI version. Binaries record the SONAME they were built against; the loader finds a file providing it. Backward-compatible library updates keep the SONAME (so old binaries still run); ABI-breaking changes bump it (so old binaries don't silently load an incompatible library).
What does dlopen give you over normal dynamic linking?
Explicit, on-demand loading of a library your program names at runtime (from config, a plugin directory), with dlsym to look up functions by string. Used for plugin architectures, optional features, and lazy loading of rarely-used heavy dependencies.
When would you statically link everything?
For maximally portable single-file deployment (copy the binary anywhere, no dependency hell), minimal containers (`FROM scratch`), reproducibility, avoiding "works on my machine" library-version drift, and slightly faster startup / no PLT indirection. Downsides: bigger images, security fixes in a library need every dependent rebuilt, and glibc static linking has caveats (NSS, locale).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which library type makes a bigger executable?
Static — the used code is copied into the binary.
Command to list a binary's shared-library dependencies?
ldd binary (Linux); otool -L on macOS.
What flag builds position-independent code for a shared library?
-fPIC.

Intermediate core

Your program runs on the build machine but fails with "libfoo.so.2: cannot open shared object file" on deploy. Fixes?
The runtime host lacks that library (or the right version) on its search path. Options: install the package providing libfoo.so.2; ship the .so alongside and set RUNPATH (-Wl,-rpath,'$ORIGIN/lib') so the loader looks next to the binary; statically link that dependency; or use a container image that bundles it. Diagnose with ldd (shows "not found") and LD_DEBUG=libs ./prog (shows the search).
Two shared libraries your app loads each bundle their own copy of a third library's symbols, and you get crashes. What's happening?
Symbol collision in the single global namespace: both copies of the third library's functions/globals have the same names, the loader binds every caller to whichever it saw first, so library A ends up calling library B's copy's state (different errno-like globals, different allocator arenas, mismatched struct layouts if versions differ). Fixes: make the third library a single shared dependency both link against (don't bundle); build the plugins with -fvisibility=hidden so only their real API is exported; load plugins with dlopen(..., RTLD_LOCAL) (and RTLD_DEEPBIND cautiously) so their symbols don't enter the global scope; or use distinct namespaces (dlmopen).

Advanced deep

Walk through what the dynamic loader does between execve and main().
The kernel maps the executable and, seeing it's dynamically linked (PT_INTERP program header naming /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2), also maps the loader and transfers control to it, not the program. The loader: (1) parses its own DYNAMIC section and self-relocates (bootstrap — it can't call anything yet). (2) Reads the executable's DT_NEEDED entries, and recursively theirs, building the dependency graph; resolves each name via DT_RUNPATH (or legacy RPATH), LD_LIBRARY_PATH, the ld.so.cache (ldconfig-built index), then default dirs; mmaps each library's segments (text shared read-only/exec, data private COW). (3) Performs relocations: for each object, processes its relocation tables — R_*_RELATIVE (add load base, cheap), and symbolic relocations that require searching the global symbol scope in load order (first definition wins — interposition). DT_BIND_NOW/LD_BIND_NOW or full RELRO does all function relocations now; otherwise lazy binding leaves PLT entries pointing at the resolver stub, bound on first call. (4) Applies RELRO: mprotects the GOT (and other relro data) read-only after relocation to harden against GOT-overwrite attacks. (5) Runs each library's init functions in dependency order — DT_INIT then the DT_INIT_ARRAY (C++ static constructors, __attribute__((constructor)), ifunc resolvers). (6) Jumps to the executable's entry point (_start), which sets up the C runtime and calls main. On exit, DT_FINI_ARRAY/atexit destructors run in reverse. LD_DEBUG=all traces every step; static-PIE binaries fold the loader's job into the program itself.
What is symbol versioning in glibc (GLIBC_2.x), and how does it let one libc.so.6 support 20 years of binaries?
Instead of bumping the SONAME every time a function's behaviour changes, glibc attaches a version node to each symbol. When the semantics of, say, memcpy or realpath or pow change in an incompatible way, glibc keeps the old implementation under the old version (memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5) and adds the new one as the default (memcpy@@GLIBC_2.14 — double-at marks the default). A binary linked years ago recorded a reference to memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5 and the loader binds it to the preserved old code; a freshly compiled binary gets memcpy@@GLIBC_2.14. This is why an ancient binary still runs on a modern system (the old symbol versions are all still present) but a binary built on a new system fails on an old one with "version `GLIBC_2.34' not found" (the new node doesn't exist there). The version map is declared in a linker version script (--version-script); the linker stamps each undefined reference with the version of the definition it saw at link time. It also enables gradual ABI evolution for third-party libraries: you can add a symbol, change one, or remove one, mark versions accordingly, and old consumers keep working — a much finer-grained tool than the all-or-nothing SONAME bump. The cost is complexity in the build (version scripts, careful "old code path" maintenance) and that it only helps for changes you anticipated versioning; a bug that changes behaviour of an unversioned path still breaks callers.

The ABI & Name Mangling

The contract two separately-compiled pieces of code must agree on to call each other.

Notes

What an ABI covers

  • Calling convention: which registers/stack slots pass arguments and return values, who cleans up, caller- vs callee-saved registers, stack alignment.
  • Type layout: sizes, alignment, struct padding, enum underlying type, bitfield order, vtable layout, RTTI, exception tables.
  • Name mangling: how source names map to linker symbols.
  • Object-file format, standard library layout, std::string/std::list representation.

The API is the source-level interface (function signatures); the ABI is the binary-level one. Code compiled separately must share an ABI to interoperate.

// same C source, the calling convention is fixed by the platform ABI:
int f(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }
// x86-64 SysV:   a->edi  b->esi  c->edx    return->eax
// Windows x64:   a->ecx  b->edx  c->r8d    return->eax   + 32 bytes "shadow space"
// -> an .o built for one CANNOT be linked into a program using the other
$ gcc -c f.c && objdump -d f.o | head

Name mangling

C:    int add(int, int);          -> symbol:  add
C++:  int add(int, int);          -> symbol:  _Z3addii
C++:  int add(double, double);    -> symbol:  _Z3adddd
C++:  namespace N { void f(); }   -> symbol:  _ZN1N1fEv

C++ encodes namespace, class, function name, parameter types (and templates, const, ref-qualifiers) into the symbol — that's how overloading and namespaces coexist at link time. C doesn't mangle. extern "C" { ... } tells a C++ compiler to emit an unmangled symbol so C and C++ can call each other; note it also disables overloading for those functions.

ABI breaks

Changes that keep the API but break the ABI — recompiling every consumer is required:

  • Adding/removing/reordering a class's data members or virtual functions; changing a member's type.
  • Changing an enum's underlying type; changing struct packing.
  • Changing a function's signature in a way that affects the mangled name or the calling convention (adding a default argument is API-compatible but callers still linked against the old symbol).
  • Switching standard-library implementation or the infamous _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI flag (pre-C++11 vs C++11 std::string).
// v1 of the shared lib's header:
struct Config { int timeout; bool verbose; };
// v2 -- API looks identical, ABI is BROKEN: sizeof/offsets changed
struct Config { int timeout; int retries; bool verbose; };
// old app (still linked against v1) passes an 8-byte Config; v2 lib reads 12 -> garbage `verbose`

// the glibc++ string ABI switch bites the same way:
$ g++ -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 a.cpp   # old std::string layout
$ g++                             b.cpp   # new layout -> "undefined reference" on std::string params

Stable-ABI techniques: a pure C interface, opaque handles + accessor functions, PImpl, versioned symbols, "only add, never change" rules.
