// stable ABI: a C surface + opaque handle. Struct changes never reach the caller.
typedef struct Session Session;        // incomplete type -- caller can't see its size
extern "C" Session *session_open(const char *url);
extern "C" int      session_get(Session *, const char *key, char *out, size_t n);
extern "C" void     session_close(Session *);
// add session_set_timeout() later -> old binaries keep working (additive only)
Cheat Sheet
  • ABI = binary contract: calling convention (regs/stack, saved regs, alignment), type/vtable/struct layout, name mangling, object format, stdlib layout.
  • API = source interface; ABI = the compiled interface. Separately compiled code needs a shared ABI.
  • C: no mangling (add). C++: mangled (_Z3addii) to encode namespace/class/params → enables overloading.
  • extern "C" → unmangled symbol for C↔C++ interop; disables overloading for those names.
  • ABI breaks (need full recompile): change data members / virtuals / their order/type, enum base, struct packing, calling convention, stdlib ABI flag.
  • Adding a default argument is API- but not ABI- relevant for already-linked callers.
  • Stable ABI: expose a C API, opaque handles, PImpl, symbol versioning, additive-only changes.
Q&A
API vs ABI?
The API is the source-level contract — function names, signatures, types — that lets code compile against a library. The ABI is the binary-level contract — calling convention, exact type layout, symbol names — that lets already-compiled code link and run against a library without recompiling.
Why does C++ mangle names?
To support overloading and namespaces at link time: f(int) and f(double) and N::f() are distinct entities but share the source name f. Encoding the enclosing scope and parameter types into the linker symbol makes each unique.
What does extern "C" do?
It tells the C++ compiler to use C linkage for the enclosed declarations — emit and expect an unmangled symbol name and the C calling convention — so a C++ program can call a C library and a C program can call C++ functions declared this way. Overloading isn't available for extern "C" names.
Give an ABI-breaking change that isn't API-breaking.
Adding a private data member to a class in a public header: the API (methods) is unchanged and consumer source still compiles, but sizeof and member offsets change, so any consumer compiled against the old header now has wrong layout — must recompile. Same for adding/reordering virtual functions (vtable slots shift).
How do library authors provide a stable ABI?
Expose a plain C interface (no mangling, no class layout), pass opaque handle pointers with accessor functions, use PImpl so the header has fixed size, only add symbols (never change existing ones), and use symbol versioning to keep old entry points alongside new ones.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Does C mangle function names?
No — the linker symbol is just the function name.
What wrapper makes a C++ function callable from C?
extern "C" around its declaration/definition.
Name two things an ABI specifies.
Calling convention (argument/return registers, stack alignment) and type/struct layout — also name mangling and vtable layout.

Intermediate core

A plugin built with GCC crashes when loaded by a host built with an older GCC, though both compiled fine. Likely cause?
A C++ standard-library ABI mismatch — most famously libstdc++'s dual std::string/std::list ABI toggled by _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI. If the host passes a std::string across the boundary and the two sides disagree on its layout (old copy-on-write vs new SSO), you read garbage. Also possible: exception-handling table or vtable-layout differences between compiler versions, or an inline function whose definition differs. Fixes: build host and plugins with the same toolchain and stdlib ABI flags, or use a pure C ABI at the plugin boundary (opaque handles + C functions).
You demangle a crash symbol with c++filt: _ZN3lib6WidgetC1ERKNS_6ConfigE. Roughly what is it?
lib::Widget::Widget(lib::Config const&) — the C1 is a complete-object constructor, RK = reference to const, NS_ = the lib namespace again (substitution compression). So the crash is in a Widget constructor taking a const Config&.

Advanced deep

Why is there no standard C++ ABI, and how do the Itanium C++ ABI and MSVC differ in consequence?
The C++ standard deliberately specifies only source semantics, leaving layout, mangling, exception mechanism, RTTI format, and calling details to the implementation — partly historical (no single vendor could dictate), partly to allow platform/perf freedom. In practice the industry converged on the Itanium C++ ABI for everything except Microsoft: GCC, Clang, ICC on Linux/macOS/BSD all follow it, so a library built with GCC can be consumed by Clang (same mangling like _Z..., same vtable layout, same __cxa_* exception runtime, same guard-variable scheme for function-local statics). This is why mixed GCC/Clang C++ codebases mostly "just work". MSVC uses its own mangling (?add@@YAHHH@Z-style), its own vtable and RTTI layout, SEH-based exceptions, and different calling conventions — so a C++ library built with MSVC and one built with Clang-for-Windows historically couldn't interoperate at the C++ level at all (only via a C interface). (clang-cl narrows this by targeting the MSVC ABI on Windows.) Consequences: on Linux you get a de-facto stable cross-compiler C++ ABI (though still not cross compiler-version for stdlib types, and not guaranteed by any standard); on Windows the C ABI has long been the only reliable cross-toolchain boundary, which is why Windows plugin/SDK interfaces are overwhelmingly C or COM (which pins vtable layout explicitly). The lesson for library authors: if you must ship binaries consumed by unknown toolchains, expose a C ABI; C++-across-the-boundary only works when everyone uses the same compiler family, version, standard-library, and flags.
Explain how function-local static initialization is made thread-safe at the ABI level (the "guard variable").
For void f(){ static Heavy h(args); ... }, C++11 requires h to be constructed exactly once, on the first call that reaches it, with concurrent callers blocking until it's done. The Itanium ABI implements this with a per-static guard variable (in .bss) and two runtime calls: on entry to the static's scope the compiler emits (roughly) if (__cxa_guard_acquire(&guard)) { construct h; __cxa_guard_release(&guard); atexit_register(destructor); }. __cxa_guard_acquire does a fast unlocked check of the guard's low byte (already-initialised → return 0, no lock — this is the common path, one relaxed load); if not initialised it takes a lock (a global recursive mutex, or a futex on the guard itself in modern glibc), re-checks, and either returns 1 (you construct) or, if another thread is mid-construction, blocks until release/abort. __cxa_guard_release sets the initialised byte with release semantics and wakes waiters. There's also __cxa_guard_abort for when the constructor throws (so a later call retries). Subtleties: recursive entry (the initializer calls f again) is undefined / deadlocks depending on implementation; the fast-path load must be an acquire (or the constructed object's writes may not be visible to a thread that sees the guard set) — some early implementations got this wrong and needed a fix; and this machinery is why a function-local static is the recommended thread-safe singleton in C++11+ ("Meyers singleton") — the compiler+ABI give you the double-checked locking correctly, including the memory barriers, for free.

make & Incremental Builds

A dependency graph + timestamps — the model under every build system.

Notes

The core model

target: prereq1 prereq2      # target depends on these
<TAB> recipe                 # shell commands to (re)build target

make rebuilds target iff it's missing or older than any prerequisite (mtime comparison). It walks the dependency DAG, building leaves first. This is the whole idea: declare what depends on what, and only stale things rebuild.

Essentials

  • Pattern rules: %.o: %.c with $< (first prereq), $@ (target), $^ (all prereqs).
  • Variables: CC, CFLAGS, $(wildcard *.c), $(patsubst ...). := (immediate) vs = (lazy).
  • .PHONY: clean all test — targets that aren't files, so they always run and don't clash with a file of that name.
  • Parallelism: make -j$(nproc) — correct only if the dependency graph is complete (missing deps → race, flaky builds).
CC      := gcc
CFLAGS  := -O2 -Wall
SRC     := $(wildcard src/*.c)
OBJ     := $(SRC:.c=.o)

app: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) $^ -o $@              # $^ = all prereqs, $@ = target

%.o: %.c                       # pattern rule for every .c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@ # $< = the .c file

.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f $(OBJ) app           # always runs, even if a file named `clean` exists

Header dependency tracking

Naive Makefiles miss ".o depends on the headers the .c includes", so editing a header doesn't rebuild. The fix: gcc -MMD -MP emits a .d file listing the includes; -include $(OBJ:.o=.d) pulls them in. Now header edits trigger the right rebuilds.

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -MMD -MP -c $< -o $@   # also writes src/foo.d

-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)          # pull in "foo.o: foo.c bar.h baz.h"

# src/foo.d contains:
#   src/foo.o: src/foo.c include/bar.h include/baz.h
#   include/bar.h:        <- -MP adds empty rules so a DELETED header doesn't break the build

Why people moved on

  • Recursive make (a Makefile per directory calling sub-makes) fragments the dependency graph — "Recursive Make Considered Harmful". Use one top-level non-recursive Makefile, or a generator.
  • mtime-based staleness is fooled by clock skew, touch, and checkout order; content-hash build systems (Bazel, Buck) are more robust.
  • Hand-writing portable, correct Makefiles is tedious → CMake/Meson generate them (or Ninja files).
# mtime lies: git checkout writes NEW mtimes on unchanged files -> spurious rebuild
$ git checkout main && make    # rebuilds half the tree for no reason

# content-hash build system: rebuilds only if the INPUT BYTES changed
$ bazel build //app:server     # cache hit across machines / branches / CI

# the common middle ground: let CMake generate Ninja
$ cmake -G Ninja -B build && ninja -C build
Cheat Sheet
  • Rule: target: prereqs / TAB recipe. Rebuild if target missing or older than a prereq.
  • Automatic vars: $@ target, $< first prereq, $^ all prereqs. Pattern rule %.o: %.c.
  • := immediate assignment, = recursively-expanded (lazy), ?= default, += append.
  • .PHONY for non-file targets (all, clean, test).
  • Header deps: gcc -MMD -MP → .d files → -include $(DEPS). Without this, header edits don't rebuild.
  • make -j N for parallelism — only safe with a complete/correct dependency graph.
  • Avoid recursive make (fragmented graph); prefer one non-recursive Makefile or a generator (CMake → Ninja).
  • mtime staleness is fragile; hash-based systems (Bazel) are more reproducible.
Q&A
How does make decide whether to rebuild a target?
It compares modification times: if the target file doesn't exist, or any prerequisite is newer than the target, the recipe runs. Otherwise it's considered up to date.
Why declare clean as .PHONY?
So make always runs its recipe even if a file named clean happens to exist in the directory (which would otherwise be seen as an up-to-date target and skipped).
You edit a header but make rebuilds nothing. Why?
The Makefile doesn't record that the .o files depend on that header — only on the .c. Generate dependency files with gcc -MMD -MP and -include them so header prerequisites are tracked.
What can go wrong with make -j8?
If the dependency graph is incomplete (a target uses an output that isn't listed as its prerequisite), parallel jobs can run in the wrong order or simultaneously, producing intermittent build failures or corrupt outputs. Parallel make only works when dependencies are fully and correctly declared.
What's the problem with recursive make?
Each sub-make only knows its own directory's dependency graph, so cross-directory dependencies are invisible — leading to under-building (stale results) or over-building (rebuilding everything to be safe), broken parallelism, and repeated work. A single non-recursive Makefile (or a generator that produces one) sees the whole graph.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does $< mean in a recipe?
The first prerequisite. $@ is the target, $^ is all prerequisites.
What must precede a recipe line?
A literal TAB character (not spaces).
Flag to build with N parallel jobs?
make -j N (e.g. make -j$(nproc)).

Intermediate core

Write a minimal Makefile that builds all *.c into one binary with correct header tracking.
CC := gcc
CFLAGS := -O2 -g -Wall -MMD -MP
SRC := $(wildcard *.c)
OBJ := $(SRC:.c=.o)
app: $(OBJ)
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $^
%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
-include $(OBJ:.o=.d)
.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f app $(OBJ) $(OBJ:.o=.d)
The -MMD -MP + -include lines are what make header edits trigger rebuilds.
Your CI build passes with make but fails intermittently with make -j. Diagnosis?
Missing or incorrect dependencies let jobs run out of order: something reads a file another job is still writing, or two jobs write the same file, or a generated header isn't declared as a prerequisite of the objects that include it. Add the missing prerequisite edges (generated files, codegen outputs, link order), avoid shared scratch files, and consider a stricter tool (Ninja from CMake, which also validates the graph). make --output-sync and -j1 reproduction help isolate it.

Advanced deep

Why do content-hash build systems (Bazel, Buck2, Nix) claim better correctness and cacheability than mtime-based make, and what do they demand in return?
mtime is a proxy for "did the input change" that's wrong in many ways: git checkout / rsync can set an old file's mtime to now (over-build) or a new file's to the past (under-build — stale binary that "builds clean"); clock skew across NFS/containers; touch; and mtime granularity races. It also gives you nothing to share: two developers building the identical source get no benefit from each other's work. Hash-based systems compute a cryptographic digest of every declared input to an action — source files' contents, the exact command line, the toolchain version, environment variables, and the digests of upstream outputs — and use that as a cache key. Consequences: (1) correctness — an action re-runs iff a real input changed, regardless of timestamps; (2) remote caching — if anyone (or CI) has built this exact action before, download the output instead of rebuilding, so a clean checkout can be near-instant; (3) remote execution — farm actions out to a build cluster; (4) reproducibility — same inputs → same outputs, verifiable. What they demand: every action must declare all its inputs and outputs precisely (no reading undeclared files, no non-deterministic output — no embedded timestamps, no __DATE__, sorted archive members, stable link order), the build runs in a sandbox that enforces this (an undeclared read fails), and the toolchain itself is treated as a versioned input (hermetic toolchains). This is a large upfront cost — you can't just system("...") — which is why they pay off mainly at large-monorepo scale where the caching and parallelism dominate, and why smaller projects stay with CMake+Ninja (which is still mtime-based but with a correct, non-recursive graph and fast null builds).
Explain make's .SECONDEXPANSION, order-only prerequisites (| dir), and why they exist.
Order-only prerequisites (after a | in the prereq list): the target depends on them existing but not on their timestamp — if they're newer than the target, the target is not rebuilt. The canonical use is a build directory: build/%.o: %.c | build ensures build/ is created first, but every .o doesn't rebuild every time the directory's mtime bumps (which happens whenever a file is written into it). Without this, adding one .o to build/ touches the directory and triggers a full rebuild. .SECONDEXPANSION: normally a rule's prerequisite list is expanded once, when the Makefile is read. With .SECONDEXPANSION enabled, prerequisites are expanded a second time when the rule is actually considered, at which point automatic variables like $@ are available — so you can write $$(patsubst %.o,%.c,$$@) or per-target prerequisite lists computed from the target name ($$(DEPS_$$(notdir $$@))). It's the mechanism for data-driven rules where each target has a different, computed set of prerequisites (per-plugin sources, per-test fixtures) without writing an explicit rule for each. Both features exist because make's two-phase model (read all rules, then build) is otherwise too static: order-only deps decouple "must exist" from "affects staleness", and second expansion re-introduces target context into the dependency computation. They're powerful but a readability hazard — heavy use is a sign you want a generator instead.

CMake Fundamentals

A meta-build system: describe targets and their requirements; it generates the real build.

Notes

Model: targets carry their requirements

add_library(mylib src/a.cpp src/b.cpp)
target_include_directories(mylib PUBLIC  include
                                 PRIVATE src)
target_link_libraries(mylib PUBLIC fmt::fmt PRIVATE Threads::Threads)
target_compile_features(mylib PUBLIC cxx_std_20)

add_executable(app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE mylib)   # app inherits mylib's PUBLIC include dirs + libs

"Modern CMake" (3.x, target-based) attaches include paths, compile options, definitions, and link deps to targets, with usage requirements that propagate:

KeywordApplies to the targetPropagates to consumers
PRIVATEyesno
PUBLICyesyes
INTERFACEnoyes (header-only libs)

Avoid the old globals (include_directories(), link_libraries(), manual CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS hacking) — they leak everywhere.

Workflow

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build
cmake --install build --prefix /opt/app
  • Out-of-source: all generated files in build/, keeping the source tree clean.
  • Generators: Ninja (fast, recommended), Unix Makefiles, Visual Studio, Xcode.
  • find_package(Foo) locates dependencies (config-mode preferred, providing imported targets like Foo::Foo). FetchContent / vcpkg / Conan for fetching deps.
  • Presets (CMakePresets.json) capture configure/build/test option sets so everyone (and CI) builds identically.
Cheat Sheet
  • CMake generates a build (Ninja/Make/VS) from CMakeLists.txt; you don't run the compiler directly.
  • Modern CMake = target-based: target_include_directories / target_link_libraries / target_compile_* with PRIVATE/PUBLIC/INTERFACE.
  • PRIVATE = this target only; PUBLIC = this + consumers; INTERFACE = consumers only (header-only).
  • Consumers inherit a linked target's PUBLIC/INTERFACE requirements automatically — no manual path juggling.
  • Always out-of-source: cmake -S . -B build; cmake --build build.
  • -G Ninja for speed; -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE= (single-config generators) or --config (multi-config).
  • find_package(Foo CONFIG) → imported targets Foo::Foo. FetchContent/vcpkg/Conan to acquire deps.
  • CMakePresets.json to share exact configs with the team + CI. Avoid CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS hacking and old include_directories().
Q&A
What does CMake actually produce?
It doesn't build anything itself — it reads CMakeLists.txt and generates the input for a real build tool (Ninja files, Makefiles, a Visual Studio solution). You then invoke that tool (via cmake --build).
PRIVATE vs PUBLIC vs INTERFACE on target_link_libraries?
PRIVATE: the dependency is used to build this target but not exposed — consumers don't get it. PUBLIC: used to build this target and propagated, because it appears in this target's headers. INTERFACE: not used to build this target (it may have no sources), only propagated — for header-only libraries and pure requirement bundles.
Why do an out-of-source build?
All generated files (object files, CMake cache, the build system, config headers) go in a separate build/ directory, so the source tree stays clean, you can have multiple build configs side by side, and "clean" is just rm -rf build.
What does find_package(fmt CONFIG) give you?
It locates the installed fmt package's CMake config files and imports a target (fmt::fmt) that already carries the right include directories, compile definitions, and library path — so target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE fmt::fmt) is all you need.
What problem do CMake presets solve?
They record named sets of configure/build/test options (generator, build type, toolchain, cache variables) in CMakePresets.json, so a contributor runs cmake --preset ci and gets byte-identical configuration to CI — no "works with my flags" drift.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Command to configure into a build/ directory?
cmake -S . -B build (optionally -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release).
Which visibility keyword is for a header-only library?
INTERFACE — it has no compiled sources; its requirements only propagate to consumers.
Recommended generator for fast builds?
Ninja.

Intermediate core

Library A's public header includes <fmt/format.h>. How should A link fmt so consumers of A compile?
target_link_libraries(A PUBLIC fmt::fmt) — PUBLIC because fmt appears in A's interface (its public header), so any target linking A transitively needs fmt's include dirs and library. If fmt were only used in A's .cpp files it would be PRIVATE.
A teammate's build has different warnings/optimisation than yours despite the same repo. Likely cause and fix?
Different configure-time cache variables / generator / build type / toolchain, or leftover flags in a stale build/ cache. Fix: delete the build dir and reconfigure; standardise with CMakePresets.json so everyone uses cmake --preset dev; set compiler warnings on the target (target_compile_options(app PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)) rather than relying on environment; and don't append to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS from the environment.

Advanced deep

Explain how CMake's transitive usage requirements are actually resolved, including generator expressions and the difference between build-tree and install-tree.
Each target stores its requirements as properties: INTERFACE_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES, INTERFACE_COMPILE_DEFINITIONS, INTERFACE_COMPILE_OPTIONS, INTERFACE_LINK_LIBRARIES, plus the non-INTERFACE_ versions for the target's own build. When you target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE mylib), at generation time CMake walks the link graph: for every target reachable, it unions the INTERFACE_* properties into app's compile/link command — recursively, so mylib's PUBLIC deps' interfaces also flow through. Generator expressions ($<...>) defer evaluation to generation time because a requirement can differ per configuration, per compiler, or per "am I being built vs installed": e.g. target_include_directories(mylib PUBLIC $<BUILD_INTERFACE:${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include> $<INSTALL_INTERFACE:include>) — when another target in the same build tree consumes mylib, the BUILD_INTERFACE path (absolute, in your source tree) is used; when mylib is install()ed and its exported config is later consumed by an external project via find_package, the INSTALL_INTERFACE path (relative to the install prefix) is used instead. This is why exporting a library correctly requires install(TARGETS mylib EXPORT ...) + install(EXPORT ...) generating a mylibConfig.cmake that recreates the imported target with install-tree paths. Other genexes: $<CONFIG:Debug>, $<COMPILE_LANG_AND_ID:CXX,GNU>, $<TARGET_PROPERTY:...>. The mental model: CMakeLists.txt builds a graph of targets-with-properties; generation flattens it per (config, target) into concrete flags, with genexes as the escape hatch for anything not known until then.
Compare find_package (CONFIG vs MODULE mode), FetchContent, and a package manager (vcpkg/Conan) for dependency acquisition.
find_package(Foo) MODULE mode: CMake runs a FindFoo.cmake script (shipped with CMake or your project) that gropes around the system with find_library/find_path and sets variables (or, if well-written, imports a target). Works for libraries that don't ship CMake config, but the Find scripts are heuristic, often don't propagate transitive deps, and version handling is weak. find_package(Foo CONFIG): the library was built/installed with CMake and shipped a FooConfig.cmake that recreates proper imported targets with full usage requirements and dependency chaining — the gold standard, but requires the dependency to already be installed somewhere CMake looks (system, CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH). Neither mode fetches anything. FetchContent: declares a dependency by URL/git ref, downloads it at configure time, and add_subdirectorys it into your build so its targets become available directly — zero external tooling, great for small header/leaf libs and CI reproducibility, but it rebuilds the dep as part of your build (slower clean builds, no shared cache across projects), and version/ODR conflicts arise if two of your deps FetchContent the same thing at different versions. vcpkg / Conan: a real package manager — resolves a dependency graph with version constraints, builds/caches binary packages per configuration (triplet/profile), and integrates via a toolchain file so find_package(CONFIG) then "just works". Best for larger projects with many/transitive C++ deps and for binary caching across a team/CI, at the cost of adopting the tool, writing manifests, and occasional recipe gaps. Rule of thumb: find_package(CONFIG) for system/OS-provided libs; FetchContent for a handful of small pinned deps; vcpkg/Conan once the dependency count and version-conflict pain justify it.

Build Types, Flags & Optimization

What -O2, -g, NDEBUG, and friends actually change.

Notes

Optimisation levels

FlagEffect
-O0none — fast compile, easy debugging, slow code. Dev default.
-O1/-O2most optimisations; -O2 is the usual release level.
-O3-O2 + aggressive inlining/vectorisation; sometimes bigger and not faster — measure.
-Os / -Ozoptimise for size (embedded, code-cache-bound).
-Ogoptimise but keep debuggability — good for debug builds you also want responsive.
-ffast-mathrelax IEEE-754 (reassociation, no NaN/inf handling, FTZ) — faster FP, changes results. Opt-in, per-file ideally.
$ gcc -O0 -g   app.c -o app   && ls -l app   # dev: fast compile, step-through debug, slow
$ gcc -O2      app.c -o app                  # release baseline
$ gcc -O3 -march=native app.c -o app         # aggressive -- BENCHMARK vs -O2, can be slower
$ gcc -Os      app.c -o app                  # smallest binary (embedded)

// -ffast-math changes results -- scope it to one file, never whole-project
$ gcc -O2 -ffast-math dsp.c -c    # isnan() checks now compile away; sum reassociates

Debug info & asserts

  • -g emits DWARF debug info. It's independent of -O — you can (and CI should) ship -O2 -g, then strip or split the debug info into a separate file (objcopy --only-keep-debug + --add-gnu-debuglink).
  • -DNDEBUG disables assert() (and often triggers "release" code paths). Release builds define it; be sure asserts have no side effects you rely on.
  • -fno-omit-frame-pointer keeps frame pointers so profilers/`perf` can unwind cheaply — a small speed cost, big observability win. Often worth it in production.
# ship optimised + fully symbolicated, with zero runtime cost:
$ gcc -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer app.c -o app
$ objcopy --only-keep-debug app app.debug     # extract symbols
$ strip --strip-debug app                      # ship this (small)
$ objcopy --add-gnu-debuglink=app.debug app    # gdb/perf auto-find app.debug

// -DNDEBUG danger: side effects in an assert vanish in release
assert(init() == 0);        // release: init() is NEVER called

Target & safety flags

  • -march=native / -march=x86-64-v3 — use newer instructions (AVX2 etc.). native ties the binary to the build machine's CPU.
  • Hardening: -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -fstack-protector-strong, -fPIE -pie, -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now, -fstack-clash-protection, -fcf-protection.
  • -flto for whole-program optimisation (release/CI).
# distributable: pick a defined ISA baseline, NOT native
$ gcc -O2 -march=x86-64-v2 app.c -o app   # SSE4.2/POPCNT -- runs on ~any 64-bit CPU since 2009
# -march=native on a build box with AVX-512 -> customer's older CPU: SIGILL

# the standard hardening bundle:
$ gcc -O2 -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -fstack-protector-strong -fstack-clash-protection \
      -fcf-protection -fPIE -pie -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now app.c -o app
$ checksec --file=app     # verify: RELRO Full, Canary yes, NX yes, PIE yes

Build types in CMake

Debug (-O0 -g), Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG), RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g -DNDEBUG — the usual shipping choice), MinSizeRel (-Os -DNDEBUG).

$ cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo   # the usual ship config
$ cmake --build build

# multi-config generators (VS / Ninja Multi-Config) pick per build, not per configure:
$ cmake --build build --config Release
# override just the extra flags without clobbering the type's defaults:
$ cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE="-O2 -g"
Cheat Sheet
  • -O0 dev, -O2 release default, -O3 aggressive (measure — can be slower/bigger), -Os/-Oz size, -Og debug-friendly optimised.
  • -g is orthogonal to -O. Ship -O2 -g then split/strip debug info (objcopy --only-keep-debug).
  • -DNDEBUG kills assert() — release builds set it; keep asserts side-effect-free.
  • -fno-omit-frame-pointer for cheap profiler unwinding (small cost, worth it in prod).
  • -march=native uses the build CPU's ISA → not portable; pick an ISA baseline (x86-64-v2/v3) for distributables.
  • Hardening: _FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -fstack-protector-strong, -fPIE -pie, full RELRO (-z relro -z now).
  • -ffast-math changes results — opt-in, scoped.
  • CMake: Debug, Release, RelWithDebInfo (usual ship), MinSizeRel.
Q&A
Is -g mutually exclusive with -O2?
No — they're independent. -O2 -g gives optimised code with debug info; optimisation makes debugging less precise (inlined/reordered code, "optimized out" variables) but you can still get useful backtraces and inspect much of the state. Shipping RelWithDebInfo and keeping the symbols is standard practice.
What does -DNDEBUG do?
Defines the NDEBUG macro, which makes the standard assert() expand to nothing — so assertions are compiled out in release builds. Never put required side effects inside assert().
Why might -O3 be slower than -O2?
Its aggressive inlining and loop unrolling/vectorisation can bloat code, increasing instruction-cache pressure and sometimes triggering the AVX-512 frequency penalty, without a proportional compute benefit. It's workload-dependent — benchmark both.
What's the downside of -march=native for a released binary?
It compiles for the exact CPU features of the build machine, so the binary may use instructions (AVX2, BMI2, AVX-512) that a customer's older CPU lacks — illegal-instruction crash. For distribution, target a defined baseline (-march=x86-64-v2/-v3) or ship multiple variants / use function multi-versioning.
Why keep frame pointers (-fno-omit-frame-pointer) in production?
They let sampling profilers and perf walk the stack with a cheap, reliable method instead of relying on DWARF CFI unwinding (slow, sometimes incomplete for optimised code). The ~1% runtime cost buys you production-quality flame graphs and crash backtraces.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which optimisation level is the typical release default?
-O2.
What macro disables assert()?
NDEBUG (usually via -DNDEBUG).
Which CMake build type gives optimised code plus debug symbols for shipping?
RelWithDebInfo.

Intermediate core

Your release build is fast but crash reports have useless stack traces. Fix without slowing it down?
Build with -O2 -g (debug info doesn't slow the code), then separate the symbols: objcopy --only-keep-debug app app.debug; strip --strip-debug app; objcopy --add-gnu-debuglink=app.debug app. Ship the stripped app, archive app.debug, and load it in the debugger / symbolication service. Optionally add -fno-omit-frame-pointer for cheap unwinding. Now traces are fully symbolicated with no runtime cost.
A numerical result changed after you added -ffast-math "for speed". What happened and what do you do?
-ffast-math lets the compiler reassociate floating-point ((a+b)+c → a+(b+c)), assume no NaN/Inf, flush denormals to zero, and use less-accurate reciprocal/rsqrt — all of which change results, sometimes materially in ill-conditioned code. Options: remove it and optimise the hot loop specifically (vectorise manually, use FMA via -ffp-contract=fast which is safer than full fast-math), or scope -ffast-math to only the files/functions where the accuracy loss is acceptable (#pragma float_control / __attribute__((optimize)) / per-file CMake flags), and add a regression test pinning the numerical output.

Advanced deep

What is Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO), what does it improve that static heuristics can't, and what's the workflow cost?
Compilers guess which branches are hot, which functions to inline, and how to lay out code using static heuristics (loop depth, [[likely]], call-graph shape) — often wrong for real workloads. PGO feeds them measured behaviour: (1) build an instrumented binary (-fprofile-generate) that records, per branch/call/function, execution counts; (2) run it on a representative workload to produce profile data; (3) rebuild with -fprofile-use, so the optimiser knows the actual hot paths. Wins static analysis can't get: hot/cold splitting (move rarely-executed code — error handling, cold branches — out of line into a .text.unlikely section, so the hot path is dense and i-cache/µop-cache resident); accurate inlining (inline the calls that are actually frequent, don't bloat for cold ones); block layout so the common branch direction is the fall-through (fewer taken branches, better prefetch); better register allocation and spill placement biased to hot blocks; devirtualization when the profile shows one call target dominates; and switch/jump-table vs branch-chain decisions. Typical gains: 5–20% on branch-heavy code (compilers, browsers, databases — Chrome, Firefox, LLVM itself, MySQL all ship PGO'd). Costs: the workflow needs a stable, representative training workload (a bad profile can hurt); it doubles the build (instrument, run, rebuild); profile data must be regenerated when the code changes enough (stale profiles degrade gracefully but drift); and CI complexity. AutoFDO / CSSPGO reduce the cost by using perf samples from production (no instrumented build) at some accuracy loss. PGO composes with LTO (ThinLTO + PGO is the common high-end release config) — PGO tells LTO what's hot across the whole program. BOLT goes further, re-optimising the linked binary from profiles.
Explain the security-hardening flag set for a production Linux binary and what each mitigates.
-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2/3 (with -O1+): replaces unbounded libc calls (memcpy, sprintf, strcpy…) with __*_chk variants that know the destination buffer size (from __builtin_object_size) and abort on overflow — catches many buffer overflows at runtime with near-zero cost; level 3 handles more dynamic sizes. -fstack-protector-strong: inserts a random "canary" between local buffers and the saved return address in functions with risky stack layout; a stack buffer overflow that smashes the return address also corrupts the canary, detected on function return → __stack_chk_fail aborts before the corrupted return is used. Mitigates classic stack-smashing. -fstack-clash-protection: emits probing code when growing the stack by large amounts so a huge alloca/VLA can't "jump the guard page" and silently land in the heap (the Stack Clash class). -fPIE -pie: makes the main executable position-independent so ASLR randomises its base too (not just libraries) — defeats attacks that rely on fixed code addresses for ROP gadgets. -Wl,-z,relro -Wl,-z,now (full RELRO): resolve all dynamic relocations at load time, then mprotect the GOT and other relocation tables read-only — blocks GOT-overwrite / one-shot function-pointer hijacks (partial RELRO leaves the lazy-binding PLT GOT writable). -fcf-protection=full (Intel CET): emits endbr64 landing pads and enables a shadow stack — hardware-enforced control-flow integrity against ROP/JOP. -Wl,-z,noexecstack: mark the stack non-executable (defeats classic shellcode injection). -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks / -fwrapv in some contexts: rein in UB-based optimisations that have removed security checks. Distros compile with most of this by default (Debian/Fedora hardening flags); the cost is single-digit-percent runtime and a bit of size, universally considered worth it for anything network-facing or privileged.

Sanitizers & Static Analysis in CI

Catching memory bugs, UB, and races automatically — before they reach production.

Notes

The sanitizers (compile-time instrumentation)

FlagCatchesOverhead
-fsanitize=address (ASan)heap/stack/global buffer overflow, use-after-free, use-after-return/scope, double free, leaks~2× time, ~2–3× memory
-fsanitize=undefined (UBSan)signed overflow, misaligned/null deref, OOB shifts, bad enum/bool, invalid casts, moresmall
-fsanitize=thread (TSan)data races, some deadlocks/lock-order issues~5–15× time, ~5–10× memory
-fsanitize=memory (MSan)reads of uninitialised memory (Clang; needs instrumented libs)~3×

ASan+UBSan combine; TSan and MSan are exclusive of ASan. Build a dedicated CI job per sanitizer, run the full test suite, treat any report as a failure. Add -fno-sanitize-recover to abort on first error; symbolise with llvm-symbolizer.

$ clang -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all -g -O1 app.c -o app
$ ./app
app.c:12:5: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1   # UBSan
==4521==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ...             # ASan, both in one run

$ CC="clang -fsanitize=thread"  make check    # SEPARATE job: TSan can't combine with ASan
$ ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1 ./app

Static analysis (no execution)

  • Compiler warnings — the cheapest analyser. -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, and crucially -Werror so warnings can't accumulate. Add -Wconversion, -Wshadow, -Wnon-virtual-dtor as tolerated.
  • clang-tidy — lint + modernise + bug-prone-pattern checks; cppcheck; clang --analyze / Coverity / PVS-Studio for deeper path-sensitive analysis.
  • include-what-you-use, clang-format for hygiene.
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wshadow -Wconversion -c app.c   # the free analyser -- fails the build

$ clang-tidy --checks='bugprone-*,performance-*,modernize-*' app.c -- -std=c++20
app.cpp:8:9: warning: use range-based for loop [modernize-loop-convert]

$ cppcheck --enable=all --error-exitcode=1 src/   # path-sensitive: null derefs, leaks, dead code

CI gate structure

  1. Fast: build with -Werror, run unit tests.
  2. Per-PR: clang-tidy on changed files, format check.
  3. Nightly / pre-merge: ASan+UBSan suite, TSan suite, MSan suite, valgrind for the cases sanitizers miss, fuzzers (libFuzzer/AFL) on parsers.
  4. Release: static analyzer, LTO/PGO build, reproducible-build check.
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  fast:      { steps: [ "cmake -B b -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-Werror", "cmake --build b", "ctest --test-dir b" ] }
  tidy:      { steps: [ "git diff --name-only origin/main | grep '\\.cpp$' | xargs clang-tidy" ] }
  asan:      { steps: [ "CXX='clang++ -fsanitize=address,undefined' cmake -B b && ctest --test-dir b" ] }
  tsan:      { steps: [ "CXX='clang++ -fsanitize=thread'            cmake -B b && ctest --test-dir b" ] }
  fuzz:      { steps: [ "clang++ -fsanitize=fuzzer,address parse_fuzz.cc -o f && ./f -max_total_time=300" ] }

Reproducible builds

Same source + toolchain → bit-identical output. Requires stripping timestamps (-Wno-builtin-macro-redefined -D__DATE__=… or SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH), sorted inputs, fixed paths (-ffile-prefix-map), deterministic archive members (ar D). Enables build caching and supply-chain verification.

$ export SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$(git log -1 --format=%ct)   # stable __DATE__/__TIME__
$ gcc -ffile-prefix-map=$PWD=. -O2 -c *.c               # strip absolute build paths from debug info
$ ar Drcs libfoo.a *.o                                   # D = zero mtime/uid/gid in the archive

$ gcc ... -o app && sha256sum app        # build twice on different machines...
$ gcc ... -o app2 && sha256sum app2      # ...hashes must match -> supply-chain verifiable
Cheat Sheet
  • ASan (-fsanitize=address): OOB, use-after-free/return/scope, double free, leaks. ~2×.
  • UBSan (=undefined): signed overflow, null/misaligned deref, bad shifts/casts. Cheap; combine with ASan.
  • TSan (=thread): data races, lock-order. ~5–15×. Exclusive of ASan.
  • MSan (=memory, Clang): uninitialised reads; needs instrumented deps.
  • Run the whole test suite under each in a dedicated CI job; any report = fail. -fno-sanitize-recover.
  • Static: -Wall -Wextra -Werror (gate warnings), clang-tidy on diffs, cppcheck/Coverity for depth.
  • Fuzz parsers/decoders (libFuzzer + ASan/UBSan) on every change.
  • Reproducible builds: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, -ffile-prefix-map, sorted inputs, ar D → caching + supply-chain trust.
Q&A
What does AddressSanitizer catch that a normal build won't?
Out-of-bounds accesses (heap, stack, globals), use-after-free, use-after-return/scope, double free, and (with LeakSanitizer) memory leaks — with a precise report showing the faulting access and the relevant allocation/free stacks. Overhead ~2×, so it's a test/CI tool, not production.
Can you combine ASan and TSan?
No — they use incompatible shadow-memory schemes. Run them as separate builds/CI jobs. ASan + UBSan can be combined.
Why run tests under UBSan even though the code "works"?
Undefined behaviour (signed overflow, null/misaligned dereference, out-of-range shift, invalid enum) may produce correct results today and be miscompiled tomorrow when the optimiser exploits the "can't happen" assumption. UBSan flags it deterministically at the point it occurs.
What's the value of -Werror in CI?
It turns warnings into build failures, so they can't accumulate and drown out new ones. Combined with -Wall -Wextra, the compiler becomes a free static analyser that every developer already runs.
What makes a build "reproducible" and why care?
Given the same source and toolchain, it produces bit-identical binaries — achieved by eliminating embedded timestamps, absolute paths, non-deterministic ordering, and PRNG-seeded layout. It enables reliable build caching and lets third parties verify that a released binary really came from the published source (supply-chain security).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Flag for the thread (data-race) sanitizer?
-fsanitize=thread.
Which two sanitizers are commonly combined?
AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (-fsanitize=address,undefined).
What compiler flag makes warnings fail the build?
-Werror.

Intermediate core

ASan reports a use-after-free with no obvious owner. How do you use the report?
The report has three stacks: where the invalid read/write happened, where the block was allocated, and where it was freed. Trace the "freed here" stack to find who released it prematurely, and the "allocated here" stack to identify the object. Often it's ownership confusion — two owners, a dangling callback/iterator, or an object freed while a task referencing it is still queued. Fix by clarifying ownership (smart pointers, clear lifetime), not by suppressing.
TSan flags a race on a variable you "know" is fine because writes are rare. Response?
"Rare" doesn't make a data race defined — it's still UB and the compiler/CPU can reorder or tear it. TSan is correct to flag it. If it's a flag, make it std::atomic (relaxed is enough for a plain flag); if it guards data, add the proper lock or acquire/release. If it's genuinely a benign statistics counter where you accept approximate values, still make it a relaxed atomic so it's well-defined, and annotate/suppress only that specific access with justification.

Advanced deep

How does AddressSanitizer actually detect out-of-bounds and use-after-free — what's "shadow memory" and "redzones"?
ASan maps every 8 bytes of application memory to 1 byte of shadow memory (at address (addr >> 3) + offset), which encodes how many of those 8 bytes are addressable (0–8) or a negative code meaning "poisoned" (redzone, freed, stack-after-return, etc.). The compiler instruments every memory access to first compute the shadow address, load the shadow byte, and check whether the access is fully within addressable bytes — a few instructions, hence ~2×. Allocations are wrapped in redzones: malloc(n) actually reserves n + poisoned bytes before and after, so an overflow of a few bytes lands in a poisoned redzone and is caught immediately with the allocation stack. On free, the whole region's shadow is poisoned and the block goes into a quarantine (FIFO, bounded size) rather than being reused right away — so a use-after-free hits poisoned shadow and reports the free stack; only after the block ages out of quarantine can it be reallocated (which is why ASan can miss a UAF if quarantine is small and allocation pressure is high). Stack variables get redzones inserted by the compiler and their shadow poisoned on scope exit (catches use-after-scope) and on return (use-after-return, with fake stack frames). Globals get redzones and registration so overflows into adjacent globals are caught. Limitations: it detects spatial errors near the redzones and temporal errors within the quarantine window, but not arbitrary wild pointers into valid-but-wrong objects, not overflows that skip entirely over a redzone into another live object, and not uninitialised reads (that's MSan). It also can't see into non-instrumented code (system libraries) — hence interceptors for libc functions.
Design a CI strategy that gives strong safety guarantees for a C++ network service without making PR feedback unbearably slow.
Tier by cost vs signal. Per-commit / PR (fast, blocking, <10 min): build with -Wall -Wextra -Werror on the two primary compilers (GCC + Clang — each catches different things), run the unit + fast integration tests, run clang-tidy and clang-format only on the diff (bounded time), and a quick UBSan run (cheap overhead) of the unit suite. Cache the build (ccache/sccache) and use a fast linker (mold/lld) so incremental PR builds stay short. Merge-queue / pre-merge (medium, blocking, ~30–60 min): full ASan+UBSan run of the entire test suite (unit + integration + end-to-end), TSan run of the concurrency-relevant tests, a Release build with LTO to catch ODR/optimiser-exposed bugs, and a short (few-minutes) fuzzing run of each parser/protocol decoder seeded from the corpus, with any new crash blocking. Nightly / continuous (non-blocking, hours): long fuzzing sessions with corpus minimisation and coverage feedback (libFuzzer/AFL++ under ASan+UBSan), MSan build + suite (needs instrumented deps, so pinned), Valgrind for the subset sanitizers can't cover, the static analyzer (Coverity/clang-analyzer) full run, a sanitizer build under production-like load/soak, and a reproducible-build verification. Release: PGO+ThinLTO build with the hardening flag set, SBOM generation, and signing. Cross-cutting: keep a flaky-test quarantine so infra noise doesn't erode trust in the sanitizer gates; make sanitizer failures page the author with the symbolised report attached; and periodically run the full sanitizer matrix on main so a slow-accumulating issue in rarely-exercised code is still caught. The principle: cheap, high-signal checks block the developer loop; expensive, high-coverage checks run asynchronously but still gate the merge or the release.

Requirements → Classes → Responsibilities

The first 10 minutes of any LLD interview: turn a vague prompt into a bounded object model.

Notes

Step 1 — clarify & bound the scope

  • Ask about the core use cases, scale, and what's explicitly out of scope. "Design a parking lot" — do we handle payment? multiple floors? reservations? EVs?
  • State assumptions out loud and get agreement. A crisp, small scope beats a sprawling one.
  • List functional requirements (what it does) and a few non-functional ones (concurrency, latency, extensibility) that will shape the design.

Step 2 — find the entities

A quick heuristic (Abbott's technique): nouns → candidate classes / attributes, verbs → methods / interactions. Filter: keep nouns that have state and behaviour; drop synonyms, vague terms, and things that are really attributes of another class.

Step 3 — assign responsibilities (CRC cards)

For each class write a Class–Responsibility–Collaborator card: what it knows and does, and which other classes it needs. This surfaces:

  • Classes with too many unrelated responsibilities (split — SRP).
  • Missing classes (a responsibility with no owner).
  • Coupling (a class collaborating with everything — a "god object").

Step 4 — relationships & invariants

  • Decide association / aggregation / composition and multiplicity between classes.
  • Name the invariants each class must maintain (a ParkingFloor never reports more free spots than it has; an Account balance never goes negative) — these justify encapsulation and drive method design.
  • Only then think about patterns — and only where a real axis of change exists.
Cheat Sheet
  • 1. Clarify scope: core use cases, scale, explicit non-goals. State assumptions, get buy-in.
  • 2. Functional + a few non-functional requirements (concurrency, extensibility) that shape structure.
  • 3. Nouns → classes/attributes; verbs → methods. Drop synonyms and pure attributes.
  • 4. CRC cards: Class / Responsibilities / Collaborators — exposes god objects, missing classes, coupling.
  • 5. Relationships (assoc/agg/comp) + multiplicity; write down each class's invariants.
  • 6. Patterns last, only where there's a genuine axis of change.
  • Deliver iteratively: minimal correct model first, then extend under interviewer's prompts.
Q&A
What's the first thing to do when given an LLD prompt?
Clarify and bound the scope — ask which use cases matter, what scale, and what's out of scope — then state your assumptions explicitly. A well-scoped small design is far better than an ambitious vague one.
How do you derive candidate classes from a description?
Extract the nouns as candidate classes/attributes and the verbs as candidate methods/interactions, then filter: keep nouns that carry both state and behaviour, discard synonyms and things that are really fields of another class.
What is a CRC card and what does it reveal?
A note listing a Class's Responsibilities and its Collaborators. Doing this per class quickly reveals classes doing too much (violating SRP), responsibilities with no home (a missing class), and classes that talk to everything (excessive coupling / a god object).
Why write down invariants early?
They define what "valid" means for each object, which justifies making state private (only the class can maintain them) and drives the method set (each mutating method must preserve them). They also become your test assertions.
When should you introduce a design pattern?
Only after the core model is clear, and only where there's a real, identified axis of variation (multiple payment methods → Strategy; a family of related objects to create → Factory). Adding patterns pre-emptively is over-engineering.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Nouns in a requirement map to what?
Candidate classes or attributes.
What does CRC stand for?
Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators.
Should you start coding the full design immediately?
No — clarify scope and assumptions first, then build the minimal model and iterate.

Intermediate core

The interviewer says "design a library management system". List the clarifying questions you'd ask.
Which actors (members, librarians, admins)? Physical books only or e-books/audio? Multiple copies of a title? Reservations/holds and a queue? Fines for late returns — and payment, or just tracking? Search requirements (by title/author/ISBN/subject)? Branches/multiple locations? Membership limits (max books, loan period by member type)? Scale (books, members, transactions/day)? Concurrency (two members reserving the last copy)? Notifications? Which of these are in scope for this session?
You've listed 15 candidate classes and it feels sprawling. How do you cut it down?
Merge synonyms and near-duplicates; demote nouns that are just attributes (a "barcode" is a field of BookCopy, not a class) or transient values (a "search result" is a return type, not an entity); defer anything outside the agreed scope (payment gateway integration, analytics); and group by responsibility — if two classes always change together and have no independent behaviour, consider one class. Aim for the smallest set that expresses the core use cases; you can add classes when the interviewer pushes on an extension.

Advanced deep

How do you decide the boundary between "domain model" classes and "service/coordinator" classes?
Domain classes (entities, value objects) own state + the invariants over that state and the behaviour that's intrinsic to them: a Loan knows its due date and whether it's overdue; a BookCopy knows if it's available. Push behaviour onto these where it only needs their own data ("tell, don't ask") — a rich domain model. Service/coordinator classes own use-case orchestration that spans multiple entities and touches infrastructure: CheckoutService.checkout(member, copy) validates member limits, checks copy availability, creates a Loan, updates the copy, schedules a due-date notification, and commits a transaction. The test: if a method needs data or collaborators from several aggregates, or does I/O (persistence, messaging, external calls), it belongs in a service; if it operates on one object's own state and enforces that object's rules, it belongs on the entity. Anti-patterns at the extremes: an anemic model (entities are just getters/setters, all logic in fat services — procedural code wearing OO clothes) and a god entity (one class does orchestration + persistence + rules for the whole system). A good split keeps entities testable in isolation with no mocks, and services thin (mostly sequencing calls to entities and repositories).
What is the aggregate/aggregate-root concept and why does it matter for LLD consistency?
An aggregate (from Domain-Driven Design) is a cluster of objects treated as a single unit for data changes, with one entity designated the aggregate root — the only member outside code is allowed to hold a reference to. All mutations go through the root's methods, which enforce the invariants that span the cluster. Example: an Order root with OrderLine children — you never modify an OrderLine directly; you call order.addLine(...) / order.changeQuantity(...), and the Order re-checks "total ≤ credit limit" and "no duplicate SKU" atomically. Why it matters for LLD: (1) it gives a clear transactional/consistency boundary — one aggregate is saved atomically, and cross-aggregate consistency is eventual (via domain events), which prevents huge lock scopes and tangled object graphs; (2) it stops the "action at a distance" bug where code mutates a child object and the parent's invariant silently breaks; (3) it bounds what you load and lock — you fetch the whole Order aggregate, not a lazy-loaded graph of the entire database; (4) references between aggregates are by id, not object pointer, keeping the model loosely coupled and serializable. In an interview, identifying "what's the aggregate root here, and what's inside vs referenced by id" is a strong signal — e.g. for a parking lot, is ParkingSpot its own root or part of a ParkingFloor aggregate? The answer shapes locking, allocation, and how you'd shard/persist it.

SOLID Applied to a Real Design

Turning the five principles into concrete class splits and interfaces.

Notes

Worked example: an order-processing module

Start with a fat OrderService.placeOrder() that validates, prices, charges a card, writes to the DB, and emails a receipt. Apply SOLID:

PrincipleConcrete move
SRPSplit into OrderValidator, PricingEngine, PaymentProcessor, OrderRepository, Notifier — each with one reason to change.
OCPNew payment type = a new PaymentMethod implementation + registry entry; no edit to OrderService.
LSPEvery PaymentMethod honours the same contract (charge returns success/failure, never silently no-ops). A FreeOrderPayment that ignores the amount but still reports success is fine; one that throws "not supported" is a violation.
ISPSplit a fat Repository into OrderReader + OrderWriter so a read-only reporting path doesn't depend on write methods.
DIPOrderService depends on the interfaces (PaymentProcessor, OrderRepository, Notifier), which are injected. The concrete Stripe/Postgres/SES classes are wired at the composition root.

The payoff

  • Unit-testable: inject fakes for payment/repo/notifier; test OrderService logic in isolation.
  • Swappable infra: change DB or payment provider without touching business logic.
  • Parallel work: teams own different collaborators behind stable interfaces.

The caution

Every interface with one implementation "for testing" is a smell — introduce a seam only where change or testing genuinely needs it. Five collaborator interfaces for a stable 30-line class is over-engineering. Apply SOLID where the pain is, guided by the rule of three.

Cheat Sheet
  • SRP: one class per reason-to-change — split validate / price / charge / persist / notify.
  • OCP: extend via new implementations + registration, not by editing the coordinator.
  • LSP: every implementation fully honours the interface contract (no "not supported" throws, no strengthened preconditions).
  • ISP: split fat interfaces into role interfaces (Reader/Writer) so clients depend only on what they use.
  • DIP: high-level code depends on injected interfaces; concretes wired at the composition root.
  • Payoff: isolation-testable, swappable infra, parallel team work.
  • Caution: no speculative seams; apply where change/testing actually demands it (rule of three).
Q&A
How does DIP make a service testable?
The service depends on interfaces (PaymentProcessor, Repository) rather than concrete classes, and receives them via constructor injection. Tests pass in fakes/mocks, so the service's logic is exercised with no database, network, or real payment calls.
Give a concrete OCP-compliant way to add a discount type.
Define a DiscountRule interface with apply(cart) -> adjustment. Each discount (percentage-off, buy-one-get-one, loyalty) is a class implementing it. The pricing engine iterates a list of rules it was given. Adding a discount is a new class + adding it to the configured list — no change to the engine.
What does an LSP violation look like in a payment hierarchy?
A subtype that doesn't honour the base contract: a GiftCardPayment whose charge() throws UnsupportedOperationException for amounts over the balance instead of returning a failure result, or one that requires an extra setup call the base doesn't. Client code written against PaymentMethod breaks on that subtype.
When is splitting a class per SRP not worth it?
When the "responsibilities" always change together and for the same reason, when the class is small and stable, or when the split would just create anemic data holders plus a procedural coordinator. SRP is about reasons to change, not line count.
Why is "one interface per class, always" an anti-pattern?
It adds indirection and files without decoupling anything real — if there's only ever one implementation and no test seam need, the interface is ceremony. Introduce interfaces at genuine variation points and module boundaries.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which principle says "depend on abstractions, not concretions"?
Dependency Inversion (the D in SOLID).
A class that validates input and writes to the DB violates which principle?
Single Responsibility — two reasons to change.
What pattern typically implements OCP for "swappable behaviour"?
Strategy (an interface + interchangeable implementations, injected).

Intermediate core

Refactor a ReportGenerator that queries the DB, computes stats, and renders HTML.
Three responsibilities → ReportRepository (data access, one reason to change: schema/query), ReportCalculator (business rules), ReportRenderer (presentation, interface with HtmlRenderer/PdfRenderer/CsvRenderer implementations — OCP). A thin ReportService orchestrates: renderer.render(calculator.compute(repository.fetch(params))). Now a layout change can't break the query; you can unit-test the calculator with in-memory data; adding a format is a new renderer class.
Your team keeps editing one NotificationService switch statement to add channels (email, SMS, push, Slack). Fix.
OCP + Strategy: a NotificationChannel interface (send(recipient, message)), one class per channel, registered in a map keyed by channel type (or discovered via DI). NotificationService looks up the channel(s) for a user's preferences and delegates. Adding Slack = a new SlackChannel class + registration; the service and existing channels are untouched, and each channel is independently testable.

Advanced deep

SOLID can produce a maze of tiny classes and interfaces. How do you keep a design SOLID and readable?
Treat SOLID as a set of forces to balance, not rules to maximise. Practical guardrails: (1) Introduce seams reactively — when a second reason to change actually appears (rule of three), not in anticipation; a stable class doesn't need five injected collaborators. (2) Keep interfaces at module boundaries and true variation points (payment providers, storage backends, notification channels) — not around every collaboration. (3) Prefer a rich domain model so behaviour lives with data; don't shred everything into anemic structs + services. (4) Package by feature, not by layer — a "checkout" package containing its entities, service, and adapters reads better than parallel controllers/, services/, repositories/ trees where one feature is scattered across all of them. (5) Use language features instead of pattern scaffolding — a lambda/function type for a one-method Strategy, a sealed hierarchy + pattern matching where a Visitor would be overkill. (6) Name things by role so the design documents itself. (7) Measure with the actual goal: can a newcomer find where to make a given change, and can that change be made without touching unrelated code? If yes, the abstraction level is right regardless of class count. Over-applied SOLID and under-applied SOLID are both maintenance costs; the target is "no more indirection than the observed rate of change justifies".
How do you apply DIP without a heavyweight DI container, and what does the "composition root" actually contain?
DIP is just "depend on interfaces, inject implementations" — you don't need a framework. Manual (poor-man's) DI: every class takes its dependencies as constructor parameters and stores them; nothing news up its own collaborators (no new PostgresRepository() inside OrderService). The composition root is the single place — main(), or a small Bootstrap/AppFactory — where you construct the concrete graph: create the config, the DB connection pool, new PostgresOrderRepository(pool), new StripePaymentProcessor(apiKey), new SesNotifier(...), then new OrderService(repo, payment, notifier), and hand the top-level object to the framework/entry point. It's the only place that references concrete infrastructure classes; everything below sees only interfaces. Benefits over a container: the wiring is explicit, compile-checked, greppable, and debuggable (a stack trace shows real constructors, not reflection magic); no runtime "binding not found" surprises; startup is deterministic. A DI container earns its keep only when the graph is large (hundreds of services), you need lifecycle scoping (per-request objects), or the framework mandates one — and even then, keep the container config in the composition root and don't let @Inject/attributes leak framework knowledge into domain classes. For most LLD-interview-sized designs, constructor injection + a hand-written composition root is the right answer and shows you understand what a container would be doing.

UML Class & Sequence Diagrams

The minimal notation you need to communicate a design on a whiteboard.

Notes

Class diagram

A box per class: name, attributes, operations. Visibility: + public, - private, # protected. Relationships between boxes:

LineMeans
solid lineassociation — "knows about / uses"
hollow diamondaggregation — "has-a", shared, independent lifetime
filled diamondcomposition — "owns-a", part dies with the whole
hollow triangle, solid lineinheritance — "is-a"
hollow triangle, dashed linerealization — "implements interface"
dashed arrowdependency — transient use (a parameter/return type)

Multiplicity on the ends: 1, 0..1, *, 1..* — e.g. a ParkingLot 1 →→ * ParkingFloor.

Sequence diagram

Shows an interaction over time: participants across the top, vertical lifelines, horizontal arrows for messages (solid = call, dashed = return), activation bars for "is executing". Great for walking through one use case ("checkout flow") and spotting who talks to whom, chatty round-trips, and missing error paths.

State diagram

States as rounded boxes, transitions as labelled arrows (event [guard] / action). Essential for anything with a lifecycle: an Order (created → paid → shipped → delivered / cancelled), an elevator car, a TCP connection.

In an interview

  • You don't need perfect UML — boxes, lines, and multiplicity communicate 90% of it.
  • Draw the class diagram to show structure, one sequence diagram for the main flow, a state diagram if there's a non-trivial lifecycle.
  • Keep it legible; don't cram 20 classes — show the core, mention the rest.
Cheat Sheet
  • Class box: name / attributes / operations. Visibility + - #.
  • Relations: association (line), aggregation (hollow diamond), composition (filled diamond), inheritance (hollow triangle solid), realization (hollow triangle dashed), dependency (dashed arrow).
  • Multiplicity on ends: 1, 0..1, *, 1..*.
  • Sequence diagram: participants + lifelines; solid arrow = call, dashed = return; for tracing one use case.
  • State diagram: states + event [guard] / action transitions; for lifecycles (order, elevator, connection).
  • Interview: class diagram for structure + one sequence for the main flow + state diagram if lifecycle is non-trivial. Legible > complete.
Q&A
How do you show "class A owns B, and B is destroyed with A" in a class diagram?
Composition — a solid line with a filled diamond on the A end. Aggregation (hollow diamond) would mean B can outlive A / be shared.
What's the difference between the realization and inheritance arrows?
Both use a hollow triangle head. Inheritance ("extends a class") uses a solid line; realization ("implements an interface") uses a dashed line.
What is a sequence diagram best for?
Tracing a single scenario over time — which objects send which messages in what order — to validate the interaction, spot excessive round-trips, and check that error/timeout paths are handled.
When do you need a state diagram?
When an object has a meaningful lifecycle with rules about which transitions are allowed — an order, a document workflow, a connection, an elevator car. It makes illegal transitions and missing events obvious.
What does multiplicity 1..* on an association end mean?
"One or more" — there must be at least one linked instance on that end (e.g. an Order has 1..* OrderLines).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which diamond means composition?
The filled (solid) diamond.
What does a dashed arrow between two class boxes indicate?
A dependency — one class transiently uses the other (as a parameter, local, or return type).
What kind of diagram traces one use case's message flow?
A sequence diagram.

Intermediate core

Sketch (in words) the class relationships for: a Library has Branches; each Branch has many BookCopy; a BookCopy is a copy of a Book; a Member borrows BookCopys via Loan.
Library 1 —◊ 1..* Branch (composition — branches belong to the library). Branch 1 —◊ * BookCopy (composition). BookCopy * —→ 1 Book (association — many copies of one title; the Book exists independently). Member 1 —→ * Loan and Loan * —→ 1 BookCopy (a Loan is an association class linking a Member and a BookCopy with attributes: checkout date, due date, returned date).
Draw the state diagram for a support ticket.
States: Open → (assign) → In Progress → (resolve) → Resolved → (confirm) → Closed. Extra transitions: In Progress → (need info) → Waiting on Customer → (customer replies) → In Progress; Resolved → (reopen [within 7 days]) → In Progress; any non-closed state → (cancel) → Closed. Guards on reopen and assign (must have an assignee) make the rules explicit.

Advanced deep

When is an "association class" the right modelling choice, and how does it map to code / a database?
Use an association class when the relationship itself carries attributes or behaviour, not just the two entities it links. Classic case: Student ↔ Course is many-to-many, and the enrolment has its own data — grade, semester, attendance. You can't hang "grade" off Student (which grade? for which course?) or off Course. So Enrollment becomes a class with a link to one Student and one Course plus its attributes. In UML it's drawn as a class connected by a dashed line to the association line. In code: it's a normal entity — class Enrollment { Student student; Course course; Grade grade; Date semester; } — and the many-to-many is realised as Student.enrollments : List<Enrollment> and Course.enrollments : List<Enrollment>. In a relational DB: it's the join table with extra columns — enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade, semester) with a composite primary key (student_id, course_id) (or a surrogate id if a student can re-take a course). The subtlety interviewers probe: whether (student, course) is unique (one enrolment per pair → composite PK) or repeatable (retakes → surrogate id + a semester in the key), and whether the association class is an aggregate root of its own (has a lifecycle: enrolled → completed → withdrawn) or just a value linking two roots. Getting this right prevents the "where do I put the grade" flailing that a naive many-to-many causes.
What are the practical limits of UML in modern practice, and what do teams use instead?
Full formal UML (all 14 diagram types, MDA/round-trip code generation) largely failed in industry: the tools were heavy, the diagrams went stale the moment code changed, "executable UML" never delivered, and the notation's precision exceeded what design discussions actually need. What survived and is genuinely useful: class diagrams and sequence diagrams as lightweight communication aids (on a whiteboard, or as text-to-diagram via PlantUML / Mermaid checked into the repo so they can be diffed and reviewed), and state machines where a lifecycle is complex. For architecture (above the class level), the C4 model (Context, Container, Component, Code — Simon Brown) has largely replaced UML component/deployment diagrams because it's simpler and scoped to "diagrams for different audiences at different zoom levels". For sequences of events across services, teams draw plain flow diagrams or use tracing tools (the real sequence, from Jaeger/Zipkin, beats a hand-drawn guess). For data, ER diagrams (a UML-adjacent notation) remain standard. The pragmatic stance for an LLD interview: know class-diagram and sequence-diagram notation well enough to sketch clearly and read what an interviewer draws, use state diagrams for lifecycles, and don't get precious about strict UML conformance — the goal is shared understanding, and "boxes and labelled arrows" communicates it. Keeping diagrams as code (Mermaid in markdown, PlantUML) is how teams keep the few they maintain from rotting.

Design a Parking Lot

The canonical LLD warm-up — entities, allocation strategy, and where to leave extension points.

Notes

Scope (state assumptions)

Multi-floor lot; vehicle types (motorcycle, car, bus); matching spot sizes (small, medium, large); entry issues a ticket, exit computes a fee. In scope: spot allocation, ticketing, pricing hook. Out of scope for now: reservations, license-plate recognition, valet.

Entities

ClassResponsibility
ParkingLotowns floors; entry/exit points; overall parkVehicle/unpark
ParkingFloorowns its spots; finds a free spot for a vehicle type; tracks free counts
ParkingSpot (abstract) → Small/Medium/LargeSpotstate: free / occupied; which vehicle
Vehicle (abstract) → Motorcycle/Car/Bustype, plate; which spot sizes it can use
Ticketid, entry time, spot, vehicle; exit time on unpark
ParkingStrategy (interface)pick a spot — nearest, spread across floors, etc.
PricingStrategy (interface)compute fee from duration + vehicle type
EntryGate / ExitGateissue ticket / process payment

Key flows

  • Park: gate → lot.park(vehicle) → strategy picks a compatible free spot → mark occupied → create ticket. Fail cleanly if full (return Optional<Ticket> / throw LotFullException).
  • Unpark: lot.unpark(ticket) → set exit time → pricing.fee(ticket) → free the spot → return the fee.

Extension points (where OCP matters)

  • New vehicle/spot type → new subclass + a compatibility rule (a table or method, not a giant switch).
  • New allocation policy / pricing model → new strategy implementation.
  • EV charging spots, handicapped spots → spot attributes + a filter in the strategy.

Concurrency

Two cars racing for the last spot: allocation must be atomic — a per-floor lock around "find + mark", or an atomic compare-and-set on the spot's state, plus an atomic free-count. Keep the critical section tiny (just the claim, not ticket creation).

Cheat Sheet
  • Entities: ParkingLot ◊— ParkingFloor ◊— ParkingSpot (Small/Med/Large); Vehicle hierarchy; Ticket; gates.
  • Pluggable via interfaces: ParkingStrategy (spot selection), PricingStrategy (fee).
  • Vehicle↔spot compatibility as data/method, not a switch.
  • Park: strategy picks a compatible free spot → atomically claim → issue ticket. Full → explicit failure.
  • Unpark: stamp exit → compute fee → free spot atomically.
  • Concurrency: atomic "find + mark" (per-floor lock or CAS on spot state) + atomic free count.
  • Extensions: EV/handicapped spots = attributes + strategy filter; new types = subclass + rule.
Q&A
Why make spot selection and pricing separate strategy interfaces?
They're independent axes of change: the business may switch from "nearest spot" to "balance load across floors" without touching pricing, and change from hourly to slab pricing without touching allocation. Separate interfaces keep each swappable and testable, and keep ParkingLot closed to modification.
How do you model which vehicle fits which spot?
A compatibility rule, e.g. each Vehicle exposes the set of spot sizes it can occupy (a motorcycle fits any; a bus needs large, possibly several adjacent), and the allocation strategy filters free spots by that. Avoid a hard-coded switch so new types don't require editing the allocator.
What happens on park() when the lot is full?
Return an explicit "no spot" result — Optional<Ticket> empty, a result object, or a checked LotFullException — so the gate can show "FULL" rather than the caller getting a null or a half-created ticket.
Two cars arrive at once and only one spot is left. How do you prevent double allocation?
Make "find a free spot and mark it occupied" a single atomic step: a lock on the floor (or the spot pool) around that operation, or a compare-and-set on the spot's state (free -> occupied) with a retry if it fails. Update the free-count atomically too. The ticket creation can happen outside the lock.
How would you add reserved/handicapped/EV spots without rewriting the design?
Give ParkingSpot attributes (hasCharger, isHandicapped, reservedFor) and let the ParkingStrategy take the request context (permit, EV, reservation id) and filter accordingly. No new class hierarchy needed; the allocator just gains a predicate.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a Ticket record?
Ticket id, entry time, the assigned spot, the vehicle; and exit time (set on unpark) used to compute the fee.
Which relationship holds between ParkingFloor and ParkingSpot?
Composition — spots belong to and are managed by the floor.
Where does "hourly vs flat-rate pricing" live?
Behind a PricingStrategy interface, injected into the exit/lot.

Intermediate core

The interviewer adds: a bus needs 3 adjacent large spots. How does allocation change?
Spot selection is no longer "find one free spot" but "find k contiguous free spots of size L on one floor". Model adjacency: spots have an ordered position per row, and the floor can scan rows for a run of k free large spots. The claim must mark all k atomically (lock the floor, verify all still free, mark all). The Ticket now references a list of spots. Free/occupancy counts and unpark free all of them. Consider whether partial parking (bus spanning two floors) is allowed — probably not, keep it one floor.
How do you keep per-floor free counts fast and correct under concurrency?
Maintain an AtomicInteger free count per floor per size class, decremented/incremented in the same critical section (or CAS sequence) that flips the spot state — never as a separate step. The entry display reads these counters directly (O(1)), so you don't scan spots. On unpark, increment. Reconcile periodically (a background sweep) as a safety net against bugs, and treat the counters as a cache of truth, with the spot states being authoritative.

Advanced deep

Scale this to a chain of 500 lots with a central app showing live availability and supporting online reservations. What changes?
The single-process object model becomes a distributed system. Each lot runs its own service (or edge device) that is the source of truth for its spots — local allocation stays a fast in-process atomic operation, resilient to network partition (a lot must keep working if the WAN drops). Live availability: each lot pushes free-count deltas (or periodic snapshots) to a central store; the app reads eventually-consistent aggregates — showing "~12 free" is fine, exact isn't needed. Reservations are the hard part: a reservation is a hold on capacity, not a specific spot. Model it as a counter reservation against a size class at a lot with an expiry (hold N large spots for the next 30 min), decremented from available capacity centrally, then reconciled with the lot — the lot must honour "keep M spots for reservations" in its local allocator. Overbooking policy: since holds expire and no-shows happen, you may allow a small overbook ratio with a fallback (comp parking / refund) rather than strict capacity, tuned from no-show data. Consistency: use the central reservation service as the authority for reservable capacity (with idempotent reservation ids, and a saga/compensation if the lot later reports it's actually full), while walk-in capacity is managed lot-locally. Add: an event stream for analytics/billing, per-lot config (pricing, spot mix) served from the center, and offline mode where a lot queues events and syncs on reconnect. The LLD class model per lot barely changes; what's added is the reservation aggregate, a sync/replication layer, expiry handling, and explicit decisions about which numbers are authoritative vs eventually consistent.
Model parking fee calculation to support: free first 15 min, tiered hourly rates, daily max, different rates by vehicle type, weekend/holiday pricing, and lost-ticket flat fee. Keep it clean.
Don't put this in one method with a pile of ifs. Model it as a pipeline of pricing rules plus a rate schedule.
