The PricingStrategy takes a PricingContext (entry time, exit time, vehicle type, ticket state, lot id) and returns a Fee breakdown. Internally: (1) a RateTable data object — per vehicle type, an ordered list of tiers (0–15min: $0, 15min–1h: $4, 1–3h: $3/h, 3h+: $2/h) and a daily cap. Tiers and caps are configuration, not code. (2) A Calendar/PricingPeriod resolver that maps a date to weekday/weekend/holiday and selects the right RateTable (so holiday pricing is just a different table, chosen by a rule, not a special branch). (3) A short chain of modifier rules applied in order: GracePeriodRule (zero out the first 15 min), TieredDurationRule (walk the tiers over the parked duration, summing), DailyMaxRule (cap per calendar day, handling multi-day stays day-by-day), LostTicketRule (if ticket.state == LOST, short-circuit to the flat lost fee, ignoring duration). (4) Return a Fee with line items so the receipt and disputes are explainable. Adding "first hour free for EVs" or a "validation code" discount is a new rule class or a new row in the rate config — the calculator and the parking flow don't change (OCP). Test each rule in isolation with crafted contexts, and property-test the whole chain (fee monotonic in duration except at the daily cap, never negative, lost-ticket fee ≥ max possible normal fee).

Design an LRU / LFU Cache

O(1) get and put — the hash map + doubly linked list, and where it gets harder.

Notes

LRU: the standard structure

  • Hash map: key → node (O(1) lookup).
  • Doubly linked list: nodes in recency order, most-recently-used at the head, least at the tail. Doubly-linked so you can unlink any node in O(1).
  • get(k): map lookup; if hit, move node to head; return value.
  • put(k, v): if present, update value + move to head; else create node, add at head, insert in map; if size > capacity, evict the tail node (remove from list and map).

Use a sentinel head and tail to avoid null checks. Both operations are O(1). Many languages have this built in (Java LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true, Python OrderedDict / functools.lru_cache).

LFU (least-frequently-used)

Evict the item with the lowest access count; break ties by recency. O(1) version: a map key→node, a map frequency→(doubly linked list of nodes with that frequency), and a minFreq pointer. On access, move the node from its freq list to the freq+1 list; update minFreq. More complex; use it when access frequency is a better predictor than recency (e.g. a long-tail workload with a few very hot keys).

Real-world concerns

  • Thread-safety: wrap operations in a lock (simple), or shard the cache into N independently-locked segments (like ConcurrentHashMap) for less contention, or use a concurrent design (Caffeine uses lock-free reads + a ring buffer of access events replayed under a lock).
  • TTL / expiry: store an expiry timestamp per entry; lazily evict on access, plus a background sweep. LRU + TTL together is common.
  • Size vs bytes: cap by entry count is easy; capping by memory needs a per-entry weight.
  • Stampede: on a miss for a hot key, many threads recompute — add per-key single-flight (compute once, others wait).
Cheat Sheet
  • LRU = hash map (key→node) + doubly linked list (recency order, MRU at head). Sentinel head/tail.
  • get: lookup + move-to-head. put: upsert + move-to-head; over capacity → evict tail. Both O(1).
  • LFU O(1): key→node map + freq→list-of-nodes map + minFreq; access bumps node to next freq list.
  • Recency (LRU) for temporal locality; frequency (LFU) for stable hot sets. LRU-K / ARC / W-TinyLFU blend both.
  • Thread-safe: one lock (simple), sharded locks (scalable), or a concurrent design (Caffeine).
  • Add TTL: per-entry expiry, lazy eviction on access + background sweep.
  • Cache stampede on a hot miss → per-key single-flight.
Q&A
Why a doubly linked list, not singly?
To unlink an arbitrary node (the one you just accessed, found via the hash map) in O(1) you need its predecessor pointer. A singly linked list would require an O(n) scan to find the previous node.
What do the sentinel head/tail nodes buy you?
Every real node always has a non-null prev and next, so insert/remove code has no special cases for "list empty" or "removing the first/last node" — fewer bugs.
LRU vs LFU — when does LFU win?
When a small set of keys is accessed far more than the rest over a long period, and occasional bursts of one-time scans shouldn't evict them. Pure LRU lets a big sequential scan flush the hot set; LFU (or scan-resistant hybrids like W-TinyLFU) keeps the frequently-used items.
How do you make an LRU cache thread-safe without killing throughput?
A single mutex is correct but serialises all access. Better: shard into N segments each with its own lock and its own LRU (route by key hash), so concurrent operations on different keys don't contend. Best (libraries like Caffeine): lock-free reads that just append the access to a buffer, with the LRU order maintained asynchronously under one lock, amortising the bookkeeping.
How do you add TTL to an LRU cache?
Store an expiry timestamp on each entry. On get, if now > expiry, treat it as a miss and evict. Run a periodic background sweep (or a min-heap keyed by expiry) to reclaim expired entries that are never accessed again.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Two data structures behind an O(1) LRU cache?
A hash map (key → list node) and a doubly linked list (recency order).
Which end of the list holds the eviction candidate?
The tail (least recently used).
Does get change the cache's internal order?
Yes — a hit moves the entry to the most-recently-used position.

Intermediate core

Implement put for an LRU cache in pseudocode.
put(k, v):
  if k in map:
    node = map[k]; node.val = v; moveToHead(node); return
  node = Node(k, v)
  map[k] = node; addToHead(node)
  if map.size > capacity:
    lru = tail.prev
    removeNode(lru); del map[lru.key]
Your LRU cache is hit by a nightly full-table scan and the hot working set is evicted every night. Fix without switching to LFU entirely.
Make it scan-resistant. Options: (1) Segmented LRU / 2Q — new entries go into a small "probationary" list; only entries accessed a second time get promoted to the "protected" list. A one-time scan fills and flushes the small probationary segment, leaving the protected hot set intact. (2) W-TinyLFU (Caffeine's policy) — a tiny frequency sketch (counting Bloom filter) gates admission: a candidate for admission only evicts a victim if its estimated frequency is higher, so scan items (freq 1) can't displace hot items (freq >> 1). (3) ARC — adaptively balances recency and frequency lists based on hit history. All keep O(1) operations and dramatically improve hit rate on mixed scan + hot-set workloads over plain LRU.

Advanced deep

Design a bounded, thread-safe, TTL-aware cache for a high-QPS service. Walk through the structures and trade-offs.
Core: a concurrent hash map (key → entry) as the source of truth; entries hold value, size/weight, createAt, expireAt, and a frequency estimate. Eviction policy: W-TinyLFU (admission via a frequency sketch, victims from a small window LRU + a main SLRU) — scan-resistant and near-optimal hit rate; the policy's ordering data is maintained asynchronously: reads just record the accessed key into a lock-free ring buffer (per-thread striped to avoid contention), and a single maintenance task drains the buffers under one lock, replaying accesses to update recency/frequency and doing evictions in batches. This makes the read path essentially a map lookup + a cheap append — no per-read lock, no linked-list pointer surgery on the hot path. TTL: lazy — on get, check now > expireAt and treat as a miss; plus the maintenance task expires entries in bulk, optionally driven by a hierarchical timing wheel keyed on expiry so it's O(1) amortised rather than scanning. Weight/size bound: track total weight atomically; evict until under the limit, using the policy's victim order. Stampede control: on a miss, use single-flight per key (a small map of in-progress futures) so only one thread computes the value and the rest await it; optionally serve a slightly-stale value while refreshing asynchronously (refresh-ahead) so latency-critical reads never block on recomputation. Observability: expose hit rate, eviction count, load penalty, size — a falling hit rate is the signal to resize or revisit the policy. Trade-offs: the async policy means recency/frequency data lags reality slightly (fine — a few ms of imprecision costs almost nothing in hit rate); the ring buffers and sketch add fixed memory overhead; and correctness testing is harder (concurrency + eviction + TTL interactions) so it's worth using a proven library (Caffeine on JVM, or an equivalent) rather than hand-rolling the concurrent maintenance loop.
Extend the single-node cache to a distributed cache. What are the key design decisions?
Partitioning: spread keys across N nodes with consistent hashing (+ virtual nodes) so adding/removing a node only remaps ~1/N of keys, not everything — avoids a cache-wide stampede on scaling events. Client vs proxy: a smart client that hashes and talks directly to the owning node (memcached-style, low latency, no extra hop) vs a proxy/router layer (simpler clients, central control, extra hop) — or a replicated design (Redis Cluster) where nodes gossip topology. Replication: for a cache, often none (a lost node just means cache misses that refill from the DB — acceptable), or 1 replica for hot partitions / to survive a node loss without a thundering herd on the origin. Consistency: caches are best-effort; on a write to the DB you either invalidate the key (delete from cache, next read refills) or update it — invalidate is safer (avoids stale writes racing). Accept a small window of staleness; use short TTLs as a backstop. Hot keys: a single key hotter than one node can serve → replicate that key to multiple nodes, or add a small client-side L1 cache with a very short TTL to absorb the QPS. Failure: node down → requests to its partition fail fast and fall through to the DB (with per-key single-flight and maybe a circuit breaker to protect the DB from the surge); don't block. Coordination: topology changes via a config service / gossip; clients refresh their ring on error. This is essentially memcached/Redis-Cluster/ Tair — the interview points are consistent hashing, invalidate-don't-update, tolerate-misses-not-staleness, and protect the origin during node loss.

Design a Rate Limiter

Four algorithms, and how each handles bursts, boundaries, and distribution.

Notes

The algorithms

AlgorithmIdeaBursts
Fixed windowcount requests per key per calendar minute; reset at the boundaryallows 2× rate at the boundary (end of one window + start of next)
Sliding window logstore timestamps of recent requests; count those within the last minuteexact, but O(requests) memory per key
Sliding window counterweighted blend of current + previous fixed-window countssmooths the boundary spike; approximate; O(1) memory
Token bucketbucket of capacity tokens, refilled at rate/sec; each request takes 1allows a burst up to capacity, then steady rate. The usual choice.
Leaky bucketrequests queue; drained at a fixed rate; queue full → rejectno bursts — perfectly smooth output

Token bucket — the common implementation

Store per key: tokens (float), lastRefill (timestamp). On a request: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * rate); lastRefill = now; then if tokens ≥ 1, decrement and allow, else reject. Two numbers per key, O(1).

Where it lives

  • Per-process: an in-memory map; simplest, but each instance has its own limit → effective limit × instance count.
  • Distributed: state in Redis. Do the read-modify-write atomically — a Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE for fixed window). Watch Redis latency on the hot path; consider a local token bucket that syncs periodically for approximate limiting with low latency.

API concerns

  • Key by user / API key / IP / (user, endpoint) — and often several tiers at once.
  • Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset headers.
  • Fail-open vs fail-closed if the limiter store is down (usually fail-open for availability).
Cheat Sheet
  • Fixed window: O(1), simple, 2× burst at boundaries.
  • Sliding log: exact, O(requests) memory. Sliding counter: approx, O(1), smooths boundary.
  • Token bucket: capacity + refill rate; allows a bounded burst then steady rate — default pick. Two fields/key.
  • Leaky bucket: fixed drain rate, queue; smooth output, no bursts.
  • Per-process = simple but limit multiplies by instance count. Distributed = state in Redis, atomic RMW (Lua / INCR+EXPIRE).
  • Key by user / API key / IP / (user,endpoint); support multiple tiers.
  • Reject with 429 + Retry-After + X-RateLimit-* headers.
  • Limiter store down → usually fail-open.
Q&A
Why does a fixed-window limiter allow bursts up to twice the rate?
A client can send the full quota in the last instant of window N and the full quota in the first instant of window N+1 — 2× the limit within a span shorter than one window. Sliding-window approaches remove this boundary effect.
Token bucket vs leaky bucket?
Token bucket permits a burst (up to the bucket capacity) after an idle period, then enforces the average rate — good for APIs where occasional bursts are fine. Leaky bucket forces a perfectly smooth output rate by queuing and draining at fixed speed — good for protecting a downstream that can't absorb spikes.
What two values does a token-bucket entry need?
The current token count and the timestamp of the last refill. On each request you lazily add (now - last) × rate tokens (capped at capacity) before checking.
How do you rate-limit across many server instances?
Keep the counter/bucket state in a shared store (Redis) and make the check-and-decrement atomic — a Lua script for token bucket, or INCR with EXPIRE for fixed window. Alternatively, give each instance a share of the budget locally and reconcile periodically (approximate but low-latency).
What should a rate-limited response look like?
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, a Retry-After header telling the client when to try again, and ideally X-RateLimit-Limit, -Remaining, -Reset so well-behaved clients can self-throttle.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which HTTP status code means "rate limited"?
429 Too Many Requests.
Which algorithm naturally allows a controlled burst then a steady rate?
Token bucket.
Which algorithm gives a perfectly smooth output rate?
Leaky bucket.

Intermediate core

Implement a distributed fixed-window limiter with Redis. What's the race, and the fix?
Naively: GET key; if under limit, INCR key. The race: two requests both read the same count before either increments, so both pass and you exceed the limit. Fix: INCR first (atomic), get the new value back, and on the response that made it exceed the limit, reject — and on the request that created the key (returned 1), also set EXPIRE key window_seconds. Or do it all in one Lua script: check, incr, set expiry atomically. The key is one round trip that both increments and returns the post-increment value.
You need per-user limits AND a global limit AND a per-endpoint limit. How do you compose them?
Run the request through an ordered chain of limiters, each with its own key and config: [globalLimiter (key="global"), userLimiter (key=userId), endpointLimiter (key=userId+":"+endpoint)]. Allow only if all pass; reject with the tightest Retry-After among the failing ones. Check cheap/most-likely-to-fail limiters first to short-circuit. Be careful to only consume tokens from limiters after you know the request will proceed (or refund on later rejection), so a request blocked by limiter 3 doesn't wrongly deplete limiters 1 and 2 — either check-all-then-consume-all, or consume and compensate.

Advanced deep

Design a rate limiter for a global API gateway: 10k+ nodes, sub-millisecond added latency budget, per-key limits, and it must degrade gracefully when the central store is slow.
A pure "call Redis on every request" design blows the latency budget and makes Redis a SPOF at that scale. Use a two-tier / local-token design: each gateway node keeps an in-memory token bucket per active key, and a background process periodically (every few hundred ms) reconciles with the central store — it reports how many tokens the node consumed and requests a fresh allotment for the next interval, and the central authority divides the global budget among nodes proportional to recent demand (nodes seeing more traffic for a key get a bigger share). Between syncs, the node enforces limits purely locally — O(1), zero network latency on the request path. Consequences and tuning: (1) the limit is approximate — brief overshoot up to (per-node allotment × nodes-that-just-got-a-burst) is possible; you set the sync interval and per-node buffer to bound this (shorter interval = tighter limit, more central load). (2) Cold keys: a key with no local allotment gets a small starter grant on first hit, refined next sync. (3) Store slow/down: nodes keep enforcing with their last-known allotment (fail-open-ish but still bounded), and the central authority is not on the critical path, so gateway latency and availability are unaffected — you just lose precision until it recovers. (4) Hot key across nodes: the demand-proportional split handles skew automatically. (5) For keys that genuinely need exact limits (billing, abuse), route those through a synchronous Redis check and accept the latency for that subset. This is roughly how Stripe/CloudFlare-scale limiters work: local enforcement for speed, periodic central reconciliation for a globally coherent (if slightly fuzzy) limit, and the central component off the request path.
Compare rate limiting with load shedding and backpressure — when do you want which?
They solve overlapping but distinct problems. Rate limiting is a policy control keyed on identity (per user/API key/plan): "this client gets 1000 req/min regardless of whether the system is busy" — it's about fairness, abuse prevention, and monetisation, and it rejects with 429 deterministically. Load shedding is a self-protection control keyed on system health: when a queue depth, latency, or CPU threshold is exceeded, start dropping requests (ideally the cheapest/least-important first — priority-aware shedding) to keep the service from collapsing entirely; it returns 503 and is dynamic — off when healthy, aggressive when overloaded. Backpressure is a flow control mechanism: instead of dropping, you slow the producer — bounded queues that block/park the caller, TCP window shrinking, reactive-streams "request(n)" signalling, or gRPC flow control — propagating "I can't keep up" upstream so the source stops sending rather than the receiver drowning. You typically want all three layered: rate limiting at the edge for policy/fairness, backpressure through the internal pipeline so slow downstreams throttle upstreams instead of buffering unboundedly (which turns a latency blip into an OOM), and load shedding as the last resort when backpressure isn't enough (e.g. the slow component is a shared dependency you can't backpressure). A common mistake is using only rate limiting: it doesn't adapt to real-time capacity, so a dependency slowdown still causes a cascading failure that per-client limits never triggered on.

Design an Elevator System

A state machine plus a scheduling policy — and the multi-car dispatch problem.

Notes

Requests: two kinds

  • Hall call: a button in the lobby/floor — has a floor and a direction (up/down). Served by the system, which picks a car.
  • Car call: a button inside a car — has a target floor. Served by that car.

Single-car scheduling

Keep two sorted sets of target floors: up stops and down stops. The car follows the elevator algorithm (SCAN/LOOK): keep moving in the current direction, stopping at every requested floor along the way, until there are no more requests ahead; then reverse. This minimises direction changes and starvation vs "serve nearest request" (which can strand someone at the top).

State machine per car

IDLE  —request→  MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWN
MOVING_*  —reached a stop→  DOORS_OPENING → DOORS_OPEN → DOORS_CLOSING → MOVING_* or IDLE
any  —emergency→  STOPPED / MAINTENANCE

Guards: doors can't open while moving; can't move with doors open; overload sensor blocks close; door-obstruction re-opens.

Multi-car dispatch

On a hall call, a Dispatcher scores each car and assigns the best one. Simple score: estimated time to reach that floor = f(distance, current direction vs call direction, number of stops already queued, load). Assign to the minimum. Re-evaluate as conditions change (a closer car frees up). Real systems use "destination dispatch" (you enter your target in the lobby, the system groups passengers and assigns cars to minimise total travel time).

Classes

  • ElevatorSystem (owns cars + dispatcher), ElevatorCar (state machine, own queue), Dispatcher (interface — strategy for car selection), Request (HallCall / CarCall), Door, Button/Panel, FloorSensor.
Cheat Sheet
  • Hall call (floor + direction, system picks a car) vs car call (target floor, that car).
  • Per-car: two sorted stop sets (up/down) + SCAN/LOOK — sweep in one direction serving all stops, then reverse. Avoids starvation of "nearest request".
  • Car state machine: IDLE ↔ MOVING_UP/DOWN ↔ DOORS_OPENING/OPEN/CLOSING; + STOPPED/MAINTENANCE. Guards: no move with doors open, no open while moving, obstruction re-opens.
  • Multi-car: Dispatcher strategy scores cars (ETA from distance, direction match, queued stops, load) → assign minimum; re-evaluate on change.
  • Destination dispatch (enter target in lobby) optimises total travel; group passengers.
  • Classes: ElevatorSystem, ElevatorCar, Dispatcher (iface), Request (HallCall/CarCall), Door, Panel.
Q&A
Hall call vs car call?
A hall call comes from a floor button and carries a floor + desired direction; the system chooses which car serves it. A car call comes from a panel inside a car and carries a target floor; it's served by that specific car.
Why use SCAN/LOOK instead of "serve the nearest request"?
Nearest-request can starve far requests indefinitely if closer ones keep arriving. SCAN sweeps steadily in one direction serving everything in its path, then reverses — bounded wait for everyone and fewer energy-costly direction changes.
What invariants does the door state machine enforce?
Doors never open while the car is moving; the car never moves while doors are open or opening; an obstruction or overload during closing re-opens the doors; a close only proceeds after a dwell timeout with no obstruction.
How does the dispatcher pick a car for a hall call?
It estimates each car's time-to-serve for that call — based on distance to the floor, whether the car is already heading that way in the requested direction, how many stops it has queued, and its current load — and assigns the car with the lowest estimate, re-checking if circumstances change.
What is destination dispatch?
Passengers enter their destination floor at a lobby kiosk (not just "up"), so the system knows demand ahead of time. It groups people going to nearby floors into the same car and assigns cars to minimise total or worst-case travel time — higher throughput in busy buildings.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name the elevator scheduling algorithm.
SCAN (or the LOOK variant, which turns around at the last request rather than the physical end).
Which component decides which car answers a lobby button?
The dispatcher / controller (a strategy for car selection).
Can a car move with its doors open?
No — a state-machine guard forbids it.

Intermediate core

Model a single car's request handling. What data structures and update rules?
Two ordered sets: upStops (min-heap or sorted set) and downStops (max-heap / reverse-sorted). Current floor and direction. On a new target t: if t > floor add to upStops, if t < floor add to downStops. Step loop: if direction == UP, next stop = smallest element of upStops > floor; move there, open doors, pop it. When upStops has nothing above the current floor, switch to DOWN and serve downStops from the top. If both empty → IDLE. A hall call with a direction is added to the matching set; a hall call opposite the current sweep is deferred to the return pass.
A hall call at floor 5 (going up) arrives while car A is at 8 going down and car B is at 2 going up. Which gets it and why?
Car B: it's already moving up and will pass floor 5 in the requested direction, so its ETA is ~3 floors of travel plus any stops in between. Car A is going the wrong way — it would have to finish its downward sweep, reverse, and come back up, a much larger ETA. The dispatcher's score (direction match + distance-along-path) favours B. If B had many queued stops between 2 and 5, or was overloaded, the score might still tip to A — that's why it's an estimate, re-evaluated.

Advanced deep

Design the dispatcher for a bank of 6 elevators in a 40-floor office building, handling the morning up-peak, evening down-peak, and midday interfloor traffic. What changes by mode?
One fixed policy is poor across these regimes, so the dispatcher runs in modes selected by measured traffic (car load sensors, hall-call rates by floor/direction, time of day): Up-peak (morning): almost everyone boards at the lobby going up. Strategy shifts to "return empty cars to the lobby immediately", load cars fully before dispatching, and if destination dispatch is available, group by destination zone so a car serves floors 10–15, another 16–22, etc. — minimising stops per trip. Throughput (people/5min) is the metric. Down-peak (evening): mirror image — sweep down collecting from upper floors; cars should not linger at the lobby; anticipate and pre-position cars high. Interfloor (midday): scattered origin/destination pairs, lower volume — classic SCAN per car with ETA-based hall-call assignment, and park idle cars at "expected demand" floors (lobby + a mid floor) rather than all at the bottom. Cross-cutting: (1) Zoning even outside peak reduces average stops. (2) Coincident call handling — don't send two cars to the same hall call; lock the assignment but allow reassignment if a better car becomes free before pickup. (3) Load-based skipping — a full car passes hall calls (indicator relights for the next car). (4) Anti-bunching — penalise assigning a car that's right behind another going the same way; spread the fleet. (5) Fairness/starvation cap — a hall call older than T seconds gets a priority boost so no one waits forever during a peak. (6) The mode switch itself needs hysteresis so it doesn't oscillate. Modern real controllers (Otis Compass, KONE) use exactly this: continuous traffic estimation + destination dispatch + zoning, often with an optimisation that assigns the whole current call set to cars to minimise a cost function (total wait + total travel + energy), re-solved every few seconds.
How do you make the elevator controller robust to sensor failure, power loss, and software crash?
Safety is layered and mostly not in the dispatch software. (1) Independent hardware safety chain: overspeed governor + mechanical brakes/safeties, final limit switches, door interlocks wired in series to a safety relay — if any opens, the drive is cut regardless of what the controller software thinks. This is certified separately (EN 81 / ASME A17.1) and the software cannot override it. (2) Controller = real-time state machine with explicit guards; every transition validated against sensor inputs; an implausible sensor state (car "between floors" reported at two floors at once, door "open" while moving) forces a safe stop and a fault mode, not a best-effort continue. (3) Watchdog: hardware watchdog timer the control loop must kick; if the software hangs, the watchdog resets it and the car goes to a defined safe state (stop, doors closed, or creep to nearest floor and open, depending on standard). (4) Power loss: battery/UPS drives the car at low speed to the nearest floor and opens the doors ("automatic rescue device"), then parks; never leaves people stuck between floors if avoidable. (5) Sensor redundancy / plausibility: floor position from multiple sources (encoder + magnetic floor sensors + door-zone sensor) cross-checked; load from redundant sensors; disagreement → degrade to a slower, more conservative mode or out-of-service. (6) Fail operational vs fail safe: door obstruction fails open (re-open), motion faults fail stopped. (7) Crash recovery: on controller restart, the car does a re-levelling / homing run (creep to a known floor sensor) before accepting calls — it never trusts a persisted position across a crash. (8) The dispatcher (fleet-level optimisation) is a separate, non-safety-critical process; if it dies, each car falls back to serving its own queue with a local SCAN, so the building keeps working degraded rather than stopping. The interview point: separate the safety-critical real-time control (hard guarantees, hardware backstop, certified) from the optimisation layer (soft, restartable, degradable), and never let a software bug or sensor glitch produce an unsafe mechanical state.

Design a Logging Library

Levels, sinks, formatters, and getting logging off the hot path.

Notes

Core pieces

ConceptRole
Loggerthe API (log.info("...")); named/hierarchical; holds a level threshold
LogLevelTRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR < FATAL — a record is emitted iff its level ≥ the logger's threshold
LogRecordtimestamp, level, logger name, thread, message, structured fields, exception
Formatter / Layoutrecord → string or JSON
Sink / Appender (interface)where output goes: console, rotating file, syslog, network, ring buffer — OCP extension point
Filterextra per-record include/exclude logic (by field, rate limit, sampling)

A logger fans a record out to one or more sinks, each with its own level, formatter, and filter. Named loggers form a tree so you can set com.acme.db to DEBUG while the root stays INFO.

Performance

  • Level check first, before building the message: if (log.isDebugEnabled()) log.debug(expensive()), or lazy args / a format string so expensive() isn't called when DEBUG is off. Lambda/template APIs make this automatic.
  • Async logging: the caller writes the record into a lock-free ring buffer / bounded queue and returns; a background thread formats and writes to sinks. This takes I/O (file, network) off the request path — often 10–100× lower logging latency. (Log4j2 async, spdlog async, zap.)
  • Bounded queue policy when full: block, drop oldest, or drop the new record — a deliberate choice (usually drop with a counter, so logging can't stall the app).

Structured & contextual logging

Prefer key–value fields (logger.info("order placed", "orderId", id, "amountCents", amt)) over string interpolation — machine-parseable, queryable. MDC / context: attach request id, user id, trace id once per request (thread-local or explicit context) so every log line in that request carries them.

Cheat Sheet
  • Logger (named, hierarchical, level threshold) → builds a LogRecord → fans out to Sinks, each with level + Formatter + Filter.
  • Levels: TRACE<DEBUG<INFO<WARN<ERROR<FATAL; emit iff record level ≥ threshold.
  • Sink/Appender is the OCP extension point: console, rotating file, syslog, network, ring buffer.
  • Check level before building the message (guard, lazy args, format strings, lambdas).
  • Async: caller → lock-free ring buffer → background thread formats + writes. Takes I/O off the hot path.
  • Full-queue policy: block / drop-oldest / drop-new (+ counter) — pick deliberately; logging must not stall the app.
  • Structured (key–value) fields > string interpolation. MDC/context for request/trace ids on every line.
Q&A
Why check the level before constructing the log message?
Building the message may involve string concatenation, serialization, or calling expensive methods. If the level is disabled, all that work is wasted. A guard (isDebugEnabled()), a parameterised format string, or a lambda that's only invoked when enabled avoids it.
What does asynchronous logging buy you?
The caller enqueues the record and returns immediately; a background thread does the formatting and the slow I/O (file write, network send). This removes disk/network latency and lock contention on the sink from the application's critical path.
What should happen when the async log queue is full?
A deliberate policy: block the caller (backpressure — risky, can stall the app), drop the oldest queued records, or drop the new record. Most systems drop and increment a "dropped N messages" counter, because logging should never take the service down.
Why prefer structured logging over interpolated strings?
Key–value fields (orderId=123 status=paid) are machine-parseable, so log aggregation systems can index and query them (find all logs for orderId=123), aggregate, and alert. Interpolated free text requires fragile regex extraction.
How do you get a request/trace id onto every log line for a request?
A mapped diagnostic context (MDC) — set the id once at the start of request handling (thread-local, or an explicit context object passed/attached), and the logger reads it and includes it in every record for the duration of that request.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which is more severe: WARN or ERROR?
ERROR.
What's the extension point for "where logs go"?
The sink / appender interface (console, file, syslog, network, …).
What turns a LogRecord into text or JSON?
A formatter / layout.

Intermediate core

Design the API so log.debug("user " + expensiveLookup(id) + " did X") costs nothing when DEBUG is off.
Don't accept a pre-built string. Options: (1) parameterised message — log.debug("user {} did X", () -> expensiveLookup(id)) where the arg is a supplier invoked only if DEBUG is enabled; (2) a format string + args — log.debug("user {} did X", idOrCheapValue) where formatting is deferred and skipped when disabled (but the args are still evaluated, so keep them cheap); (3) an isDebugEnabled() guard the caller writes explicitly. Modern libraries (SLF4J fluent API, Log4j2 lambdas, Rust log macros, zap's typed fields) build (1) in so the expensive work is behind a closure that only runs past the level check.
How do you support "root at INFO, but com.acme.payments at DEBUG"?
Hierarchical named loggers. A logger's effective level is its own configured level, or, if unset, inherited from the nearest configured ancestor up to the root. getLogger("com.acme.payments.StripeClient") with no explicit level inherits com.acme.payments's DEBUG; everything else inherits root's INFO. Configuration (file / env) maps logger-name prefixes to levels; the library resolves effective levels at logger creation and caches them, invalidating on config reload.

Advanced deep

Design the async pipeline: a lock-free handoff from many producer threads to a formatting/writing consumer, with backpressure and no lost ordering within a thread.
Producer side (hot path): capture a LogRecord with only cheap fields — level, timestamp (a monotonic counter or coarse clock), logger id, thread id, the format string + its arguments by reference/value, not yet formatted, and any MDC context (copied, since it may change). Push it onto a bounded MPSC (multi-producer, single-consumer) queue: a lock-free ring buffer (LMAX Disruptor style) or a lock-free linked queue. The push is a CAS on the tail plus a store — tens of ns, no formatting, no I/O. Ordering: per-thread FIFO is naturally preserved because a single thread's pushes are sequenced; global order across threads is approximate (fine — timestamps disambiguate), and if strict global order matters you sort by timestamp in the consumer's batch. Backpressure / full queue: choose per config — drop-new + increment a dropped counter (default: app never stalls; the consumer periodically emits a "dropped N log messages in the last interval" WARN so the loss is visible), block with timeout (bounded backpressure for audit-critical logs), or overwrite-oldest (ring buffer semantics — you lose the least recent, keep the newest, good for crash forensics). Consumer side: one thread drains in batches, formats each record (now paying the string/JSON cost off the hot path), groups by sink, and does batched writes (one write() per batch to a file, one flush per interval or per N records — not per line). It handles sink errors (retry, failover to a fallback sink, or drop-with-counter), file rotation, and flush-on-shutdown. Shutdown / crash: register a shutdown hook that flips the consumer to "drain and exit", and flush the queue; for crash safety, either use a memory-mapped ring buffer that a separate reader can recover, or accept that the last few unflushed lines are lost (so fatal logs bypass the async path and write synchronously). Argument lifetime: since formatting is deferred, mutable arguments passed by reference can change before the consumer formats them — either snapshot/format eagerly for object args (a middle ground: format to string on the producer, still skip I/O), or document that log args must be effectively immutable. Libraries that do this well: Log4j2 async loggers (Disruptor-backed), Rust tracing with a non-blocking writer, Go zap, C++ spdlog async mode.
What are the pitfalls of logging in a highly concurrent, latency-sensitive service, and how do you mitigate each?
(1) Lock contention on the sink — every thread serialising on one file/console mutex. Mitigate with async logging (single writer thread) or per-thread buffers flushed periodically. (2) I/O on the request path — a slow disk or a blocked network sink stalls request threads. Async + bounded queue + drop-on-full; never let the sink apply backpressure to request handlers. (3) Log volume / cost — DEBUG left on in prod, or logging in a tight loop, generates GB/min, saturates disk and the log pipeline, and the formatting CPU shows up in profiles. Mitigate: correct levels, rate-limited and sampled loggers (log 1 in N, or "at most once per 10s for this message key"), and structured events instead of chatty lines. (4) Allocation churn — each log call allocating strings/objects pressures the GC/allocator. Mitigate: object pooling for LogRecords, pre-sized buffers, avoid boxing (typed field APIs like zap), format lazily. (5) Sensitive data — PII/secrets in logs is a compliance incident. Mitigate: field-level redaction filters, allowlist structured fields rather than dumping objects, and review at the sink. (6) Log injection — unsanitised user input containing newlines forging fake log lines, or (Log4Shell) being interpreted. Mitigate: escape control chars, never interpret message content, keep the logging lib patched. (7) Time/ordering confusion across threads and machines — interleaved lines from concurrent requests are unreadable. Mitigate: always include a request/trace id (MDC) so you can filter one request's lines, and prefer a trace/span view for causality. (8) Observability tunnel vision — logs alone are expensive for high-cardinality questions; complement with metrics (cheap aggregates) and distributed tracing (causality), and reserve verbose logging for errors and sampled requests.

Thread-Safety in Low-Level Design

Design the object model so concurrency is contained, not sprinkled everywhere.

Notes

Strategy hierarchy (cheapest to most complex)

  1. Immutability — an object that never changes after construction is thread-safe with no locks. Value objects, config, events. Return new instances instead of mutating.
  2. Confinement — only one thread ever touches the object (thread-local, an actor's private state, per-connection objects). No sharing → no synchronisation.
  3. Guarded shared state — wrap all access to the mutable shared object in the same lock; keep the critical section small; document the locking discipline.
  4. Concurrent building blocks — use ConcurrentHashMap, blocking queues, atomics, thread pools instead of hand-rolled locking.
  5. Lock-free — last resort, for a proven hot single-word contention point.

Design-level moves

  • Monitor object: a class whose every public method acquires the same instance lock; callers see a simple sequential API. Fine for low-contention coordinators (a ParkingLot).
  • Split the object: separate the rarely-changing config from the hot mutable counters so they can have different (or no) synchronisation.
  • Copy-on-write: for read-mostly collections (listener lists, routing tables) — readers are lock-free, a write swaps in a new copy.
  • Message passing: give a resource to one owner thread and send it requests via a queue (actor model) — turns shared-state bugs into ordering questions.
  • Keep lock scope out of your public API — don't return a reference to internal mutable state, and don't call user callbacks while holding a lock.

Thread-safe singleton

Prefer eager init (a static final instance) or the initialisation-on-demand holder idiom (a private static nested class) — both give lazy, thread-safe, lock-free access via the language's class-init guarantees. Double-checked locking needs a volatile/atomic field to be correct; an enum singleton (Java) is the simplest correct lazy-ish form.

Cheat Sheet
  • Order of preference: immutability > confinement (thread-local / actor) > one lock per shared object > concurrent library types > lock-free.
  • Monitor object: every public method takes the same instance lock → simple sequential API for low-contention coordinators.
  • Split hot mutable state from cold config so they synchronise differently (or not).
  • Copy-on-write for read-mostly lists/maps (lock-free reads).
  • Message passing: single owner thread + request queue turns races into ordering.
  • Don't leak internal mutable references; don't run callbacks under a lock.
  • Singleton: eager static final or holder-class idiom; DCL needs volatile; enum is simplest.
Q&A
What's the cheapest way to make an object thread-safe?
Make it immutable — if state never changes after construction, any number of threads can read it concurrently with no locks and no memory-visibility concerns (given safe publication).
What is thread confinement?
Ensuring an object is only ever accessed by one thread — via thread-local storage, being private to an actor, or being created and used within a single request handler. No sharing means no synchronisation is needed.
What is a monitor object?
A class that guards all of its state with a single lock acquired at the start of every public method, so callers get a straightforward "one operation at a time" API without managing locks themselves. Suitable when contention is low.
Why split a shared object into "hot" and "cold" parts?
Configuration that rarely changes and a set of frequently-updated counters have very different synchronisation needs. Keeping them separate lets the counters use lightweight atomics (or sharding) while the config is effectively immutable, instead of one coarse lock over everything.
Simplest correct lazy singleton in a language with class-init guarantees?
The holder-class idiom: a private static nested class holds the instance; it's not initialised until first referenced, and the runtime guarantees class initialisation is thread-safe and happens once. No volatile, no explicit lock.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

An immutable object needs how many locks to be shared safely?
Zero (given it's safely published).
What concurrent collection replaces a manually-locked HashMap?
ConcurrentHashMap (or the language's equivalent).
Should a class return a reference to its internal mutable list?
No — return a copy or an unmodifiable view, or expose specific operations. Leaking the reference breaks encapsulation and thread-safety.

Intermediate core

You're designing a BookingService where two users may book the last seat concurrently. Design for correctness.
Make "check availability and claim" a single atomic operation. Options: (1) a per-show lock around if (seat.isFree()) seat.hold(user); keep it tiny — just the claim, not payment. (2) An atomic compare-and-set on the seat's state (FREE -> HELD); the loser gets false and is told "seat taken". (3) A DB unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) so the second INSERT fails. Add a hold with expiry (release if payment doesn't complete in N minutes) via a background sweeper. The service API stays simple ("bookSeat returns a confirmation or a SeatUnavailable"); concurrency is confined to that one claim step.
A class exposes addListener() and fires events to listeners from many threads. How do you make the listener list safe without locking on every fire?
Copy-on-write: store listeners in an immutable array/list; addListener/removeListener create a new list and atomically swap the reference (under a small lock, since writes are rare); firing an event just reads the current reference (lock-free) and iterates. Readers never block and never see a partially-updated list. Caveat: a listener added during a fire won't get that event, and you must not hold any lock while calling listener callbacks (they can call back into you → deadlock/reentrancy).

Advanced deep

Design a thread-safe object pool (e.g. DB connections). What are the concurrency and correctness concerns?
Structure: a bounded set of reusable objects; acquire() hands one out (blocking or with timeout when none free), release() returns it. Back it with a concurrent queue of idle objects plus a semaphore initialised to max size (so acquire = semaphore.acquire() then poll the queue, lazily creating up to max; release = validate + return to queue + semaphore.release()). Concerns: (1) Leaks — a caller that forgets release() permanently shrinks the pool; mitigate with try-with-resources / RAII wrappers, and a leak detector (track acquire stack + max-checkout-time, log/reclaim stale ones). (2) Double release — returning the same object twice corrupts the count/queue; use a one-shot handle that marks itself returned. (3) Validation — a pooled connection may have died (server closed it, network dropped); validate on borrow (cheap ping) or on return, and discard+replace bad ones rather than handing out a broken object. (4) Fairness / starvation — use a fair semaphore or a FIFO wait queue so a burst of new requests doesn't starve a waiter. (5) Shutdown — drain: stop accepting acquires, wait for outstanding releases (with timeout), then close all idle objects; forcibly close leaked ones after the timeout. (6) Thundering herd on startup — if all N objects are created lazily on first load spike, that's N slow connects at once; pre-warm a minimum pool size in the background. (7) Sizing — too small → contention/queueing; too large → overloading the downstream (a DB has its own connection limit); expose metrics (in-use, idle, wait time, timeouts) to tune it. (8) Thread affinity / state — if pooled objects carry per-use state (transaction, prepared-statement cache, session variables), release must reset them (ROLLBACK, clear settings) or the next borrower inherits stale state. Don't hand-roll this in production — use HikariCP / a proven pool — but the interview is about naming these hazards and the semaphore-plus-queue core.
When would you choose an actor / single-owner-thread model over shared-state-with-locks for a subsystem, and what do you give up?
Choose actors when: the subsystem has complex mutable state with many invariants that are painful to lock correctly (a game world region, a matchmaking pool, a stateful protocol handler, an in-memory order book); when you want to eliminate data races by construction (only one thread touches the state, so there are none) and reason about behaviour as a sequential state machine processing a message stream; when the workload is naturally partitionable (one actor per user / per connection / per shard) so you scale by adding actors, not by making one lock finer-grained; and when you want failure isolation (an actor can crash and restart with fresh state without corrupting neighbours). What you give up: (1) Synchronous call convenience — every interaction is now an async message + reply (or a future), which is more code and changes error handling (timeouts instead of exceptions, no stack traces across the boundary). (2) Cross-actor consistency — an operation spanning two actors' state can't be a single atomic step; you need a saga/2-phase protocol or you accept eventual consistency — the same problem as distributed transactions, in-process. (3) Throughput ceiling per actor — one actor processes its mailbox serially, so a hot actor is a bottleneck (mitigate by sharding it, but then you're back to partitioning problems). (4) Mailbox as a hidden queue — unbounded mailboxes leak memory under overload; bounded ones need a backpressure story. (5) Debuggability — the flow is spread across message handlers and time; you rely on tracing/logging rather than stepping through a call stack. (6) Tooling / discipline — it's easy to accidentally share mutable state via a message payload (send a mutable object, both actors mutate it) — payloads must be immutable or copied. For a low-contention coordinator (a parking lot, a small in-memory registry), a monitor object with one lock is simpler and perfectly adequate; reach for actors when the locking is getting genuinely hard to keep correct or the partitioning is a natural fit.

Evolving a Design & Over-Engineering

Just enough structure now, and cheap seams for the changes you'll actually make.

Notes

YAGNI vs extensibility

  • YAGNI ("You Aren't Gonna Need It"): don't build a plugin framework, generic rules engine, or config-driven abstraction for a single case that isn't varying yet. Speculative flexibility usually guesses the wrong axis and adds cost forever.
  • But: keep the code changeable — small classes, clear boundaries, dependency injection at true seams — so adding the abstraction later is a local refactor, not a rewrite.

The rule of three

Write it inline the first time. Copy it the second time (duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction). On the third occurrence, you understand the real variation — now extract the abstraction. Premature abstraction from two examples often captures a coincidence.

Refactoring seams

A "seam" is a place you can change behaviour without editing in place: an interface, a factory, a strategy parameter, a hook method. Good design leaves seams where change is likely (payment providers, storage, notification channels) and keeps everything else concrete and direct. Adding a seam later: extract an interface from the concrete class, inject it, done.

When patterns pay off

Add a pattern when…
you have (or clearly will have) 3+ variants of one behaviour → Strategy
object creation is spread out and type is chosen at runtime → Factory
you're adding responsibilities in combinations → Decorator
a big switch on a type/state keeps growing → polymorphism / State
an object has a real lifecycle with rules → State machine

Signals you over-engineered

Interfaces with one implementation and no test need; layers that only forward calls; config for things that never change; a framework where a function would do; more time reading the indirection than the logic. The fix is usually to inline and delete.

Cheat Sheet
  • YAGNI: don't build speculative flexibility; it guesses wrong and costs forever.
  • Keep code changeable (small classes, clear boundaries) so adding abstraction later is local.
  • Rule of three: inline once, duplicate twice, abstract on the third — by then you know the real variation.
  • Leave seams (interface/factory/strategy/hook) only where change is likely; concrete + direct elsewhere.
  • Adding a seam later = extract interface + inject — cheap if the class was small.
  • Patterns when: 3+ behaviour variants (Strategy), runtime type choice (Factory), combinable responsibilities (Decorator), growing type/state switch (polymorphism/State).
  • Over-engineering smells: one-impl interfaces, pass-through layers, config for constants, framework where a function fits → inline and delete.
Q&A
What does the rule of three say about abstraction?
Don't abstract from two examples — you're likely capturing a coincidence. Duplicate the second time; on the third occurrence you can see what genuinely varies and what's common, so the extracted abstraction fits.
How do you reconcile YAGNI with "design for change"?
Don't build the flexible mechanism now, but do keep the code in small, well-bounded pieces with clean interfaces at module edges, so when the change actually arrives you can introduce the abstraction with a local refactor instead of a rewrite. Changeability ≠ pre-built flexibility.
Give a concrete "over-engineering" smell.
An interface that has exactly one implementation, isn't a module boundary, and isn't needed for testing — it's pure indirection. Also: config parameters for values that have never changed, and "manager/service/handler" layers that only forward calls.
When is a big switch statement a problem worth a pattern?
When it keeps growing with new cases, the same switch is duplicated in several places, and each case has non-trivial behaviour. Then replace it with polymorphism (a type per case) or the State pattern — adding a case becomes a new class, not an edit to every switch.
What's a cheap way to add a seam to existing concrete code?
Extract an interface from the concrete class (same method signatures), have callers depend on the interface, and inject the concrete implementation at the composition root. If the class was small and its dependencies were already injected, this is a mechanical change.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How many occurrences before you extract a shared abstraction?
Three (the rule of three).
What does YAGNI stand for?
"You Aren't Gonna Need It."
An interface with one implementation and no test seam is usually what?
Over-engineering — unnecessary indirection.

Intermediate core

The interviewer asks you to "make it support multiple databases" but there's only Postgres today. Response?
Note the axis of change is plausible, so put data access behind a repository interface (a real module boundary that also helps testing) — but implement only the Postgres one, and don't build a generic query abstraction or ORM layer speculatively. If a second database is genuinely on the roadmap, the interface is enough of a seam; when it arrives you add one implementation and the composition root wires it. Building the abstraction for two hypothetical databases now risks leaking Postgres-isms (or the wrong lowest-common-denominator) into the interface.
You inherit a codebase with 5 layers of pass-through services and interfaces with single implementations. How do you improve it?
Collapse the indirection incrementally. For each interface with one implementation and no test/module reason: inline it (merge interface into class or remove the pass-through layer), guided by tests. Keep interfaces only at genuine boundaries (external I/O, plugin points, where a fake is needed for testing). Re-package by feature so a change is local. Do it under test coverage, one seam at a time, verifying behaviour is unchanged — the goal is fewer files to read per change, not a big-bang rewrite.

Advanced deep

How do you decide, in a real project, where to invest in flexibility — what evidence do you use?
Use observed and reasonably-certain change, not imagination. Evidence sources: (1) Git history — which files/modules churn the most? High-churn areas are where seams pay off; stable areas should stay concrete. (2) The backlog / roadmap — a committed requirement to add payment providers next quarter is real evidence for a PaymentGateway interface now; a vague "maybe we'll go multi-region someday" is not. (3) The rule of three in practice — the moment you're writing the third variant, extract; not before. (4) Bug clusters — if the same class breaks every time a certain kind of change is made, its responsibilities need splitting. (5) Domain knowledge — some axes are inherently variable (tax rules, notification channels, report formats, external integrations) and worth a seam even at two examples; others (the core aggregate's invariants) rarely change and should be direct. (6) Cost asymmetry — if adding the abstraction later would be a cheap local refactor (small class, injected deps), defer it; if it would be a cross-cutting rewrite (a persistence model baked throughout), invest earlier. The meta-rule: make the likely changes cheap and accept that unlikely changes will be expensive — you can't make everything cheap to change without making everything expensive to read. Review this periodically: an abstraction that was speculative and never got a second implementation is debt to remove; a concrete area that's now churning is a candidate for a seam.
Describe refactoring a "big ball of mud" module toward a clean design without a rewrite.
Work in small, safe steps under a growing test net — the "strangler fig" approach at module scale. (1) Characterisation tests first: pin the current behaviour (including its bugs) with tests at the module's boundary, so any refactor that changes observable behaviour fails loudly. Use approval/golden-master tests if the module is hard to assert on. (2) Find seams: identify the module's real inputs/outputs and introduce an interface at that boundary; route callers through it. Now you have a place to insert new implementations. (3) Extract the easy wins: pull pure functions out (no dependencies → trivially testable), then classes with a single clear responsibility, using automated refactorings (extract method/class) which are behaviour-preserving. (4) Break dependencies: where the tangle is a class that news up its collaborators / hits the DB / reads globals, apply "dependency-breaking" techniques (extract-and-override, parameterise constructor, wrap the static) to get it under test, then refactor its internals. (5) Introduce the new design alongside the old: build the clean version of a slice behind a feature flag or a routing switch; migrate one use case at a time; delete the old path once traffic is fully on the new one. (6) Package by feature as you go, so each extracted piece lands in a cohesive home. (7) Keep each commit shippable and reviewed — never a multi-week branch. The discipline: every step is small enough to verify, the module keeps working the whole time, and you can stop at any point with the codebase better than you found it. This is slower than a rewrite on paper but far less risky — rewrites of understood-badly systems routinely lose edge-case knowledge and take longer than estimated.

Interview Framework & Estimation

A repeatable structure for the 45 minutes, and the numbers to do capacity math in your head.

Notes

The structure

  1. Clarify (5 min) — functional requirements, non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency), and explicit non-goals. Nail down the 2–3 features you'll design.
  2. Estimate (3 min) — QPS (avg & peak), storage/year, bandwidth, and whether it fits on one machine. These numbers drive every later decision.
  3. API (3 min) — the handful of endpoints, their shapes.
  4. Data model (5 min) — entities, access patterns, then choose storage (SQL / KV / doc / column / blob) from the access patterns.
  5. High-level design (10 min) — boxes and arrows: clients → LB → stateless app tier → caches / DB / queue / object store. Walk the main read and write paths.
  6. Deep dive (10 min) — the interviewer picks 1–2 areas; go deep: sharding key, cache invalidation, fan-out, consistency.
  7. Bottlenecks & wrap (5 min) — single points of failure, hot spots, what breaks at 10× scale, monitoring.

Latency numbers to know (order of magnitude)

Operation~Time
L1 / branch mispredict~1 ns / ~5 ns
Main memory reference~100 ns
Mutex lock/unlock~25 ns
Compress 1 KB~1–3 µs
SSD random read~16–100 µs
Datacenter round trip~0.5 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD~50–200 µs
Disk seek (HDD)~5–10 ms
Cross-continent round trip~100–150 ms

Estimation shortcuts

  • 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s. So 1M requests/day ≈ ~12 QPS average; multiply by 2–10 for peak.
  • 1 char ≈ 1 byte; a "tweet" ~300 B; a small row ~1–2 KB; a photo ~1–5 MB; a minute of video ~10–50 MB.
  • Storage/year = writes/sec × bytes/write × 3×10⁷ s.
  • A modern server: ~tens of thousands of simple QPS, ~64–256 GB RAM, ~10–40 TB SSD, ~10–25 Gbps NIC.
Cheat Sheet
  • Flow: clarify → estimate → API → data model → high-level (LB → stateless app → cache/DB/queue/blob) → deep dive → bottlenecks.
  • Always: functional + non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency) + non-goals.
  • Estimate QPS (avg & peak ×2–10), storage/year, bandwidth; check "fits on one box?".
  • 1M/day ≈ 12 QPS avg. Day ≈ 10⁵ s. Storage/yr = wps × bytes × 3×10⁷.
  • Memory ~100 ns, SSD read ~50 µs, DC RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~100 ms, HDD seek ~10 ms.
  • Choose storage from access patterns, not by default.
  • Keep the app tier stateless (state in DB/cache/session store) so it scales horizontally.
Q&A
Roughly how many QPS is 1 million requests per day?
~12 average (1M / 86,400). Design for peak, which is typically 2–10× the average depending on the traffic pattern — so plan for ~50–120 QPS.
What's the order-of-magnitude latency of a main-memory access vs a datacenter round trip?
~100 nanoseconds for memory; ~0.5 milliseconds (500,000 ns) for an in-datacenter RPC round trip — about 5000×. Cross-continent is ~100–150 ms, another ~300×.
Why estimate before designing?
The numbers decide the architecture: 10 QPS and 10 GB fits on one machine (design accordingly); 1M QPS and 100 TB/year forces sharding, caching, and async processing from the start. Designing without numbers leads to over- or under-engineering.
Why keep the application tier stateless?
So you can add/remove instances freely behind a load balancer without session affinity, and any instance can serve any request. Session/user state goes to a shared store (Redis, DB, or a signed token).
How do you pick a datastore in the interview?
From the access patterns: key lookups by id → KV; queries across fields / transactions → relational; whole-aggregate documents / flexible schema → document; huge write volume with known query shapes → wide-column; large binary objects → blob store; relationships / traversal → graph. State the pattern, then the choice.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

First step when given a system design prompt?
Clarify requirements — functional, non-functional (scale/latency/availability/consistency), and what's out of scope.
Seconds in a day, to one significant figure?
~90,000 (86,400) — often rounded to 10⁵ for mental math.
Where should user session state live in a horizontally scaled web tier?
In a shared store (Redis / DB) or a signed client token — not in an app instance's memory.

Intermediate core

Estimate storage for a service ingesting 5,000 events/sec, each ~500 bytes, retained 1 year.
5,000 × 500 B = 2.5 MB/s. × 86,400 s/day ≈ 216 GB/day. × 365 ≈ ~79 TB/year raw. Add ~1.5–3× for indexes/replication overhead → ~120–240 TB. Conclusion: doesn't fit one node → you need partitioning + a retention/compaction strategy (or tiered storage: hot in a fast store, cold in object storage / parquet).
A read-heavy service does 50k QPS, each request 1 DB query at 2 ms. How many DB connections/replicas roughly?
By Little's Law, concurrency = throughput × latency = 50,000 × 0.002 s = 100 in-flight queries at any instant. So you need ~100 usable connections (plus headroom, say 150–200) across the read replicas. If one replica sustains ~10k QPS of this query, you need ~5–6 replicas (plus one for redundancy). Caching the hot reads (say 90% hit rate) cuts DB QPS to ~5k → 1–2 replicas.

Advanced deep

How do you reason about the "does it fit on one machine?" question, and why does it matter so much?
Compare your estimated working set and throughput against a single modern server: ~128–512 GB RAM, ~10–40 TB NVMe, ~25–100 Gbps network, and — for the CPU — anywhere from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands of "simple" operations/sec depending on how much work each does (a Redis GET: ~100k+/s/core; a complex query with joins: dozens/s). Check four dimensions: (1) Does the hot dataset fit in RAM? If yes, you can serve reads from memory on one box and the design collapses to "one replicated node + backups". If no, you're doing disk I/O per read and need caching or sharding. (2) Does peak QPS × per-request CPU exceed one machine's cores? If yes, you need a horizontally scalable stateless tier. (3) Does storage/year exceed one machine's disk? If yes, sharding or object storage. (4) Does peak bandwidth exceed the NIC? (matters for media/CDN-shaped systems). It matters because the moment you can't fit on one machine, you inherit distributed-systems problems — partitioning, replication, consistency trade-offs, partial failure, cross-node coordination — which are an order of magnitude more design and operational complexity. A strong answer explicitly says "at this scale it fits on one primary with read replicas and we're done; at 100× we'd shard by X" — showing you scale the design effort to the actual requirements rather than reaching for Kafka and 20 microservices for 100 QPS.
What non-functional requirements do candidates most often forget to pin down, and how does each change the design?
(1) Consistency requirement per operation — "must a user see their own write immediately?" (read-your-writes), "can two users briefly see different values?" (eventual OK), "does money/inventory need strict serializability?". This decides single-primary vs multi-primary, sync vs async replication, whether you can use a cache freely, and whether you need distributed transactions or can use a saga. (2) Availability target — 99.9% (~8.8 h/yr down) vs 99.99% (~52 min) vs 99.999% changes whether you need multi-AZ, multi-region, active-active, and how much redundancy/failover automation. (3) Latency SLO and at which percentile — "p50 < 100 ms" is very different from "p99.9 < 200 ms"; tail latency drives timeouts, hedged requests, connection-pool sizing, and whether synchronous fan-out is acceptable. (4) Durability — "can we lose the last few seconds of writes on a crash?" decides sync vs async commit, replication factor, and whether an in-memory queue is acceptable. (5) Read:write ratio — 100:1 (cache everything, read replicas) vs 1:1 (caching helps less, write path is the bottleneck) vs write-heavy (LSM storage, batching, async). (6) Data retention & deletion — GDPR "delete on request", retention limits, and audit requirements change storage choice and add a deletion pipeline. (7) Traffic shape — steady vs spiky (flash sale, viral event) decides autoscaling, queue buffering, and pre-provisioning. (8) Cost sensitivity — sometimes a stated constraint. Asking about these early, and restating "so we're optimising for availability over consistency here, correct?", is a strong signal and prevents designing the wrong system confidently.

Load Balancing

Spreading traffic across servers, removing dead ones, and where the LB itself can fail.

Notes

L4 vs L7

L4 (transport)L7 (application)
Routes byIP + portURL path, Host, headers, cookies
Sees payloadnoyes (terminates the connection, often TLS)
Cost / featuresfast, cheap, protocol-agnosticretries, rewrites, path routing, WAF, canary — more CPU
ExamplesAWS NLB, IPVS, hardware LBsnginx, HAProxy, Envoy, ALB

Algorithms

  • Round robin (+ weighted) — simple, good when requests are uniform.
  • Least connections / least response time — adapts to uneven request cost.
  • Consistent hashing — same key → same backend (cache affinity, sticky routing) with minimal remap on membership change.
  • IP hash — cheap client→backend stickiness.

Health checks & failure

  • Active: LB probes each backend (/healthz) and ejects failing ones. Passive: mark a backend down after N consecutive request errors.
  • Distinguish "liveness" (process up) from "readiness" (can serve — DB connected, caches warm). Drain connections gracefully on deploy.
  • The LB is a SPOF → run it redundantly: a VIP with failover (keepalived/VRRP), an anycast address, or a managed LB across AZs. Global traffic uses DNS/GeoDNS/anycast to pick a region, then a regional LB.

Sticky sessions

Pin a client to one backend (cookie or IP hash). Needed only if the backend holds per-session state — the better fix is stateless backends (session in Redis / signed token) so any request can go anywhere, enabling free scaling and deploys.

Autoscaling

Scale the backend pool on a signal (CPU, request rate, queue depth, p99 latency). Scale out fast, in slowly (avoid flapping). Pre-warm for known spikes. The LB must pick up new instances automatically (service discovery / target groups).

Cheat Sheet
  • L4: routes by IP:port, payload-blind, fast, connection-preserving. L7: reads HTTP, path/host/header routing, TLS termination, retries, canary.
  • Algorithms: round-robin / weighted (uniform), least-connections / least-latency (uneven cost), consistent-hash (cache affinity), IP-hash (cheap stickiness).
  • Health: active probe (/healthz) + passive ejection; separate liveness vs readiness; graceful connection draining on deploy.
  • LB is a SPOF → redundant (VIP+VRRP, anycast, multi-AZ managed LB). Global: DNS/GeoDNS/anycast → regional LB.
  • Sticky sessions only if backends are stateful — prefer stateless (session in Redis/token).
  • Autoscale on CPU / RPS / queue depth / p99; out fast, in slow; service discovery so the LB sees new instances.
Q&A
When do you need an L7 load balancer?
When routing decisions depend on request content — send /api and /static to different pools, route by Host for multi-tenant, do path-based canary/blue-green, terminate TLS centrally, or apply a WAF. If you only need "spread TCP connections across identical servers", L4 is faster and cheaper.
Liveness vs readiness health check?
Liveness = "is the process alive?" (restart it if not). Readiness = "can it serve traffic now?" (has DB connections, caches warm, not overloaded). The LB routes only to ready instances; an instance can be live but temporarily not ready (starting up, reconnecting).
Why is consistent hashing used for load balancing in front of caches?
It maps a key to the same backend most of the time, so cache hit rates stay high, and when a backend is added/removed only ~1/N of keys move — avoiding the mass cache-miss stampede that plain modulo hashing causes.
The load balancer is a single point of failure. How do you address that?
Run it redundantly: an active/standby pair sharing a virtual IP with fast failover (VRRP/keepalived), an anycast IP announced from multiple nodes, or a cloud managed LB that's inherently multi-AZ. For multi-region, DNS or anycast directs users to a region and a regional LB pair handles it from there.
How do you avoid needing sticky sessions?
Make the backends stateless — store session data in a shared store (Redis) or a signed/encrypted cookie/JWT the client sends each request. Then any instance can serve any request, so you can scale and deploy without worrying about affinity.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which LB layer can route by URL path?
Layer 7 (application).
Which algorithm adapts to backends handling requests of very different cost?
Least connections (or least response time).
What removes a crashed backend from rotation?
Health checks (active probing or passive error-based ejection).

Intermediate core

After a deploy, users get errors for ~30 s even though the new instances are healthy. Cause and fix?
Old instances were killed before the LB stopped sending them traffic, or new instances were added to rotation before they were actually ready (still warming caches / opening DB pools). Fix: on shutdown, first fail the readiness check (LB drains), wait for in-flight requests to finish (connection draining with a timeout), then exit. On startup, don't pass readiness until dependencies are connected and warm. Use rolling deploys with maxUnavailable small, and health-check grace periods.
Your service is behind one LB in one AZ. Design for AZ failure.
Run backends in ≥2 (ideally 3) AZs, and a cross-AZ load balancer (cloud managed LBs span AZs by default; for self-managed, an LB pair per AZ behind a global entry). The database needs a multi-AZ setup too (a standby in another AZ with automatic failover, or a quorum across 3 AZs). DNS/anycast at the top so if a whole region degrades you can shift traffic. Test with game days / chaos experiments that actually kill an AZ's instances.

Advanced deep

Why can "least connections" load balancing perform badly, and what's the modern alternative?
Classic least-connections works well only when every backend is identical and every request costs the same amount of the resource that matters. Failure modes: (1) a backend that's slow (GC pause, degraded disk, noisy neighbour) accumulates connections and, counterintuitively, attracts more under least-connections in some implementations, or is avoided so hard it never recovers — and "connection count" doesn't capture "this box is at 95% CPU". (2) In a large fleet behind multiple LB instances, each LB only sees its own connections, so global balance is poor. (3) Long-lived connections (HTTP/2, gRPC, websockets) break the model — connection count is nearly constant regardless of load. The modern approach: power of two choices (pick two backends at random, send to the less-loaded — provably close to optimal balance with O(1) state and no global coordination, used by Envoy, Finagle, NGINX Plus); latency-/EWMA-based weighting where each backend's recent response-time and error-rate feed a dynamic weight (Netflix's approach), so a degrading backend sheds load automatically; outlier detection (eject a backend that's returning 5xx or timing out at an anomalous rate, re-admit gradually); and for request-level fairness with expensive requests, concurrency limiting per backend (a token per in-flight request) plus load-based shedding. For gRPC/HTTP-2 you also need request-level LB (each RPC balanced independently) not connection-level, often via a client-side LB (xDS/Envoy) or an L7 proxy that de-multiplexes streams.
Explain how a large service actually routes a user request from their browser to a specific backend process, layer by layer.
(1) DNS: the browser resolves api.example.com; the authoritative DNS (often GeoDNS / a traffic manager like Route 53, NS1, Akamai) returns an IP for the nearest healthy region/PoP based on the resolver's location and per-region health, with a low TTL so it can shift traffic. Some providers return an anycast IP instead, and BGP routes the packets to the nearest edge. (2) Edge / CDN PoP: the anycast IP terminates at a CDN edge that may serve cached static content directly, or (for dynamic API traffic) terminates TLS and proxies onward over a warm, optimised backbone connection to the origin region. (3) Regional L4 LB: at the origin, a layer-4 load balancer (hardware, or IPVS/Maglev-style ECMP where routers hash flows across many LB nodes, each LB node consistently hashing the 4-tuple to a backend so connections stay pinned) spreads connections across the L7 proxy tier. Google's Maglev and Cloudflare's Unimog are examples — they give per-flow consistency without shared state so LB nodes are stateless and horizontally scalable. (4) L7 proxy tier (Envoy / nginx / a service mesh ingress): parses HTTP, does path/host routing, applies auth/rate-limit/WAF, picks the target service, and load-balances at the request level across that service's instances — using power-of-two-choices or EWMA weights, honouring outlier detection and per-instance concurrency limits, and re-resolving the instance list from service discovery (Consul, EDS/xDS, Kubernetes endpoints) as instances come and go. (5) Backend instance: the request lands on one process; if that process is itself multi-threaded/async, an internal work queue or thread pool assigns it to a worker. Cross-cutting: every hop has its own health checking and connection draining, timeouts are set to decrease at each inner layer (so an inner call times out before the outer one gives up), retries are budgeted (retry only at one layer, with a cap, to avoid retry storms), and the whole path is traced (a trace/span id propagated in headers) so you can see where a slow request spent its time.

Caching Strategies & Invalidation

Where to cache, which read/write pattern, and the two hard problems: invalidation and stampede.

Notes

Where

Client / browser → CDN edge → API gateway → in-process (per app instance) → distributed (Redis/Memcached) → database buffer pool. Cache as close to the client as the freshness requirement allows.

Read patterns

PatternHow
Cache-aside (lazy)app checks cache; on miss, reads DB, populates cache. Most common; cache only holds what's asked for.
Read-throughapp asks the cache; the cache library fetches from DB on miss. Same effect, logic in the cache layer.

Write patterns

PatternTrade-off
Write-throughwrite DB + cache synchronously — cache always fresh, writes slower.
Write-back (write-behind)write cache, flush to DB async — fast writes, risk of loss on cache crash, DB lags.
Write-aroundwrite DB only, skip cache — avoids polluting cache with write-once data; next read is a miss.

Common combo: cache-aside reads + write-through-or-invalidate on writes. On a write, either update the cache entry or (safer) delete it so the next read repopulates — avoids stale-write races.

The hard problems

  • Invalidation: keeping the cache consistent with the source. Options: short TTLs (accept bounded staleness), explicit delete on write, versioned keys (user:123:v7), or a change-data-capture stream that invalidates. "There are only two hard things… cache invalidation."
  • Stampede / dogpile: a hot key expires and thousands of requests all miss and hit the DB at once. Fixes: per-key single-flight (one request recomputes, others wait), probabilistic early expiry (refresh slightly before TTL), serve-stale-while-revalidate, or a lock in the cache.
  • Hot key: one key hotter than a single cache node can serve — replicate it to multiple nodes, or add a tiny local L1 with a 1–5 s TTL.
  • Thundering herd on cold start: a fresh/flushed cache means every request misses — warm it, or ramp traffic.
Cheat Sheet
  • Layers: client → CDN → gateway → in-process → Redis/Memcached → DB buffer pool.
  • Reads: cache-aside (app manages) or read-through (cache library manages). Cache-aside is the default.
  • Writes: write-through (fresh, slower), write-back (fast, lossy), write-around (skip cache for write-once).
  • On write: delete the cache key (repopulate on next read) — safer than update against races.
  • Invalidation: short TTL, explicit delete, versioned keys, or CDC-driven.
  • Stampede: per-key single-flight, early/probabilistic refresh, stale-while-revalidate, lock.
  • Hot key: replicate across nodes or add a short-TTL local L1. Cold cache: warm it / ramp.
  • Cache hit rate is the metric — watch it; a drop means wrong keys, too-short TTL, or churn.
Q&A
What is cache-aside?
The application checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, then writes the value into the cache before returning. The cache only ever holds data that's been requested. It's the most common pattern and keeps caching logic in the app.
On a write, should you update the cache entry or delete it?
Deleting is safer. Updating from the write path can race with a concurrent read that repopulates with a stale DB value, leaving the cache wrong. Deleting forces the next read to fetch fresh from the DB. (Update is fine if you have a single writer per key or a version check.)
What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
