(2) Cold start — new users/posts have no engagement features; fall back to popularity + demographic priors, explore deliberately. (3) Filter bubble — pure engagement optimisation narrows the feed; inject exploration and source diversity. (4) Staleness — if the ranking pipeline lags, users see an old feed; have a chronological fallback and cap end-to-end latency. (5) Latency budget — ranking must complete in tens of ms for a feed load; if the model service is slow, serve a cheaper heuristic ranking rather than blocking. (6) Metric myopia — optimising short-term clicks can hurt long-term retention and wellbeing; teams add long-horizon and survey-based objectives. (7) Consistency — the same user refreshing shouldn't see a totally reshuffled feed; add position stability / seen-item suppression. The system is deliberately layered so each stage can degrade independently (skip recommendations, skip ranking → chronological) under load or failure.

The Object Model: Blob, Tree, Commit

Everything in Git is an object in a content-addressed store — understand this and the rest follows.

Notes

A content-addressed key-value store

At its core Git is a key-value database. You hand it content, it stores the content and returns a hash (SHA-1 historically; SHA-256 in newer repos). The hash is the key: the same content always produces the same hash, and any change to the content produces a completely different hash. Objects live in .git/objects/ (loose objects, then packed into .pack files for efficiency).

The four object types

TypeWhat it holds
blobThe raw contents of one file. No filename, no permissions, no history — just bytes. Two files with identical content anywhere in the repo share one blob.
treeA directory listing: a list of entries, each being (mode, type, hash, name). Entries point at blobs (files) or other trees (subdirectories). This is where filenames and the executable bit live.
commitA snapshot pointer: the hash of one root tree, zero or more parent commit hashes, author + committer (name, email, timestamp), and the commit message.
tag (annotated)A named, described pointer to another object (usually a commit) with its own author, message, and optional signature. Lightweight tags are just a ref, not an object.

How a commit represents your whole project

A commit points to one tree — the root directory. That tree points to blobs and subtrees, which point to more blobs and subtrees, all the way down. So a single commit hash transitively names the exact content of every file and every directory. Git stores a full snapshot conceptually (not diffs); it just deduplicates via hashing, so unchanged files across commits reuse the same blob and unchanged directories reuse the same tree. Packfiles then delta-compress similar objects on disk, but that's a storage optimisation invisible to the model.

History = a DAG of commits

Each commit records its parent(s), so commits form a directed acyclic graph. A normal commit has one parent; the first commit has none (a "root commit"); a merge commit has two or more. Branches and tags are just named pointers ("refs") into this graph, stored as files under .git/refs/ (or in packed-refs). HEAD usually points at a branch ref.

Inspecting objects

git hash-object -w file.txt      # store content as a blob, print its hash
git cat-file -t <hash>           # show an object's type
git cat-file -p <hash>           # pretty-print an object's content
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}      # dump the root tree of the current commit
git rev-parse HEAD               # resolve a ref/expression to a full hash
git count-objects -v             # loose vs packed object stats
Cheat Sheet
  • Git = content-addressed KV store; the SHA of the content is the key. Same content → same hash; any change → new hash.
  • blob = file contents (no name). tree = directory (entries: mode, type, hash, name). commit = one root tree + parent(s) + author/committer + message. annotated tag = named pointer object with message/signature.
  • A commit → a tree → blobs + subtrees: one hash names your entire project state.
  • Snapshots, not diffs — but unchanged blobs/trees are reused across commits; packfiles delta-compress on disk.
  • History is a DAG: 1 parent = normal, 0 = root commit, ≥2 = merge.
  • Refs (branches, tags) = files in .git/refs/ holding a commit hash. HEAD → current branch.
  • Poke around: git cat-file -p <hash>, git cat-file -t, git rev-parse, git hash-object -w.
Q&A
What are the four Git object types?
Blob (file contents), tree (a directory listing pointing at blobs and subtrees), commit (a pointer to one root tree plus parent commits and metadata), and annotated tag (a named pointer object with its own message/signature).
Does a blob store the filename?
No. A blob is just the file's bytes. The filename, path, and mode (e.g. executable bit) are stored in the tree entry that points at the blob. That's why two identically-named files with different content are different blobs, and two differently-named files with identical content are the same blob.
Does Git store diffs between commits?
Conceptually no — each commit is a full snapshot (a complete tree). Git avoids bloat by reusing unchanged blob and tree objects across commits (dedup via hashing) and by delta-compressing objects inside packfiles on disk. The model is snapshots; deltas are an invisible storage detail.
What is a branch, physically?
A tiny file (e.g. .git/refs/heads/main, or a line in packed-refs) containing a single 40-hex-character commit hash. "Moving a branch" just rewrites that file. This is why branching and deleting branches are instant.
Why is the commit hash different if I commit the same tree twice?
Because the commit object includes the committer timestamp (and usually a different parent). The tree hash would be identical, but the commit object's bytes differ, so its hash differs.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is used as the key for a Git object?
A cryptographic hash of the object's content (SHA-1, or SHA-256 in newer repositories).
Which object type contains filenames?
The tree object — each entry is (mode, type, hash, name).
How many parents does the very first commit in a repo have?
Zero — it's a root commit.

Intermediate core

You copy config.yaml to config.bak without changing it and commit. How many new blobs are created?
Zero new blobs. The content is identical, so it hashes to the same blob that already exists; Git just adds a second tree entry (config.bak) pointing at that same blob hash. A new tree object (the directory now has an extra entry) and a new commit object are created, but no new blob.
Explain how one commit hash can guarantee the exact state of a 10,000-file project.
The commit points to a single root tree hash. That tree's bytes include the hashes of all its entries (files as blobs, subdirectories as subtrees). Each subtree in turn includes its children's hashes, recursively. Because every hash is derived from content, changing any byte of any file changes that blob's hash, which changes its parent tree's hash, which propagates up to the root tree hash, which changes the commit hash. So the commit hash is a Merkle-root over the entire directory structure — it cryptographically fixes every file and folder.
What's the difference between an annotated tag and a lightweight tag?
A lightweight tag is just a ref — a file under .git/refs/tags/ holding a commit hash, with no extra data. An annotated tag creates a real tag object containing a tagger name/email/date, a message, and optionally a GPG signature; the ref then points at that tag object, which points at the commit. Releases should use annotated (or signed) tags so there's a recorded author and message; lightweight tags are fine as private bookmarks.

Advanced deep

Git historically used SHA-1, which has known collision attacks. Why hasn't this broken Git, and what has been done about it?
Several reasons it hasn't been catastrophic: (1) Git hashes a type/length header plus the content, and for commits the object includes parent hashes and timestamps, so a useful collision must be a valid Git object of the right type that also fits the surrounding DAG — much harder than a raw SHA-1 collision. (2) The known attacks (SHAttered, 2017) are identical-prefix / chosen-prefix collisions requiring the attacker to craft both colliding blobs; they can't produce a collision for an existing object they don't control (no preimage attack on SHA-1 is known). (3) Git added a collision-detection library (sha1dc / "hardened SHA-1") that detects the SHAttered attack pattern and aborts, so those specific PDFs can't even be added. (4) The real fix is the SHA-256 object format: repositories can be created with --object-format=sha256, making all object names 256-bit. Interop with SHA-1 repos is still maturing (hosting support, a mapping between the two hashes), so migration has been gradual, but the transition design exists and new security-sensitive repos can opt in today.
What is a packfile, how does git gc build one, and what problem does it solve?
Storing every object as its own zlib-compressed file ("loose objects") wastes space (no cross-object compression) and inodes, and makes network transfer chatty. A packfile (.git/objects/pack/*.pack with a companion .idx) bundles many objects into one file and stores similar objects as deltas against a chosen base object (delta chains), then compresses. git gc (invoked automatically past thresholds, or manually) runs git repack: it walks reachable objects, groups likely-similar ones (heuristics on type, size, path/filename, and recency — newer objects are kept whole or shallowly-deltated for fast access), picks base objects, computes deltas up to a max chain length, and writes the pack plus an index for O(log n) lookup by hash. It also prunes unreachable loose objects older than the expiry (default 2 weeks, and only those not referenced by the reflog). The result: dramatically smaller repos, fewer files, and packs can be sent almost as-is over the wire ("thin packs" during fetch/push send deltas against objects the other side already has). Trade-off: deep delta chains cost CPU to reconstruct an object, so Git caps chain depth and keeps a delta cache.

The Three Trees: Working Tree, Index, HEAD

Almost every confusing Git command makes sense once you track which of the three trees it moves.

Notes

The three "trees" (states)

TreeWhat it is
HEADThe last commit on the current branch — the snapshot your next commit will be based on. "What I last committed."
Index (staging area / cache)A binary file (.git/index) listing the exact file contents (blob hashes) + metadata that will go into the next commit. "What I've proposed to commit."
Working treeThe actual files on disk you edit. "What I'm working on right now."

The basic workflow moves content between them

edit file        # working tree changes, index & HEAD unchanged
git add file     # copy working-tree version into the index
git commit       # write the index as a new commit; HEAD moves to it

After a clean commit, all three trees match. git status is essentially a diff report: "Changes to be committed" = index vs HEAD; "Changes not staged" = working tree vs index; "Untracked files" = in working tree, not in index.

reset moves things between the three trees

CommandHEADIndexWorking tree
reset --soft <c>→ cunchangedunchanged
reset [--mixed] <c>→ c→ cunchanged
reset --hard <c>→ c→ c→ c (discards changes)

So git reset --soft HEAD~1 "uncommits" but keeps everything staged; git reset HEAD~1 also unstages; git reset --hard HEAD~1 throws the work away entirely.

checkout / restore / switch

  • git checkout <commit> — moves HEAD (detaches it) and updates index + working tree to that commit; refuses if it would clobber uncommitted changes.
  • git checkout <branch> — same, but HEAD follows the branch (not detached).
  • git checkout -- <file> / git restore <file> — overwrite the working-tree file from the index (discard unstaged edits).
  • git restore --staged <file> — copy HEAD's version into the index (unstage), leaving the working tree alone. git restore --staged --worktree <file> resets both.
  • Newer split: git switch for branches, git restore for files — less overloaded than checkout.

Other index operations

git add -p          # stage selected hunks interactively
git reset -p        # unstage selected hunks
git rm --cached f   # remove from index (stop tracking) but keep on disk
git diff            # working tree vs index
git diff --staged   # index vs HEAD  (aka --cached)
git diff HEAD       # working tree vs HEAD (both combined)
Cheat Sheet
  • HEAD = last commit. Index = next commit's staged content (.git/index). Working tree = files on disk.
  • add = working tree → index. commit = index → new commit, HEAD moves.
  • git status: "to be committed" = index vs HEAD; "not staged" = worktree vs index; "untracked" = not in index.
  • reset --soft = move HEAD only. reset --mixed (default) = HEAD + index. reset --hard = HEAD + index + working tree (destroys changes).
  • git restore <file> = discard unstaged edits (from index). git restore --staged <file> = unstage (from HEAD).
  • git diff = worktree vs index. git diff --staged = index vs HEAD. git diff HEAD = worktree vs HEAD.
  • git rm --cached = untrack but keep file. git add -p / reset -p = hunk-level staging.
Q&A
What is the index / staging area?
A file (.git/index) that holds the complete list of file paths and their blob hashes that will form the next commit. git add writes working-tree content into it; git commit turns it into a commit. It lets you build a commit incrementally and commit only some of your changes.
Difference between git diff and git diff --staged?
git diff (no args) shows working tree vs index — your unstaged changes. git diff --staged (or --cached) shows index vs HEAD — what you've staged and would commit. git diff HEAD shows everything (staged + unstaged) vs the last commit.
What do --soft, --mixed, and --hard control in git reset?
Which of the three trees get updated to the target commit. --soft: only HEAD moves (index and working tree untouched → your changes are left staged). --mixed (default): HEAD and index move (changes left unstaged in the working tree). --hard: all three move (working-tree changes are discarded — the only destructive one).
How do I unstage a file I accidentally git added?
git restore --staged <file> (modern) or git reset HEAD <file> (classic). Both copy HEAD's version of that path back into the index; your working-tree edits are preserved.
What's the difference between git rm and git rm --cached?
git rm file deletes it from both the index and the working tree (staged for deletion). git rm --cached file removes it only from the index — Git stops tracking it, but the file stays on disk. Use --cached when you committed something that should have been gitignored.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command copies a change from the working tree into the index?
git add.
After a clean git commit with nothing else changed, how do the three trees compare?
All three (HEAD, index, working tree) are identical — git status reports "nothing to commit, working tree clean".
Which reset mode discards your uncommitted working-tree changes?
git reset --hard.

Intermediate core

You've made 3 commits that should really be 1. You want to keep all the changes staged and re-commit once. Which command?
git reset --soft HEAD~3. HEAD moves back 3 commits, but the index and working tree are untouched — so all the combined changes from those 3 commits are sitting staged, ready for a single new git commit. (git reset --mixed HEAD~3 would also work but leaves them unstaged, so you'd need to git add again.)
You run git checkout <some-old-commit> and Git warns about "detached HEAD". What does that mean and what's the risk?
Normally HEAD points at a branch name, and that branch points at a commit. In detached HEAD, HEAD points directly at a commit with no branch in between. You can look around and even make commits, but those commits aren't on any branch — if you then git checkout main, nothing references them and they become candidates for garbage collection (recoverable via the reflog for a while). To keep work done in detached HEAD, create a branch first: git switch -c new-branch.
What does git add -p do and when is it useful?
It walks through your unstaged changes hunk by hunk and asks, for each, whether to stage it (y/n/split/edit). It lets you separate unrelated changes that live in the same file into different commits — e.g. stage a bug fix now while leaving a half-finished refactor in the same file unstaged. It operates purely on the index; nothing is committed.

Advanced deep

Walk through exactly what git commit -a -m "msg" does in terms of the three trees, and name a case where -a silently does the wrong thing.
-a makes Git, just before committing, automatically stage modifications and deletions of already-tracked files (equivalent to git add -u) — it copies the current working-tree content of every tracked, modified path into the index. Then it commits the index as a new commit and advances HEAD. Sequence: (working tree → index) for tracked changes, then (index → new commit), then HEAD moves. Cases where it does the wrong thing: (1) New files are not tracked yet, so -a ignores them — you think you committed everything but new files were left out. (2) If you had carefully staged only some hunks with git add -p, -a overrides that by staging the entire current content of those files, silently including the hunks you deliberately left out. (3) A file you'd staged and then further edited: -a commits the newer working-tree version, not the version you reviewed and staged. So -a is a convenience for the "I edited tracked files and want all of it" case and a footgun whenever your index was intentionally different from your working tree.
Why is the index a performance feature, not just a UX feature? What metadata does it cache and how is that used?
The index is a flat, sorted binary file listing every tracked path with its blob hash and cached stat data from the last time Git saw that file: mtime, ctime, inode, device, size, and mode. On git status / git diff, Git doesn't re-hash every file in the repo — it lstat()s each path and compares the stat fields to the cached ones. If they match, Git assumes the content is unchanged and skips reading and hashing the file entirely. Only files whose stat data differs get their content hashed to confirm a real change. For a large repo this turns an O(total bytes) operation into O(number of files) syscalls. Extensions build on this: the untracked cache stores directory mtimes so Git can skip scanning unchanged directories for new files; the fsmonitor integration (Watchman / built-in) lets the OS tell Git which paths changed since last time, avoiding even the full lstat() walk; the split index and sparse index reduce the cost of writing and carrying the index itself. The "racy git" problem (a file modified in the same second the index was written, so mtime matches but content changed) is handled by treating entries with mtime ≥ index mtime as dirty and re-checking them.

Branches, HEAD & Fast-Forward

A branch is just a movable pointer — once that clicks, merges and rebases stop being mysterious.

Notes

A branch is a pointer, not a copy

A branch is a 41-byte file under .git/refs/heads/ containing one commit hash. Creating a branch writes that file; it does not copy any files. When you commit on a branch, Git creates the commit and then updates the branch file to point at the new commit. That's the whole mechanism — branches are cheap because they're one line of text.

HEAD

  • HEAD is a file (.git/HEAD) that normally contains ref: refs/heads/main — a symbolic reference to the current branch. "The current branch" is defined as whatever HEAD points to.
  • When you commit, Git follows HEAD → branch, and moves that branch.
  • Detached HEAD: HEAD contains a commit hash directly (from git checkout <hash> or git checkout v1.0). Commits you make advance HEAD but no branch — create a branch to keep them.

Fast-forward vs true merge

Say main is at commit C and you branch feature, then add D and E on feature. main has not moved.

C ← D ← E   (feature, HEAD)
^
main

git checkout main; git merge feature: since main's commit C is an ancestor of feature's E, Git can just slide the main pointer forward to E. No new commit, no merge — a fast-forward. History stays linear.

Now suppose someone else committed F on main while you worked:

      D ← E   (feature)
     /
C ← F         (main)

The branches have diverged. A fast-forward is impossible. Git creates a merge commit M with two parents (E and F) that combines both lines. This is a "true" / "3-way" merge (it uses E, F, and their common ancestor C).

Controlling merge behaviour

git merge feature              # FF if possible, else a merge commit
git merge --no-ff feature      # always create a merge commit (keeps the branch visible)
git merge --ff-only feature    # only if it can FF, else fail (good for scripts / pulls)
git config pull.ff only        # make 'git pull' refuse to create surprise merge commits
git merge --squash feature     # stage the combined diff, no merge; you commit once, no link to feature

Everyday branch commands

git switch -c feature           # create + switch (old: git checkout -b)
git branch                      # list local branches (* = current)
git branch -vv                  # + upstream tracking + ahead/behind
git branch -d feature           # delete (refuses if not merged)
git branch -D feature           # force delete
git branch -m old new           # rename
git switch -                    # jump back to previous branch
git push -u origin feature      # push + set upstream tracking

Tracking branches & remotes

origin/main is a remote-tracking branch — Git's local cache of where main was on origin at your last fetch. It only moves when you fetch/pull. Your local main can be "ahead 2, behind 1" relative to it. git status reports this when your branch has an upstream set.

Cheat Sheet
  • Branch = file in .git/refs/heads/ holding one commit hash. Committing moves it. Creating/deleting is instant.
  • HEAD = symbolic ref to the current branch (ref: refs/heads/…). Detached HEAD = points straight at a commit.
  • Fast-forward: target branch's tip is an ancestor of the source → just slide the pointer, no merge commit, linear history.
  • True / 3-way merge: branches diverged → new merge commit with 2 parents, using the common ancestor.
  • merge --no-ff = always a merge commit. merge --ff-only = FF or fail. merge --squash = flatten, no parent link.
  • git switch -c new branch; git branch -d safe delete; -D force; switch - = previous branch.
  • origin/main = remote-tracking branch, a snapshot from your last fetch; "ahead/behind" is measured against it.
Q&A
What actually happens when you create a branch?
Git writes a new file under .git/refs/heads/ containing the current commit's hash. No files are copied, nothing is duplicated. Switching to it just updates HEAD to point at that ref and updates the working tree/index to match its commit.
What is a fast-forward merge?
When the branch you're merging into has not diverged — its tip commit is a direct ancestor of the branch you're merging from — Git doesn't need a merge commit. It simply moves the current branch pointer forward to the other branch's tip. History remains a straight line.
When is a fast-forward not possible?
When both branches have commits the other doesn't — they've diverged from a common ancestor. Git then performs a three-way merge and records a merge commit with two parents.
What does --no-ff achieve?
It forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward would be possible. Teams use it so that every feature branch leaves a visible "merge bubble" in history, making it easy to see which commits belonged together and to revert a whole feature with one git revert -m 1.
What is origin/main and why doesn't it update as I work?
It's a remote-tracking branch: a local, read-only pointer recording where main was on the remote origin the last time you communicated with it. It only advances on git fetch (or pull, which fetches then merges/rebases). Between fetches it's a stale-but-useful reference point for "ahead/behind" counts.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

How much data is copied when you run git branch new-feature?
Essentially none — Git writes one small file containing a commit hash.
What does HEAD normally point to?
The current branch (a symbolic ref like ref: refs/heads/main), not a commit directly.
Does a fast-forward merge create a merge commit?
No — it just moves the branch pointer forward.

Intermediate core

git branch -d feature fails with "not fully merged". What does that check, and when is -D safe?
-d refuses to delete a branch whose tip commit is not reachable from HEAD (or from its configured upstream) — i.e. it has commits that would become unreferenced. It's protecting you from losing work. -D (force) is safe when you know those commits are unwanted (an abandoned experiment), or when they are reachable another way — e.g. you already merged the branch with --squash or rebased its commits onto main under new hashes, so the original commits are redundant. Even after -D, the branch's old tip is in the reflog for a couple of weeks, so an accidental force-delete is recoverable.
Your teammate asks why git pull sometimes creates a weird "Merge branch 'main' of …" commit on their branch. What's happening and how do you prevent it?
git pull = git fetch + git merge origin/<branch> by default. If they have local commits and the remote also advanced, the two have diverged, so the merge can't fast-forward and Git records a merge commit right there on their branch — often with an ugly auto-generated message, and it clutters history with tiny merge bubbles. Prevention options: git config --global pull.ff only (pull refuses and tells them to decide) combined with git pull --rebase when they do have local work (replays their commits on top of the updated remote, keeping history linear); or set git config --global pull.rebase true to make rebase the default. For shared long-lived branches, merges are fine; for a personal feature branch, rebase-on-pull is usually what people want.

Advanced deep

Explain how Git computes "ahead 3, behind 2", and why that count can be misleading after a rebase or force-push.
Given your branch tip L and its upstream tip R, Git finds the merge base B (their most recent common ancestor) and counts commits on each side: "ahead" = commits reachable from L but not R (i.e. on B..L), "behind" = commits reachable from R but not L (B..R). It's literally git rev-list --left-right --count R...L. This is a graph comparison by commit identity (hash), not by content. After you rebase your branch, every one of your commits gets a new hash even though the diffs are identical. So if upstream hasn't changed, you'll now show "ahead N, behind N" — N brand-new commits ahead, and the N original pre-rebase commits (still reachable from origin/branch until you push) counted as "behind" — because Git sees two disjoint sets of commit objects that happen to represent the same changes. Similarly, after someone force-pushes a rewritten upstream, your local remote-tracking branch is stale and the ahead/behind numbers reflect the divergence between old and new histories, not real unmerged work. The fix is to fetch and then reconcile deliberately (reset your local branch to the new upstream, or rebase onto it), after which the counts become meaningful again. The lesson: ahead/behind answers "how do these two commit graphs differ?", which only equals "how does the work differ?" when no history rewriting has happened.
What is a symbolic ref, how does git symbolic-ref differ from a normal ref, and where else does Git use them besides HEAD?
A normal ref (.git/refs/heads/main) contains a 40-hex commit hash — it points at an object. A symbolic ref contains the text ref: refs/heads/<name> — it points at another ref, forming one level of indirection. HEAD is the canonical example: "current branch" is implemented as HEAD being a symbolic ref to a branch, so that committing updates the branch HEAD names, and detaching just means overwriting HEAD with a raw hash instead. git symbolic-ref HEAD reads it; git symbolic-ref HEAD refs/heads/other repoints it without touching the working tree (unlike switch, which also updates files). Other uses: refs/remotes/origin/HEAD is a symbolic ref recording the remote's default branch (what git clone checks out, and what a bare origin means in some commands) — you can retarget it with git remote set-head origin -a. During an interactive rebase or a merge, Git writes transient symbolic/plain refs like ORIG_HEAD, MERGE_HEAD, REBASE_HEAD to track state. Worktrees each get their own HEAD. The indirection is also why the reflog is per ref: HEAD's reflog records every value HEAD took (including branch switches), while main's reflog records only where main pointed.

Merge vs Rebase

Two ways to combine work — one preserves history as it happened, the other rewrites it to look tidy.

Notes

The setup

      D ← E     feature
     /
A ← B ← C       main

You want feature to include main's new commit C.

Merge

git checkout feature; git merge main creates a merge commit M with two parents (E and C):

      D ← E ← M     feature
     /       /
A ← B ← C ←--/     main
  • Nothing is rewritten. E, D, C keep their hashes.
  • M records "these two lines of development were joined here", with the exact state at that time.
  • History is truthful but can become a tangle of criss-crossing lines ("merge bubbles") on busy repos.

Rebase

git checkout feature; git rebase main takes your commits (D, E), sets them aside, moves feature to C, then replays D and E on top as brand-new commits D′ and E′:

A ← B ← C ← D′ ← E′     feature
        ^
        main
  • D′ and E′ have new hashes (new parent, new committer date) — the originals are now unreferenced.
  • History is linear: it looks like you started your work from C all along.
  • Each replayed commit can hit conflicts; you resolve, git rebase --continue, repeat.

The golden rule

Don't rebase commits that others have based work on (anything already pushed to a shared branch that teammates pulled). Rebasing rewrites hashes; when you force-push the rewritten branch, everyone else's history diverges from yours and they get painful conflicts. Rebase freely on your own unpushed / unshared commits.

When to use which

Use mergeUse rebase
Integrating a shared/long-lived branchUpdating your local feature branch onto latest main
You want the true record of when things joinedYou want a clean, linear, reviewable history
The branch is public and others use itCleaning up your own commits before opening/merging a PR
Preserving context of parallel workAvoiding "Merge branch 'main'" noise commits

Related commands

git pull --rebase             # fetch, then rebase your local commits onto the new upstream
git rebase --onto A B feature # replay feature's commits that are after B, onto A
git merge --no-ff feature     # force a merge bubble even if FF is possible
git rebase -i main            # interactive: also reorder/squash/edit while replaying
git rebase --abort            # bail out, restore pre-rebase state
git config rerere.enabled true# reuse recorded conflict resolutions across replays

Semi-linear / "rebase and merge" workflows (common on GitHub/GitLab): rebase the feature branch onto main first, then merge with --no-ff — linear commits plus a merge commit marking the feature boundary.

Cheat Sheet
  • Merge: joins two branches with a 2-parent merge commit. Non-destructive, hashes unchanged, true history, can get tangled.
  • Rebase: replays your commits on top of another branch as new commits (new hashes). Linear history, "as if you started from latest". Rewrites history.
  • Golden rule: never rebase/rewrite commits others have already pulled from a shared branch.
  • Rebase conflicts are resolved per replayed commit: fix → git add → git rebase --continue (or --abort).
  • git pull --rebase avoids "Merge branch 'main'" noise on your feature branch.
  • Rule of thumb: rebase to update your branch onto main; merge to bring a finished branch into main (often --no-ff).
  • Enable rerere to auto-reapply conflict resolutions during long rebases.
Q&A
Core difference between merge and rebase?
Merge combines two branches by creating a new commit with both branch tips as parents — existing commits are untouched. Rebase moves your branch's commits so they replay on top of another branch, creating new commits with new hashes and discarding the originals — producing a linear history.
Why does rebase change commit hashes?
A commit's hash is derived from its content including its parent hash and committer date. Rebasing gives each replayed commit a different parent (and a new committer timestamp), so its bytes differ and it gets a new hash. The original commits still exist until garbage-collected but nothing points to them.
What is "the golden rule of rebasing"?
Never rebase commits that exist outside your local repo — i.e. that others may have pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else into a divergent state and messy recovery. Only rebase private, unpushed (or unshared) work.
How are conflicts handled differently in merge vs rebase?
A merge resolves conflicts once, at the single merge commit. A rebase replays commits one at a time and can stop with a conflict on each commit; you fix each, git add, and git rebase --continue. It's more interruptions but each is smaller and localised to that commit's change.
What does git pull --rebase do?
It fetches the upstream, then instead of merging origin/<branch> into your local branch (which would create a merge commit when you have local commits), it rebases your local commits on top of the updated upstream. Result: linear history, no "Merge branch" commits on your branch.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which operation produces a linear history?
Rebase.
How many parents does a standard merge commit have?
Two (or more, for an octopus merge).
Is it safe to rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared main that colleagues pulled?
No — that violates the golden rule and forces everyone into a divergent history.

Intermediate core

Your feature branch is 20 commits behind main. Compare the review/history outcome of git merge main into it vs git rebase main.
merge main: one merge commit is added to your feature branch; your 20-behind situation is resolved in a single conflict-resolution pass; history now shows a merge bubble, and when the PR is eventually merged, reviewers see your original commits plus a "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commit mixed in. Diffs against main include the merge. rebase main: your feature commits are replayed on top of current main as new commits, so the branch becomes a clean linear series that applies directly to main's tip; the PR diff is exactly your changes with no merge noise; reviewers can read commit-by-commit. Cost: you may resolve conflicts multiple times (once per replayed commit that touches contested code), the commits get new hashes (fine, since the branch is yours and unshared or you'll force-push-with-lease), and you lose the information about when you integrated main. Most teams prefer rebase here for review clarity, reserving merge for when the branch is shared.
What does git rebase --onto do that a plain git rebase can't? Give a concrete use.
Plain git rebase <base> replays "all commits on the current branch since its merge base with <base>" onto <base>. git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> [<branch>] decouples which commits to replay from where to put them: it replays the commits in <upstream>..<branch> onto <newbase>. Concrete use: you branched featureB off featureA, but featureA got abandoned. You want featureB's commits (only the ones unique to it) to sit on main instead. git rebase --onto main featureA featureB takes exactly the commits after featureA and lands them on main, dropping featureA's commits from the branch. Another use: dropping a range of commits from the middle of a branch by rebasing --onto the commit before the range, over the commit at the end of the range.

Advanced deep

A teammate force-pushed a rebased shared branch and now three people's local copies are broken. Walk through what went wrong and how each person recovers safely.
What happened: the branch origin/shared used to point at history H1 (commits …X–Y–Z). The teammate rebased, producing H2 (…X–Y′–Z′ with new hashes) and force-pushed, so origin/shared now points at H2 and Y, Z are no longer referenced on the remote. Everyone else still has H1 as their local shared plus possibly new local commits on top. On their next git pull, Git fetches H2, sees local shared (H1-based) and origin/shared (H2) have diverged, and either creates a mess of a merge (re-introducing Y and Z alongside Y′ and Z′ — duplicated commits, spurious conflicts) or refuses. Recovery per person: (1) git fetch to get H2. (2) If they had no local commits beyond H1: git checkout shared && git reset --hard origin/shared — discard the old-history local branch and match the remote. (3) If they did have local work on top of the old Y–Z: identify just those commits (e.g. git log origin/shared@{1}..shared using the reflog of the remote-tracking branch, or the range since the old merge base) and rebase --onto them from the old tip to the new one: git rebase --onto origin/shared <old-shared-tip> shared. This drops the now-duplicated Y/Z and lands only their genuinely-new commits on the rewritten history. (4) Verify with git range-diff <old> <new> that nothing was lost. Prevention going forward: don't rebase shared branches; if a shared branch must be rewritten, coordinate a freeze, use --force-with-lease (fails if someone else pushed in the meantime), announce it, and have everyone reset rather than pull. Better: only ever rebase private branches; integrate shared branches with merges.
Explain how git rebase decides which commits to replay, and why "already applied upstream" commits are silently dropped. How does this interact with cherry-picks?
git rebase <upstream> computes the commit list as roughly git rev-list <upstream>..HEAD — commits reachable from your branch tip but not from <upstream> — in topological order, then replays each with an internal cherry-pick. Before replaying, it runs a patch-id equivalence check (like git cherry / git patch-id): for each of your commits it computes a hash of the diff (whitespace- and context-normalised, independent of commit metadata and line numbers) and compares against the patch-ids of commits in <upstream> that aren't in your branch. If a match is found, that commit is considered already present upstream (someone cherry-picked it, or an earlier version of your branch was merged) and it is skipped to avoid applying the same change twice (which would usually conflict or create an empty commit). This is why, after a maintainer cherry-picks two of your five commits into main, rebasing your branch onto main cleanly replays only the other three. Caveats: the patch-id match requires the diffs to be essentially identical — if the upstream version was modified during cherry-pick (conflict resolution, a squash, an amended hunk), the patch-ids differ and your commit is not recognised as duplicate, so it replays and conflicts against the already-present change. git rebase --keep-empty / --empty=keep and --no-reapply-cherry-picks (or the older --reapply-cherry-picks) control this behaviour; --interactive shows you the computed list (with dropped commits commented out) before you commit to it. The same patch-id machinery powers git cherry -v and git format-patch's duplicate detection.

Interactive Rebase & Editing History

Reword, squash, split, reorder, and drop commits before anyone else sees them.

Notes

Starting it

git rebase -i HEAD~5        # edit the last 5 commits
git rebase -i main         # edit every commit on this branch since it left main
git rebase -i --root       # edit from the very first commit

Git opens an editor with the commits listed oldest first, each prefixed with pick. You change the verbs and/or reorder lines, save, and Git replays the list top to bottom.

The commands (the "todo list")

VerbEffect
pick (p)Use the commit as-is.
reword (r)Use the commit's changes, but stop to edit its message.
edit (e)Stop after applying the commit so you can amend it, split it, add files, etc. Then git rebase --continue.
squash (s)Merge this commit into the previous one; combine both messages (editor opens).
fixup (f)Like squash but discard this commit's message. fixup -C keeps this message instead.
drop (d)Delete the commit entirely (same as removing the line).
reorderJust move the lines — commits replay in the new order.
exec (x)Run a shell command (e.g. tests) at that point; a non-zero exit pauses the rebase.
break (b)Stop here unconditionally; resume with --continue.

Common recipes

# Fix the message of the last commit (nothing else)
git commit --amend

# Squash the last 3 commits into one
git rebase -i HEAD~3     # set lines 2 and 3 to 'fixup' (or 'squash')

# Auto-squash: make review fixups that collapse into the right commit later
git commit --fixup <hash>          # message becomes "fixup! <subject>"
git rebase -i --autosquash main    # fixup!/squash! lines auto-placed & marked

# Split one commit into two
git rebase -i <before>   # mark the target 'edit'
git reset HEAD~          # un-commit it, changes now unstaged
git add -p; git commit   # stage & commit piece 1
git add -p; git commit   # ... piece 2
git rebase --continue

# Drop a secret that was committed 6 commits ago
git rebase -i HEAD~6     # 'edit' that commit, remove the file, amend, continue
                          # (for something already pushed/shared, use git-filter-repo)

Safety & recovery

  • git rebase --abort at any pause restores the exact pre-rebase state.
  • Before starting, the branch tip is saved as ORIG_HEAD and in the reflog — git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD undoes a finished rebase.
  • Set git config rerere.enabled true so repeated conflicts (common when squashing) are resolved automatically after the first time.
  • Pushing a rebased branch needs git push --force-with-lease (safer than --force: it refuses if the remote moved since your last fetch).
  • Only do this on unshared commits — the golden rule from Merge vs Rebase applies.
Cheat Sheet
  • git rebase -i <base> → editor lists commits oldest-first, all pick. Change verbs / reorder / delete lines, save.
  • reword = edit message; edit = pause to amend/split; squash = fold into prev (keep both msgs); fixup = fold in, drop msg; drop = remove; exec = run a command.
  • Amend just the last commit: git commit --amend.
  • Auto-squash flow: git commit --fixup <hash> … then git rebase -i --autosquash <base>.
  • Split a commit: mark edit → git reset HEAD~ → stage & commit in pieces → --continue.
  • Undo a whole rebase: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD. Bail mid-rebase: git rebase --abort.
  • Push rewritten branch: git push --force-with-lease. Never rewrite shared/pushed-and-pulled history.
  • rerere.enabled true reuses conflict resolutions across the replay.
Q&A
Difference between squash and fixup in an interactive rebase?
Both combine a commit into the one above it. squash opens an editor so you can craft a combined commit message from both. fixup silently discards the squashed commit's message and keeps only the earlier commit's message — ideal for "oops, typo" commits.
How do you edit a commit that isn't the most recent one?
git rebase -i <commit-before-it>, change that commit's line to edit, save. The rebase stops right after applying it; make your changes and git commit --amend, then git rebase --continue. Later commits are replayed on top with new hashes.
What is --autosquash and how do you set it up?
While working, run git commit --fixup=<hash> (or --squash=<hash>); Git makes the message fixup! <original subject>. Later, git rebase -i --autosquash <base> automatically moves each such commit directly below its target and pre-marks it fixup/squash, so you just save. Set git config rebase.autosquash true to make it the default.
You started a rebase, hit conflicts, and it's a mess. How do you get back to safety?
git rebase --abort. It restores the branch, index, and working tree to exactly how they were before you ran git rebase. If the rebase already finished and you don't like the result, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (or a reflog entry) puts it back.
Why do you need --force-with-lease after an interactive rebase?
Rebasing rewrites commit hashes, so your local branch and the remote branch have diverged — a normal push is rejected. --force-with-lease overwrites the remote branch but only if it still points where you last saw it (i.e. nobody else pushed in the meantime), preventing you from clobbering a colleague's work the way plain --force would.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

In the interactive-rebase todo list, are commits shown newest-first or oldest-first?
Oldest-first (the reverse of git log).
Which verb only changes a commit's message?
reword.
What command undoes a rebase you just completed?
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (or reset to the pre-rebase reflog entry).

Intermediate core

You have 8 messy WIP commits on your branch. The reviewer wants "one commit per logical change" — you decide there are 3. Outline the process.
git rebase -i main. In the todo list, arrange the 8 lines so commits belonging to the same logical change are adjacent (reorder lines as needed — watch for dependencies that would cause conflicts). Keep the first commit of each group as pick (or reword to give it a good message), and mark the rest of that group fixup (or squash if their messages have content worth merging). Save. Resolve any conflicts as each group replays (git add + git rebase --continue), enabling rerere first if the same conflict recurs. End with 3 clean commits. Then git push --force-with-lease. If reordering causes too many conflicts, an alternative is git reset --soft main to collapse everything to staged changes, then git add -p + git commit three times to rebuild the history from scratch.
What does an exec line do in the todo list, and how would you use it to guarantee every commit builds?
exec <cmd> runs <cmd> in the shell at that point in the replay; if it exits non-zero, the rebase pauses so you can fix things, then git rebase --continue. To check that every commit builds/tests, run git rebase -i --exec "make test" main — Git inserts exec make test after every picked commit. The rebase stops at the first commit where tests fail; you amend that commit to fix it and continue. This is how you enforce "no broken commits" (important for git bisect later) across a whole branch in one pass.

Advanced deep

A password was committed 40 commits ago and the branch has been pushed. Interactive rebase can "fix" it — why is that insufficient, and what's the correct remediation?
Why rebase -i alone is insufficient: (1) It's error-prone for deep history and doesn't touch other branches or tags that also contain the commit. (2) The old commits still exist in your local repo (reflog, ORIG_HEAD) and, crucially, on the remote — force-pushing the branch doesn't delete unreachable objects on the server immediately; they linger until the host runs gc (and many hosts keep them reachable via PR refs, forks, and caches essentially forever). (3) Anyone who already cloned/fetched has the secret. (4) Search engines / dorking and automated scanners may have already indexed it. Correct remediation, in order: (a) Rotate the credential immediately — assume it's compromised; this is the only step that truly fixes the exposure. History rewriting is damage-limitation, not the fix. (b) Rewrite history with a purpose-built tool: git filter-repo --replace-text (or the older BFG Repo-Cleaner) to strip the secret from every commit on every ref, not just one branch. filter-branch is deprecated and slow. (c) Force-push all rewritten refs (--force-with-lease), and have all collaborators re-clone or hard-reset — merging old clones would reintroduce the secret. (d) Ask the hosting provider (GitHub/GitLab) to expire the cached views and run gc, and invalidate any PRs that reference the old SHAs; on GitHub, old commit SHAs can remain accessible directly until support purges them. (e) Delete and recreate affected forks. (f) Add prevention: a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks, trufflehog), server-side push protection, and store secrets in a vault / env, never in the repo. Bottom line: rotate first, rewrite with filter-repo across all refs second, coordinate re-clone third.
How does interactive rebase implement "split a commit", and what happens to authorship, dates, and signatures of the rewritten commits?
Mechanism: when you mark a commit edit, the rebase applies that commit normally (so HEAD is now at the commit, working tree clean) and then pauses. git reset HEAD~ (a mixed reset) moves the branch pointer back one commit while leaving the working tree untouched — so the commit's changes are now present as unstaged modifications, and the commit itself is no longer on the branch. You then stage subsets with git add -p and make as many commits as you want. git rebase --continue resumes, replaying the remaining todo entries on top of your new commits. Every subsequent commit is recreated with a new hash (new parent). Regarding metadata: the author name/email and author date are preserved from the original commits by default (rebase reuses them), which is why git log still shows the original author and time; the committer identity and committer date are set to you/now (visible with git log --format=fuller). For the commits you manually created during the split, both author and committer default to you/now unless you pass --author=. Use git rebase --committer-date-is-author-date or --ignore-date/--reset-author-date to control this. GPG/SSH signatures are not carried over — a rewritten commit is a new object with different bytes, so the old signature can't apply; the commit becomes unsigned unless you rebase with -S (or set commit.gpgsign true and rebase.gpgSign true), which re-signs each replayed commit as you. This is why signature-verification policies and rebase-heavy workflows need explicit configuration to coexist.

The Reflog & Recovering Lost Work

Git almost never truly loses a commit — the reflog is your undo history for refs.

Notes

What the reflog is

Every time a ref (a branch, or HEAD) changes where it points — commit, checkout, reset, rebase, merge, pull, amend — Git appends a line to that ref's reflog under .git/logs/. It records the old hash, the new hash, who/when, and the action. It is local-only (never pushed or fetched) and per-clone.

git reflog                       # HEAD's reflog (most useful)
git reflog show main             # a specific branch's reflog
git log -g --oneline             # reflog as a log, with dates

Entries are addressable: HEAD@{2} = "where HEAD was 2 moves ago", main@{1} = "main's previous position", HEAD@{yesterday}, main@{2.hours.ago}.

The core recovery move

You did something destructive (reset --hard, a bad rebase, deleted a branch, a botched merge). The commits look gone — nothing points to them — but the objects still exist and the reflog still names them.

git reflog                        # find the good state, e.g. "HEAD@{4}: commit: add parser"
git reset --hard HEAD@{4}         # move the current branch back there
#   -- or, non-destructively: --
git switch -c recovered HEAD@{4}  # put the lost commits on a new branch
git branch recovered <hash>       # if you have the raw hash from reflog / log -g

Recovering a deleted branch

git reflog                        # look for "... : checkout: moving from feature to main"
                                  # the hash before that line is feature's old tip
git branch feature <that-hash>    # recreate it
# HEAD's reflog persists even after 'git branch -D feature'

When the reflog can't help: git fsck

If even the reflog entry expired or you're in a fresh clone, dangling objects can still be found directly:

git fsck --lost-found            # lists dangling commits / blobs
git fsck --unreachable
git show <dangling-hash>         # inspect
git cat-file -p <blob-hash> > recovered.txt   # rescue a single lost file

Expiry & garbage collection

  • Reachable-from-reflog commits are protected from git gc.
  • Reflog entries expire: 90 days for reachable entries (gc.reflogExpire), 30 days for entries pointing at now-unreachable commits (gc.reflogExpireUnreachable).
  • After that, git gc can prune the objects (loose objects also have a 2-week grace period via gc.pruneExpire). So recover sooner rather than later.
  • git gc --prune=now or git reflog expire --expire=now --all then gc will destroy unreachable history immediately — occasionally what you want (see the secrets question), usually not.

Other undo anchors

ORIG_HEAD is set by reset, merge, rebase, and pull to the pre-operation tip — git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD is a quick one-step undo for the last such operation. git merge --abort / git rebase --abort / git cherry-pick --abort use it too.

Cheat Sheet
  • Reflog = per-ref local log of every position a ref (esp. HEAD) has held. Not pushed, not shared.
  • git reflog to browse; address entries as HEAD@{n}, main@{1}, HEAD@{1.hour.ago}.
  • Undo a bad reset/rebase: git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git switch -c rescue HEAD@{n}.
  • Quick single-step undo of last reset/merge/rebase/pull: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD.
  • Recover a deleted branch: find its old tip hash in git reflog, then git branch <name> <hash>.
  • Reflog gone? git fsck --lost-found / --unreachable lists dangling commits & blobs; git show / cat-file -p to inspect & rescue.
  • Expiry: 90 days (reachable), 30 days (unreachable), then gc may prune. Recover promptly.
Q&A
What is the reflog and where does it live?
A local log, under .git/logs/HEAD and .git/logs/refs/…, recording every change to where a ref points — each line has the old hash, new hash, and the action (commit, checkout, reset, rebase, …). It's private to your clone and never transferred by push/fetch.
You ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 and realise you needed those 3 commits. Recovery?
git reflog, find the entry for the tip before the reset (e.g. HEAD@{1}), then git reset --hard HEAD@{1} (or git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD, which the reset set for you). The commits were never deleted — only the branch pointer moved.
Does git branch -D feature permanently destroy that branch's commits?
No, not immediately. The branch ref is deleted, but the commits remain as unreachable objects, and HEAD's reflog still contains the hash of the branch's last tip (from when you last checked it out). Recreate it with git branch feature <hash-from-reflog>. They're only gone after reflog expiry (~30 days unreachable) plus a gc.
What's the difference between the reflog and git log?
git log walks the commit graph by parent pointers — it shows history as it currently exists and is the same for everyone. The reflog is a chronological local record of your actions on refs — it includes commits that are no longer reachable, shows checkouts and resets, and is unique to your machine.
When does the reflog stop being able to save you?
After entries expire (default 90 days if the commit is still reachable some other way, 30 days if unreachable) and git gc subsequently prunes the now-unreferenced objects. A fresh clone has no reflog at all. Also, git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now wipes it deliberately.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Is the reflog shared when you push a branch?
No — the reflog is entirely local to your clone.
How do you refer to "where HEAD pointed two moves ago"?
HEAD@{2}.
What single ref does reset/merge/rebase/pull set to the previous tip, for easy one-step undo?
ORIG_HEAD.

Intermediate core

A colleague force-pushed over your feature branch and your local copy auto-updated after a pull. Can the reflog recover your lost commits? From which reflog?
Yes, if it hasn't expired. The commits you had are still objects in your local repo, and the remote-tracking branch's reflog (git reflog show origin/feature or git log -g origin/feature) plus your local branch's reflog (git reflog show feature) record the pre-pull tip. Find that hash and either git reset --hard <hash> on your local feature, or git branch feature-rescue <hash>. Then reconcile with the new upstream (rebase your genuinely-unique commits onto it). Note: this only works on a machine that had those commits before the force-push; a fresh clone can't see them.
You did an interactive rebase that squashed 10 commits, then realised commit #4 had a change you now can't find in the working tree. How do you retrieve just that change?
The pre-rebase branch tip is in the reflog (git reflog → the entry labelled rebase (start) or the commit just before it, also available as ORIG_HEAD). You don't want to undo the whole rebase, just inspect the old commit #4. Get the old tip: OLD=$(git rev-parse ORIG_HEAD). Then git log --oneline $OLD to find commit #4's hash, and git show <hash> to see its diff. To reapply just that change onto your current squashed history: git cherry-pick -n <hash> (no-commit, so you can review/adjust) or git checkout <hash> -- path/to/file to grab a specific file version, then commit or amend. git range-diff ORIG_HEAD HEAD is also excellent here — it shows commit-by-commit what the rebase changed, making a dropped hunk obvious.

Advanced deep

Explain the full lifecycle of an "orphaned" commit from the moment it becomes unreachable to when its bytes are actually deleted from disk. Which knobs control each stage?
Stage 1 — becomes unreachable: a ref move (reset, rebase, branch delete, amend) leaves commit C with nothing in refs/ pointing to it. C is still on disk (loose object or inside a packfile) and is still named by one or more reflog entries, which count as "reachable" for gc purposes — so C is fully protected. Stage 2 — reflog expiry: git gc (or an explicit git reflog expire) prunes reflog entries older than gc.reflogExpire (default 90 days) if the entry's commit is otherwise reachable, or older than gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (default 30 days) if not. Per-ref overrides exist (e.g. keep refs/stash forever — Git sets gc.refs/stash.reflogExpire=never by default). Once C's last reflog entry is gone, C is truly unreferenced. Stage 3 — object pruning: git gc calls git repack (which writes a new pack of reachable objects, leaving unreachable ones as loose) and then git prune, which deletes loose objects whose mtime is older than gc.pruneExpire (default "2 weeks ago"). The two-week grace protects objects that were just written by an in-progress operation (a concurrent git commit that hasn't updated its ref yet) from being reaped by a simultaneous gc. Objects that were inside a pack and became unreachable are handled by --cruft packs (modern Git) or fall out when the pack is rewritten, again respecting the expiry via cruft-pack mtimes. Stage 4 — gone: after prune, the bytes are unlinked. Forcing it: git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now collapses every stage immediately. Auto-gc: most commands opportunistically run git gc --auto, which triggers a real gc once loose objects exceed gc.auto (6700) or packs exceed gc.autoPackLimit (50); until that threshold, orphaned commits can linger well past the nominal expiry. On hosted platforms, server-side gc scheduling, plus hidden refs for pull requests and fork networks, mean an "unreachable" commit can remain fetchable by hash far longer than these local defaults suggest.
The stash is built on the same machinery as the reflog. Explain how git stash stores data and how you'd recover a stash you accidentally dropped.
git stash creates commit objects — it doesn't use a special file format. A single stash entry is a merge commit W with two (or three) parents: parent 1 is the current HEAD, parent 2 is a commit I capturing the index state, and (with -u) parent 3 captures untracked files; W's tree is the full working-tree state. That commit W is pointed to by the ref refs/stash, and — crucially — every stash you make is pushed onto refs/stash's reflog: stash@{0}, stash@{1}, … are literally reflog entries of that one ref. git stash pop applies stash@{0} and then drops it (deletes that reflog entry, shifting the rest down). If you drop or pop a stash and regret it: the underlying commit W is now unreachable but not yet gc'd, and its hash may still be in the refs/stash reflog (git reflog stash / git log -g stash) if other entries remain, or in HEAD's reflog, or findable via git fsck --unreachable | grep commit and inspecting each with git show --stat (a stash commit is recognisable: message like "WIP on branch: …", a merge commit with that parent structure). Once you have the hash, recover with git stash apply <hash> or git stash store -m "recovered" <hash> to put it back on the stash list, or just git branch recovered <hash>. This works only before gc removes it — and because refs/stash has reflogExpireUnreachable=never by default, dropped stash commits are actually somewhat more durable than other orphans, though an explicit gc --prune=now still kills them.

bisect for Regression Hunting

Binary search over history to find the exact commit that introduced a bug — in log₂(n) steps.

Notes

The idea

You know the bug is present now (a "bad" commit) and absent at some older commit (a "good" commit). Somewhere between them one commit flipped it. git bisect checks out the midpoint, you test, tell it "good" or "bad", it halves the remaining range, and repeats. 1000 commits → ~10 tests.

Manual session

git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current HEAD is broken
git bisect good v2.3           # this tag/commit was fine
# Git checks out a commit in the middle...
#   build & test it
git bisect good                # ...or 'git bisect bad'
#   repeat until:
# "<hash> is the first bad commit"  + shows the commit
git bisect reset              # return to where you were (or 'git bisect reset <ref>')

Automated: git bisect run

Give it a script/command whose exit code classifies a commit: 0 = good, 1–124 & 126–127 = bad, 125 = skip (can't be tested), ≥128 = abort the bisect.

git bisect start HEAD v2.3     # bad good, in one line
git bisect run ./test.sh      # or: make check / pytest -q tests/test_x.py / cargo test foo
# Git drives the whole search unattended and prints the first bad commit.
git bisect reset
# typical test.sh
#!/bin/sh
make -s || exit 125           # build broken here -> skip, don't call it "bad"
./run-repro || exit 1         # repro fails -> bad
exit 0                        # repro passes -> good

Handy extras

  • git bisect skip — the current commit can't be judged (won't build, unrelated breakage). Git picks a nearby one. Too many skips → result is "somewhere in this range".
  • git bisect terms --term-old <x> --term-new <y> or git bisect start --term-new slow --term-old fast — rename good/bad when you're hunting a performance regression or a fix rather than a break.
  • git bisect log — dump the session; git bisect replay <file> — re-run it (great after a misclassification: fix the log, replay).
  • git bisect visualize / --stat — see the remaining suspect range.
  • git bisect start -- <path> — only consider commits touching that path, shrinking the search.

Requirements & pitfalls

  • Needs a reliable, fast repro — a flaky test makes bisect converge on the wrong commit. Make the repro deterministic first.
  • Works cleanly when every commit builds. Messy WIP history → lots of skips; consider bisecting merge commits only (first-parent) or a cleaned-up branch.
  • The "first bad commit" might be a merge that pulled in a bad branch — then bisect within that branch's commits.
  • A regression that was introduced and later temporarily masked can confuse the good/bad monotonicity assumption.
Cheat Sheet
  • git bisect start → git bisect bad [rev] → git bisect good [rev]. Then test each checkout and mark good/bad.
  • One-liner start: git bisect start <bad> <good>.
  • Automate: git bisect run <cmd>. Exit codes: 0=good, 1–127 (not 125)=bad, 125=skip, ≥128=abort.
  • git bisect skip for untestable commits; git bisect reset when done.
  • Narrow it: git bisect start -- <path>. Rename terms for perf hunts: --term-new slow --term-old fast.
  • git bisect log → save; git bisect replay <file> after fixing a wrong answer.
  • Prerequisites: deterministic repro, ideally every commit builds. Complexity ~log₂(commits).
Q&A
What does git bisect do?
It performs a binary search across a range of commits to find the first one where some property changed (typically a bug appeared). You mark one end "good" and one "bad"; Git repeatedly checks out the midpoint for you to test, halving the candidate range each round, until it names the first bad commit.
How many tests for 1000 commits?
About log₂(1000) ≈ 10. Each answer eliminates half the remaining commits.
What's the exit-code contract for git bisect run?
The command is run at each step: exit 0 means the commit is good; exit 1–124 or 126–127 means bad; exit 125 means "skip, can't test this one" (e.g. it doesn't compile); exit 128 or higher aborts the whole bisect.
When would you use git bisect skip?
When the checked-out commit can't be evaluated — it doesn't build, or an unrelated bug prevents running the test. Git then picks another nearby commit. If too many commits in a region are skipped, Git reports a range of possible first-bad commits instead of a single one.
Why does bisect need a deterministic reproduction?
Because a single wrong "good"/"bad" answer sends the search down the wrong half and it converges on an innocent commit. A flaky test that sometimes passes on a genuinely-bad commit (or fails on a good one) produces exactly that. Make the repro reliable before bisecting.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What two labels do you give Git to start a bisect?
A "bad" commit (bug present) and a "good" commit (bug absent).
Which command automates the search using a test script?
git bisect run <command>.
What exit code tells bisect run to skip the current commit?
125.

Intermediate core

Write the test.sh for git bisect run to find which commit made a specific pytest case start failing, given the build sometimes doesn't compile on old commits.
#!/bin/sh
# reinstall/build; if it can't build, this commit is untestable -> skip
pip install -e . -q || exit 125
# run only the one test; -x stops on first failure, -q quiet
python -m pytest -q -x tests/test_orders.py::test_discount
status=$?
# pytest: 0 = passed (good). 1 = test failed (bad).
# 2-5 = usage/collection error -> treat as skip rather than bad
if [ $status -eq 0 ]; then exit 0; fi
if [ $status -eq 1 ]; then exit 1; fi
exit 125
Then: git bisect start HEAD <known-good-tag>; git bisect run ./test.sh; git bisect reset. Mapping collection errors to skip (125) rather than bad avoids blaming a commit where the test simply couldn't run.
You suspect a performance regression, not a functional break — the code works at every commit but got 3× slower somewhere. How do you bisect that?
Rename the terms so the monotonic property is "speed": git bisect start --term-old fast --term-new slow, then git bisect fast <old-rev> and git bisect slow HEAD. Write a run script that benchmarks deterministically and thresholds: build, run the workload N times (discard warm-up), take the median duration, and exit 0 if it's under a chosen cutoff (say 1.5× the known-fast baseline), exit 1 if over, exit 125 if it won't build or the benchmark is too noisy that round. Pin things that add variance: fixed input size, single thread or fixed thread count, CPU frequency governor set to performance, no other load, enough iterations that the fast/slow gap dwarfs the noise. git bisect run ./bench.sh then converges on the commit that crossed the threshold.

Advanced deep

How does bisect choose the next commit to test in a non-linear history (branches and merges), and why isn't it just "the middle of the list"?
The suspect set isn't a line, it's a DAG subgraph: all commits that are descendants of a good commit and ancestors of the bad commit (commits reachable from bad but not from any good). "Halving" means picking the commit whose classification eliminates as close to half of that set as possible — but eliminating in a DAG is asymmetric: marking commit X bad removes X and everything not an ancestor of X (the search continues below X), while marking X good removes X and all its ancestors. So for each candidate X, Git computes the number of ancestors of X within the suspect set; the best test commit is the one where that count is nearest to half the total, because whichever answer you give, the larger remaining side is minimised (this is a minimax choice). Git does this efficiently by counting, for every commit, how many suspect commits are reachable from it, then choosing the max–min. Merges complicate it: a merge commit's "ancestors" include both branches, so testing near a merge can collapse the range fast if the bug came in through one parent. Git also weights toward commits it can actually check out cleanly. If several commits tie, it prefers ones with more even splits. This is why bisect on a repo with lots of parallel feature branches sometimes seems to jump around unintuitively — it's optimising graph-reachability reduction, not list position. Practical corollary: a cleaner, more linear history (or bisecting --first-parent to treat each merge as one step) makes each bisection step more predictable and is often faster overall, then you bisect inside the guilty feature branch as a second pass.
Your git bisect run finished and blamed commit C, but C looks totally unrelated to the bug. List the ways this can happen and how to validate or correct the result.
Causes: (1) Flaky repro — the test is nondeterministic, so a genuinely-good commit was marked bad (or vice versa) once, sending the search astray. (2) Non-monotonic bug — the bug was introduced at A, accidentally masked at B (unrelated change hid the symptom), then unmasked at C; bisect assumes "once bad, stays bad" and lands on C. (3) Build/env contamination — stale build artifacts, a cached __pycache__, an installed package not reinstalled per step, or a generated file not regenerated, so you tested the wrong code. (4) Wrong good baseline — the "good" commit actually already had the bug (just not noticed), so the true culprit is outside the searched range and bisect converges on the earliest in-range commit. (5) Test script exit-code bug — e.g. returning 1 for a compile failure instead of 125, so untestable commits were called bad. (6) Skips — heavy skipping left ambiguity and Git reported a plausible-but-not-certain commit. (7) The culprit is a merge and C is a random commit on the merged branch. Validation/correction: run git bisect log and eyeball every classification; manually re-test C and its parent several times to confirm the flip is real and reproducible; git show C — if truly unrelated, widen the good end (git bisect good <much-older>) and re-run; fix the repro to be deterministic (seed RNG, pin clock, isolate state) and use git bisect replay on a corrected log; add make clean / fresh venv to the run script; bisect with --first-parent to blame the merge, then bisect inside that branch; if non-monotonic, bisect for the masking change separately. Finally, once you have a candidate, prove it: git revert it (or checkout its parent) and confirm the bug disappears, and inspect the diff for a plausible mechanism.

cherry-pick, revert & reset

Copy a commit, safely undo a commit on shared history, or move a branch pointer around.

Notes

cherry-pick — copy a commit onto the current branch

git cherry-pick <hash>             # apply that commit's diff as a NEW commit here
git cherry-pick A^..B              # a range (A exclusive .. B inclusive)
git cherry-pick -n <hash>          # apply but don't commit (stage only) so you can tweak
git cherry-pick -x <hash>          # append "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message
git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge>       # pick a merge commit, relative to parent 1
# on conflict:
git cherry-pick --continue / --skip / --abort
  • Takes the diff of the target commit and reapplies it here; the result is a brand-new commit with a new hash (author preserved, committer = you).
  • Classic uses: backport a fix from main to a release branch; grab one commit from an abandoned branch; move a commit made on the wrong branch.
  • Overusing it across long-lived branches creates duplicate commits (same change, different hash) that later merges/rebases must reconcile via patch-id.

revert — undo a commit by making an inverse commit

git revert <hash>                  # new commit that applies the reverse diff
git revert --no-commit <a> <b>     # stage several reverts, commit once
git revert -m 1 <merge-hash>       # undo a merge, keeping parent-1 line; re-merging later needs care
  • Doesn't rewrite history — it adds a commit. Safe on main / anything already pushed and shared.
  • The reverted change stays visible in history; you can revert the revert to bring it back.
  • Contrast with reset, which removes commits from the branch and is unsafe to push to shared branches.

reset — move the current branch pointer (and optionally index / working tree)

ModeHEAD/branchIndexWorking treeUse
--softmoves——uncommit but keep changes staged (re-commit differently)
--mixed (default)movesreset—uncommit & unstage; changes remain in working tree
--hardmovesresetresetdiscard commits and changes (destructive)
git reset --soft HEAD~1           # undo last commit, keep everything staged
git reset HEAD~1                  # undo last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard origin/main      # make local branch exactly match remote (loses local work)
git reset <path>                   # unstage just that path (no mode = mixed, path-limited)
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD        # undo the last reset/merge/rebase

Choosing

  • Undo a commit on a shared branch → git revert.
  • Undo commits only on your local, unpushed branch → git reset.
  • Bring one specific commit from elsewhere → git cherry-pick.
  • Discard all local changes to match upstream → git reset --hard @{upstream}.
Cheat Sheet
  • cherry-pick = reapply another commit's diff as a new commit here. -n stage-only, -x record origin, -m 1 for merges, range A^..B.
  • revert = add a commit that undoes a commit. History-safe, use on shared branches. -m 1 to revert a merge.
  • reset = move current branch pointer. --soft (keep staged) / --mixed default (keep unstaged) / --hard (discard). Unsafe to push if it drops shared commits.
  • Undo last commit keep work: git reset --soft HEAD~1. Match remote exactly: git reset --hard origin/<branch>.
  • Unstage a file: git reset <path> (or git restore --staged <path>).
  • Undo a reset/merge/rebase: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD.
  • Rule: revert for public history, reset for private history, cherry-pick to copy a change.
Q&A
Difference between git revert and git reset?
revert creates a new commit whose diff is the inverse of a target commit — history grows, nothing is rewritten, safe to push to shared branches. reset moves the branch pointer to an earlier commit, effectively removing the later commits from the branch — it rewrites which commits the branch contains and is unsafe on anything others have pulled.
What does git cherry-pick actually apply?
The diff between the target commit and its parent, reapplied onto your current HEAD, then committed as a new commit (new hash, original author retained). It does not link back to the original commit unless you pass -x.
How do you cherry-pick or revert a merge commit?
A merge has multiple parents, so Git needs to know which parent's line represents "mainline". Pass -m 1 (usually parent 1 = the branch you were on) so the diff is computed relative to that parent. git revert -m 1 <merge> undoes the merged-in changes; git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge> replays them elsewhere.
You committed to main but it should have been on a feature branch. Fix?
On main: note the hash, then git reset --hard HEAD~1 (assuming it's unpushed) to drop it. Then git switch -c feature and git cherry-pick <hash> — or, if you switched before resetting, cherry-pick onto the feature branch first, then reset main. If main was already pushed, use git revert on main instead of reset.
Which reset mode is destructive?
--hard — it overwrites the working tree and index, discarding uncommitted changes. --soft and --mixed leave your file changes intact (staged / unstaged respectively).
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command is safe to use on an already-pushed shared branch to undo a commit?
git revert — it adds an inverse commit instead of rewriting history.
Does git cherry-pick keep the original commit's hash?
No — it creates a new commit with a new hash (the author is preserved).
Which reset mode leaves your changes staged?
--soft.

Intermediate core

A critical fix landed on main as commit F. You need it on release/1.8 without pulling in the other 30 commits on main. Steps and caveats?
git switch release/1.8; git cherry-pick -x F. The -x annotates the new commit with "(cherry picked from commit F)" so the provenance is recorded. If F depends on earlier changes not present on the release branch, the cherry-pick will conflict — resolve, git add, git cherry-pick --continue, and verify the fix actually works in the release context (it may need adaptation). Caveats: F now exists as two commits with different hashes on two branches; if release/1.8 is ever merged back into main (or vice versa), Git's patch-id detection usually recognises them as equivalent and avoids a double-apply, but a conflicting resolution during cherry-pick can defeat that and cause a spurious conflict later. Tag or note the backport in the PR. If several related commits form the fix, cherry-pick the whole range (git cherry-pick F1^..F3).
You merged feature branch X into main (merge commit M, already pushed), then discovered X is broken. You revert M. Two weeks later X is fixed — why won't a plain re-merge work, and what do you do?
When you git revert -m 1 M, Git adds commit R to main that undoes X's changes — but the merge M is still in history, so from Git's graph perspective X's commits are "already merged into main". If you now git merge X again, Git sees nothing new to bring in (X's tip is an ancestor of main via M) and either fast-forwards nothing or produces an empty/partial merge — the fixed code doesn't actually land, because R already removed the old version and the merge won't re-add it. Options: (a) Revert the revert: git revert R on main to restore X's original changes, then merge the branch containing the fixes on top. This is the documented approach (see "Reverting a faulty merge" in the Git docs) — but it also re-introduces any genuinely bad parts of the original X, so the fix branch must correct them. (b) Rebuild the feature branch from current main and re-apply the (now-fixed) work as new commits, then merge that — cleaner history, no double-negative. (c) Cherry-pick just the fixed commits onto main. Most teams prefer (b) or (c) unless X was large.

Advanced deep

Contrast the three-tree effect and the safety profile of git reset --hard <C>, git checkout <C>, and git restore --source=<C> --staged --worktree .. When is each the right tool?
git reset --hard C: moves the current branch ref to C, then forces index and working tree to match C. Effect on trees: branch→C, index→C, worktree→C.
