Routing — transforms.conf: [to_security] REGEX = (sshd|sudo|authentication failure) DEST_KEY = _MetaData:Index FORMAT = security; reference from props.conf: [linux_secure] TRANSFORMS-route = to_security. Order matters — list masking before routing in TRANSFORMS- if the routing regex shouldn't see the raw SSN. Then set RBAC so only the security team's role has srchIndexesAllowed including security. Validate with a sample through "Add Data" / a test index first.

Advanced deep

Design a data onboarding standard for an org onboarding ~5 new sourcetypes a week, covering naming, config packaging, testing, and license governance.
Naming: a controlled vocabulary — indexes by data domain + retention tier (net_fw_90d, os_linux_30d, app_payments_1y), sourcetypes vendor:product:format (palo:pan:traffic, myco:orders:json), reusing CIM-compliant sourcetypes from official TAs wherever one exists. No auto-generated sourcetypes (disable [sourcetype]::learned drift; set explicit sourcetypes on every input). Config packaging: every onboarding is a versioned Technology Add-on in Git — inputs.conf (forwarder-side, deployed via Deployment Server serverclasses), props.conf/transforms.conf split into an index-time TA (to indexer cluster via Cluster Manager, and to HFs) and a search-time TA (to SHC via Deployer). No config edited directly on servers. CI lints the .conf (btool-style checks, regex compiles, no overlapping stanzas) and runs on a schedule. Testing: a staging Splunk with a dedicated onboarding index; the requester provides a representative sample (ideally 24h incl. edge cases — multiline stack traces, DST boundary, max-length lines); reviewer verifies in "Add Data" preview: correct event breaking, timestamp (incl. TZ and sub-second), truncation not triggering, all expected fields extracting, CIM mapping if applicable, and volume/EPS estimate. A checklist PR template. License governance: estimate daily GB before approval; require a nullQueue plan for known noise (health checks, debug); tag each index with an owner and a monthly GB budget; a daily report of ingest by index/sourcetype/host vs budget, alerting on >20% overage or a new unexpected sourcetype; use the license pool warnings and, on Cloud, the ingest/entitlement dashboards. Workflow: request (form) → TA PR → CI + staging validation → review → merge → Deployment Server / Cluster Manager / Deployer push → post-onboard validation search (count > 0, no parsing errors in index=_internal) → hand back a saved search + dashboard link. This keeps 5/week sustainable without snowflake configs or license surprises.
Explain how Splunk determines an event's timestamp, every setting involved, and the failure modes when data spans time zones and DST.
Order of precedence per event: (1) If DATETIME_CONFIG = CURRENT, use ingest time (no parsing). If = NONE, no timestamp processing at all. Otherwise use the datetime config (default /etc/datetime.xml patterns) plus sourcetype overrides. (2) Splunk looks for the timestamp starting at TIME_PREFIX (a regex; scanning begins right after the match) — without it, Splunk scans from the start of the event. (3) It reads up to MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD characters (default 128) looking for something matching TIME_FORMAT (strptime spec). If TIME_FORMAT is unset, it tries the datetime.xml pattern library. (4) Time zone resolution: if TIME_FORMAT includes %z/%Z and the data has an offset, that wins. Else the TZ attribute for that sourcetype/host/source (an IANA name like America/New_York) is used. Else the forwarder/indexer's system TZ is assumed (a classic bug source). Per-host TZ can be set with [host::<h>] TZ = .... (5) Sanity clamps: events older than MAX_DAYS_AGO (default 2000) or newer than MAX_DAYS_HENCE (default 2) are rejected/clamped; MAX_DIFF_SECS_AGO/MAX_DIFF_SECS_HENCE flag events whose time is wildly off from the surrounding stream. Failure modes: (a) No offset + wrong assumed TZ — a log in US Eastern parsed on a UTC indexer lands 4–5h off; dashboards and correlation searches silently mis-bucket. Fix: explicit TZ. (b) DST transitions — if TZ is a fixed offset (TZ = GMT-5) rather than a zone name, half the year is wrong; always use the IANA zone so DST is handled. The "fall back" hour where local time repeats can also mis-order events — source data with an explicit offset avoids this. (c) Ambiguous formats — 02/03/04 (D/M/Y vs M/D/Y) parsed by the generic patterns can flip; pin TIME_FORMAT. (d) Lookahead too short — timestamp deep in the line (e.g. after a long JSON prefix) never found → falls back to ingest time; raise MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD and set TIME_PREFIX. (e) Multiline events — wrong line breaking makes Splunk read the timestamp of the wrong physical line for a merged event. (f) Future data rejected — a source with a badly-set clock or a TZ mistake putting events > 2 days ahead gets dropped by MAX_DAYS_HENCE; you see gaps and DateParserVerbose warnings in index=_internal. Diagnosis: search index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=DateParserVerbose, and compare _time vs _indextime (| eval lag = _indextime - _time) to spot systematic offsets.

SPL Fundamentals

A search is a pipeline: retrieve events, then transform them command by command.

Notes

The pipeline model

index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500   <-- base search (retrieval)
| stats count by uri_path                          <-- transforming command
| sort - count
| head 10

Everything before the first | is the base search that pulls events from indexes. Each | pipes results into the next command. Commands are applied left to right.

The base search

  • Implied AND: error timeout host=web01 = all three must match.
  • OR, NOT, parentheses; != and </> for fields.
  • Always constrain index (and ideally sourcetype) — a bare term searches every index you can see.
  • Time range is a first-class filter (the time picker, or earliest=-24h latest=now, earliest=-1d@d). Narrow time = fast search.
  • TERM(1.2.3.4) / CASE() match against the raw lexicon (fast, exact, respects major breakers).
  • Wildcards: trailing fail* is fine; leading *fail is slow (can't use the index).
  • Quote phrases: "connection refused". Escape with \.

Fields

  • _raw (the event text), _time (event time, epoch), index, source, sourcetype, host, linecount, _indextime.
  • Search-time extracted fields appear automatically (status, uri_path…). fields command keeps/drops fields (do it early to speed things up).
  • | eval creates/overwrites fields; | rename; | table for a columnar view.

Streaming vs transforming commands

Streaming (distributable)Transforming (centralising)
eval, where, rex, fields, rename, lookup, searchstats, chart, timechart, top, rare, dedup (partly), sort
Run on indexers, in parallel, per eventForce results back to the search head to aggregate

The first transforming command is the "reduce" point. Do as much filtering/field work in streaming commands before it as possible.

Search modes

  • Fast: only fields needed by the search; no event-list field discovery. Use for reporting.
  • Smart (default): fast for transforming searches, verbose-ish for event searches.
  • Verbose: discover all fields for every event — slow; use only when exploring.

Subsearches

index=web [ search index=threat action=block | fields src_ip | format ]

The bracketed search runs first, its results become part of the outer search (as an OR of src_ip=…). Powerful but limited (default 10k rows / 60s) — often stats/join/lookups are better.

Common early commands

| fields status uri_path bytes        # keep only what you need (speed)
| eval kb = bytes/1024
| where kb > 500
| rex field=uri "id=(?<id>\d+)"       # ad-hoc extraction
| dedup session_id
| eval _time = strptime(ts, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
Cheat Sheet
  • Search = base retrieval (before first |) then commands piped left→right.
  • Base search: implied AND; OR/NOT/parens; always set index= and sourcetype=; narrow time.
  • TERM() for fast exact lexicon match; trailing * ok, leading * slow; quote "phrases".
  • Default fields: _raw, _time, index, source, sourcetype, host, _indextime.
  • Streaming (eval, where, rex, fields, lookup) runs on indexers; transforming (stats, chart, timechart, top, sort) reduces on the search head. Filter before the first transforming command.
  • | fields early = faster. | eval to compute, | where to filter on computed values, | rex for ad-hoc fields.
  • Modes: Fast (reporting), Smart (default), Verbose (exploring, slow).
  • Subsearch [ ... ] runs first; capped at ~10k rows / 60s — prefer stats/lookup.
Q&A
Why always specify index=?
Without it, Splunk searches every index your role can access, scanning far more data and buckets than needed — slow and wasteful. Naming the index (and sourcetype) lets Splunk skip irrelevant buckets immediately.
What's the difference between a streaming and a transforming command?
Streaming commands process one event at a time and can run on the indexers in parallel (eval, rex, where, fields). Transforming commands aggregate events into a results table and must run centrally on the search head (stats, timechart, top). The first transforming command is where the distributed search "reduces".
Why is a leading wildcard (*error) slow?
Splunk's index is a lexicon of terms; it can match error* by prefix but can't use the index for *error, so it must scan and filter raw events. Restructure the search or extract a field instead.
When would you use TERM()?
To match an exact string that contains minor breakers (like an IP 10.1.2.3 or a path) as a single indexed term, avoiding Splunk splitting it. It's faster and more precise than a quoted phrase for such tokens.
How does a subsearch execute relative to the main search?
The subsearch (in square brackets) runs first, to completion; its output is turned into search terms and spliced into the outer search, which then runs. It's bounded (default 10,000 results, 60 seconds), so for large result sets use stats, a lookup, or join instead.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What separates commands in SPL?
The pipe |.
Which field holds the event's timestamp?
_time (epoch seconds).
Which command filters on the value of a computed field?
where (e.g. | eval r=a/b | where r>0.5).

Intermediate core

This search is slow: index=* "*exception*" | stats count by host. Rewrite it and explain each change.
Problems: index=* hits every index; "*exception*" has a leading wildcard so the lexicon can't help; no time bound; Verbose-style field discovery. Better: index=app_logs sourcetype=myapp:log earliest=-1h ( "exception" OR "Exception" ) | fields host | stats count by host. Changes: (1) name the index and sourcetype so only relevant buckets are opened; (2) drop the leading * — match the term exception (trailing wildcard if you need exceptions); (3) add an explicit time range; (4) | fields host before stats so only that field is pulled from raw events; (5) run in Fast mode. If "exception" appears mid-token, extract a field at index or search time and filter on that instead of substring matching.
You want events from web whose src_ip also appears in today's threat index. Show a subsearch version and a better non-subsearch version.
Subsearch: index=web [ search index=threat earliest=-1d@d | stats count by src_ip | fields src_ip ] — the subsearch yields src_ip="a" OR src_ip="b" ... spliced into the outer search. Risk: if there are > 10k distinct threat IPs it's silently truncated, and it's slow. Better: build a lookup. Either a scheduled search index=threat earliest=-1d@d | stats count by src_ip | outputlookup threat_ips.csv, then index=web | lookup threat_ips.csv src_ip OUTPUT count as is_threat | where isnotnull(is_threat). Or, for ad hoc, use stats across both: (index=web OR index=threat) | stats values(index) as idx by src_ip | where mvcount(idx)>1 ... then join back. The lookup approach scales, is cacheable, and can be a KV Store collection for frequent updates.

Advanced deep

Explain how a distributed search executes: parsing, the map/reduce split, what runs where, and how | stats is actually computed across indexers.
(1) Parse & expand: the search head parses the SPL, expands macros, event types, tags, and | tstats/data-model references, resolves knowledge objects, and determines the time range and which indexes/sourcetypes are needed. (2) Split into remote + local: Splunk walks the pipeline and finds the first non-streamable (centralising) command. Everything up to and including the streamable prefix becomes the remote search (the "map"); the rest is the local/reduce part run on the SH. Purely streaming commands (eval, rex, where, fields, lookup with a replicated file) are pushed to the indexers; stats, timechart, sort, dedup, top centralise. (3) Dispatch: the SH sends the remote search to all search peers (indexers) holding relevant data; in a clustered index it targets exactly one searchable copy of each bucket (the primary) to avoid duplicate results. (4) On each indexer: use the time index (tsidx) to select candidate buckets, use the lexicon to select candidate events (keyword/TERM), read raw events, apply search-time extraction and the streaming prefix, and — crucially — for a transforming command, compute a partial aggregate. For | stats count by host, each indexer returns per-host partial counts, not raw events; for | stats avg(x) by y it returns per-y running sum and count (so the SH can combine correctly); for dc() it returns partial sketches; for values()/list() it returns partial sets. This "prestats" mode is why stats scales — the network only carries small partials. (5) On the search head: merge the partials (add the counts, combine sums/counts into final averages, union the distinct-value sketches), then run the remaining local commands (sort, head, eval on aggregated rows, another stats). (6) Stream to UI: results are written to the dispatch directory and streamed/paginated to the browser; for real-time or long searches, partial results update as peers report. Commands that can't be pre-aggregated (e.g. transaction, streamstats across the whole set, sort before a stats) force raw events to the SH and are slow — hence "filter and reduce early, sort late". | tstats skips step 4's raw read entirely by querying the tsidx directly.
A dashboard runs 12 panels, each a full search over 24h of a large index, and it's hammering the indexers. How do you restructure with base searches, acceleration, and scheduling?
(1) Base/post-process searches: in the dashboard, define one or a few base searches that retrieve the shared event set once (e.g. index=web sourcetype=access earliest=-24h | fields _time status uri_path bytes host), and make each panel a post-process search that only adds | stats ... / | timechart ... on the base results. 12 retrievals → 1. Constraint: post-process is capped (default 500k events / limited) and only works when panels share the base filter — group panels by their common base. (2) Report acceleration or a summary index: if the panels are aggregations, schedule a search that computes the per-interval aggregates (| sitimechart / | sistats span=5m count by status, uri_path) into a summary index or an accelerated report; dashboard panels then query the small summary (| timechart span=5m ... over the summary) — orders of magnitude cheaper, and consistent across panels. (3) Data model acceleration + | tstats: if the data fits a CIM/data model, accelerate it and rewrite panels as | tstats count FROM datamodel=Web WHERE ... BY _time span=5m Web.status — reads tsidx only, extremely fast, and the acceleration is maintained incrementally by Splunk. (4) Scheduling & caching: set the dashboard/panels to use scheduled saved searches with a refresh (e.g. every 5 min) so all users share one cached result rather than each triggering ad-hoc runs; stagger schedules to avoid a thundering herd; use | loadjob to reuse the latest scheduled artifact. (5) Scope: tighten time defaults, add | fields, run Fast mode, cap panel result counts, and lazy-load below-the-fold panels. (6) Governance: move heavy shared searches to a dedicated scheduler SH / pool so interactive users aren't starved, and watch index=_internal search concurrency and skipped-search metrics. Net: shared base search for grouped panels + acceleration (data model + tstats, or summary index) for the aggregates + scheduled shared results.

stats, chart & timechart

The transforming commands that turn a pile of events into a report.

Notes

The three

CommandOutput shape
statsA table: one row per BY group; columns = the aggregations. No implicit time.
timechartstats with _time as the implicit X axis. BY <field> makes one column per value of that field. Single split field only.
chartLike timechart but you choose the X axis: chart count OVER host BY status. Two dimensions (OVER + BY).

stats functions

count, count(field), dc(field)           # distinct count
sum, avg, min, max, median, mode, range
stdev, var, perc95(field), p99(field)
first(field), last(field)                # by search order (not time!)
earliest(field), latest(field)           # by _time
values(field), list(field)              # multivalue: unique / all

index=web | stats count AS hits,
                  dc(clientip) AS uniq_visitors,
                  avg(response_ms) AS avg_ms,
                  perc95(response_ms) AS p95_ms
            BY uri_path
| sort - hits

timechart

index=web | timechart span=5m count BY status
index=web | timechart span=1h avg(response_ms) AS avg, perc95(response_ms) AS p95
index=web | timechart span=1d count BY uri_path limit=10 useother=t usenull=f
  • span sets the bucket; omit it and Splunk auto-picks from the time range.
  • BY takes one field; high-cardinality splits get bucketed into OTHER unless you raise limit (0 = all, careful).
  • cont=f to not connect gaps; usenull/useother to control the extra series; fixedrange=f.

Streaming cousins — eventstats / streamstats

  • eventstats: computes the same aggregates but adds them as fields to every event instead of collapsing — e.g. attach the overall avg to each row so you can compare.
  • streamstats: running/windowed aggregates in event order — running totals, deltas (streamstats current=f last(x) as prev | eval d = x - prev), rolling averages (window=10), per-group sequence numbers.
  • bin (aka bucket): quantise a field into ranges (bin _time span=1h, bin bytes span=1000) — what timechart does to _time internally.

tstats — the fast one

| tstats count WHERE index=web BY _time span=1h, status
| tstats `summariesonly` count FROM datamodel=Web BY Web.http_method

Runs against the tsidx (indexed fields / accelerated data models) without reading raw events — dramatically faster for big aggregations, but limited to indexed/accelerated fields.

Gotchas

  • first()/last() are search-order dependent, not time — use earliest()/latest() for "by time".
  • timechart only splits by one field; for two dimensions over time, use chart ... OVER _time won't help — concatenate fields or use multiple panels.
  • Aggregating a rate: stats gives totals; divide by the window yourself, or use timechart per_second(count).
  • stats drops _raw and all fields not named — put eval/rex before it.
Cheat Sheet
  • stats <funcs> BY <fields> → table, one row per group, no time axis.
  • timechart span=<s> <funcs> BY <one field> → time on X, one series per value; extra values → OTHER (raise limit, useother=f, usenull=f).
  • chart <funcs> OVER <x> BY <y> → pick both axes.
  • Funcs: count, dc(), sum/avg/min/max/median, perc95()/p99(), stdev, values()/list(), earliest()/latest() (by time), first()/last() (by search order — careful).
  • eventstats = same aggregates added as fields to every event (no collapse). streamstats = running/windowed aggregates in order (totals, deltas, rolling avg).
  • bin _time span=1h to quantise manually. | tstats ... BY _time span=1h for tsidx/data-model speed.
  • stats keeps only named fields — do eval/rex first.
Q&A
Difference between stats and timechart?
timechart is stats with _time automatically as the X axis, bucketed by span. It produces a time series suitable for a line/area chart; stats produces a plain aggregate table with no time dimension. timechart also only allows a single BY split field.
What does eventstats do that stats doesn't?
stats collapses events into aggregate rows. eventstats computes the same aggregates but writes them back onto every event as new fields, keeping all the events — so you can, say, compare each request's latency to the overall average in the same pipeline.
When do you use streamstats?
For order-dependent calculations: running totals, cumulative counts, deltas between consecutive events (current=f last(x)), moving averages (window=N), or numbering events within a group. It processes events in stream order and emits a value per event.
Why prefer earliest()/latest() over first()/last()?
first() and last() return values based on the order events arrive in the pipeline (usually newest-first from the index), which is easy to misuse. earliest() and latest() explicitly use _time, so "the first status for this session" means chronologically first regardless of search order.
What makes | tstats fast?
It answers the query from the time-series index files (tsidx) — and from accelerated data model summaries — without reading and parsing raw events. That skips the most expensive part of a search, at the cost of only being able to use indexed or accelerated fields.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command puts _time on the X axis automatically?
timechart.
What function counts distinct values?
dc() (distinct count).
How many split fields can timechart ... BY take?
One.

Intermediate core

Write a search for p50/p95/p99 API latency per endpoint over the last 24h as a table, sorted by p99.
index=api sourcetype=api:access earliest=-24h | stats count AS calls, perc50(response_ms) AS p50, perc95(response_ms) AS p95, perc99(response_ms) AS p99 BY endpoint | sort - p99. Notes: perc<n>() (or p<n>()) computes the percentile; include count so you can ignore endpoints with tiny sample sizes; add | where calls > 100 if you only care about meaningful traffic. For a time trend instead, | timechart span=1h perc95(response_ms) BY endpoint limit=10.
You need the time between each user's consecutive logins. How?
Sort ascending by user then time, then use streamstats to reach back one event within each user group: index=auth action=login | sort 0 user _time | streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time BY user | eval gap_secs = _time - prev_time | where isnotnull(gap_secs) | table _time user gap_secs. current=f excludes the current event so last() is the previous one; BY user resets per user; sort 0 avoids the 10k default sort cap. Convert with | eval gap = tostring(gap_secs, "duration") for readability.

Advanced deep

Explain how stats, timechart, and tstats differ in where and how the aggregation is computed, and the performance implications of each on a clustered deployment.
stats: a transforming command that runs in prestats mode on the indexers — each peer computes partial aggregates over its buckets (partial counts, sum+count pairs for avg, distinct-value sketches for dc, partial sets for values) and ships only those partials to the search head, which merges them into final rows. Cost is dominated by reading and applying search-time extraction to every matching raw event on each indexer; network transfer is small. Scales well with more indexers as long as the streaming prefix filters hard first. timechart: same engine as stats plus an implicit bin _time span=...; indexers emit per-(time-bucket, split-value) partials, SH merges and pivots into columns. Same cost profile as stats; the extra work is bucketing and the pivot, and high-cardinality BY forces an OTHER rollup or a wide result. Both still require the raw-event read. tstats: queries the tsidx directly — the time index and indexed-field index — or an accelerated data model's summary tsidx. It never reads journal.gz raw events, never runs search-time field extraction. On each indexer it scans compact index structures and returns partials; the SH merges. This is often 10–100× faster for large-window aggregations. Constraints: only indexed fields (index, sourcetype, host, source, _time, and any index-time extracted fields) or accelerated data model fields (datamodel=X, referenced as Model.field); WHERE filters must be on indexed/accelerated fields; results are counts/sums/etc. of events, not the events themselves. Clustered implications: for all three, the SH dispatches the remote search to one searchable copy (primary) of each relevant bucket, so search factor ≥ 1 must hold; a peer down triggers primary re-assignment (brief) — searches still complete via other copies. stats/timechart load is I/O + CPU on indexers proportional to matched raw events, so a broad search over billions of events is heavy regardless of clustering — add indexers, or accelerate. tstats spreads the (much lighter) tsidx scan across the same peers; data model acceleration builds and incrementally maintains summary tsidx files per bucket on the indexers (extra disk + a background workload), which is the price for the query speed. Rule of thumb: exploratory / arbitrary-field aggregation → stats/timechart with tight filters; known, repeated, large-scale aggregation → model the data, accelerate it, and use tstats.
A timechart ... BY user over 7 days shows almost everything lumped into "OTHER" and the p95 line looks wrong. Diagnose and fix.
OTHER lumping: timechart's BY keeps only the top limit series (default 10) by their aggregate over the whole range and rolls the rest into OTHER; with thousands of users almost every user is "other". Fixes depend on intent: if you actually want per-user lines, timechart is the wrong tool for high cardinality — instead stats per user without time, or filter to a specific cohort (| search user IN (...)), or raise limit (e.g. limit=50) knowing the chart gets unreadable, or set limit=0 (all — can explode result size/memory). If you want an aggregate trend, drop the BY user entirely and just timechart span=1h perc95(response_ms), optionally splitting by a low-cardinality field (status class, region). Use useother=f/usenull=f to hide the noise series. Wrong p95: several causes — (1) percentiles per time bucket are computed from only that bucket's events; a 1h bucket with 3 events gives a meaningless p95, and mixing bucket sizes across the range makes the line jumpy. Choose a span that yields enough samples per bucket. (2) If you first did stats/timechart and then another percentile on top, you're taking a percentile of aggregates, not of raw latencies — percentiles don't compose; compute perc95(response_ms) directly on raw events in one timechart. (3) With BY user + OTHER, the OTHER series' p95 is across many users' merged latencies, which isn't what you think it is. (4) Splunk's perc uses a fast approximate algorithm by default (radix/t-digest style) with a small error; use exactperc95() if you need precision (slower, more memory). (5) Unit/field issues — multivalue response_ms, or some events measuring ms and others seconds, skew it; normalise with eval first. Fix: index=api earliest=-7d | timechart span=1h exactperc95(response_ms) AS p95, count, sanity-check count per bucket, and split only by a low-cardinality dimension.

eval, Calculated Fields & Lookups

Compute new fields inline, or enrich events with data from CSV / KV Store tables.

Notes

eval

| eval kb = bytes/1024
| eval status_class = case(status>=500,"server", status>=400,"client", status>=300,"redirect", 1==1,"ok")
| eval host = lower(host)
| eval full = src . ":" . port                       # . = string concat
| eval is_err = if(status>=500, 1, 0)
| eval ts = strftime(_time, "%F %T")
| eval epoch = strptime(raw_ts, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
| eval tags = mvappend(tags, "reviewed")
| eval domain = mvindex(split(email,"@"), 1)

Key functions: if, case, coalesce, validate; tonumber/tostring (tostring(x,"duration"|"commas"|"hex")); round/ceiling/floor; len, substr, lower/upper/trim, replace, match (regex bool), mvcount/mvindex/mvjoin/mvfilter; strftime/strptime; cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", ip); isnull/isnotnull/nullif.

eval vs where vs fieldformat

  • eval f = expr — assign a field. In a boolean context it yields 1/0/null.
  • where <boolean expr> — keep rows where the expression is true (uses eval syntax, so where response>avg compares fields, unlike search).
  • fieldformat f = expr — change only the display of f; the underlying value (used by sort/stats) is unchanged.

Calculated fields (props.conf)

[api:access]
EVAL-kb          = bytes/1024
EVAL-status_class = case(status>=500,"server", status>=400,"client", 1==1,"ok")

An EVAL-<name> in props.conf applies the eval automatically at search time for that sourcetype — so kb just exists on every event without typing | eval. Great for standardising derived fields across searches and dashboards.

Lookups — enrich events from a table

TypeWhat
CSV lookupA file (lookups/ in an app). Static-ish reference data (asset inventory, code→description).
KV Store lookupA MongoDB-backed collection on the SH. Read/write via outputlookup, REST, or a form; better for large or frequently-updated data, supports keys & types.
External / scripted lookupA script (e.g. DNS, GeoIP, threat-intel API) invoked per lookup call.
Geospatial lookupKMZ polygons → region name, for choropleth maps.
time-bounded lookupCSV/KV with a time field so the "correct" row depends on the event's _time.
| lookup asset_inventory ip AS src_ip OUTPUT owner, criticality
| lookup dnslookup clientip                       # match & output default fields
| inputlookup threat_ips.csv                       # read the table AS the result set
| outputlookup append=t seen_ips.csv              # write current results to a lookup
  • lookup: for each event, match input field(s) to the table, add the OUTPUT fields. OUTPUTNEW = only if not already present.
  • Automatic lookups (props.conf LOOKUP-<name> = <lookup> ip AS src_ip OUTPUT owner) apply on every search for that sourcetype — no | lookup needed.
  • inputlookup can start a search from the table (great with append to combine with events).
  • Match modes: exact, WILDCARD, CIDR (mark the field in the lookup definition), case-sensitivity toggle.

Gotchas

  • Big CSV lookups are loaded per search — move large/dynamic data to KV Store, or index it.
  • Lookup files must be replicated to indexers if referenced in a streaming lookup pushed to the indexing tier (they usually are via bundle replication).
  • eval null propagates: any null operand often makes the whole expression null — guard with coalesce/if(isnull(...)).
  • String vs number: "10" < "9" is true (lexical). tonumber() first.
Cheat Sheet
  • eval f = expr: if/case/coalesce, tonumber/tostring(x,"duration"), strftime/strptime, match, cidrmatch, mv*, . for concat.
  • where = filter with eval syntax (field-vs-field ok). fieldformat = change display only, keep sort/stats value.
  • EVAL-<name> in props.conf = automatic calculated field per sourcetype.
  • Lookups: CSV (static ref), KV Store (large/updatable, read/write), external/scripted (DNS/GeoIP/API), geospatial, time-bounded.
  • | lookup <name> <in> AS <field> OUTPUT[NEW] <out>; | inputlookup to read the table as results; | outputlookup to write.
  • Automatic lookup: LOOKUP-x in props.conf applies enrichment on every search.
  • Match modes: exact / WILDCARD / CIDR (set in the lookup definition). Move big/dynamic tables to KV Store.
Q&A
Difference between eval and a calculated field?
They do the same computation; a calculated field is an EVAL-<name> stanza in props.conf that Splunk applies automatically at search time for a sourcetype, so the derived field exists on every event without writing | eval. Use it to standardise a derivation across many searches/dashboards.
When do you use KV Store instead of a CSV lookup?
When the table is large, changes frequently, needs per-record updates (write from a search with outputlookup, or via REST/a form), needs typed fields or an _key, or must be queried directly. CSV lookups are simplest for small, mostly-static reference data.
What's an automatic lookup?
A LOOKUP-<name> definition in props.conf tied to a sourcetype, so the enrichment (match input field to table, add output fields) happens on every search of that data with no explicit | lookup. E.g. every firewall event automatically gets src_owner from an asset table.
What does | inputlookup do?
It reads a lookup table (CSV or KV Store collection) and emits its rows as the search result set — you can start a search from a table, or combine it with events using | inputlookup append=t. | outputlookup is the reverse: write the current results into a lookup.
Why might an eval produce null unexpectedly?
Null propagation: if any operand in an arithmetic or string expression is null, the result is usually null. Also type surprises — comparing strings lexically, or strptime failing to parse. Guard with coalesce(x, default), if(isnull(x), ..., ...), and tonumber().
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command changes only how a field is displayed, not its stored value?
fieldformat.
What operator concatenates strings in eval?
. (dot).
Which command reads a lookup table as the result set?
inputlookup.

Intermediate core

Classify each source IP as internal/external using CIDR, then enrich internal ones with their owner from an asset CSV. Show the SPL.
index=fw | eval scope = if(cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", src_ip) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", src_ip) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", src_ip), "internal", "external") | lookup asset_inventory ip AS src_ip OUTPUTNEW owner, business_unit, criticality | eval owner = coalesce(owner, "unknown"). Notes: cidrmatch() handles the RFC1918 ranges; OUTPUTNEW won't clobber an existing owner; coalesce fills misses. If the asset table is large or updated often, make it a KV Store collection and/or an automatic lookup on the firewall sourcetype so every search gets owner for free. To only enrich internal IPs, you can't conditionally skip lookup, but non-matching rows just get null outputs, which is fine.
You want a running list of every unique client IP ever seen, updated by a scheduled search. Design it.
Use a KV Store collection (better than CSV for continual growth and concurrent writes). Define a collection seen_ips with fields ip, first_seen, last_seen, hits, and a lookup definition over it. Scheduled search (every 15m, over -20m for overlap): index=web earliest=-20m | stats min(_time) AS first_seen, max(_time) AS last_seen, count AS hits BY clientip | rename clientip AS ip | inputlookup append=t seen_ips | stats min(first_seen) AS first_seen, max(last_seen) AS last_seen, sum(hits) AS hits BY ip | outputlookup seen_ips. This merges new observations with the existing table (min first_seen, max last_seen, summed hits) and writes it back. Guard size with a retention step (| where last_seen > relative_time(now(), "-90d")) before outputlookup. For very high IP cardinality, consider a summary index instead, or accept the KV Store growing and add a TTL sweep.

Advanced deep

Compare CSV lookups, KV Store lookups, automatic lookups, and indexing the reference data outright. Give the decision criteria and the performance/consistency trade-offs.
CSV lookup: a flat file in an app's lookups/, distributed to search peers via bundle replication. Loaded into memory per search that uses it. Pros: trivial to create/edit/version (it's in the app, goes through your deploy pipeline), fast for small tables, supports WILDCARD/CIDR match. Cons: whole file re-read/parsed per search; large files (> tens of MB / hundreds of thousands of rows) bloat the knowledge bundle replicated to every indexer and slow every search; no concurrent-safe partial updates (rewrite the whole file); no indexing/keys. Use for < ~1M rows of mostly-static reference data (country codes, HTTP status text, small asset lists). KV Store lookup: MongoDB-backed collection on the SH (replicated across SHC members). Pros: supports large datasets, per-record CRUD (from searches via outputlookup, REST, or forms), typed fields, an _key, accelerated fields (indexes) for fast lookups, no giant file in the bundle. Cons: lives on the SH tier so a streaming lookup that would run on indexers can't use it directly (it's pulled to the SH, breaking full distribution for that stage); SHC replication and Mongo operational concerns; slightly more setup. Use for big, frequently-updated, or programmatically-maintained tables (threat intel, session state, entity stores). Automatic lookup: not a storage type — a props.conf binding that applies a CSV or KV lookup on every search of a sourcetype. Pros: consistency (every search/dashboard gets the enrichment, no one forgets | lookup), central control. Cons: hidden cost — it runs even when you don't need those fields, so a heavy automatic lookup taxes all searches of that sourcetype; ordering/override subtleties with other knowledge objects; harder to debug ("where did this field come from?"). Use for enrichment that essentially every consumer wants and that's cheap. Indexing the reference data (ingest the asset/CMDB feed as events, then stats latest() or a data model): Pros: scales to any size, time-aware natively (you can ask "who owned this IP at the time of the event"), searchable/reportable on its own, no bundle bloat. Cons: more moving parts (an input, scheduled search to snapshot current state or a lookup-gen search writing to KV/CSV), and joining events to it needs a subsearch/lookup-generation step anyway. Use when the data is huge, time-varying, or you need historical correctness. Decision flow: tiny + static → CSV; needs writes / large / dynamic → KV Store; "everyone needs it" + cheap → make it automatic; huge or time-travel semantics required → index it and periodically materialise a KV/CSV lookup from the latest state. Consistency: CSV changes propagate on bundle push (seconds to a minute); KV writes are immediate on the SH but SHC replication has a small lag; indexed reference data is only as fresh as its feed + snapshot cadence. Always dedupe/normalise keys (case, whitespace) or matches silently fail.
A dashboard's automatic lookup makes every search of a high-volume sourcetype 3× slower. Walk through diagnosis and options.
Diagnose: confirm the lookup is the cause — run the same base search with | noop vs. and check the Job Inspector's command.lookup time and dispatch.evaluate.lookup; look at index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd for lookup reload messages; check the lookup file size and whether it's CIDR/WILDCARD match (those are far more expensive than exact — every row is tested against every event). Check if it's a scripted/external lookup (per-event process invocation — brutal at volume). Check bundle replication size if it's a huge CSV. Options: (1) Narrow the trigger — if only some searches need the enriched fields, remove the LOOKUP- automatic binding and call | lookup explicitly where needed, or bind it to a more specific sourcetype. (2) Use OUTPUTNEW and fewer output fields so it does less work. (3) Switch match mode — if it's WILDCARD but the data is actually exact, use exact match (indexable, hash lookup). For CIDR, ensure the lookup is sorted/optimised and the field is properly typed; consider bucketing IPs. (4) Move CSV → KV Store with accelerated (indexed) fields so matches are O(log n) not O(n) per event — big win for large tables. (5) Replace scripted lookup with a materialised table — run the script's logic in a scheduled search that writes results to a CSV/KV lookup, then do a plain lookup against that. (6) Index-time enrichment — if the mapping is stable, do it once at ingest (an index-time LOOKUP/transform) so search-time is free. (7) Pre-aggregate — if dashboards only need aggregates, build a summary index / accelerated data model that already includes the enriched fields, so the lookup runs during summarisation (once) not per dashboard load. (8) tstats where possible to skip raw events (and thus the per-event lookup) entirely. (9) Cache: raise the lookup's memory/row limits so it isn't spilling; ensure it isn't being reloaded every run. Best long-term for high volume: index-time enrichment or an accelerated data model with the fields baked in; short-term: de-automate the lookup and move it to KV Store with indexed match fields.

Field Extraction & rex

Turning raw text into fields — at search time (flexible) or index time (rare, costly).

Notes

Search-time vs index-time extraction

Search-time (default, preferred)Index-time (rare)
WhenApplied each search, from knowledge objectsBaked into the event as it's indexed
Change later?Yes — edit and it applies retroactivelyNo — needs re-index
CostCPU at search timeStorage (bigger tsidx) + slower indexing
Use forAlmost everythingFields you must filter on at massive scale, or need for routing; segmenting punctuation

Automatic search-time extraction

  • KV pairs — key=value in the raw text is auto-extracted (KV_MODE=auto). KV_MODE=json / xml parse structured events into fields (nested → a.b.c / a{}.b).
  • Indexed extractions — for pure JSON/CSV/TSV, INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=JSON at ingest gives structured fields cheaply.
  • The Field Extractor (FX) UI: pick sample events, highlight values, it generates a regex or delimiter rule → saved as an EXTRACT- or REPORT-/transforms stanza.

rex — inline extraction

| rex field=_raw "user=(?<user>\w+)\s+ip=(?<src_ip>\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
| rex field=uri "/(?<section>[^/]+)/"
| rex field=msg max_match=0 "id=(?<ids>\d+)"          # multivalue: all matches
| rex mode=sed field=card "s/\d(?=\d{4})/X/g"          # sed mode: transform in place
  • Named capture groups (?<name>...) become fields. Default field=_raw.
  • max_match=0 → capture every match into a multivalue field.
  • mode=sed → substitute (masking, cleanup) rather than extract.
  • PCRE syntax; non-greedy *?; anchor and be specific — broad .* is slow and fragile.

Persisting extractions in props.conf

[my:sourcetype]
# inline regex, one field or more
EXTRACT-login = user=(?<user>\w+)\s+result=(?<result>\w+)

# regex via transforms.conf (reusable, supports DELIMS, MV, cleaning)
REPORT-kv = my_kv_transform

# transforms.conf
[my_kv_transform]
DELIMS = " ", "="            # delimiter-based KV extraction
# or:
REGEX = (?<field>\w+)=(?<value>[^;]+)
FORMAT = $1::$2               # dynamic field names from capture groups
MV_ADD = true
  • EXTRACT- = self-contained regex. REPORT- = points at a transforms.conf stanza (needed for delimiter-based, dynamic-name, or multivalue extraction).
  • Field aliases (FIELDALIAS-x = src AS src_ip) normalise names (CIM). Calculated fields (EVAL-) derive values.

Precedence & debugging

  • Order roughly: index-time / indexed extractions → search-time EXTRACT/REPORT → KV auto → field aliases → calculated fields (EVAL-) → lookups → event types / tags. Later stages can use earlier fields.
  • More specific sourcetype/source/host stanza wins; local over default; app priority via ASCII order unless set.
  • Debug: Job Inspector, | extract to force, erex to generate a regex from examples, and test regex in the FX or rex before persisting.
Cheat Sheet
  • Prefer search-time extraction (editable, retroactive). Index-time only for scale/routing/punct — needs re-index to change.
  • key=value auto-extracts (KV_MODE=auto); KV_MODE=json/xml for structured; INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=JSON/CSV for pure structured feeds.
  • | rex field=X "(?<name>pattern)" — named groups become fields; max_match=0 for multivalue; mode=sed to substitute.
  • Persist: EXTRACT-name (inline regex) or REPORT-name → transforms.conf (for DELIMS, dynamic FORMAT=$1::$2, MV_ADD).
  • FIELDALIAS- to rename (CIM), EVAL- for calculated fields, LOOKUP- for enrichment.
  • Precedence: indexed → EXTRACT/REPORT → KV auto → aliases → EVAL → lookups → eventtypes/tags. Specific stanza + local wins.
  • Tools: Field Extractor UI, erex (regex from examples), Job Inspector.
Q&A
Why is search-time extraction preferred over index-time?
It's flexible and non-destructive: you can add or fix an extraction and it immediately applies to all existing data, with no re-indexing. Index-time extraction is fixed at ingest, enlarges the index, and slows indexing — justified only for fields you must filter on at very large scale, or need for index-time routing.
What's the difference between EXTRACT- and REPORT- in props.conf?
EXTRACT-<name> holds a self-contained regex right there. REPORT-<name> references a transforms.conf stanza, which you need for delimiter-based extraction (DELIMS), dynamically-named fields (FORMAT = $1::$2), multivalue fields (MV_ADD), or reusing one transform across sourcetypes.
How do you get every occurrence of a repeating pattern into one field?
| rex max_match=0 "id=(?<ids>\d+)" — max_match=0 tells rex to keep matching and collect all captures into a multivalue field ids. In transforms.conf the equivalent is MV_ADD = true.
What does rex mode=sed do?
It performs a sed-style substitution on a field's value instead of extracting — e.g. | rex mode=sed field=ssn "s/\d{5}/XXXXX/g" to mask. It changes the field value in the pipeline (search-time only; for index-time masking use SEDCMD in props.conf).
Two apps define a field user for the same sourcetype differently. Which wins?
Config precedence decides: a stanza matching a more specific key (source:: > sourcetype > host:: ordering aside, specificity and local vs default matter), and between apps, priority order (by app directory name / explicit priority). Use btool props list --debug to see the effective value and which file won.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command extracts fields inline during a search?
rex.
What regex construct creates a field in rex?
A named capture group: (?<fieldname>pattern).
Does fixing a search-time extraction require re-indexing?
No — it applies to existing data immediately.

Intermediate core

Logs look like 2024-05-01 lvl=ERROR svc=checkout msg="db timeout" dur=1423ms. What extracts automatically, and what needs help?
lvl=ERROR, svc=checkout, dur=1423ms are key=value pairs and extract automatically under KV_MODE=auto. msg="db timeout" extracts too (quoted value handled). The date isn't key=value, but it's the timestamp so it becomes _time via TIME_FORMAT, not a field. Things needing help: (1) dur=1423ms gives a string "1423ms" — add EVAL-duration_ms = tonumber(replace(dur,"ms","")) as a calculated field for numeric math. (2) If you want msg split into an error category, add a rex/EXTRACT. (3) Normalise names for CIM: FIELDALIAS-svc = svc AS service, alias lvl AS severity. Persist the eval/alias in props.conf for the sourcetype so every search benefits.
A rex works on 5 sample events but misses 20% in production. How do you make it robust?
Causes: format variants (optional fields, different delimiters, quoting, IPv6 vs IPv4, extra whitespace, multiline), greedy matching grabbing too much, and anchoring assumptions. Steps: (1) Sample the failures: ... | rex "..." | where isnull(myfield) | head 100 and eyeball the variety. (2) Loosen the rigid parts: \s+ not a single space, make trailing fields optional (?:\s+extra=(?<extra>\S+))?, allow quotes "?(?<v>[^"\s]+)"?. (3) Tighten the greedy parts: use [^\s]+ / [^,]+ / non-greedy .*? with a following anchor instead of .*. (4) Anchor to a stable nearby token (user=) rather than position. (5) Consider multiple EXTRACT- stanzas, one per format variant, or a transforms.conf with alternation. (6) If the log is actually structured (JSON), stop regexing — set KV_MODE=json or INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS. (7) Add a monitoring search that alerts when extraction success rate for the sourcetype drops (| eval ok=if(isnotnull(myfield),1,0) | timechart avg(ok)) so a future format change is caught.

Advanced deep

Explain the full search-time field precedence chain and give a concrete case where getting the order wrong breaks a dashboard.
Order (each stage can reference fields produced by earlier stages): (1) Indexed fields / INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS — present from the tsidx, always first. (2) Explicit search-time extractions: EXTRACT- (inline regex) and REPORT- (→ transforms.conf, incl. DELIMS, dynamic FORMAT, MV). Among these, config precedence applies (specific stanza, local > default, app priority). (3) KV auto-extraction (KV_MODE) — generic key=value/JSON/XML parsing; runs after explicit extractions, so an explicit EXTRACT for the same name wins. (4) Field aliases (FIELDALIAS-) — copy/rename existing fields (e.g. src AS src_ip); runs after extraction so the source field must already exist. (5) Calculated fields (EVAL-) — can use extracted and aliased fields. (6) Lookups (automatic LOOKUP-) — can key off extracted/aliased/calculated fields and add more. (7) Event types and tags — evaluated last, can match on any field above. Also: | rex / | eval / | lookup in the SPL itself run at their pipeline position, after all the props.conf-driven stuff. Broken-dashboard case: a CIM dashboard filters | tstats ... WHERE nodename=Web.action=blocked or a panel does | stats count BY action. The raw field is act; the app defines FIELDALIAS-action = act AS action. Someone then adds a calculated field EVAL-action = case(...) in a different app to "clean up" action values, intending it to post-process. But EVAL- runs after FIELDALIAS-, and if the eval references action which the alias just created, fine — however if the eval is EVAL-action = coalesce(action, "unknown") and the alias in the lower-priority app didn't fire (because a more specific sourcetype stanza in yet another app redefined action via EXTRACT- to something empty on non-matching events), you get action="unknown" everywhere and the dashboard's BY action collapses to one row. Or: the dashboard relies on the automatic lookup to add action_category, but the lookup keys on action, and because an EXTRACT- in a higher-priority app now produces action with different casing than the lookup table, every lookup misses and action_category is null — panels that filter action_category=denied go blank. Diagnosis is btool props list <sourcetype> --debug to see every contributing stanza and file, plus removing stages one at a time. The fix is to not stack redefinitions of the same field name across apps: use distinct names, respect that aliases precede evals precede lookups, and keep CIM normalisation in one owned TA.
When is index-time extraction genuinely worth the cost, and what exactly does it change on disk and in search behaviour?
Worth it when: (1) You must WHERE/filter on a field across enormous event volumes where search-time regex per event is too slow even after other tuning, and the field can't be an accelerated data model instead. (2) The field is needed for index-time routing or index-time masking decisions (you can't route on a search-time field). (3) You want the field usable by | tstats directly without a data model (tstats can query index-time fields). (4) Punctuation/segmentation needs (SEGMENTATION, custom major/minor breakers) so TERM()/keyword search treats a token the way you need. (5) Very stable schema (a field that will never need redefinition), because changing it means re-indexing. What it changes on disk: index-time extracted fields (via transforms.conf with WRITE_META = true / INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS) are stored in the bucket's tsidx as additional indexed key-value terms, and can be written to the metadata. This enlarges the tsidx (often significantly for high-cardinality fields — watch disk and the cost of building/replicating tsidx in a cluster), and adds work to the indexing pipeline (lower max ingest throughput per indexer). It does not change journal.gz raw storage (unless you also alter _raw via SEDCMD). Search behaviour: queries filtering on the indexed field can be answered from the tsidx (fast, and tstats-eligible) instead of reading raw events; fields for it is free; but the field is now immutable — a parsing mistake is permanent for existing data (re-index or accept it), and you've traded storage + ingest capacity for query speed. High-cardinality warning: indexing something like request_id or user_id at index time bloats the tsidx enormously and can hurt overall search performance (larger indexes to scan) — the classic anti-pattern. Prefer: search-time extraction for flexibility; accelerated data models + tstats for repeated large aggregations; index-time only for a small number of low-cardinality, stable, must-filter-at-scale or must-route-on fields.

Search Performance

Filter early, reduce data before the search head, and use the tsidx when you can.

Notes

The four levers, in order of impact

  1. Time range — the single biggest filter. Every extra day is more buckets scanned. Default dashboards to the smallest useful window.
  2. Index & sourcetype — name them; never index=*. Lets Splunk skip whole buckets by metadata.
  3. Selective terms in the base search — put the most distinctive keyword/field=value before the first |, so the lexicon narrows candidate events. status=500 beats | where status=500.
  4. Reduce before the first transforming command — | fields to keep only needed fields, filter with where/search, extract only what you need. The first stats/timechart is the map→reduce boundary.

Dense vs sparse vs rare vs "needle in haystack"

TypeMatch ratioBound by
Dense> ~1% of eventsCPU to process matches (aggregation)
Sparse~0.01–1%Mix of I/O + CPU
Rare< ~0.01%I/O to seek matching events; lexicon helps a lot
Needle-in-haystack1 in millionsPure seek; make the term indexed/TERM()

Fast wins

  • No leading wildcards (*fail). Trailing (fail*) is fine.
  • Use TERM() for exact tokens with minor breakers (IPs, paths, GUIDs).
  • Prefer stats over transaction (transaction keeps raw events on the SH, no prestats).
  • Prefer stats over join/subsearch where possible — join runs a subsearch (10k/60s limits) and centralises.
  • dedup is cheaper than stats latest(*) by when you just need one event per key; but | stats distributes better for aggregates.
  • Put | fields immediately after the base search.
  • Run reporting searches in Fast mode; avoid Verbose.
  • | tstats against indexed fields or an accelerated data model — skips raw reads entirely.

Acceleration options

MechanismBest for
Report accelerationOne specific transforming search run often over a long range. Splunk auto-builds summaries per bucket.
Data model acceleration + tstatsMany searches/dashboards over a shared schema (CIM). Incrementally maintained tsidx summaries.
Summary indexing (collect / si* commands)Custom rollups you control; historical aggregates; when built-in acceleration doesn't fit.
Scheduled search + loadjobShare one result set across users/panels instead of everyone re-running.

Diagnosing with the Job Inspector

  • Total run time and the command.* breakdown — which command ate the time.
  • scan count vs event count vs result count — how much was read vs matched vs returned. Huge scan/tiny result = your filter isn't selective.
  • dispatch.stream.remote (indexer work), dispatch.evaluate (SH work), command.search.index (lexicon), command.search.rawdata (bucket reads).
  • index=_audit action=search / index=_internal for skipped/deferred scheduled searches and concurrency limits.
  • The Monitoring Console for indexer load, search concurrency, and skipped searches org-wide.

Concurrency & scheduling

  • Each SH has caps: max_searches_per_cpu, historical vs real-time, scheduled-search quota (a fraction of total). Exceed → searches are skipped or queued.
  • Stagger schedules (avoid every :00), lengthen intervals, use schedule_window, and move heavy scheduled work to a dedicated SH.
  • Real-time searches are expensive (a persistent search per) — use indexed real-time or short historical instead where possible.
Cheat Sheet
  • Levers by impact: time range → index/sourcetype → selective terms before the first | → | fields + filter before the first transforming command.
  • status=500 in base search > | where status=500. No leading *. TERM() for IPs/paths/GUIDs.
  • Prefer stats over transaction and over join/subsearch (those centralise + have 10k/60s caps).
  • Fast mode for reporting; not Verbose.
  • | tstats on indexed / accelerated-data-model fields = no raw read.
  • Acceleration: report acceleration (one heavy search), data model acceleration + tstats (shared schema / dashboards), summary indexing (custom rollups), scheduled search + loadjob (share results).
  • Job Inspector: compare scan count vs event count vs result count; check command.* timings. Watch skipped scheduled searches / concurrency in the Monitoring Console.
Q&A
Why is filtering in the base search better than | where later?
Base-search terms use the index (time index + lexicon) to avoid reading non-matching events at all, and they run distributed on the indexers. | where (and | search after the first pipe) runs on already-retrieved events, so Splunk has already paid the I/O to read them.
What does a large scan count with a tiny result count tell you?
Splunk read a lot of events to produce very few results — your search isn't selective at retrieval time. Add index/sourcetype constraints, a more distinctive keyword, or a field=value filter to the base search, or narrow the time range.
Why avoid transaction when stats will do?
transaction groups raw events into transactions on the search head, keeping all events in memory, with no prestats optimisation — it doesn't distribute. stats (e.g. stats range(_time) count by session_id) computes partial aggregates on the indexers and only ships small partials. Use transaction only when you truly need the grouped raw events or complex start/end conditions.
When should you accelerate a data model vs use a summary index?
Accelerate a data model when many searches/dashboards share a schema (especially CIM) and you want tstats speed with Splunk maintaining the summaries automatically. Use summary indexing when you need a custom rollup Splunk's acceleration doesn't express, want full control of the summarised data's retention/schema, or need to backfill history.
Your scheduled searches are being "skipped". Why and what do you do?
Search concurrency limits are exceeded — too many scheduled (and ad-hoc) searches want to run at once, and the scheduler's quota is full. Stagger schedules off the top of the hour, lengthen intervals, add schedule_window / priority, reduce per-search cost (acceleration, tighter scope), or add search-head capacity / a dedicated scheduling SH.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What's the highest-impact thing to constrain in a slow search?
The time range.
Which is faster: error* or *error?
error* (trailing wildcard can use the lexicon; leading cannot).
Which command reads the tsidx instead of raw events?
tstats.

Intermediate core

A dashboard panel: index=* | search sourcetype=api | stats count by endpoint | join endpoint [search index=* sourcetype=api_meta | fields endpoint owner]. Rewrite for performance.
Problems: index=* twice; | search sourcetype=api after the pipe instead of in the base search; join with a subsearch (10k/60s caps, centralised); no time bound. Rewrite: put both datasets in one search and aggregate, or use a lookup for the metadata. If api_meta is small/stable: generate a lookup (index=api_meta earliest=-1d | stats latest(owner) as owner by endpoint | outputlookup api_owners.csv on a schedule), then the panel is index=api sourcetype=api:access earliest=-24h | fields endpoint | stats count by endpoint | lookup api_owners.csv endpoint OUTPUT owner | sort - count. If it must be live, combine: (index=api sourcetype=api:access) OR (index=api sourcetype=api_meta) earliest=-24h | stats count(eval(sourcetype="api:access")) as calls, values(owner) as owner by endpoint. Both avoid join, name the index, filter in the base search, add a time range, and | fields early.
The Job Inspector shows command.search.rawdata dominating the runtime. What does that mean and what are your options?
Splunk is spending its time reading and decompressing raw events from buckets (journal.gz), i.e. it matched a lot of events and had to pull them off disk to process — a dense search, or one whose selective filtering happens too late. Options: (1) Make the base search more selective so fewer events are retrieved (better keyword, field=value, tighter time). (2) If you only need aggregates on indexed fields, switch to | tstats so raw data is never read. (3) Accelerate a data model covering this data and query via tstats/pivot. (4) Build a summary index / report acceleration so the heavy read happens once during summarisation, not per dashboard load. (5) Ensure hot/warm buckets are on fast storage (NVMe) and cold isn't on something slow for frequently-searched ranges. (6) Add indexers to spread the bucket-read I/O. (7) Reduce output fields with | fields so less per-event work follows the read. If instead command.search.index dominated, the lexicon lookup is the cost — often leading wildcards or very broad term matching.

Advanced deep

Design an acceleration strategy for an org where 300 analysts run ad-hoc security searches, ~2,000 scheduled correlation searches run continuously, and executives load heavy dashboards — all on the same data. How do you keep it performant and fair?
Separate the workloads onto tiers: (a) a search-head cluster for interactive analysts; (b) a dedicated SH (or SHC) for the scheduled correlation searches (e.g. Enterprise Security's) so a burst of scheduled work never starves humans; (c) optionally a small SH for executive dashboards. Use workload management (resource pools with CPU/memory limits and rules by user/app/search type) to cap ad-hoc searches, guarantee the scheduler a slice, and de-prioritise dashboard auto-refreshes. Model and accelerate the data: map the security data to CIM data models (Authentication, Network Traffic, Web, Endpoint…) and enable data model acceleration with retention matched to detection needs (e.g. 7–30 days). Rewrite correlation searches and dashboard panels to | tstats/| pivot against the accelerated models — this is the single biggest win: thousands of searches read compact summary tsidx instead of raw events. Accept the cost: acceleration builds background summaries on the indexers (disk + a maintenance workload) — size indexers for it. For long-range reporting (exec dashboards, trend reports): summary indexing — scheduled si*/collect jobs roll data into small summary indexes with long retention; dashboards query those. Share results: exec dashboards use scheduled saved searches with a refresh and loadjob so all viewers hit one cached artifact; base + post-process searches within each dashboard so shared data is retrieved once. Schedule hygiene: stagger the 2,000 scheduled searches (schedule_window, cron spread, priorities), lengthen intervals where detection latency allows, and continuously watch index=_internal for skipped searches and lag; alert on skip rate. Ad-hoc guardrails: default time ranges, search filters/macros that inject index constraints, Fast mode defaults, per-role concurrency and disk quotas, and training. Capacity: size the indexing tier for (ingest + acceleration maintenance + peak concurrent search), N+1 per site, and monitor the Monitoring Console health checks. Net: CIM + data model acceleration + tstats for the bulk, summary indexing for long-range, workload management + tiered SHs for fairness, scheduled/shared results for dashboards, and constant skip/lag monitoring.
Explain exactly what "scan count", "event count", and "result count" mean in the Job Inspector, how they relate through a pipeline, and how to read them to find the bottleneck.
scan count: the number of events Splunk examined from buckets to satisfy the base search — roughly, candidate events the lexicon/time-index pointed at that were read and tested. It is not "all events in the index"; the index prefilters. A high scan count means the retrieval isn't selective (broad terms, wide time, dense term). event count: the number of events that matched the base search (passed the retrieval-time filter) and entered the pipeline — the input to your first command after the base search. result count: the number of rows in the final result set after all commands (post-stats, post-head, etc.). Relationship: scan count ≥ event count ≥ (usually) result count, though result count can exceed event count if a command multiplies rows (mvexpand, some eval+append patterns) and equals event count for a pure streaming search with no aggregation. Reading them: (1) scan count >> event count → the base search reads far more than it keeps; the lexicon isn't narrowing well — add distinctive terms, index/sourcetype, tighter time, or TERM(); check for leading wildcards. Pair with command.search.rawdata/command.search.index timings. (2) scan count ≈ event count and both huge → genuinely dense search; the cost is in processing matches — reduce fields (| fields), push filtering earlier, or accelerate/tstats. (3) event count huge, result count tiny, and a big command.stats/command.sort time → you're shipping/aggregating too many events on the SH; move filtering before the first transforming command, or aggregate on indexers with a streamable prefix. (4) event count small but total time large → the cost is elsewhere: an expensive lookup (scripted/CIDR/large), rex with catastrophic backtracking, transaction, a subsearch/join, or field discovery in Verbose mode — check the per-command timings and dispatch.evaluate.*. (5) Compare dispatch.stream.remote (indexer work) vs local — if local dominates, too much is being done on the SH; if remote dominates and it's slow, indexers are I/O-bound (dense search or slow storage) — accelerate or add indexers. Also watch elapsed_time vs run_duration (queuing/concurrency), and whether the search was finalized early by a limit. The quick heuristic: scan≈event≈result and fast = well-targeted; scan≫event = fix retrieval selectivity; event≫result with slow stats/sort = reduce before the reduce.

Data Models, tstats & CIM

A schema over your events, an acceleration that makes it fast, and a shared vocabulary so content is portable.

Notes

Data models

  • A hierarchical schema defined on top of raw events: a tree of datasets (formerly "objects"), each with constraints (a search that selects its events) and fields (extracted / eval / lookup / geoip).
  • Child datasets inherit parent constraints and fields and add more — e.g. Web → Web.Errors (adds status>=400).
  • Fields are typed and can be auto-extracted, calculated, or lookup-based — the model is where you normalise messy events into a clean shape.
  • Consumed by Pivot (GUI reporting, no SPL), by | datamodel, and by | tstats … FROM datamodel=….

Acceleration

  • Enable "Accelerate" on a model + a retention window (e.g. 30 days). Splunk builds and incrementally maintains per-bucket summary tsidx files on the indexers containing the model's fields.
  • | tstats … FROM datamodel=X then reads those summaries — no raw event access, huge speedup.
  • summariesonly=t → only return accelerated data (fast, but misses very recent un-summarised events); summariesonly=f (default) fills the gap by searching raw for the unsummarised tail (slower but complete). allow_old_summaries=t to tolerate schema drift.
  • Costs: extra disk on indexers, a background summarisation workload, and rebuilds if you change the model. Only accelerate models people actually query a lot.

tstats against a model

| tstats summariesonly=t count
    FROM datamodel=Web
    WHERE Web.status>=500 AND Web.http_method=POST
    BY Web.dest, _time span=1h
| rename Web.* AS *
  • Reference fields as <Model>.<field> in WHERE/BY.
  • Only fields in the model are available; no arbitrary raw regex.
  • | tstats … prestats=t … | timechart … to feed charting; or | pivot.

The Common Information Model (CIM)

  • A Splunk-provided add-on defining standard data models (Authentication, Network Traffic, Web, Endpoint / Processes / Ports, Malware, Intrusion Detection, Change, DLP, Email, Vulnerabilities, Certificates, …) with standard field names (src, dest, user, action, signature, bytes_in…) and tags (tag=authentication, tag=network tag=communicate).
  • You make a data source "CIM-compliant" by writing a Technology Add-on that: extracts/aliases fields to the CIM names, adds the required tags/eventtypes, and sets any needed evals — so the vendor's usr becomes user, act becomes action, etc.
  • Payoff: any content written against the CIM (Enterprise Security correlation searches, dashboards, community apps) works on your data with no rework — | tstats … FROM datamodel=Authentication spans every auth source you've normalised.

Enterprise Security & the CIM

ES ships hundreds of correlation searches, dashboards, and risk rules that all query the accelerated CIM data models via tstats. Onboarding a new log source into ES = CIM-normalise it with a TA + confirm the relevant data model is accelerated + validate the events appear via | datamodel … search.

Cheat Sheet
  • Data model = tree of datasets, each with constraints (selecting search) + typed fields (extract/eval/lookup); children inherit + narrow.
  • Consumed by Pivot (no SPL), | datamodel, and | tstats FROM datamodel=X.
  • Acceleration: per-bucket summary tsidx on indexers, incrementally maintained; tstats reads it → no raw access.
  • summariesonly=t = only accelerated data (fast, misses recent tail); =f = fill tail from raw (complete, slower).
  • | tstats count FROM datamodel=Web WHERE Web.status>=500 BY Web.dest, _time span=1h — fields as Model.field, model fields only.
  • CIM = Splunk add-on of standard data models + field names (src/dest/user/action…) + tags.
  • Make a source CIM-compliant via a TA: alias/extract to CIM fields, add tags/eventtypes. Payoff: Enterprise Security & CIM apps work unmodified.
Q&A
What is a data model in Splunk?
A structured, hierarchical schema layered over raw events: datasets with constraint searches and typed fields, arranged so child datasets inherit and refine parents. It lets non-SPL users build reports via Pivot and, when accelerated, powers fast tstats queries.
How does data model acceleration make searches fast?
Splunk pre-computes and incrementally maintains compact summary index files (tsidx) for the model's fields, stored per bucket on the indexers. | tstats FROM datamodel=X answers queries from those summaries without reading or parsing raw events — often 10–100× faster.
What does summariesonly=t trade off?
Speed for completeness. With summariesonly=t, tstats returns only data that's already been summarised, so the most recent events (not yet rolled into summaries) are missing. summariesonly=f also searches raw for that unsummarised tail, giving complete results but slower.
What is the CIM and why does it matter?
The Common Information Model is a set of standardised Splunk data models and field names (e.g. src, dest, user, action). If you normalise your log sources to the CIM (via Technology Add-ons that alias/extract fields and add tags), then any content built against the CIM — Enterprise Security correlation searches, prebuilt dashboards, community apps — works on your data without modification.
How do you make a new log source "CIM-compliant"?
Write or install a Technology Add-on for it that: extracts the relevant fields, uses FIELDALIAS-/EVAL- to map them to CIM names, adds the required eventtypes and tags (e.g. tag=authentication), and sets any needed lookups. Then verify with | datamodel Authentication Authentication search that your events show up with the right fields.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which command queries an accelerated data model without reading raw events?
tstats.
What GUI feature lets non-SPL users report off a data model?
Pivot.
What does CIM standardise?
Data model structure and field names (and tags) across data sources.

Intermediate core

Your firewall data is onboarded but doesn't show up in Enterprise Security's Network Traffic dashboards. What's the likely gap and how do you fix it?
The data isn't CIM-normalised for the Network Traffic data model. ES dashboards run | tstats FROM datamodel=Network_Traffic, which only sees events that (a) match the model's constraints — typically tag=network tag=communicate — and (b) have the CIM fields (src, dest, src_port, dest_port, action, bytes_in, bytes_out, transport, …). Fix: install/author the vendor's Technology Add-on (Palo Alto TA, etc.) on the search heads (and indexers for index-time bits), which provides the field extractions, FIELDALIAS-/EVAL- to CIM names, and the eventtype+tag assignments. Verify: | datamodel Network_Traffic All_Traffic search | search sourcetype=pan:traffic returns events with populated CIM fields; tag=network matches. Then ensure the Network Traffic data model is accelerated (ES relies on acceleration) and let it backfill. If some fields are missing, extend the TA's props/transforms. Re-check the ES dashboard after acceleration catches up.
When would you build a custom data model instead of using the CIM?
When your use case is a bespoke business/application domain the CIM doesn't cover — e.g. an order-processing pipeline with fields like order_id, fulfilment_stage, warehouse, sla_breached. The CIM is aimed at IT/security telemetry (auth, network, endpoint, web); forcing business events into it gains nothing. A custom model gives you: Pivot-based self-service for analysts, acceleration + tstats speed for dashboards over that schema, and a clean normalised layer over possibly-messy app logs. You'd still CIM-normalise the infrastructure aspects (the web tier serving the orders) so security content works, and keep the custom model for the domain metrics. Also build a custom model when you need acceleration for a specific heavy reporting workload that doesn't map to any CIM model.

Advanced deep

Explain how data model acceleration is built and maintained across a clustered deployment, the failure/rebuild scenarios, and how summariesonly, allow_old_summaries, and retention interact.
Build/maintain: when you accelerate a model, the SH schedules a special search (an "acceleration search", visible as _ACCELERATE_DM_...) that runs frequently (default every 5 min). It generates, per bucket on each indexer, a summary tsidx file containing just the model's fields for events matching the model's constraints in that bucket's time span. Because it's per-bucket, it's incremental: new hot/warm buckets get summarised as they appear; already-summarised warm/cold buckets are skipped. Buckets outside the acceleration retention window (acceleration.earliest_time, e.g. -30d) are not summarised, and their summaries are removed as they age out. In an indexer cluster, summary tsidx files are treated like other bucket data — they're built on the primary searchable copy and the cluster ensures other searchable copies also have them (rebuilt on the peer if missing), so search factor still applies. On a SHC, the acceleration search is owned/scheduled by the cluster (captain coordinates) so it isn't run N times. Progress is visible in Settings → Data Models (percent complete, size, last build). Failure/rebuild scenarios: (1) You edit the model (add/change a field or constraint) → existing summaries no longer match the schema; Splunk marks them stale and rebuilds — potentially re-summarising the whole retention window (expensive; plan changes). allow_old_summaries=t on a tstats lets queries keep using the old summaries meanwhile (results may lack the new field) instead of falling back to raw. (2) An indexer is down / a bucket is unsearchable → that bucket's summary is unavailable; summariesonly=t silently under-reports for that slice until the cluster restores a searchable copy and rebuilds the summary. (3) Acceleration search skipped (concurrency limits) → summaries lag; the unsummarised tail grows, so summariesonly=f queries get slower (more raw backfill) and summariesonly=t queries miss more recent data. Monitor skipped _ACCELERATE searches. (4) Disk pressure on indexers → summary builds fail; watch summary size (can be a large fraction of the model's raw data for wide models). (5) Bucket roll to frozen → summary goes with it. Interactions: summariesonly=t = "trust only the summary" → fast, deterministic cost, but excludes the unsummarised tail (recent minutes) and any slice whose summary is missing/stale — good for scheduled correlation searches where a few minutes' latency is acceptable and consistent performance matters; pair with a separate real-time-ish check for the very recent window if needed. summariesonly=f = "summary + raw for the gap" → complete, but latency spikes when the tail is large (lagging acceleration) — better for ad-hoc/interactive correctness. allow_old_summaries=t = "use summaries even if the model definition changed" → avoids a total raw fallback during a rebuild, at the risk of stale schema/results; use temporarily around model changes. Retention: the acceleration window should be ≥ the longest lookback of the searches that use it; making it longer multiplies summary disk and build cost. ES ships sensible defaults per CIM model; extend deliberately.
You're normalising 40 log sources to the CIM for Enterprise Security. Design the process, the validation, and the ongoing governance so detections don't silently break.
Process per source: (1) Identify the relevant CIM data model(s) (a source can feed several — e.g. an EDR feeds Endpoint, Processes, Ports, Malware). (2) Prefer an official/Splunkbase TA for that vendor — it already has the extractions, aliases, eventtypes, and tags; only extend it. If none exists, author a TA: search-time EXTRACT-/REPORT- for raw fields, FIELDALIAS-/EVAL- to CIM names, eventtypes.conf + tags.conf to set the model's required tags (tag=authentication, tag=network tag=communicate, …), lookups for enrichment (vendor action codes → CIM action values like success/failure/blocked). (3) Deploy the TA to SHs (search-time) and indexers/HFs (any index-time bits) via Deployer/Cluster Manager, versioned in Git. Validation per source: (a) | datamodel <Model> <Dataset> search | search sourcetype=<yours> returns events. (b) Use the CIM Validation tooling / | tstats count values(sourcetype) BY <required fields> to check every required and recommended field is populated (not null, correct type, expected value domain — e.g. action is one of the CIM's allowed values). (c) Confirm the model's tags match. (d) Check a representative correlation search that uses that model now fires on test data from the new source. (e) Verify acceleration picks it up (count via summariesonly=t after a build cycle). Ongoing governance: (1) A scheduled "CIM health" dashboard/alert per model: field fill-rate over time per sourcetype (| tstats count, count(eval(isnotnull(Model.user))) ... BY sourcetype), alerting when fill-rate for a required field drops (catches a vendor format change or a TA regression). (2) Coverage alert: each expected sourcetype still contributes events to its model in the last N hours (catches a broken input). (3) Change control: TA changes go through PR + CI (btool/regex lint, and a test that runs CIM validation against sample events) + staging validation before prod; pin TA versions. (4) Model change discipline: editing a CIM model (or the CIM add-on upgrade) triggers acceleration rebuilds and can shift field semantics — schedule, announce, and re-validate detections after. (5) Acceleration monitoring: alert on skipped _ACCELERATE searches and acceleration lag/percent-complete per model. (6) Track a source→model→detection matrix so when a source breaks you know which detections are blinded.
