Guard: the error-budget policy must be agreed by engineering and product leadership up front, with a real freeze mechanism and an escalation path; report budget status in the same review as feature progress; make burn-rate pages actually page; retro on whether the policy was followed. Other: too many SLOs (every metric becomes an "SLO", diluting meaning — keep a handful per service tied to user journeys); SLOs on things users don't touch; windows that hide slow burns (only alerting on 1h windows misses a 0.5× erosion) — hence the multi-window set and a 28d budget view. Keeping them honest ultimately means: few, user-derived SLIs measured near the user; stable targets changed only by process; every exclusion justified in the open; a real, leadership-backed error-budget policy; and regular reconciliation of the SLI against actual user-reported pain.

Alerting Philosophy

Every page should be urgent, actionable, and about a real user-facing problem.

Notes

The test for a page

Before something is allowed to page a human at 3am, it should pass all of:

  • Real — a genuine problem, not a threshold twitch.
  • User-impacting (or imminently so) — a symptom, not an internal curiosity.
  • Actionable — there is something the responder can do right now.
  • Urgent — it can't wait for business hours.

If it fails "actionable" or "urgent", it's a ticket or a dashboard, not a page.

Symptoms vs causes

  • Alert on symptoms — the user-visible SLO/RED signals: error ratio, latency past SLO, SLO burn rate, "requests failing". These catch any cause, including ones you didn't predict.
  • Don't page on causes — "CPU 90%", "disk 80%", "GC time up", "one pod restarted". A cause that isn't hurting users is a dashboard line; a cause that is hurting users already tripped a symptom alert.
  • Exception: a small number of leading-indicator alerts where the fix takes long enough that waiting for the symptom is too late — "disk will be full in 4 hours", "certificate expires in 7 days", "no successful backup in 25 hours". These page/ticket because they're actionable and time-boxed.

Three delivery tiers

TierMeansExample
PageWake someone nowSLO fast-burn, checkout error rate 20%, whole service down
TicketLook within a day, business hoursSLO slow-burn, a single replica unhealthy, cert expiring in 10 days
Log / dashboardAvailable when investigatingPer-pod CPU, retry counts, cache hit ratio

Reducing noise

  • Multi-window burn-rate alerting (see SLIs/SLOs) — fast + slow window both must trip; auto-resolves quickly.
  • for: duration so a 30-second blip doesn't page.
  • Grouping / inhibition: one page for "region down", not 400 pages for each service in it; inhibit downstream alerts when an upstream cause is firing.
  • Dedup & routing: by team/severity; sensible repeat_interval.
  • Maintenance windows / silences for known work.
  • Delete alerts that have never been actioned; every alert has an owner and a runbook.

Runbooks & context

  • Every alert links a runbook: what it means, how to confirm, first mitigations, escalation, dashboards.
  • The alert payload carries: the SLO/graph link, affected scope (service/region), recent deploys, and severity.
  • Goal: responder goes from page to "I know what's wrong and the first thing to try" in under a minute.

On-call health

  • Track pages per shift (target: a responder can sleep most nights), actionability rate, and false-positive rate. Alert fatigue is an incident risk — ignored pagers.
  • Every page reviewed: was it valid? actionable? could it be a ticket? Tune or delete.
  • Compensate on-call; keep rotations big enough; hand off cleanly.
Cheat Sheet
  • A page must be real + user-impacting + actionable + urgent. Fails any → ticket or dashboard.
  • Alert on symptoms (SLO burn, error ratio, latency) — catches unknown causes. Don't page on causes (CPU/disk/GC/pod restart).
  • Exception: leading indicators with slow fixes — disk-will-fill, cert-expiring, backup-missing.
  • Tiers: page (now) / ticket (today) / dashboard (when investigating).
  • Noise control: multi-window burn-rate, for: duration, grouping + inhibition, silences for maintenance, delete never-actioned alerts.
  • Every alert: an owner + a runbook + rich payload (SLO link, scope, recent deploys).
  • Track pages/shift, actionability %, false-positive %. Review every page; fatigue = missed real incidents.
Q&A
Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
A symptom alert (error ratio, latency, SLO burn) fires for any underlying cause, including ones you never anticipated, and it directly reflects user pain. Cause alerts ("CPU high") are noisy, often not user-impacting, and you can't enumerate every cause. If a cause is actually hurting users, the symptom alert already caught it; the cause metrics are for diagnosis on the dashboard.
When is it legitimate to alert on a cause?
When it's a leading indicator whose remedy takes longer than the time until it becomes a user-facing outage: "disk full in 4 hours", "TLS cert expires in 7 days", "no successful backup in 25 hours", "approaching a hard quota". These are actionable and time-boxed, so acting before the symptom appears is correct.
What makes an alert "actionable"?
There's a specific thing the on-call person can do right now to mitigate — roll back, fail over, scale up, disable a feature, follow a runbook. If the only response is "watch it" or "file a bug for tomorrow", it shouldn't page.
How do you stop one big outage from generating hundreds of pages?
Grouping and inhibition in the alert manager: group related alerts (by cluster/region/service) into a single notification, and configure inhibition rules so a high-level alert ("region unreachable") suppresses the flood of dependent alerts it obviously causes. Combined with sensible dedup and one notification per group.
What metrics tell you your alerting is unhealthy?
High pages-per-shift (people can't sleep), low actionability rate (most pages need no action), high false-positive rate, alerts that are routinely silenced or ignored, and a growing set of alerts nobody owns. These predict alert fatigue, which causes real incidents to be missed.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Should "CPU at 90%" page someone?
No — it's a cause, not a symptom, and often not user-impacting. Dashboard it; page on the symptom if users are affected.
Name the three delivery tiers for alerts.
Page (now), ticket (today), and dashboard/log (when investigating).
What should every alert link to?
A runbook (and it should have a named owner).

Intermediate core

Your on-call gets ~15 pages a night, most needing no action. Give a concrete plan to fix it.
(1) Audit every alert: for each, pull the last N firings and label them real/actionable/user-impacting. (2) Delete or downgrade the ones that are never actioned or aren't urgent — convert to tickets or dashboards. Typical culprits: per-pod resource alerts, single-replica-unhealthy, transient network blips, cause metrics. (3) Replace cause alerts with symptom/SLO alerts: one multi-window burn-rate alert per service SLO instead of a dozen threshold alerts. (4) Add for: durations and multi-window conditions so blips don't page and alerts auto-resolve. (5) Group and inhibit: collapse related alerts; suppress downstream alerts when an upstream cause fires. (6) Fix flapping: hysteresis / different fire vs clear thresholds. (7) Route by severity: only true "wake up" alerts page; the rest go to a daytime queue. (8) Set a target (e.g. ≤ 2 actionable pages/shift, 0 nights with > 1) and review weekly, tuning or deleting until you hit it. (9) Make a rule: a new paging alert requires an owner, a runbook, and a symptom justification.
An engineer wants to page on "database replica lag > 30s". Is that right? Discuss.
It depends on whether replica lag is a symptom of user impact or just a cause. Ask: do reads serve from replicas? If yes, lag > 30s means users can see stale data — that is user-facing, so a symptom-style alert (e.g. "stale-read SLI violated" or "replica lag past the freshness SLO") is legitimate, ideally tied to an actual freshness SLO rather than a raw 30s threshold. If replicas are only for failover/analytics, lag is a cause: it doesn't hurt users now, but it degrades your recovery capability, so it's better as a ticket (or a page only if it's severe and sustained, because failover readiness is time-sensitive). Also check actionability: is there a runbook (throttle writes, add replica capacity, investigate long transactions)? And avoid flapping with a for: 5m and a clear threshold below the fire threshold. Net: reframe it around the freshness SLO if reads use replicas; otherwise ticket it, page only on sustained severe lag.

Advanced deep

Design the complete alerting policy for a platform team owning 40 services: what pages, what tickets, routing, escalation, suppression, and how it's governed.
What pages (symptom-only, per service, from SLOs): multi-window multi-burn-rate on each service's availability and latency SLOs (14.4×/1h+5m and 6×/6h+30m → page; 1×/3d+6h → ticket); "service hard down" (no successful requests for N minutes); and a small set of platform-wide symptoms (ingress error rate, auth service down, global DB primary unavailable). Plus leading indicators as page-or-ticket by lead time: disk-full-in-<4h (page), cert-expiry-<72h (page) / <14d (ticket), backup-missing->25h (page), quota->90% (ticket). Everything else (per-pod CPU/mem, GC, retry counts, cache ratios, single replica unhealthy, queue depth below danger) is dashboard-only or a ticket. Routing: alert labels team, service, severity, slo. Alertmanager tree: per-owning-team route → severity split (page → PagerDuty/Opsgenie rotation; ticket → the team's daytime queue); a platform catch-all for unrouted alerts → platform on-call (and that's a bug to fix). Group by service,region,alertname; group_wait 30s, group_interval 5m, repeat_interval 3–4h. Escalation: page → primary on-call; no ack in 5–10 min → secondary; still nothing → team lead / incident commander; sev1 auto-opens an incident channel and notifies stakeholders. Suppression: inhibition rules so "region down" / "cluster unreachable" / "ingress down" suppress dependent per-service alerts; maintenance silences via a self-service tool that requires a reason and an end time; a "deploy in progress" silence scoped to the service for the rollout window; dependency-outage silences with expiry. Governance: alerts are code (in the service's repo or a central alerts repo), reviewed via PR; a new severity=page alert must include an owner, a runbook URL, a symptom/lead-time justification, and burn-rate/for tuning — CI checks these fields exist. A weekly alert review: dashboard of pages per service, actionability rate, false-positive rate, MTTA/MTTR, nights-disturbed; any alert below an actionability threshold or above a noise threshold is tuned or deleted that week. Quarterly: prune unused alerts and dashboards, re-check SLO targets. On-call health metrics reported to leadership; rotations sized so median is a quiet week; comp/policy for after-hours. The north star: a page means "a user-facing thing is broken or about to be, and you can fix it now" — anything else is a ticket or a graph.
Symptom-based alerting is the standard advice, but it has real weaknesses. Enumerate them and how a mature setup compensates.
1. Detection lag. A symptom alert fires only once users are already affected; for a fast, severe failure that's fine, but for slow-building problems (a leak, a slowly filling disk, creeping cardinality, cert expiry) waiting for the symptom means an avoidable outage. Compensate: a curated set of leading-indicator alerts with explicit lead times and runbooks — the sanctioned exceptions to "symptoms only". 2. Low signal on the cause. "Error ratio is up" tells you that something's wrong, not what. Compensate: rich alert payloads (which SLO, which endpoints/regions, recent deploys/flags), correlated traces/logs one click away, and cause metrics on the linked dashboard so the responder can localise fast. Good MTTD from symptoms + good tooling for the localise/explain steps. 3. Blind spots for low-traffic services. A ratio-based symptom SLI is statistically noisy or silent when request volume is tiny — a couple of errors swing the ratio, or an outage produces no requests so the error ratio stays 0. Compensate: minimum-volume guards, absolute-count alerts alongside ratios, and outside-in synthetic probes that generate steady traffic and alert on probe failure (catches "service is down so there are no requests"). 4. Partial / dimensional failures hidden by aggregates. One broken tenant, region, shard, or endpoint can be invisible in the global SLI. Compensate: multi-dimensional SLOs (per region / tier / critical endpoint), and alerts that fire on "any dimension breaching", not just the aggregate. 5. Correctness failures that return 200. Availability/latency symptoms miss wrong-but-successful responses (bad data, empty results, silent truncation). Compensate: correctness/freshness SLIs, response validation, and business-outcome metrics ("successful checkouts/min" vs baseline). 6. Recovery/resilience erosion. Symptoms don't tell you you've lost redundancy (one of three replicas down, failover untested, backup failing) until the next failure takes you down. Compensate: ticket-level alerts on redundancy/DR state, and periodic failover/restore drills. 7. Cascading-failure ambiguity. When everything is on fire, hundreds of symptom alerts don't point at the root. Compensate: alert grouping/inhibition, a dependency model, and an incident process with a commander rather than relying on alerts to diagnose. 8. "No alert" isn't "healthy". A broken exporter or a paused scrape produces silence. Compensate: dead-man's-switch / heartbeat alerts (alert if a known-always-firing test alert stops), scrape-health monitoring, and alerting-pipeline monitoring. A mature setup is therefore: symptom/SLO alerts as the backbone for "users are hurting now", plus a small, governed set of leading-indicator and resilience alerts, plus synthetics for low-traffic and outside-in coverage, plus multi-dimensional SLOs, plus heartbeats and pipeline monitoring — and strong localise/explain tooling so the thin symptom signal is enough to act on.

Designing Effective Dashboards

A dashboard is a tool for answering one question fast — not a museum of every metric.

Notes

Start from the question

  • Each dashboard answers one question: "is service X healthy?", "what is the DB doing?", "how is the fleet?".
  • Know the audience & moment: on-call triage (fast, few panels, health-first), deep-dive debugging (detailed, drill-down), capacity planning (trends, long windows), exec/status (SLOs, high level).
  • If you can't say the question in a sentence, split the dashboard.

Layout: top-down, most-important-first

  1. Header: a text panel — what this is, who owns it, links to runbook and related dashboards.
  2. Summary row: SLO / RED at a glance (availability, error ratio, latency percentiles, saturation) as stat panels colored by threshold. Answer "OK?" in two seconds.
  3. Supporting detail: time series for the summary signals, broken down by endpoint / dependency / region.
  4. Deep-dive rows: per-pod, runtime (GC, heap), pools, queues — collapsed by default, lazy-loaded.

Panel hygiene

  • Set the correct unit so axes/tooltips auto-scale; set Y-min to 0 for rates/counts (a non-zero baseline exaggerates wiggles); don't force 0 for latency.
  • Name series ({{label}}); hide legends on dense panels or use a table legend with last/min/max for comparison.
  • Colour: consistent semantics (red = bad) everywhere; don't rely on colour alone; limit to topk so the graph is readable.
  • Thresholds drawn on latency/error panels to show the SLO line.
  • Percentiles for latency (p50/p95/p99), not averages. Rates for counters, not raw.
  • Every panel has a description (what it shows, what "bad" looks like).

Context

  • Annotations for deploys, config changes, incidents, feature-flag flips — so a change in a graph has an explanation.
  • Shared time range across all panels; a time picker default that matches the use (15m–1h for triage, 7–30d for capacity).
  • Template variables (env, region, service, instance) so one dashboard covers the fleet; cascade them; provide sensible defaults.
  • Data links from panels to logs, traces, and the next dashboard down — carry the time range and labels.

Consistency & maintenance

  • Use a house template (a standard RED row, USE row, SLO header) so every service dashboard looks the same — responders build muscle memory.
  • Dashboards as code (Jsonnet/grafonnet, Terraform) for anything shared — reviewable, consistent, regenerable.
  • Kill dashboards nobody opens; a graveyard of stale dashboards is worse than none.

Performance

  • Fewer panels; sane refresh (don't auto-refresh a capacity dashboard every 5s); adaptive rate windows ($__rate_interval).
  • Recording rules for heavy aggregations; collapsed rows lazy-load; shared base queries where the tool supports it.
  • Target: a triage dashboard loads in < 2–3 seconds.
Cheat Sheet
  • One dashboard = one question. Know the audience (triage / debug / capacity / exec) and match density + time range.
  • Layout top-down: header text → SLO/RED summary stats → supporting time series → collapsed deep-dive rows.
  • Correct units; Y-min 0 for rates; name series ({{label}}); topk to bound; SLO threshold lines; percentiles not averages; per-panel descriptions.
  • Annotate deploys/config/incidents; shared time range; template vars (env/region/service) with defaults; data links to logs/traces/next dashboard.
  • House template + dashboards-as-code for shared ones. Delete unused dashboards.
  • Perf: fewer panels, sane refresh, $__rate_interval, recording rules, lazy rows; triage board < 2–3s.
Q&A
What's the single most common dashboard anti-pattern?
The "everything wall" — 50+ panels trying to answer every question at once. It loads slowly, buries the important signals, and nobody can find anything under pressure. Split into a fast health/triage dashboard plus focused drill-down dashboards linked from it.
How should a triage dashboard be laid out?
Top-down by importance: a header explaining ownership and links, then a summary row of SLO/RED stat panels colored by threshold that answers "is it OK?" instantly, then supporting time series broken down by endpoint/dependency, then deep-dive rows collapsed by default. Everything shares the time range; deploys are annotated.
Why set Y-axis minimum to 0 for rate graphs?
If the axis auto-scales to the data's min, small fluctuations look like huge swings and you misjudge severity. Anchoring at 0 shows the true proportion of the change. (For latency, don't force 0 — you want to see the working range clearly.)
Why annotate deployments on dashboards?
So that when a metric moves you can immediately see whether a release, config change, or flag flip happened at the same moment. It turns "something changed at 14:03" into "the 14:03 deploy did this", which is usually the fastest path to root cause.
How do template variables improve a dashboard?
They let one dashboard definition serve the whole fleet: pick env/region/service/instance from dropdowns and every panel re-scopes. Chained variables narrow each other (region → service → instance). This means one reviewed, consistent dashboard instead of hundreds of near-duplicates, and it's the basis for overview→drill-down navigation via data links.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Roughly how many questions should one dashboard answer?
One.
What goes at the very top of a service dashboard?
A summary/SLO row (and a header text panel with ownership + links).
Average latency or latency percentiles on a dashboard?
Percentiles (p50/p95/p99) — the average hides the tail.

Intermediate core

Design the panel list for a per-service triage dashboard.
Header (text): service name, team, on-call, links to runbook, logs, traces, dependencies, and the drill-down dashboards. Summary row (stat panels, threshold-colored): current availability SLI + remaining error budget; request rate; error ratio; p50/p95/p99 latency vs SLO line; saturation headline (in-flight vs limit, or pool usage); count of firing alerts for this service. Traffic & errors row (time series): request rate by route; error ratio by route and by status class; 4xx vs 5xx split. Latency row: p50/p95/p99 over time (success only) with SLO threshold line; latency heatmap; slowest routes table. Dependencies row: error rate and latency of each downstream call (DB, cache, other services, queues); circuit-breaker / retry counts. Saturation row: CPU + run-queue, memory + GC, connection pool in-use/wait/timeouts, thread pool, work-queue depth. Deep-dive rows (collapsed): per-pod resource use, per-pod restarts, JVM/runtime detail, host-level. Context: deploy/config annotations on every time series; template vars for env, region, version; default range 1h, 15s–30s refresh; data links to logs/traces filtered by the current selectors.
A team's dashboard has 45 panels and takes 8 seconds to load. Give the rework plan.
(1) Split by question/audience: a ≤ 8-panel health/triage dashboard (SLO, error rate, p95 latency, traffic, saturation headline, recent deploys, firing alerts) that answers "is it OK?" in 2s; separate drill-down dashboards (endpoints, dependencies, runtime, infra) linked via data links carrying the time range and variables. (2) Collapse + lazy-load any remaining detail rows. (3) Cut query cost: $__rate_interval, correct Max data points, recording rules for the heavy aggregations, raise the min refresh, remove sub-30s auto-refresh, use shared base queries where supported. (4) Standardise units and colours, add a header with owner + runbook. (5) Templating ($service, $env, $region) so it's one dashboard for the fleet, not 45 panels for one service. (6) Re-measure; target < 2–3s. (7) Delete panels nobody references (check with usage analytics if available).

Advanced deep

Design a dashboard system for a 300-service org so an on-call engineer goes from "something's wrong" to a root-cause signal in under a minute. Cover the hierarchy, templating, linking, and maintenance.
Hierarchy (3 tiers): (1) Fleet / triage — one screen: per-service SLO burn-rate table or heatmap (sortable, worst first), global error rate and latency, deploy annotations across the org, a panel of all firing alerts (ALERTS{alertstate="firing"}). Each row links to… (2) Service dashboard — a single templated definition ($service/$env/$region/$version): RED summary vs SLO, dependency health matrix (error+latency of each downstream), saturation, recent deploys/flags, top-erroring endpoints. Data links from every panel to logs (same selectors), traces (Tempo), and… (3) Drill-down dashboards per concern (endpoint detail, each dependency type, runtime/GC, k8s pod, host). Templating: consistent variable names everywhere; chained (env → region → service → instance); SLO thresholds pulled from a per-service config (a recording rule or lookup) so the same panel colours correctly for every service. Linking: exemplars on latency histograms → traces; trace→logs and logs→trace configured; panel data links and cross-source "correlations" so the same jumps work from any panel, always carrying ${__url_time_range} and label values; alert notifications deep-link to the service dashboard at the incident time (dashboardUID/panelId in the alert). Consistency: all service dashboards are generated from one Jsonnet/grafonnet (or Terraform) template — identical layout, so muscle memory works on any of the 300; onboarding a service = it emits the standard labels and appears automatically. Performance: recording rules for every summary metric (burn rate, RED per service) so the fleet dashboard is cheap across 300 services; collapsed lazy-loaded detail; sensible refresh. Maintenance: dashboards-as-code in Git with CI (lint JSON, forbid hard-coded datasource names, validate queries, "does it render" smoke test); shared dashboards are read-only (provisioned), teams get editable personal folders; a scheduled job flags dashboards with zero views for deletion; the golden template is versioned and changes go through review. On-call flow: page deep-links to the service dashboard at the right time → RED + dependency matrix shows which endpoint/dependency is bad → click to its traces/logs → root-cause signal; the fleet dashboard is the fallback for vague pages. Under a minute because the path is always the same and always one or two clicks.
What are the trade-offs of "dashboards as code" vs click-built dashboards, and how do you get the benefits of both?
Click-built: pros — fast to iterate, low barrier, great for exploration and one-off investigations, WYSIWYG, anyone can do it. Cons — drift (everyone's slightly different), no review, no history beyond the tool's version list, hard to apply a fix across 200 similar dashboards, easily lost/edited, "snowflake" dashboards, and they rot silently. As code (Jsonnet/grafonnet, Terraform provider, Grizzly): pros — consistency (one template → N dashboards), code review, Git history and rollback, DRY (fix a panel once, regenerate everywhere), parameterisation, CI validation (schema, queries, no bad datasource refs), reproducible across environments, and it scales to hundreds of services. Cons — higher barrier (you write code, not drag panels), slower iteration loop (edit → render → deploy), verbose (raw dashboard JSON is huge; libraries mitigate), schema migrations on Grafana upgrades create churn, and it can discourage quick experimentation. Getting both: (1) Explore in the UI, promote to code — give people an editable dev folder (or dev Grafana) to build and iterate; when a dashboard is worth keeping, export it, normalise it (strip volatile fields, parameterise datasource), and PR it into the code repo where it becomes provisioned/read-only. (2) Code the shared, click the personal — fleet/service/golden dashboards are code and locked; individual engineers and teams keep click-built dashboards in their own folders for ad-hoc needs, accepting those are disposable. (3) Libraries not raw JSON — grafonnet / a house library of panel and row functions so "as code" is concise and the barrier is low. (4) Library panels for shared components even within click-built dashboards, so a common panel is edited once. (5) Drift detection — a job that diffs live provisioned dashboards against the repo and alerts, so manual edits to golden dashboards are caught. (6) Fast deploy — CI renders and deploys on merge in under a minute so the code loop feels close to the click loop. The rule of thumb: if more than one team relies on it or there's more than one of it, it should be code; if it's your personal scratch view, click away.

Label Cardinality & Cost

Every unique label-value combination is a time series — and series count is what a metrics system pays for.

Notes

What cardinality is

  • A time series is identified by its metric name + the full set of label key/value pairs. http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/x",status="200"} is one series.
  • Cardinality of a metric ≈ the product of the number of distinct values of each of its labels (minus impossible combos). Add a label with 1,000 values and you multiply series count by up to 1,000.
  • A histogram multiplies again by its bucket count.
  • Cost drivers: Prometheus holds an in-memory index and per-series memory for the head block; queries touch every matching series; remote-write and long-term stores charge per series/sample.

Cardinality-explosion offenders (never put these in labels)

  • User ID, account ID, session ID, request ID, trace ID.
  • Full URL / path with IDs (/orders/48213) — use the route template (/orders/:id).
  • Email, IP address, hostname of clients, container ID, pod name hash, git SHA as a per-request label.
  • Timestamps, durations, or any continuous value as a label.
  • Error message text, stack traces, SQL query strings.
  • Unbounded enums that grow over time (feature-flag names, experiment IDs, dynamic tags).

These belong in logs or trace/span attributes, where high cardinality is fine.

Churn — the sneaky one

Even if active cardinality is bounded, rapidly changing label values create many series over time: pods that restart with new names, autoscaling, short-lived jobs, deploy-versioned labels. Prometheus keeps churned series for the staleness/retention window; the index grows; queries over a range see all of them. Fix: relabel ephemeral identifiers away (map to a stable instance), don't label with pod name / start time / version-per-scrape.

Controlling it

  • Governance in a shared client library: fix the allowed label set per metric; make adding a label a code review.
  • Templating: route/path normalisation middleware; collapse status to status_class (2xx/4xx/5xx) unless you truly need per-code.
  • metric_relabel_configs at scrape time: drop offending labels or whole series (action: labeldrop, action: drop).
  • Recording rules that aggregate away high-cardinality dimensions into a small series for dashboards/alerts, then short-retain the raw.
  • Limits: sample_limit / label_limit / target_limit per scrape; per-tenant series limits in Mimir/Cortex; alert on per-job series count growth.
  • Downsampling & retention tiers: raw high-res short; rollups long (Thanos/Mimir/VictoriaMetrics).
  • Native/exponential histograms to cut bucket-driven cardinality.

Finding the problem

topk(10, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"}))        # biggest metrics by series
count(count by (label_you_suspect) (some_metric))      # cardinality of one label
prometheus_tsdb_head_series                            # total head series (trend it!)
sum(scrape_samples_scraped) by (job)                   # samples per job
# Prometheus UI: Status -> TSDB Status -> top label value pairs
Cheat Sheet
  • 1 series = metric name + full label set. Metric cardinality ≈ product of per-label distinct values (× buckets for histograms).
  • Never label with: user/session/request/trace ID, raw URL with IDs, email/IP, pod-name-hash/container ID, error text, SQL, timestamps, durations, unbounded enums. → logs / span attributes instead.
  • Churn: changing label values (pod restarts, autoscale, per-deploy labels) pile up series over the retention window even if active count is low. Relabel ephemeral IDs to a stable instance.
  • Control: shared client lib fixes label sets; template routes; status_class not raw code; metric_relabel_configs to drop; recording rules to aggregate + short-retain raw; sample_limit/series limits; downsampling tiers; native histograms.
  • Find it: topk(10, count by (__name__)(...)), count(count by (label)(metric)), prometheus_tsdb_head_series (trend), TSDB Status page.
Q&A
What determines a metric's cardinality?
Roughly the number of distinct combinations of its label values that actually occur — close to the product of each label's distinct-value count. For a histogram, multiply by the number of buckets. Each combination is a separate stored time series.
Why is putting user_id in a label catastrophic?
It's unbounded and grows with your user base, so the metric's series count becomes proportional to the number of users (times every other label). Prometheus's in-memory index and per-series overhead blow up, ingestion and queries slow or OOM, and long-term storage costs soar. User-level data belongs in logs or span attributes.
What is series churn and why does it matter even with low active cardinality?
Churn is the rate at which label-value sets change — e.g. pods restarting with new names, autoscaling, per-deploy version labels. Each new set is a new series that Prometheus retains for the staleness/retention window, so the total series count and index size grow even though only a few are active at once, and range queries must consider all of them.
How do you keep per-code HTTP status from inflating cardinality?
Use a status_class label with a handful of values (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx) instead of the raw code, unless you have a specific need for per-code data (then keep it only on the endpoints that need it). Similarly, template the route so paths with IDs collapse to /orders/:id.
Name two mechanisms to cap cardinality at ingestion.
metric_relabel_configs in the scrape config (drop labels with labeldrop, or drop whole series with action: drop on a regex), and per-scrape sample_limit / label_limit / target_limit (or per-tenant series limits in Mimir/Cortex) so a misbehaving target is rejected rather than allowed to overwhelm the server.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What is one time series identified by?
The metric name plus its complete set of label key/value pairs.
Should a full URL path with an order ID be a metric label?
No — use the route template (/orders/:id).
Where should a request ID go instead of a metric label?
In logs and/or as a trace/span attribute.

Intermediate core

Prometheus is OOMing. Walk through how you'd find and fix the cardinality problem.
(1) Confirm it's cardinality: trend prometheus_tsdb_head_series and process_resident_memory_bytes; a steady climb = growth, a step = a new bad target/metric. (2) Find the biggest metrics: topk(20, count by (__name__)({__name__=~".+"})), and the Prometheus Status → TSDB Status page (top metrics, top label-value pairs, label names with most values). (3) Find the bad label: for the top metric, count(count by (suspect_label)(metric)) for each label — the one with thousands+ values is the culprit; also check for churn by comparing series count over a range vs instantaneously. (4) Fix at the source if possible: remove the label from instrumentation, template the route, collapse status codes, stop labelling with pod name / start time / version. (5) Fix at scrape as a stopgap: metric_relabel_configs with labeldrop on the offending label or action: drop on the metric; set sample_limit so the target can't do it again. (6) Aggregate: recording rule that sums away the high-card dimension for the series dashboards/alerts need; short-retain the raw. (7) Prevent recurrence: per-job series-count alert, label governance in the client library, and a review gate for new labels. (8) If it's genuinely needed data, move to a system built for it (Mimir with per-tenant limits, or push it to logs/traces).
A histogram metric has 15 buckets and labels service (20), route (50), method (4), status (30 codes). Estimate the series and propose cuts.
Series ≈ buckets × product of label cardinalities = 15 × 20 × 50 × 4 × 30 = 1,800,000 series for this one metric (plus _sum and _count: × ~1.13 → ~2.03M). That's huge. Cuts: (1) status → status_class: 30 → 4, dividing by 7.5 → ~240k. (2) Trim buckets to the ~8 that bracket the SLO: 15 → 8, ×0.53 → ~128k. (3) Do you need per-route latency for all 50 routes? Often only ~10 matter for SLOs; keep the full histogram for those and a coarse one elsewhere, or drop route from the histogram and keep it only on the request counter → another big cut. (4) method: usually keep (only 4). (5) Consider a native/exponential histogram, which collapses the bucket dimension to a compact sparse structure — often 5–10× fewer series and better tail resolution, removing the bucket-count multiplier entirely. Combined (status_class + native histogram + route only on the SLO endpoints): from ~2M down to tens of thousands, with equal or better SLO visibility via a recording rule.

Advanced deep

Design a cardinality governance program for a 100-team org so metrics cost stays bounded without killing useful observability.
Standards & libraries: publish a metrics style guide (naming, units, the "never label with" list, route templating, status_class) and ship a shared instrumentation library per language that enforces it — fixed label sets per metric type, automatic route normalisation middleware, no API to add arbitrary labels at call sites without declaring them. Adding a label to a shared metric is a code review with a cardinality estimate. Budgets & chargeback: each team gets an active-series budget (and remote-write/long-term sample budget) with cost attribution (by team/namespace label). A dashboard shows usage vs budget per team, trended; alerts at 80% and on sudden growth (deriv(series_count[1h])). Exceeding budget triggers a conversation, not an outage. Guardrails in the pipeline: per-scrape sample_limit, label_limit, label_value_length_limit, target_limit; in Mimir/Cortex, per-tenant max_global_series_per_user and max_label_names_per_series, so a runaway is rejected at ingest with a clear error rather than degrading everyone. A shared metric_relabel_configs layer that drops known-bad labels org-wide as a backstop. Detection & review: a weekly automated report of top metrics by series, fastest-growing metrics, highest-cardinality labels, and biggest churn contributors, routed to the owning team. New metrics flagged for review. CI check on instrumentation PRs that estimates cardinality from the declared label sets and fails if over a threshold without sign-off. Aggregation tiers: encourage/require recording rules that produce the low-cardinality series dashboards and alerts actually use, with the raw high-cardinality metric on short retention (e.g. 3–7 days) and rollups long. Provide templates for common ones (RED per service). Escape hatches: when a team genuinely needs high-cardinality analysis (per-customer, per-experiment), route them to the right tool — logs/wide-events/traces or a purpose-built high-card store — not the metrics system. Education: onboarding covers the model ("a label is a multiplier"), and office hours for instrumentation design. Enforcement ladder: report → nudge the team → auto-relabel-drop the offending label → ingest limit. The goal is that the default path (use the library, follow the guide) is cheap, high-cardinality needs are consciously chosen and go elsewhere, and cost is visible and owned.
Explain how high cardinality actually degrades a Prometheus/TSDB server: memory, ingestion, query, and compaction. Where are the cliffs?
Memory: Prometheus keeps an inverted index (label name/value → series IDs) and the head block (the most recent ~2h of samples) largely in RAM, plus per-series metadata (label sets, chunk references). Each active series costs on the order of a few KB resident. Millions of series → multi-GB just for the head and index, before samples. The index also holds every historical label value seen in the retention window, so churn inflates it even past active count. Cliff: when resident memory approaches the host limit, the OOM killer takes Prometheus; there's no graceful shedding by default (limits help). Ingestion: every scrape must, per sample, look up or create the series in the index (a write path with locking), append to the head chunk, and update the WAL. More series = more index operations per scrape cycle and a bigger WAL to replay on restart (slow startup — a real operational cliff: a restart of a high-card Prometheus can take many minutes to become ready). sample_limit rejects a target's whole scrape if it exceeds the cap, protecting the server. Query: a PromQL selector resolves to a set of series via the index, then reads chunks for each. Cost scales with matched series × time range. A query like sum(rate(metric[5m])) over a metric with 1M series must touch 1M series' chunks even though the result is one line — slow, memory-hungry (can OOM the query, or hit max_samples), and it evicts useful chunks from the page cache. Range queries over churned series are worse. Cliff: dashboards/alerts start timing out; the query engine's memory guard aborts queries; alert evaluation lags, delaying pages. Compaction: every ~2h the head block is written to a persistent block; periodically blocks are merged (compaction) and stale series are dropped after retention. High series counts make blocks bigger, compaction longer and more I/O- and memory-intensive, and index files on disk larger (mmap'd, competing for page cache). Compaction stalls can back up the head block, raising memory further — a feedback loop. Downstream: remote_write queues and long-term stores (Mimir/Thanos/Cortex/VM) charge and shard by series; a cardinality spike can saturate the remote-write queue (dropped samples), blow per-tenant limits, or balloon object-storage cost and compactor load. Summary of cliffs: (1) head+index memory → OOM; (2) WAL size → multi-minute restart / not-ready; (3) query fan-out → dashboard/alert timeouts and query OOM; (4) compaction time/I/O → head backup → more memory. The defenses are all about bounding series: relabel/drop at ingest, limits, recording-rule aggregation with short raw retention, sharding by tenant, and killing the label at the source.

Pull vs Push, Scraping & Agents

How measurements get from a process into a monitoring backend — and why Prometheus pulls.

Notes

Pull vs push

Pull (Prometheus scrape)Push (StatsD, OTLP push, remote_write)
Who initiatesThe monitoring server calls each target's /metrics on an intervalThe app/agent sends metrics to the backend
Target livenessFree — a failed scrape = up == 0Must infer from absence / heartbeats
DiscoveryServer needs service discovery to know targetsTargets need to know the endpoint
Short-lived jobsHard — may finish before a scrape → PushgatewayNatural
NetworkServer → targets (firewall/NAT can block)Targets → server (easier outbound)
Cardinality controlServer enforces limits at scrapeClient controls what it sends

Prometheus chose pull mainly for the free liveness signal, simple local testing (curl the endpoint), and the server controlling scrape rate and limits.

Exporters

  • An exporter translates some system's stats into Prometheus format on /metrics: node_exporter (host), cAdvisor/kubelet (containers), blackbox_exporter (probe HTTP/TCP/ICMP/DNS from outside), *_exporter for databases, queues, hardware, cloud APIs.
  • Direct instrumentation (client library in the app) is preferred where you own the code; exporters bridge things you don't.

Service discovery & relabeling

  • SD backends: Kubernetes, EC2/GCE/Azure, Consul, DNS, file_sd, HTTP SD. Prometheus continuously refreshes the target list.
  • relabel_configs (before scrape): filter which targets to keep (keep/drop on SD meta labels), set the __address__, job, instance, and attach labels (namespace, team) from SD metadata.
  • metric_relabel_configs (after scrape, before ingest): drop noisy metrics/labels, rename, cut cardinality.

Pushgateway — use sparingly

  • For service-level batch jobs that exit before they can be scraped: the job pushes its final metrics to the Pushgateway, which Prometheus scrapes.
  • Caveats: it's a single point, metrics persist until overwritten/deleted (a dead job's last values linger — use push --delete or grouping), and it breaks up semantics. Not for per-instance or high-frequency pushing.

Agents & the OpenTelemetry Collector

  • Prometheus Agent mode / Grafana Alloy / vmagent / OTel Collector: a local process that scrapes (or receives) and remote_writes to a central store (Mimir/Thanos/Cortex/VictoriaMetrics/vendor). No local querying; just collect & forward.
  • OTel Collector pipeline: receivers (OTLP, Prometheus scrape, statsd, host metrics) → processors (batch, memory_limiter, attributes, filter, tail-sampling for traces, transform) → exporters (Prometheus remote write, OTLP, vendor). One agent for metrics, logs, and traces.
  • remote_write: durable queue with retries, sharding, and backpressure; used for HA, long-term storage, and multi-tenant fan-in.

Scrape hygiene

  • Pick a sane scrape_interval (15–60s); keep it consistent (rate windows depend on it).
  • scrape_timeout < interval; watch scrape_duration_seconds and scrape_samples_scraped.
  • Every scrape yields up, scrape_duration_seconds, scrape_samples_* — alert on up == 0 and on sample-limit hits.
  • Staleness: if a series disappears from a scrape, Prometheus marks it stale after ~5 min so rate() and instant queries behave.
Cheat Sheet
  • Pull (Prometheus): server scrapes /metrics on an interval → free liveness (up), server controls rate/limits, needs service discovery. Push: app/agent sends → natural for short-lived jobs and outbound-only networks.
  • Exporters translate external systems to Prometheus format (node_exporter, cAdvisor, blackbox_exporter, DB/queue exporters). Prefer direct instrumentation for your own code.
  • relabel_configs: pre-scrape — choose targets, set job/instance/labels from SD meta. metric_relabel_configs: post-scrape — drop metrics/labels, cut cardinality.
  • Pushgateway: only for service-level batch jobs that exit before a scrape; values linger, breaks up, single point — use sparingly.
  • Agents (Prometheus Agent, Grafana Alloy, vmagent, OTel Collector): scrape/receive → remote_write to central store; no local queries. OTel Collector: receivers → processors → exporters, one pipeline for metrics/logs/traces.
  • Consistent scrape_interval; scrape_timeout < interval; alert on up == 0; staleness marks vanished series after ~5m.
Q&A
Why does Prometheus pull instead of push?
Pulling gives a free target-liveness signal (a failed scrape sets up == 0), lets the server control scrape frequency and enforce limits centrally, makes targets trivially testable (just curl /metrics), and avoids every target needing to know and reach the backend. The cost is needing service discovery and special handling for short-lived jobs.
What is an exporter?
A small process that exposes a /metrics endpoint translating some system's internal stats into Prometheus format — node_exporter for host metrics, cAdvisor for containers, database/queue exporters, blackbox_exporter for external probes. It's the bridge for systems you can't instrument directly.
Difference between relabel_configs and metric_relabel_configs?
relabel_configs runs before a target is scraped — it decides which discovered targets to keep and sets their labels (job, instance, and metadata like namespace/team). metric_relabel_configs runs after the scrape, on each sample — used to drop noisy metrics or labels and control cardinality before ingestion.
When should you use the Pushgateway, and what are the pitfalls?
Only for service-level batch/cron jobs that finish before Prometheus could scrape them — the job pushes its final metrics and Prometheus scrapes the gateway. Pitfalls: pushed values persist until overwritten or deleted (a failed job's last-known values linger and look current), it's a single point of failure, and it doesn't give you up/liveness for the job. Don't use it as a general push endpoint.
What does the OpenTelemetry Collector do?
It's a vendor-neutral agent/gateway with a pipeline of receivers (OTLP, Prometheus scrape, host metrics, statsd…), processors (batching, memory limiting, attribute editing, filtering, tail sampling), and exporters (Prometheus remote write, OTLP, vendors). One deployment handles metrics, logs, and traces, decoupling your apps from any specific backend.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What metric tells you a scrape target is up?
up (1 = last scrape succeeded, 0 = failed).
Which relabel stage controls cardinality after scraping?
metric_relabel_configs.
What's the Pushgateway for?
Service-level batch/cron jobs that exit before Prometheus can scrape them.

Intermediate core

Your apps run in a private network Prometheus can't reach; you also want long-term storage and HA. Design the collection path.
Run a lightweight agent inside the private network — Prometheus in agent mode, Grafana Alloy, vmagent, or an OTel Collector — that scrapes the local targets (it can reach them) and remote_writes outbound to a central store. Outbound HTTPS is usually allowed even when inbound isn't, solving the reachability problem without exposing /metrics publicly. For long-term storage, the central store is Mimir / Cortex / Thanos / VictoriaMetrics / a vendor — the agent just forwards; queries, rules, and retention live centrally. For HA, run two agents per network scraping the same targets, both remote-writing (the central store dedupes / accepts both, and you can use external_labels + the store's HA-dedup, e.g. Mimir's __replica__ handling). remote_write's queue gives retries and backpressure across a flaky link. Keep up/liveness meaningful by also remote-writing the agent's own up and scrape_* series and alerting centrally on them, plus a heartbeat/dead-man's-switch so a dead agent is noticed.
You need to monitor a fleet of cron jobs. Compare Pushgateway, the "textfile collector", and a job-status metric approach.
Pushgateway: each job, on completion, pushes metrics (last run time, duration, records processed, exit status) to the gateway under a grouping key (job name + instance); Prometheus scrapes the gateway. Pros: works for jobs with no persistent host, captures the final values. Cons: values persist forever until overwritten/deleted (a job that stops running silently keeps reporting its last success — you must alert on time() - job_last_success_timestamp > threshold, not on absence), single point, no up. Good for ephemeral/containerised jobs. node_exporter textfile collector: the job writes a .prom file to a directory that node_exporter on the host exposes alongside host metrics. Pros: no extra component, natural up via the host's node_exporter, atomic file replace. Cons: needs a persistent host with node_exporter (not for pure-container jobs), stale file = stale metrics (again alert on last-success age), file management. Good for cron on VMs. Job-status metric via a wrapper / batch-aware system: a Kubernetes CronJob + kube-state-metrics exposes kube_job_status_succeeded/failed, start/completion times, and you alert on failed jobs or missed schedules directly; or a wrapper script emits a structured event to your events/logs pipeline. Pros: designed for the lifecycle, gives missed-schedule detection, no lingering-value problem. Cons: depends on the orchestrator; less custom detail unless you also emit job-specific metrics (which then still need Pushgateway/textfile). Recommendation: on k8s, lean on CronJob + kube-state-metrics for schedule/success/failure, and add Pushgateway (with --delete on success or grouping) only for custom business metrics from the job. On VMs, textfile collector. In all cases the key alert is "no successful run within the expected interval" (age of last success), because batch failures manifest as silence.

Advanced deep

Design metrics collection for a 5,000-node Kubernetes estate across 8 clusters with central long-term storage, HA, and per-team multi-tenancy.
Per-cluster collection: in each cluster run collectors in agent mode (Prometheus Agent, Grafana Alloy, or OTel Collector) — not full Prometheus — deployed as a sharded set (e.g. via the Prometheus Operator's sharding, or Alloy clustering) so no single agent scrapes 5,000 nodes' worth of targets; each shard owns a hash slice of targets. Scrape: node_exporter (DaemonSet), kubelet/cAdvisor, kube-state-metrics, the API server, CoreDNS, ingress, and app /metrics via ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor discovery. Apply relabel_configs to attach cluster, region, team/tenant (from namespace labels), and metric_relabel_configs to drop known-noisy series and enforce cardinality at the edge. HA: 2 replicas per shard, both remote-writing, with external_labels including a __replica__ so the central store dedupes (Mimir/Cortex HA tracker) — you get no gaps if one replica dies, no doubles in queries. Central store: a horizontally-scalable multi-tenant TSDB — Grafana Mimir (or Cortex / Thanos receive / VictoriaMetrics cluster) — behind a gateway that maps each agent's tenant (from an auth token / header) to an X-Scope-OrgID. Object storage (S3/GCS) for long-term blocks; a compactor for downsampling (5m and 1h rollups) and retention tiers (raw 15d, 5m 13mo, 1h 3y). Multi-tenancy: one tenant per team (or per cluster-team), with per-tenant limits (max global series, ingestion rate, query concurrency, max samples per query) so one team can't starve others; per-tenant retention overrides; usage/chargeback dashboards. Agents route each namespace's metrics to the owning team's tenant via relabeling the tenant header. Query & rules: central query frontend (with results caching and query sharding) behind Grafana; the ruler component runs recording rules (RED per service, SLO burn) and alerting rules per tenant, sharded — agents don't evaluate rules. Recording rules keep dashboard/alert queries cheap despite the fleet size. Alerting: central Alertmanager (HA pair/cluster) with per-team routing; a dead-man's-switch heartbeat per cluster so a whole cluster's collection going dark is detected. Meta-monitoring: monitor the agents themselves (remote_write queue length, dropped samples, shard balance, scrape_duration, up), the ingesters, and the compactor lag — ideally from a small independent Prometheus so the monitoring of the monitoring doesn't share fate. Cardinality governance: per-tenant series budgets + alerts on growth, edge relabel drops, and the shared-client-library standards. Rollout: everything via the Prometheus Operator / Helm / GitOps so 8 clusters are identical and adding cluster #9 is a config change.
Explain remote_write end to end: batching, sharding, the WAL, retries/backpressure, ordering, and the failure modes you must monitor.
Path: as samples are appended to the local TSDB (or agent-mode WAL), a remote_write component tails the WAL (write-ahead log) — it reads newly-written series and samples from WAL segments. This decouples scraping from sending: the scrape just writes locally; remote_write catches up from the WAL. Sharding: samples are distributed across N in-memory shards (queues), hashed by series, each shard with its own sender goroutine. The number of shards auto-scales between min_shards and max_shards based on the backlog (samples pending in the WAL vs sent) and throughput — if it's falling behind, add shards; if caught up, reduce. Batching: each shard accumulates up to max_samples_per_send (or flushes after batch_send_deadline), Snappy-compresses a protobuf WriteRequest, and POSTs it to the endpoint. Retries/backpressure: on 5xx or network error the batch is retried with backoff (min_backoff..max_backoff); on 429 it also backs off. If the endpoint stays slow/down, shard queues fill and the component stops reading new WAL as fast — the WAL grows on disk (bounded by local retention; if the outage outlasts WAL retention, samples are lost, oldest first). It does not block scraping (scrapes still write locally) until disk fills. Ordering: within a series, samples are sent in timestamp order; the receiver (Mimir/Cortex/Thanos receive) generally requires monotonically increasing timestamps per series and rejects out-of-order (there is now optional out-of-order ingestion support with a window). Across series there's no ordering guarantee. Exactly-once isn't guaranteed — a retry after a partial success can resend a batch; receivers dedupe by (series, timestamp) so it's idempotent in practice. HA dedup: two Prometheis with external_labels: {__replica__: a|b, cluster: x} both send; the receiver's HA tracker picks one replica as leader per (cluster) and drops the other's samples, failing over if the leader goes quiet. Failure modes to monitor: prometheus_remote_storage_samples_pending / _samples_in_total vs _samples_out_total (growing backlog = falling behind); prometheus_remote_storage_shards vs _shards_max (pinned at max = under-provisioned or endpoint slow); prometheus_remote_storage_samples_failed_total and _retried_total (endpoint errors); prometheus_remote_storage_samples_dropped_total and prometheus_remote_storage_exemplars_dropped_total (data loss — page on this); prometheus_wal_watcher_current_segment vs the WAL's newest segment (watcher lag); local disk usage (WAL growth during an outage); prometheus_remote_storage_highest_timestamp_in_seconds minus prometheus_remote_storage_queue_highest_sent_timestamp_seconds (send latency / lag in seconds — the most human-readable "how far behind are we"); and receiver-side 4xx (bad data, out-of-order, limit exceeded) vs 5xx (receiver unhealthy). Tuning levers: max_shards, max_samples_per_send, capacity (per-shard queue), batch_send_deadline, WAL retention (headroom for outages), and receiver-side ingestion limits. The key operational alert is "remote_write lag > X minutes" or "dropped samples > 0", because that's where you silently lose data.

Distributed Tracing

Follow one request as a tree of timed spans across every service it touches.

Notes

The model

  • A trace = all the work done for one logical request, identified by a trace_id.
  • A span = one unit of work (an HTTP handler, a DB query, a function): span_id, parent_span_id, name, start/end time, status, plus attributes (key/values), events (timestamped logs on the span), and links (to related spans in other traces).
  • Spans form a tree (or DAG with links); the root span is the entry point. A waterfall view shows each span's start offset and duration.
  • Span kind: server, client, producer, consumer, internal — tells the UI how to connect them.

Context propagation

  • The trace_id + current span_id + trace flags travel with the request across process boundaries in headers: W3C traceparent/tracestate (the standard), or legacy B3.
  • Each service extracts the incoming context, starts a child span, injects the context into outbound calls (HTTP, gRPC, and message queues via message headers/attributes).
  • Instrumentation: auto (agents/SDK hooks for common frameworks and clients) + manual spans for business-meaningful operations. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for APIs, SDKs, and the wire format (OTLP).
  • A gap in propagation = a broken trace (orphan spans, a new trace starting mid-request).

Sampling

Head-basedTail-based
Decision whenAt the root, before the request runs (e.g. keep 1%)After the whole trace completes, at a collector
Can select on outcome?No — doesn't know yet if it'll error / be slowYes — keep all errors, all slow traces, sample the rest
CostCheap, stateless, consistent if propagatedCollector must buffer all spans of a trace; memory + complexity
ConsistencyPropagate the decision so all services agreeCentral, so naturally consistent

Common: low head sampling as a floor + tail sampling to always keep errors and outliers. Keep trace_id in logs so you can find a trace even when the request wasn't sampled (then only its logs exist).

What tracing answers

  • Where did the latency go? Which span dominates; serial vs parallel calls; N+1 query patterns; retries; queue wait time.
  • Which hop failed? The erroring span and its status/attributes, plus its events (exception stack).
  • Service dependency map — derived from span parent/child + kind across many traces.
  • RED metrics from spans ("span metrics" / metrics generated by the collector) — rate/error/duration per service+operation without separate instrumentation.

Correlation

  • Exemplars: a latency histogram bucket carries an example trace_id → click a spike on a graph, open a slow trace.
  • Trace ↔ logs: logs include trace_id/span_id; span → its logs, log line → its trace.
  • Trace → profiles: link a span to a CPU profile of that time window.

Pitfalls

  • Missing propagation through async/queues, thread pools, batching — the common cause of broken traces.
  • Too many tiny spans (overhead, noise) vs too few (no detail). Span the meaningful boundaries.
  • High-cardinality attributes are fine on spans, but don't turn them into metric labels downstream.
  • Clock skew between hosts makes child spans appear to start before their parent — UIs clamp; keep NTP tight.
  • Sampling math: if you compute rates from sampled traces, weight by the sampling rate.
Cheat Sheet
  • Trace (one trace_id) = tree of spans (span_id + parent_span_id, name, start/dur, status, attributes, events, links). Root = entry point; waterfall = timeline view.
  • Span kind: server / client / producer / consumer / internal.
  • Context propagation via W3C traceparent/tracestate headers (or B3); extract → child span → inject into outbound calls incl. queue messages. OpenTelemetry + OTLP is the standard.
  • Head sampling: decide at root before outcome known (cheap, propagate the decision). Tail sampling: decide at collector after trace completes — keep all errors + slow, sample the rest (needs buffering).
  • Answers: where latency went, which hop failed, dependency map, RED-from-spans (span metrics).
  • Correlate: exemplars (graph → trace), trace_id in logs (trace ↔ logs), trace → profile.
  • Pitfalls: broken propagation through async/queues/threadpools; span granularity; clock skew; weight rates by sample rate.
Q&A
What's the difference between a trace and a span?
A trace is the whole request — everything done to serve one logical operation, tied together by a trace_id. A span is one timed step within it (a handler, a DB call), with its own ID, a parent pointer, timing, status, and attributes. Spans form a tree; the trace is the tree.
How does trace context move between services?
Via propagation headers — the W3C traceparent (and tracestate) header carries the trace ID, the caller's span ID, and sampling flags. Each service reads the incoming header, creates a child span, and writes the header onto its outbound requests (including onto message-queue records for async work).
Head-based vs tail-based sampling?
Head-based decides whether to keep a trace at the very start, before the request runs, so it can't preferentially keep errors or slow traces — but it's cheap and stateless. Tail-based decides at a collector after all the trace's spans arrive, so it can keep 100% of errors and slow outliers and sample the boring ones — at the cost of buffering every trace's spans in memory until it decides.
What are exemplars and how do they help?
Exemplars attach an example trace_id (and its value) to a histogram bucket sample. On a latency graph, a spike's data point links directly to a trace that experienced that latency — one click from "p99 jumped" to "here's a slow request's full breakdown".
Why do child spans sometimes appear to start before their parent?
Clock skew — the child's host clock is slightly ahead of the parent's. Timestamps come from each host independently, so a few milliseconds of NTP drift can invert the apparent order. Trace UIs usually clamp children within the parent's bounds; keeping NTP tight minimises it.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What identifies all the spans belonging to one request?
A shared trace_id.
Which HTTP header is the W3C standard for trace context?
traceparent (with tracestate for vendor data).
Which sampling type can guarantee you keep every error trace?
Tail-based sampling.

Intermediate core

A trace for a slow request shows the root span at 900 ms but the child spans only sum to 200 ms. What does that tell you and what next?
700 ms of the root span is unaccounted — time spent in the entry service that isn't inside any child span. Possible causes: (1) work not instrumented (JSON serialisation, business logic, in-process computation, template rendering) — add manual spans around the suspect code sections. (2) Waiting on something not spanned: acquiring a connection from a pool, a mutex/lock, thread-pool queue time before the handler ran, GC pauses — instrument pool checkout and add runtime/GC metrics; check if the gap is at the very start (queueing/admission) or middle (lock) or end (response write / slow client). (3) A downstream call whose client isn't instrumented, so its span is missing entirely — check outbound calls and library instrumentation coverage. (4) Blocking on a synchronous call to an external system without a client span. Next steps: add spans/events at the boundaries of the unaccounted region, look at CPU profile for that window (trace→profile link), check GC and pool-wait metrics for the pod at that timestamp, and compare to a fast trace to localise where the gap opens.
Requests that go through your message queue produce two disconnected traces instead of one. Why, and how do you fix it?
Context isn't propagated across the queue. The producer finishes its trace when it publishes; the consumer starts a brand-new trace when it picks the message up, because the traceparent wasn't carried on the message. Fix: on publish, inject the current trace context into the message's headers/attributes (most brokers support per-message headers; OTel messaging instrumentation does this automatically for supported clients). On consume, extract that context and start the processing span as a child (span kind consumer, with a link to the producer span if the relationship is fan-out/batch rather than 1:1). For batch consumers that pull many messages at once, use span links (one processing span linking to N producer spans) rather than forcing a single parent. Also propagate through any intermediate thread pool / executor inside the consumer (context must be captured and restored around the async hand-off), which is the other common break point. After this, the producer→queue→consumer path shows as one trace (or linked traces) with the queue wait time visible as the gap between publish and receive.

Advanced deep

Design a tracing setup for a 100-service platform at 500k req/s on a budget: instrumentation, sampling, collection, storage, and how you keep it useful.
Instrumentation: OpenTelemetry everywhere — auto-instrumentation (SDK/agent) for HTTP/gRPC servers & clients, DB drivers, queue clients, caches; plus a thin house wrapper that adds standard resource attributes (service.name, service.version, deployment.environment, k8s.*) and a few manual spans around business-critical operations. W3C propagation; ensure context flows through thread pools, async runtimes, and message headers (the usual break points) — CI check that a canary request stays one trace end to end. Sampling: two-stage. (1) Head sampling at the root at a low floor (e.g. 1–5%), decision propagated so all services agree — this bounds the span volume every service emits. (2) Tail sampling at a layer of OTel Collectors (the "gateway" tier): buffer spans by trace for a few seconds, then keep 100% of traces with an error span, 100% over a latency threshold (per-service p99-ish), a small % of the rest, and boost specific services/routes during incidents via config. Use consistent-probability sampling so rate math is recoverable (weight by 1/p). Keep trace_id in every log line so unsampled requests are still debuggable via logs. Collection: agent Collector as a DaemonSet/sidecar (receives OTLP from local pods, batches, adds k8s attributes, memory_limiter) → gateway Collector deployment (does tail sampling, which needs all of a trace's spans on one instance, so route by trace_id hash with the loadbalancing exporter) → storage. This tier also generates span metrics (RED per service/operation) and a service graph, so you get dashboards/alerts without extra instrumentation. Storage: a trace backend built for it — Grafana Tempo (object storage, cheap, trace-ID lookup + TraceQL), or Jaeger with a scalable backend, or a vendor. Retention short (7–14 days — traces age out of usefulness fast); object storage keeps cost low; index only what you query by (trace_id, service, duration, a few attributes) — Tempo's model of "cheap storage, search via metrics/logs then jump by trace_id" fits a budget. Keeping it useful: wire correlation — exemplars on latency histograms → traces; trace↔logs via trace_id; trace→profiles. Standard per-service dashboard includes a "slow traces" and "error traces" panel (from tail-sampled data). Alert on span-metric RED, not raw traces. Watch the collectors themselves (queue length, refused spans, sampling decisions, memory). Govern span attributes (no PII, bounded keys). Document the sampling policy so people know "your request may not have a trace, but it has logs with the trace_id". Net: low head floor keeps emission cheap; tail sampling keeps the interesting traces; span metrics give always-on RED; cheap object storage + short retention keeps the bill bounded; correlation makes the kept traces findable.
Tail-based sampling sounds strictly better than head-based. Explain its real operational costs and failure modes, and when head sampling is still the right choice.
How tail sampling works: a collector must hold all spans of a trace in memory until the trace is "complete" (a timeout after the last span, since there's no explicit end signal), then run policies (error, latency, rate, attribute-match, composite) to decide keep/drop. Costs / failure modes: (1) Memory — proportional to (traces in flight) × (spans per trace) × (span size) over the decision window; a latency spike or a slow downstream means traces stay open longer → buffer grows exactly when you're busiest; OOM drops traces silently. You must cap with num_traces/memory limits, which then drop traces under load — losing data when you most want it. (2) Span routing constraint — all spans of a trace must reach the same collector instance for the decision, so you need a load-balancing exporter that hashes by trace_id in front of the tail-sampling tier. That tier can't autoscale freely (rebalancing splits traces across instances → partial traces → wrong decisions); scaling events cause transient data loss/misdecisions. (3) Late spans — a span arriving after the decision window (slow service, retry, long-running job, clock issues) is dropped or creates an orphan; long traces (streaming, batch, websockets) don't fit the model well. (4) Latency to storage — traces are delayed by the decision window (seconds), so "live" trace search lags. (5) Complexity & cost — a stateful, carefully-sized tier to run and monitor (its own queue/refused/decision metrics), plus the compute to evaluate policies on every trace. (6) Consistency across a fleet — if some traces cross regions/clusters with separate collector pools, no single instance sees the whole trace; you either accept per-segment decisions or ship all spans to one global tier (bandwidth). (7) Rate math — non-probabilistic keep rules make "how many requests errored" from trace data non-trivial; you still need span-metrics for accurate RED. When head sampling is right: (a) very high volume where the tail-sampling buffer/compute cost is prohibitive — a low head rate is stateless and cheap and scales linearly. (b) When you primarily use traces for aggregate latency analysis / dependency mapping rather than catching individual rare errors (span-metrics + exemplars cover the "find a slow one" case). (c) Multi-region/multi-cluster where assembling whole traces centrally is too expensive. (d) Simplicity/reliability priorities — head sampling has no stateful tier to fail. (e) When errors are already well-covered by logs (with trace_id) and metrics, so you don't strictly need every error trace. Common pragmatic answer: both — a low head-sampling floor for baseline coverage and cheap scaling, plus a modest tail-sampling tier tuned to keep errors and slow outliers, sized and capped so that under extreme load it degrades to roughly head-sampling behaviour rather than falling over.

Incidents, Postmortems & Alert Fatigue

Respond in a structured way, learn without blame, and keep the pager survivable.

Notes

Incident response structure

  • Severity levels (SEV1–4 / P1–P4): defined by user impact and scope, not by how stressed anyone is. SEV1 = major outage / data loss / security; lower sevs = degraded / partial / single-tenant.
  • Roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, decides, doesn't fix), Ops/Responders (investigate & mitigate), Communications (stakeholders, status page), Scribe (timeline). One person can wear several hats on a small incident; separate them as it grows.
  • Mitigate before diagnose: stop the bleeding (roll back, fail over, disable the feature, scale, shed load) first; root cause can wait.
  • Comms cadence: regular updates even if "still investigating"; internal channel + external status page; declare start and all-clear explicitly.
  • Standard tooling: a declared incident opens a channel/bridge, a doc/timeline, and a tracking ticket automatically.

Key metrics

MetricMeaning
MTTDMean time to detect — incident start → someone/something notices. Improved by better symptom alerting & synthetics.
MTTAMean time to acknowledge — alert → a human owns it. Improved by routing/escalation.
MTTRMean time to recover/repair/resolve/mitigate (define which!). Improved by runbooks, safe rollbacks, practice.
MTBFMean time between failures — reliability of the system over time.

Time to mitigate (user impact ends) usually matters more than time to full resolution.

Blameless postmortems

  • Blameless: assume everyone acted reasonably with the information and tools they had. Ask "how did the system/process allow this?", not "who broke it". People must be safe to be honest, or you lose the facts.
  • Contents: summary & impact (users, duration, $ / SLO budget), a factual timeline (detection, key decisions, mitigation, resolution), root cause(s) and contributing factors, what went well / poorly / got lucky, and action items (each with an owner, a due date, and a priority; tracked to done).
  • Not just "the" root cause: complex failures have multiple contributing factors (a latent bug + a config change + a missing alert + a slow rollback). Use techniques like the 5 Whys carefully (it can tunnel on one chain) or a contributing-factors / causal-tree analysis.
  • Trigger criteria: every SEV1/2, any customer-visible outage, any near-miss worth learning from — agreed in advance, not discretionary after the fact.
  • Action items should reduce likelihood (fix the bug, add a guardrail), impact (graceful degradation, faster rollback), or detection (add the missing alert). Avoid "be more careful" items.

Alert fatigue

  • Definition: so many low-value alerts that responders desensitise, delay, or ignore — and then miss the real one. It's a reliability risk, not just a morale issue.
  • Signals: high pages/shift, low actionability rate, routine silencing, alerts nobody owns, "we always get that one at night".
  • Fixes: symptom/SLO-based alerting; multi-window burn rate; for: durations; grouping & inhibition; delete never-actioned alerts; require owner + runbook for every alert; a weekly alert review that tunes or deletes; track pages/shift with a target.
  • On-call health: rotations large enough that a normal week is quiet; compensation; clean handoffs with an on-call log; a "you may fix noisy alerts on shift" mandate.

Operational review loop

Weekly/biweekly: review incidents, page volume & actionability, action-item burn-down, SLO status, and recurring toil. Feeds prioritisation — reliability work competes with features via the error-budget policy.

Cheat Sheet
  • Severity by user impact/scope, not stress. Roles: Incident Commander (coordinates, doesn't fix), Responders, Comms, Scribe.
  • Mitigate before diagnose — roll back / fail over / disable feature / shed load first.
  • Regular comms cadence (internal + status page); explicit start & all-clear.
  • MTTD detect, MTTA acknowledge, MTTR recover (define it), MTBF between failures. Time-to-mitigate > time-to-full-resolution.
  • Blameless postmortem: how did the system allow this, not who. Summary+impact, factual timeline, contributing factors (not one root cause), action items with owner/date/priority tracked to done.
  • Trigger postmortems by pre-agreed criteria (every SEV1/2, customer-visible outage, notable near-miss).
  • Action items reduce likelihood / impact / detection — never "be more careful".
  • Alert fatigue = ignored pagers = missed incidents. Fix with symptom alerting, burn-rate, grouping, deletion, weekly review, quiet rotations.
Q&A
What does the Incident Commander do?
Coordinates the response — tracks what's known, assigns investigation/mitigation tasks, makes or brokers decisions (roll back? fail over? escalate?), manages comms cadence, and keeps the incident moving. The IC explicitly does not dig into the fix themselves; that's the responders' job. Separating coordination from hands-on-keyboard is what keeps a big incident from descending into chaos.
Why mitigate before diagnosing root cause?
Users are hurting now and the error budget is burning. A rollback, failover, feature-flag disable, or capacity bump often stops the impact in minutes, while root-causing can take hours. You buy time to investigate calmly. Diagnose fully afterward in the postmortem.
What makes a postmortem "blameless"?
It starts from the assumption that everyone involved made reasonable decisions given the information, time pressure, and tools they had, and it focuses on the systemic and process factors that allowed a mistake to become an incident — missing guardrails, confusing UIs, inadequate testing, slow rollback, absent alerts. Naming and blaming an individual destroys the psychological safety needed for people to report what actually happened, so you lose the ability to learn.
MTTR is ambiguous — why?
The "R" is used for repair, recovery, resolve, respond, and restore, and teams measure to different endpoints: end of user impact (mitigation), full service restoration, or closure of all follow-up. Time-to-mitigate is usually the number that matters to users. Always define which endpoint you mean before comparing MTTR across teams or over time.
Why is alert fatigue a reliability problem, not just a morale problem?
When most pages are non-actionable, responders learn to delay, batch, or ignore them — so when a genuine incident pages, it's acknowledged late or missed entirely, increasing MTTD/MTTA and thus impact. Noisy alerting directly degrades your ability to respond, on top of burning out the on-call.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Should the Incident Commander be the one fixing the problem?
No — the IC coordinates; responders investigate and mitigate.
What does MTTD measure?
Mean time to detect — from incident start to someone/something noticing.
What must every postmortem action item have?
An owner, a due date, and a priority — and it must be tracked to completion.

Intermediate core

A deploy at 14:00 caused a 40-minute partial outage. Sketch the postmortem's structure and two good vs two bad action items.
Structure: (1) Summary & impact: ~18% of checkout requests failed for 40 min (14:03–14:43), ~X orders lost, ~35% of the monthly error budget consumed, one SEV2. (2) Timeline (facts + timestamps): 14:00 deploy of vN; 14:03 error rate alert fires (fast-burn); 14:06 on-call acks; 14:09 IC declared, channel opened; 14:15 suspicion on the deploy; 14:22 rollback started; 14:31 rollback complete but caches still poisoned; 14:43 error rate normal; 14:50 all-clear. (3) Contributing factors: the bug (a null-handling regression on a code path only hit for guest checkout); it passed CI because tests lacked a guest-checkout case; canary was 5% for 2 min — too small/short to catch an 18%-of-a-subset failure; rollback took 9 min because it required a manual approval and a full redeploy; a poisoned cache extended impact 12 min past rollback. (4) What went well / poorly / lucky: alert & ack fast (good); rollback slow and cache handling unclear (poorly); lucky it was mid-afternoon with full staffing. (5) Action items. Good AIs: "Add guest-checkout path to the pre-merge integration suite" (owner, 1 wk, high) — reduces likelihood; "Make rollback one-click, no approval, target < 3 min; add a game-day to verify" (owner, 3 wks, high) — reduces impact; "Increase canary to 10% for 15 min with automatic error-rate abort" (owner, 2 wks, high) — reduces impact/detection; "Add cache-invalidation step to the rollback runbook and automate it" (owner, 1 wk, med).
