Bad AIs: "Engineers should review deploys more carefully" (not actionable, blames people); "Be more cautious with canaries" (vague, no owner/mechanism); "Add an alert for this specific null error" (over-fits the last incident instead of fixing the class); "Freeze deploys on Fridays" (cargo-cult, doesn't address the cause).
Leadership wants to track MTTR as a KPI and reward teams for lowering it. What are the risks and how do you set it up well?
Risks / gaming: (1) Definition drift — teams measure to the earliest defensible endpoint (mitigation, or even "alert cleared") to make the number small. (2) Under-declaring incidents — if it's not declared, it doesn't count; small outages get handled quietly and lessons are lost. (3) Severity deflation — classify SEV2s as SEV3 to keep them out of the tracked pool. (4) Discouraging thorough diagnosis — "mitigate and move on" without root cause to keep the clock short, so the same incident recurs. (5) Averaging hides the tail — a few very long incidents matter more than the mean; one team with rare-but-severe outages looks "better" than one with frequent minor ones. (6) It's a lagging, low-frequency metric — noisy quarter to quarter, easy to over-interpret. Doing it well: define endpoints precisely and publish them (time-to-detect, time-to-mitigate = user impact ends, time-to-resolve = service fully restored, time-to-close = action items done) and report all of them, not one blended MTTR. Use the distribution (median and p90), not just the mean, and pair with frequency (incident count / MTBF) and impact (user-minutes, budget burned) so a team can't win by hiding incidents. Make declaration criteria objective and audited. Treat the numbers as inputs to a conversation ("MTTM went up — why? rollback got slower?"), not a leaderboard with bonuses attached — rewarding the raw number is what drives the gaming. Complement with process metrics you actually want to improve: rollback time, canary coverage, action-item completion rate, alert actionability, and postmortem-on-time rate.

Advanced deep

Design an incident-management and learning program for a 300-engineer org: declaration, roles, comms, postmortems, action tracking, and how you keep it from becoming bureaucracy.
Declaration: anyone can declare; a single command (/incident) spins up a dedicated channel, a video bridge, an incident doc from a template, a tracking ticket, and pages the on-call IC pool. Objective severity rubric (user impact × scope × duration/uncertainty) posted in the channel; err toward declaring — a quick "actually fine, resolving" is cheap, a missed incident is not. Roles: a trained, rostered Incident Commander rotation separate from service on-call (so the IC isn't also the fixer); for SEV1 also assign Comms and Scribe; SEV3/4 can run with just the service on-call. IC training is a short course + shadowing. The IC runs the loop: assess → assign → decide (mitigate first) → communicate → repeat. Comms: internal updates on a fixed cadence (e.g. every 30 min for SEV1, or on state change) even if "no change"; external status page owned by Comms with pre-approved templates so legal/support don't gate each word; explicit "incident declared" and "resolved" markers; a stakeholder list per service. Postmortems: mandatory and pre-triggered for every SEV1/2 and any customer-visible outage; optional-but-encouraged for near-misses and SEV3s with a lesson. Blameless by policy and by facilitation (a trained facilitator for SEV1s, not the team that owns the service). Standard template: impact, timeline, contributing factors (plural), what went well/poorly/lucky, action items. Draft within 3 business days; review meeting within ~1 week, open to anyone, focused on systemic factors. Publish org-wide and searchable — other teams learn. Action tracking: every AI is a real ticket with owner, priority, and due date, linked from the postmortem; a dashboard tracks open incident AIs per team and their age; SEV1 AIs get a committed timeline and show up in the ops review; stale high-priority AIs escalate. Tie funding to it — the error-budget policy and the ops review are where reliability work gets prioritised against features. Anti-bureaucracy: keep the template short; SEV3/4 use a lightweight one-pager; automate everything mechanical (channel/doc/ticket creation, timeline capture from the channel, status-page prompts); don't require postmortems for trivial self-resolved blips; time-box the review meeting; measure the program by outcomes (repeat-incident rate, AI completion rate, MTTD/MTTM trend, on-call page load) not by paperwork volume; and periodically prune process steps nobody finds valuable. Feedback loop: a monthly reliability review aggregates incidents, page volume/actionability, AI burn-down, SLO status, and recurring toil into a prioritised list; themes (e.g. "deploys cause 40% of incidents") become funded initiatives. The goal is fast, calm response + honest learning + tracked follow-through, with the ceremony scaled to severity.
"Root cause" is a contested idea in incident analysis. Explain the critique, and what a mature postmortem practice does instead.
The critique (from resilience engineering / safety science — Woods, Cook, Dekker, Allspaw): (1) Complex systems fail in complex ways. A real incident is almost never one cause; it's a confluence — a latent bug that existed for months, plus a config change, plus a load spike, plus an alert that was missing, plus a rollback that was slow, plus the one engineer who knew the system being on holiday. Picking "the" root cause is choosing where to stop looking, and that choice is political and hindsight-biased. (2) Hindsight bias. After the fact, the path to failure looks obvious and the operators' "wrong" decisions look negligent. But they were acting on the information available then, under time pressure, with normal-looking signals. "They should have noticed X" ignores that X was one of fifty things and only looks salient now. (3) Counterfactual reasoning is a trap. "If only they had checked the dashboard" — you can always construct a counterfactual that would have prevented it; it doesn't tell you how to build a more robust system. (4) Human error as a cause is a dead end. "Operator error" is a starting point for investigation, not a conclusion — ask why the action made sense to them and why the system permitted it to cause harm. (5) Focusing on the failure ignores normal work. The same actions that "caused" this incident are how work gets done successfully every day; the system usually adapts around latent problems — understanding that adaptive capacity matters as much as the failure. What mature practice does instead: (a) Contributing factors, plural — enumerate the conditions that had to co-occur, technical and organisational, without ranking one as "the" cause. Tools: causal/contributing-factor trees, timelines annotated with "what did people know and believe at each point", and explicitly separating triggering event from the systemic conditions. (b) Second stories — for every "human error", the "second story" of why that was a reasonable action in context (bad tooling, misleading signal, unclear ownership, production pressure). (c) Multiple perspectives — interview the responders about their experience; the goal is to understand how the incident looked from inside, not to grade decisions. (d) Look at what went right — how was it detected, what made mitigation possible, where did the system or people successfully adapt; invest in those. (e) Action items across the three levers — reduce likelihood (fix bugs, add guardrails), reduce impact (graceful degradation, fast safe rollback, blast-radius limits), reduce detection time (the missing alert) — and also strengthen adaptive capacity (runbooks, game days, cross-training, better observability for the unknown-unknowns). (f) Blameless facilitation so the real narrative surfaces. (g) Accept that you're reducing risk, not eliminating a cause — the system will fail again differently, and the practice is continuous learning, not a search for the one fix. Some orgs rename the section "contributing factors" or "analysis" and ban the phrase "root cause" precisely to break the single-cause habit.

Issues, Types, Fields & Screens

Everything in Jira is an issue — and what an issue looks like is controlled by three layered schemes.

Notes

The issue is the atom

  • Every work item — story, bug, task, epic, sub-task, incident, change — is an issue with a key (PROJ-123), a type, a status, and a set of fields.
  • An issue belongs to exactly one project; its behaviour is governed by that project's schemes.

Issue types

  • Standard types: Story, Task, Bug, plus Epic (a parent that groups stories). Sub-task is a special child type — always has a parent, can't exist alone, doesn't appear on the backlog independently.
  • The issue type scheme defines which types a project can use; the issue type screen scheme maps each type to the screens it shows.
  • Hierarchy levels (base): Sub-task < Standard (Story/Task/Bug) < Epic. Higher levels (Initiative…) need Advanced Roadmaps / Jira Premium.

Fields

CategoryExamples
System fieldsSummary, Description, Assignee, Reporter, Priority, Labels, Components, Fix Version/s, Affects Version/s, Due date, Environment.
Custom fieldsStory Points, Sprint, Epic Link (older) / Parent, Team, Acceptance Criteria, Severity, plus anything you add (text, select, user picker, cascading, number, date).
  • Components — project-scoped sub-parts (e.g. "API", "Billing"); can have a default assignee. Labels — free-form, global, no config.
  • Versions — project-scoped release markers; Fix Version = "shipped/planned in", Affects Version = "bug found in".
  • Custom fields are global objects — adding many, especially with unrestricted contexts, slows indexing and clutters every project. Reuse and scope with field contexts (per project / issue type).

Screens

  • A screen is an ordered list of fields. Three uses, wired by the screen scheme + issue type screen screen scheme: the Create screen, the Edit screen, the View screen, and additionally screens attached to workflow transitions (e.g. a "Resolve" screen that asks for Resolution + comment).
  • A field that isn't on any screen for an issue type is effectively hidden (still exists, still settable via API/automation).
  • Field configuration (scheme) controls per-field: required/optional, hidden/visible, description, default value, and renderer (wiki vs plain).

Company- vs team-managed

  • Company-managed (classic): schemes are shared across projects, changed by Jira admins — consistency and scale, more governance.
  • Team-managed (next-gen): each project owns its own types/fields/workflow, configured by the project admin — fast and independent, but no cross-project scheme reuse and some features differ.
Cheat Sheet
  • Everything is an issue (PROJ-123): one project, a type, a status, fields.
  • Types: Story/Task/Bug (standard), Epic (parent), Sub-task (always has a parent, not on backlog alone). Allowed types = issue type scheme.
  • Fields: system (Summary, Assignee, Priority, Components, Fix Version…) + custom (Story Points, Sprint, Parent…). Custom fields are global — scope with contexts, don't over-create.
  • Components = project sub-parts (default assignee possible). Labels = global free-form. Fix Version = ships in; Affects Version = found in.
  • Screen = field list for Create / Edit / View / a transition. Not on a screen → hidden in UI. Field configuration sets required/hidden/default/renderer.
  • Company-managed = shared schemes, admin-governed. Team-managed = project owns its own config.
Q&A
What's special about a sub-task?
It's a child issue type that must have a parent, can't exist on its own, and doesn't appear independently on the backlog or as a standalone board card (it shows under its parent). It's for breaking one story into execution steps; it's not a way to model a real hierarchy of deliverables.
Difference between a Component and a Label?
Components are defined per project (an admin creates "API", "Frontend"…), can carry a default assignee and a component lead, and are structured. Labels are global, free-form text anyone can add, with no configuration — convenient but prone to typos and sprawl.
Fix Version vs Affects Version?
Affects Version records which release(s) a bug was found in; Fix Version records which release the work is planned for or was delivered in. Release reports and the "Releases" page are driven by Fix Version.
Why are unnecessary custom fields discouraged?
Custom fields are global objects. Each one adds to the Lucene index, appears in field pickers everywhere, and (with an unrestricted context) shows on every project's screens and JQL. Thousands of custom fields measurably slow indexing, search, and page loads. Reuse existing fields and restrict contexts to the projects/issue types that need them.
If a field isn't on the Edit screen, can it still be changed?
Yes — the field still exists and can be set by the REST API, automation rules, CSV import, or a workflow transition screen. It's just not editable in the normal issue UI. "Hidden" via field configuration is a stronger hide but still not a security control.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What controls which issue types a project can use?
The issue type scheme.
Which version field drives the Releases page?
Fix Version/s.
What is a screen, in Jira terms?
An ordered list of fields shown for a particular operation (Create, Edit, View, or a workflow transition).

Intermediate core

A team wants "Severity" required on the Create screen for Bugs only, not for other types, in one project only. Walk through the config.
(1) Create a custom field Severity (select list) if it doesn't exist; give it a context scoped to this project and issue type = Bug, with the option values. (2) Add Severity to the Create screen used by Bugs in this project — find the project's issue type screen scheme, see which screen scheme maps to Bug, and add the field to that screen scheme's Create screen (you may need a Bug-specific screen scheme so other types aren't affected). (3) In the project's field configuration scheme, find the field configuration applied to Bug, and mark Severity required there (create a Bug-specific field configuration if the current one is shared with other types). (4) Because contexts and field configurations are per project/issue type, other projects and other types are untouched. Team-managed projects skip most of this — you'd just add the field to the Bug type in that project's settings and mark it required. Test by creating a Bug (blocked without Severity) and a Story (no Severity field).
What breaks when you move an issue from a company-managed project to a team-managed one (or vice versa)?
Cross-type mismatches: the target project may not have the same issue type (mapped to a fallback), the same statuses (the move wizard forces a status mapping), or the same custom fields. Team-managed projects have their own field and status definitions, so a "Story Points" value from the company-managed field won't land in the team-managed project's separate Story Points field unless mapped — often data is dropped. Sprint history and Epic/parent links can be lost or need re-linking because sprints and epics are project-scoped in team-managed. Components and versions are project-scoped and won't carry. Workflow resolution and status semantics differ. Attachments, comments, and history move; structured metadata frequently doesn't. Best practice: avoid routine cross-style moves; if migrating, plan a field/status mapping, export first, and expect to re-apply sprint/epic associations.

Advanced deep

An instance with 400 projects has 3,000+ custom fields and search/indexing is slow. Design a rationalization program.
Measure: use the admin "Custom fields" view (or a marketplace app / the REST API) to pull, per field: type, number of contexts, whether context is "global" (all projects/all types), last used, screens it's on, and number of issues with a non-null value. Also check index size and reindex time trend. Categorize: (a) Duplicates — many "Story Points", "Sprint", "Team", "Root Cause", "Environment" fields created independently per project/team. (b) Unused — zero or near-zero populated issues, or not on any screen. (c) Over-scoped — a field only one team needs but with a global context, so it hits every project's screens/JQL. (d) Locked — app-managed fields (leave alone). Consolidate: pick one canonical field per concept; for duplicates, migrate values with a script/automation (copy old→new across affected issues), repoint screens and JQL/filters/dashboards/automation, then delete the duplicates. For unused fields, remove from screens, confirm no filter/board/automation/API references (search filters and gadgets by field), then delete. For over-scoped fields, replace the global context with project/issue-type-restricted contexts. Guardrails going forward: a request/approval process for new custom fields (justify why an existing one won't do), naming conventions, mandatory scoped contexts, a quarterly audit report, and admin-only field creation (remove that permission from project admins in company-managed). Execution safety: do it in waves, communicate to affected teams, snapshot filters/dashboards first, and schedule the big reindex in a maintenance window. Track index size and reindex time as the success metric, plus field count trending down.
Explain how Jira resolves what a user sees on an issue: the chain from project to the actual rendered Edit screen and a field's required/visible state.
The issue belongs to a project and has an issue type. Jira walks several scheme associations, all set at the project level: (1) Issue type scheme → is this type even allowed in the project. (2) Workflow scheme → maps the issue type to a workflow, which defines the issue's possible statuses and the transitions (and any transition screens). (3) Issue type screen scheme → maps the issue type to a screen scheme. (4) The screen scheme maps each operation (Create / Edit / View) to a specific screen; if an operation isn't mapped it falls back to the Default. (5) The screen is the ordered list of fields (tabs). A field must be (a) on this screen and (b) applicable to the project/type via its custom field context to appear at all. (6) The field configuration scheme maps the issue type to a field configuration, which per field sets: hidden vs visible (hidden wins over "on a screen"), required vs optional (enforced on Create/Edit/transition submit), the description text, the default value, and the renderer (wiki markup vs plain text). (7) Permission scheme and issue security scheme gate whether the user can see the issue and use Edit at all; field-level behaviour can be further constrained by workflow properties (e.g. jira.issue.editable=false in a status) or by validators on transitions. So the rendered Edit screen = (screen fields) − (hidden by field config) − (not in context) − (blocked by workflow status property), with "required" markers from the field configuration and additional required-ness possibly enforced by transition validators. Team-managed projects collapse most of this into the single project's own type/field/workflow settings, so the chain is shorter but the concepts (which fields, required, statuses) are the same.

Workflows, Statuses & Transitions

A workflow is a state machine for issues — and the Resolution field is the part everyone gets wrong.

Notes

Anatomy

  • A workflow = a set of statuses (states) + transitions (directed edges) an issue can take.
  • Statuses are global objects shared across workflows, each mapped to a status category: To Do (grey), In Progress (blue), Done (green). Boards and reports use the category, not the name.
  • The workflow scheme maps issue types → workflows for a project. Editing a workflow that's in use requires a draft → publish; changing which statuses exist may force a migration mapping for existing issues.

Transitions have four hook points

HookRunsExamples
ConditionsBefore the transition is even offeredOnly assignee can transition; only if a sub-task is done; user in role.
ValidatorsOn submit, can block with an errorField required (Resolution, Fix Version); comment required; field has a value.
Post-functionsAfter the transition succeedsSet Resolution, clear Resolution, assign to reporter, update a field, fire an event, add a comment.
TriggersFired by dev-tool events"Branch created" → move to In Progress; "PR merged" → move to In Review.

A special transition from "Any status" (the All node) lets you go to a status from anywhere (e.g. a global "Close").

Status vs Resolution — the classic trap

  • Status = where the issue is in the process ("In Progress", "Done").
  • Resolution = why it left the active process ("Done", "Won't Do", "Duplicate", "Cannot Reproduce"). A non-empty Resolution is what Jira treats as "this issue is resolved/closed".
  • Rule: a Set Resolution post-function (or a resolution screen) on every transition into a done status; a Clear Resolution post-function on every transition back out (Reopen). Forget the clear step and reopened issues stay "resolved" — they vanish from "open issues" filters, burndown, and notifications while sitting in an active status.
  • Never make Resolution a normal field on the Create/Edit screen — only set it via transitions.

Design guidance

  • Keep it small: To Do → In Progress → In Review → Done covers most teams. Every extra status is a board column and a place work stalls.
  • Map statuses to the right category so the board's Done column and "Complete sprint" behave.
  • Reuse a shared workflow across projects (company-managed) for consistent reporting; per-team workflows fragment cross-project metrics.
  • Prefer automation rules over heavy post-functions/scripted conditions for maintainability, unless you need the guarantee that it runs as part of the transition.
  • Avoid too many conditions that hide transitions — users get confused when the button they expect isn't there.
Cheat Sheet
  • Workflow = statuses + transitions (a state machine). Workflow scheme maps issue types → workflows per project.
  • Statuses are global; each has a category: To Do / In Progress / Done. Boards & reports use the category.
  • Transition hooks: conditions (show/hide), validators (block on submit), post-functions (act after), triggers (dev events).
  • Status = where in the process. Resolution = why it left the process; non-empty Resolution = "resolved".
  • Set Resolution on transitions into Done; Clear Resolution on Reopen — or reopened issues stay hidden from open-issue filters/burndown.
  • Never put Resolution on Create/Edit screens — only set via transitions.
  • Keep workflows small; reuse across projects for consistent metrics; prefer automation over scripted post-functions.
Q&A
What's the difference between Status and Resolution?
Status is the issue's position in the workflow ("In Progress", "Done"). Resolution explains why work stopped ("Done", "Won't Do", "Duplicate"). Jira considers an issue resolved when Resolution is non-empty, independent of the status name — which is why they must be kept in sync via transitions.
Why do "reopened" issues sometimes disappear from reports?
Because the Reopen transition moved the status back to an active state but didn't clear the Resolution. The issue still has Resolution = "Done", so filters like resolution = EMPTY, the sprint burndown, and "open issues" gadgets exclude it even though it's actively being worked. Add a Clear Resolution post-function to every transition out of a done status.
What runs in what order on a transition?
Conditions are evaluated first (they decide whether the transition button appears at all). On submit, validators run and can reject the transition with an error. If validators pass, the status changes and then post-functions execute (set/clear fields, assign, fire the event, re-index). Automation rules subscribed to the "issue transitioned" event run after.
How do you add a "Close" action available from any status?
Add a transition from the special "Any status" source to your Closed/Done status (a "global transition"). It shows on every status. Put a Set Resolution screen or post-function on it.
You edited a live workflow — why didn't it take effect?
Editing a workflow that's associated with a project creates a draft. You must publish the draft for it to apply. If your edit added/removed statuses, publishing prompts a status migration mapping so existing issues in removed statuses get moved.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What field does Jira use to decide an issue is "resolved"?
Resolution (non-empty = resolved).
Which transition hook can block a transition with an error message?
A validator.
What three categories can a status belong to?
To Do, In Progress, Done.

Intermediate core

Design the workflow config so Resolution is always correct, including reopen.
Statuses: To Do → In Progress → In Review → Done, plus a global "Won't Do". On the transition(s) into Done: a Resolution screen (so the user picks Done / Duplicate / etc.) or, for a simple team, a Set Resolution = Done post-function. On the "Won't Do" transition: Resolution screen or Set Resolution = Won't Do. On every transition whose destination is a non-Done status from a Done status — i.e. Reopen, or "Done → In Progress" — a Clear Resolution (Set Resolution = None) post-function, plus optionally reassign to the reporter and add a comment. Add a validator on the into-Done transitions requiring Resolution to be set. Keep Resolution off the Create and Edit screens entirely. Verify with JQL: status = Done AND resolution = EMPTY (should be zero) and statusCategory != Done AND resolution != EMPTY (should be zero).
A team wants issues to auto-move to "In Progress" when a branch is created and to "In Review" when a PR opens. Two ways to do this — compare.
Workflow triggers: on the target transition, add a trigger for "Branch created" / "Pull request created" (requires the Git provider integrated via the dev-tool connection). Pros: it's part of the workflow, runs as the transition (respecting conditions/validators/post-functions), no separate rule to maintain, works per project via the workflow scheme. Cons: configured per workflow (repeat for each), limited to the trigger types Jira ships, and only fires when the smart-commit/branch name references the issue key. Automation rules: a project or global rule with a "Branch created" / "Pull request created" trigger → "Transition issue to In Progress/In Review". Pros: centralized, easy to see/edit all rules in one place, can add conditions (only if currently in To Do), branch across multiple actions (assign, comment, notify), and reuse one global rule for many projects. Cons: runs after the event as a separate actor ("Automation for Jira"), so it can race with other rules, is subject to rule-execution limits/queues, and won't run if automation is disabled. Recommendation: automation rules for flexibility and central management, unless you specifically need the change to be enforced as part of the transition itself.

Advanced deep

50 teams each have a bespoke workflow; cross-team reporting (cycle time, throughput, "% done") is unreliable. Design a consolidation without a revolt.
Root problem: different status names, different numbers of stages, and inconsistent status category mapping mean board "Done" columns, sprint completion, and any cross-project JQL/report mean different things per team. Approach: (1) Define a small canonical workflow — e.g. Backlog (To Do) → Selected (To Do) → In Progress → In Review → Done, with correct categories — as the standard for company-managed projects. Allow one or two optional extra statuses (e.g. "Blocked", "In Test") from an approved list, each with a fixed category, so teams keep some flavour without fragmenting metrics. (2) Map every team's current statuses to the canonical set (a spreadsheet exercise with each team), being strict that anything representing "not started" is To Do, active work is In Progress, and shipped is Done — the category mapping is the non-negotiable part; names can vary a little if you must. (3) Migrate in waves: create the shared workflow + workflow scheme, associate it per project, run the status migration mapping, publish. Keep team boards working by adjusting column→status mappings. (4) Rebuild shared dashboards/filters on status category and standard fields, plus control-chart / cycle-time reports that now compare like-for-like. (5) Governance: new projects get the standard workflow by default; changes go through a review; team-managed projects are steered to the same status set via a template. (6) Change management: bring team leads in early, show them the broken cross-team reports as motivation, preserve their board experience, pilot with 3–5 friendly teams, provide a migration runbook, and give a deadline with support. The pitch is "you lose almost nothing on your board; the org gains trustworthy delivery metrics".
Post-functions vs automation vs app (ScriptRunner) for workflow logic: give the decision criteria, including ordering, reliability, and auditability.
Built-in post-functions / conditions / validators: run synchronously as part of the transition, in a defined order, before the user sees success. Use when the logic must be guaranteed atomic with the transition (set/clear Resolution, required-field validation, "block unless sub-tasks done"). Limits: the built-in set is basic (set a field, assign, fire event); ordering of post-functions matters and the "re-index"/"fire event" ones must stay in the right place; hard to see all of them across many workflows. Automation for Jira rules: run asynchronously after the event, as the "Automation" actor, from a central rule list. Use for cross-issue effects (update parent, create sub-tasks, sync fields), notifications, multi-step branching, scheduled jobs, and anything you want visible/editable in one place with an audit log per rule. Limits: eventual (a fraction of a second to seconds later, longer under load), subject to per-plan execution limits and queue throttling, can race with other rules and with the user's next action, silently skipped if automation is disabled or the rule errors, and loops need guarding. Not suitable when the change must be enforced before the transition completes. ScriptRunner / other apps (scripted post-functions, listeners, behaviours): run synchronously (scripted post-functions/validators) or on events (listeners), with full API access. Use for complex synchronous validation/mutation the built-ins can't express, dynamic field behaviour ("behaviours"), and bulk/admin scripting. Limits: code you own and must test; upgrades/Jira version changes can break scripts; performance risk if a script does slow work inside a transition; auditability depends on your logging discipline; another vendor dependency and cost; Cloud vs Data Center capabilities differ. Decision criteria: (1) Must it be atomic with the transition and block it? → validator/post-function (built-in if possible, ScriptRunner if the logic is complex). (2) Is it cross-issue, multi-step, or "nice to have if it runs a moment later"? → automation rule (best auditability and central management). (3) Does it need real code and can tolerate a marketplace dependency? → ScriptRunner, but keep scripts small, logged, and covered by a test project. (4) Prefer the least powerful tool that works for maintainability: config > automation > script. (5) Watch ordering: built-in post-functions have a fixed sequence you can reorder; automation and listeners fire after and among themselves in undefined order — don't have two mechanisms fighting over the same field.

Boards: Scrum vs Kanban

A board is a saved filter plus a column layout — not a container of issues.

Notes

What a board actually is

  • A board = a filter (the JQL that selects which issues appear) + configuration (columns, swimlanes, quick filters, card layout, estimation, working days).
  • Issues aren't "on" a board — they match the board's filter. One issue can appear on many boards; a board can span multiple projects if its filter does.
  • Columns map to one or more statuses. Moving a card between columns transitions the issue (if a valid transition exists). Statuses not mapped to any column are "hidden" from the board.

Scrum vs Kanban board

Scrum boardKanban board
CadenceTime-boxed sprints; a Backlog screen to plan themContinuous flow; no sprints (optional "Kanban backlog" column)
Board showsOnly the active sprint's issuesEverything matching the filter, minus done older than N days
Key reportsBurndown, Sprint Report, VelocityCumulative Flow Diagram, Control Chart, Cycle time
WIP controlSprint scope (commitment)Column WIP limits
Best forPredictable planning cycles, forecasting with velocityOps/support, steady intake, continuous delivery

Both use the same underlying issues/workflow; the board type just changes planning UI and reports. You can switch, or run a "Scrumban" hybrid.

Board configuration knobs

  • Columns & statuses: add/remove columns, map statuses, set column WIP limits (min/max), set the "Done" column (drives sprint completion & the done-issue aging).
  • Swimlanes: horizontal grouping — by Epic, Assignee, Story (parent), Query (custom JQL rows, e.g. "Expedite"), or none. Query swimlanes are ordered top-down.
  • Quick filters: one-click JQL toggles ("Only my issues", "No sub-tasks", "Recently updated").
  • Card layout: which fields show on cards (up to a few extra), card colours (by priority / assignee / issue type / JQL).
  • Estimation: Story Points / original time / issue count; and the tracking unit for burndown.
  • Working days: for burndown day calculations.
  • Sub-task handling: whether the board shows parent+sub-tasks or rolls up.

Common pitfalls

  • Filter too broad/narrow: cards missing = they don't match the filter, or their status isn't mapped to a column. Check the board's filter and column mapping first.
  • Board filter has no ORDER BY Rank: drag-to-rank on the backlog stops working; the filter must order by Rank.
  • Editing the board's filter affects everyone using that board; boards sharing a filter move together.
  • Only board admins (and the filter owner) can change config; a departed owner can orphan a board's filter.
Cheat Sheet
  • Board = saved filter + config (columns, swimlanes, quick filters, card layout, estimation). Issues match a board, aren't contained by it.
  • Columns → statuses; dragging a card transitions the issue. Unmapped statuses are hidden.
  • Scrum board: sprints + Backlog planning; shows active sprint; Burndown/Velocity/Sprint Report; WIP via sprint scope.
  • Kanban board: continuous flow, no sprints; CFD/Control Chart/cycle time; WIP via column limits.
  • Swimlanes: by Epic / Assignee / Story / Query / none. Quick filters = one-click JQL toggles.
  • Board filter must ORDER BY Rank for drag-ranking to work.
  • Same issues/workflow underneath — board type only changes planning UI + reports.
Q&A
What is a Jira board, technically?
A saved filter plus display configuration. The filter's JQL decides which issues show; the config defines columns (mapped to statuses), swimlanes, quick filters, card fields/colours, and estimation. Issues appear on any board whose filter they match.
A card isn't showing on the board even though the issue exists. First checks?
(1) Does the issue match the board's filter (project, type, any extra JQL clauses)? (2) Is the issue's status mapped to a column? Unmapped statuses are hidden. (3) On a Scrum board, is the issue in the active sprint? (4) Is a quick filter or swimlane hiding it? (5) On Kanban, is it a Done issue older than the board's "days" setting?
Scrum board vs Kanban board — when to choose which?
Scrum when work comes in planned batches and the team wants sprint commitments, velocity-based forecasting, and a regular cadence. Kanban when work arrives continuously (support, ops, platform), priorities shift often, and you care about flow metrics (cycle time, WIP) rather than sprint burndown.
What do column WIP limits do?
On a Kanban board (and optionally Scrum), you set a max (and min) number of issues for a column; Jira highlights the column red when exceeded. It's a visual nudge to finish work before starting more — Jira doesn't hard-block adding cards.
Why did backlog drag-and-drop ranking stop working?
The board's filter must end with ORDER BY Rank ASC. If someone changed the filter's sort (or it never had one), Jira can't persist manual rank order and drag-ranking is disabled. Re-add the Rank ordering to the saved filter.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What two things make up a board?
A saved filter (JQL) and its display configuration (columns, swimlanes, etc.).
Which board type has sprints?
Scrum.
What happens to the issue when you drag its card to another column?
Jira runs the workflow transition to the status that column maps to (if a valid transition exists).

Intermediate core

One team's work spans three projects. How do you give them a single board without merging the projects?
Create a saved filter with JQL like project in (ALPHA, BETA, GAMMA) AND (labels = team-orion OR component in (…)) ORDER BY Rank — whatever precisely identifies this team's issues across the three projects. Then create a board from that filter. Configure columns to map the union of statuses used across the three projects' workflows (they may differ — map each real status to the right column, and be careful about status category consistency so "Done" behaves). Set swimlanes by project or by epic if useful. Caveats: the three projects may have different workflows/fields, so transitions available from a card depend on that issue's own workflow; estimation should use a field all three populate (Story Points); sprint planning only works cleanly if the board is Scrum and all three projects share the sprint field (they do — Sprint is global in company-managed). Board admins are set separately from project admins. This is the standard "cross-project team board" pattern.
A support team's Kanban board is chaotic: everything's "In Progress", nothing finishes. What board-level changes help?
(1) Set WIP limits per column, especially on In Progress and In Review, sized to the team (e.g. ~1–1.5× headcount); the red overflow highlight forces the "stop starting, start finishing" conversation. (2) Split the "In Progress" column into meaningful stages (e.g. Analysis / Doing / Waiting-on-customer / In Review) so blocked vs active work is visible — and add a "Blocked" flag or a query swimlane for blocked items so they don't hide. (3) Add a dedicated "Expedite" query swimlane at the top for true urgent items, with its own (tiny) WIP limit, so urgent work doesn't just mean "everything's urgent". (4) Add quick filters ("Mine", "Waiting on others", "Older than 3 days") to surface stalled work. (5) Turn on the Control Chart and Cumulative Flow Diagram to make cycle time and where work piles up visible in retros. (6) Trim done-issue aging so the board isn't cluttered. The board changes won't fix the process alone, but WIP limits + explicit stages + blocked visibility are what make a flow problem impossible to ignore.

Advanced deep

Explain how the board, its filter, sprints, and rank interact — and the failure modes when multiple boards share a filter or a sprint spans boards.
Rank is a single global field (a lexicographic "LexoRank" string) per issue — there is one rank order across the whole instance, not per board. Every board that orders its filter by Rank shows issues in that same global order, filtered to its subset. Dragging to reorder on any board rewrites the global rank of the moved issue, so reordering on board A also reorders those issues relative to each other on board B. This is usually fine but surprising when two teams "own" overlapping issue sets. Sprints are objects with an ID, name, state (future/active/closed), and start/end dates; an issue's Sprint field can hold multiple sprint IDs (its history). A sprint is created from and associated with an "origin board", but issues carry the sprint value regardless of board. So an issue can be in Sprint 42 and appear on any board whose filter matches it — if two Scrum boards both match an issue that's in an active sprint, it shows in the active-sprint view of both, and completing the sprint from either board closes it for the issue everywhere. Failure modes: (1) Shared filter — two boards pointing at the same saved filter: editing the filter (or its ORDER BY) changes both; deleting/!editing column mappings is per-board but the filter is shared, so a filter change to fix board A can break board B's visible set. (2) Sprint started on the "wrong" board — a sprint's origin board determines which board's Backlog screen manages it; if the team plans on a different board, they can't start/complete that sprint there and see "no sprint" confusion. Keep one canonical board per team for sprint operations. (3) Overlapping board filters + sprints — an issue matching two teams' boards, put into team A's sprint, now clutters team B's active sprint and burndown; scope board filters so teams don't overlap, or use a component/team field in the filter. (4) Rank thrash — two teams re-ranking a shared pool fight each other; the fix is disjoint filters. (5) LexoRank rebalancing — when rank strings get too long, Jira runs a background rebalance; huge instances can see slow ranking during it. (6) Filter permissions — if the filter isn't shared with everyone who uses the board, they see an empty or partial board. Design rule: one board per team with a filter that cleanly partitions that team's work; do sprint operations only from that board; accept that Rank is global.
A director wants "one big board" showing all 12 teams' work for a portfolio view. Why is that usually the wrong tool, and what do you build instead?
Why a giant board is wrong: (1) A board is an execution tool — columns are workflow statuses, cards are individual issues, and it's tuned for a team moving work day to day. 12 teams' issues in one column list is unreadable and slow to render. (2) The 12 teams likely have different workflows, so status→column mapping is lossy or misleading. (3) Rank is global — a portfolio board that lets anyone drag-rank creates cross-team rank fights. (4) Sprints are per-team; an aggregate board can't show 12 concurrent sprints coherently. (5) The director doesn't need issue-level detail; they need epic/initiative status, delivery forecasts, and risks. What to build instead: (a) Advanced Roadmaps / Plans (Jira Premium) — a plan aggregating the 12 teams' boards/projects, showing the epic/initiative hierarchy on a timeline, capacity, dependencies, and scenario planning; this is the actual "portfolio view". (b) A dashboard with gadgets: epic progress (per team), created-vs-resolved, sprint health, cumulative flow, an "at risk" filter (e.g. due < endOfMonth() AND statusCategory != Done), and a two-dimensional filter statistics gadget (team × status). (c) A filter/JQL saved view at epic level: issuetype = Epic AND "Team[Dropdown]" in (…) ORDER BY due with status, % done (via linked issues or a progress field), target date. (d) If they insist on a board, make a read-mostly epic-level Kanban: filter issuetype in (Epic, Initiative), columns = a simple Not started / In progress / Done, swimlanes by team — a legible one-card-per-epic status wall, not 3,000 stories. The principle: boards are for teams executing; portfolios need roll-up (Plans), summary (dashboards), or an epic-level board, not a firehose.

Backlog, Sprints & Estimation

Turning an ordered list of work into time-boxed, forecastable delivery.

Notes

The backlog

  • The Backlog screen (Scrum boards) shows the ranked list of issues not in an active/future sprint, plus a section per planned sprint.
  • Ranking = drag to order (global Rank field); rank expresses priority sequence, not commitment.
  • Grooming / refinement: keep the top of the backlog small, clear, estimated, and dependency-free enough to pull into a sprint. Lower items can stay vague.
  • Bulk actions, inline create, and "send to top/bottom of sprint" speed planning.

Sprints

  • Create a sprint (from the Backlog), drag issues in, set the goal, then Start sprint (name, duration, start/end). Only one active sprint per board by default (Jira allows parallel sprints as an option — use sparingly).
  • Complete sprint: incomplete issues go back to the backlog or a future sprint; the Sprint Report snapshots what was committed vs added vs completed.
  • Scope changes mid-sprint are recorded (scope creep line on the burndown).

Estimation

MethodNotes
Story pointsRelative size (effort + complexity + uncertainty), often a modified Fibonacci scale (1,2,3,5,8,13). Not hours. Team-relative — not comparable across teams.
Time (original estimate)Hours/days. Concrete but tempts false precision and per-person accounting.
Issue countJust count stories; works if stories are sliced to similar size.
T-shirt / bucketsCoarse sizing for backlog items not yet ready.
  • The board's Estimation setting picks the field used for backlog/sprint totals and the burndown's Y axis.
  • Planning poker to estimate collaboratively and surface hidden assumptions.
  • Estimate stories, not sub-tasks (sub-tasks are execution breakdown; some teams put remaining time on sub-tasks for a separate task burndown).

Velocity & capacity

  • Velocity = points completed per sprint (from the Velocity report). Use a rolling average of the last 3–5 sprints to forecast; don't treat it as a target or a performance metric.
  • Capacity planning: account for holidays, on-call, support rotation, meetings; commit below raw velocity when the sprint is short-staffed.
  • Only fully completed issues count toward velocity — a nearly-done 8-pointer scores 0 that sprint (don't split points on carry-over; re-estimate the remainder if needed).

Anti-patterns

  • Converting points to hours (defeats relative estimation).
  • Comparing velocity between teams or demanding it always increase (invites point inflation).
  • Committing to 100% of velocity every sprint (no slack for the unexpected).
  • Carrying the same story for 4 sprints — it's too big or blocked; split it.
  • Adding lots of scope mid-sprint without acknowledging the goal is at risk.
Cheat Sheet
  • Backlog = ranked list of issues not in a sprint. Rank = priority order (global field). Groom the top; leave the tail rough.
  • Sprint: create → add issues → set goal → Start (duration) → Complete (incomplete issues roll to backlog/next; Sprint Report snapshots committed vs done).
  • Estimation options: story points (relative, Fibonacci-ish, team-local, not hours), time, issue count, buckets. Board Estimation setting picks the burndown unit.
  • Estimate stories, not sub-tasks. Use planning poker.
  • Velocity = points completed/sprint; rolling avg of 3–5 to forecast; not a target, not cross-team comparable. Only fully-done issues count.
  • Capacity: subtract holidays/on-call/support; commit below velocity when short-staffed; keep slack.
  • Anti-patterns: points→hours, velocity as KPI, 100% commitment, 4-sprint carry-over, silent scope creep.
Q&A
What are story points and why not just use hours?
Story points estimate relative size — effort, complexity, and uncertainty combined — usually on a coarse Fibonacci-like scale. They're deliberately not hours because relative sizing is faster, more consistent across people, avoids false precision, and lets the team forecast via velocity without per-person time accounting. Converting them back to hours throws away all of that.
How is velocity calculated and how should it be used?
Velocity is the sum of estimates of issues completed in a sprint (shown in the Velocity report). Use a rolling average of the last few sprints to forecast how much the team can likely take on and roughly when a backlog will be done. It is not a productivity score, not a target to grow, and not comparable between teams (each team's points are its own scale).
A story was 90% done at sprint end. What happens to its points?
It counts as 0 toward that sprint's velocity — only completed issues count. It rolls to the next sprint (or backlog) with its estimate intact; teams generally re-estimate the remaining work rather than splitting the original points. Recurring carry-over is a signal the story is too big or blocked and should be split.
What's the difference between ranking and committing?
Ranking is ordering the backlog by priority — it says nothing about when work will be done. Committing is pulling issues into a sprint with the team's agreement that they'll aim to finish them by the sprint end. You rank the whole backlog; you commit only the top slice that fits capacity.
Why keep slack instead of committing to 100% of velocity?
Because real sprints have interruptions — production issues, urgent requests, sick days, underestimated stories. Committing to exactly the average velocity means any surprise blows the sprint goal. Teams typically commit somewhat below velocity (and adjust for known capacity gaps) so they can absorb the unexpected and still hit the goal.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Do story points represent hours?
No — they're a relative measure of size/complexity/uncertainty.
What counts toward a sprint's velocity?
Only issues fully completed in that sprint.
Where do incomplete issues go when you complete a sprint?
Back to the backlog or into a selected future sprint.

Intermediate core

A team's velocity is 40, 12, 45, 38, 41. How do you forecast, and what do you do about the outlier?
The 12 is an outlier — almost certainly a holiday sprint, a major incident, or a big release freeze. Investigate and, for forecasting, exclude it (or annotate why). Forecast from the remaining sprints: mean ≈ 41, range ~38–45, so plan around ~38–40 committed points per normal sprint (use the low end for commitments, the average for roadmap projections). To forecast a backlog of, say, 400 points: ~10–11 sprints, and present it as a range (9–12) not a single date. Adjust each sprint for known capacity (a person on leave, on-call load) rather than blindly using 40. Keep watching — if another low sprint appears, the "outlier" may be a pattern (chronic interruptions) worth fixing. Don't let the team chase "back to 45"; that just inflates estimates.
Product keeps injecting "urgent" work mid-sprint and the team never hits the sprint goal. What Jira mechanics and practices address this?
Make it visible: the burndown already shows a scope change line — review it every sprint retro and in sprint review with product, quantifying "we committed 38, 22 points of unplanned work was added, goal missed". The Sprint Report's "added during sprint" section does the same. Mechanics: (1) Reserve explicit capacity for unplanned work — commit to (velocity − historical injection average), effectively a buffer. (2) Use a distinct issue type or label ("Expedite"/"Unplanned") and a query swimlane at the top of the board so injected work is tracked and countable, not silently absorbed. (3) A rule that adding scope means removing equivalent scope ("one in, one out") — product chooses what drops. (4) For genuinely continuous interrupt work, consider moving that stream to a Kanban board with a WIP-limited expedite lane, and keep the Scrum sprint for planned work. (5) Protect the sprint goal as the real commitment (not the full issue list) so the team can still "succeed" by delivering the goal even if filler stories slip. Practice: agree an interrupt policy with product (what qualifies as sprint-breaking urgent vs "next sprint"), route non-urgent requests through backlog refinement, and if injection stays high, that's a prioritization/planning problem to escalate, not a team execution problem.

Advanced deep

Leadership wants to standardize story points across 15 teams so they can "add up capacity". Explain why that's flawed and what actually enables cross-team planning.
Why it's flawed: story points are deliberately relative to a team's own baseline — a team calibrates "a 3" against their reference stories, their codebase, their skills, their definition of done. Team A's 5 and Team B's 5 represent different amounts of work, and forcing a shared scale just moves the calibration problem without solving it (teams will drift back, or game the scale). Summing points across teams to get "org capacity" produces a number with no real meaning, and it invites the worst dynamics: point inflation, cross-team comparison as a performance cudgel, and estimation becoming a political exercise. Velocity is a per-team forecasting aid, not a currency. What actually enables cross-team / portfolio planning: (1) Plan at a coarser unit that is comparable — epics/features with T-shirt sizes or a rough sprint-count estimate per team, or "number of teams × number of sprints". (2) Use each team's own velocity to forecast that team's portion of a roadmap, then compose the timelines — Advanced Roadmaps / Plans does exactly this (per-team capacity from their velocity, rolled up with dependencies on a timeline). (3) Track throughput (features/epics completed per quarter per team) and cycle time for delivery-rate comparisons — these are unit-free and meaningful across teams. (4) For "can we take this on?", ask each team to forecast against their own backlog and velocity and report a confidence range, then aggregate the answers, not the points. (5) Keep story points as an internal team tool and explicitly tell leadership the org-level metrics are throughput, cycle time, epic burn-up, and forecast confidence — not summed points. The one legitimate standardization is a shared process (consistent definition of done, similar story-slicing guidance, refinement discipline) so each team's forecasts are individually trustworthy.

JQL: Searching & Filters

Jira Query Language — SQL-ish clauses over issue fields, powering filters, boards, dashboards, and automation.

Notes

Shape of a query

field OPERATOR value [AND|OR field OPERATOR value ...] [ORDER BY field ASC|DESC]

No SELECT — a JQL query is just the WHERE + ORDER BY. It always returns issues.

Operators

OperatorUse
= !=exact match / not
> >= < <=ordered fields (dates, numbers, priority, votes)
IN (a, b) / NOT INset membership
~ / !~text "contains" (indexed word match, not substring) — for summary, description, comment, text
IS EMPTY / IS NOT EMPTYnull check (use for resolution, fixVersion, custom fields)
WAS / WAS IN / WAS NOThistorical value of status/assignee/etc. (with AFTER, BEFORE, DURING, ON, BY)
CHANGEDfield changed (FROM, TO, AFTER, BY, DURING)

Functions (value generators)

  • Dates: now(), startOfDay()/endOfDay(), startOfWeek(), startOfMonth(), and relative math: -1w, -3d, "-1w 2d". e.g. due <= endOfWeek(), created >= -14d.
  • People: currentUser(), membersOf("jira-developers").
  • Agile: sprint in openSprints(), sprint in closedSprints(), sprint in futureSprints().
  • Versions: fixVersion in releasedVersions(), unreleasedVersions(), earliestUnreleasedVersion(PROJ).
  • Links/hierarchy (varies by version/app): issuesInEpics(), parentEpic(), issueLinkType, linkedIssues("KEY", "blocks"), portfolioChildrenOf().
  • issueHistory() (recently viewed), votedIssues(), watchedIssues().

Common recipes

project = PLAT AND statusCategory != Done AND assignee = currentUser() ORDER BY priority DESC, due ASC
project = WEB AND created >= -7d AND type = Bug
resolution = EMPTY AND updated <= -30d AND statusCategory = "In Progress"     # stale in-progress
status WAS "In Progress" BY jsmith DURING ("2024-01-01", "2024-03-31")
status CHANGED TO Done AFTER startOfMonth() AND assignee in membersOf("team-orion")
sprint in openSprints() AND type != Sub-task AND statusCategory != Done       # sprint scope remaining
project = SUP AND labels = escalation AND priority in (Highest, High) ORDER BY created ASC
filter = "Team Orion Base" AND due < now() AND statusCategory != Done          # compose saved filters

Saved filters

  • Save a query → a filter with an owner and share permissions (private / project / group / public). Boards, dashboard gadgets, and other filters (filter = "Name" ) reference it.
  • Subscriptions: email the filter results on a schedule (cron), to you or a group.
  • Permissions gotcha: a viewer only sees issues they have Browse permission on, and only sees the filter if it's shared with them. A board backed by a filter the team can't see shows empty.
  • An orphaned filter (owner deactivated) needs an admin to change the owner; boards/gadgets break meanwhile.

Notes

  • ~ matches whole indexed words with stemming, not arbitrary substrings; wildcards text ~ "cust*" work, leading wildcards don't.
  • Custom field names with spaces or duplicates: quote them, or use cf[10021] by ID.
  • ORDER BY Rank is required on a board's filter for manual ranking.
  • JQL is also the language for automation conditions/branches and bulk-change selection.
Cheat Sheet
  • JQL = field OP value [AND/OR ...] [ORDER BY ...]. No SELECT; always returns issues.
  • Ops: = != >… IN/NOT IN, ~/!~ (word contains), IS [NOT] EMPTY, WAS/WAS IN, CHANGED (with FROM/TO/AFTER/DURING/BY).
  • Functions: currentUser(), membersOf(), now()/startOfDay()/endOfWeek() + -1w, openSprints()/closedSprints(), releasedVersions()/unreleasedVersions(), linkedIssues().
  • Use statusCategory (To Do/In Progress/Done) for status-agnostic queries; resolution = EMPTY for "open".
  • Compose filters: filter = "Saved Name" AND .... Reference custom fields by cf[10010] if names collide.
  • Saved filter = query + owner + share scope; feeds boards, gadgets, subscriptions (scheduled email).
  • Viewer sees only issues they can Browse and filters shared with them; unshared filter → empty board.
Q&A
Why use statusCategory != Done instead of status not in (Done, Closed)?
Status names vary by project and workflow; statusCategory is one of three fixed values (To Do, In Progress, Done) that every status maps to. A query on the category works across all projects and survives someone renaming or adding statuses, so it's the portable way to say "not finished".
What does the ~ operator actually match?
It's a full-text "contains" against the Lucene index — it matches whole words (with stemming), not arbitrary substrings. summary ~ "login" matches "login failed" and "logins" but not "weblogins". Trailing wildcards (~ "log*") work; leading wildcards don't.
How do you find issues that were in "In Progress" at some point last month?
status WAS "In Progress" DURING (startOfMonth(-1), startOfMonth()). The WAS operator queries status history; DURING bounds the time window. You can add BY someuser to restrict to who made the change.
What is a saved filter and what can reference it?
A named, saved JQL query with an owner and share settings. Boards are built on a filter; dashboard gadgets take a filter; other JQL can embed one with filter = "Name"; and you can attach an email subscription to run it on a schedule. Sharing controls who can see and use it.
A colleague's board shows no issues for you but works for them. Likely cause?
Either the board's underlying filter isn't shared with you (so you can't see the board's query), or you lack Browse Project permission on the projects it covers (so the issues are invisible to you), or an issue security level hides them. Filter results are always intersected with the viewer's permissions.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which JQL keyword sorts results?
ORDER BY.
How do you query "assigned to me"?
assignee = currentUser().
How do you check a field has no value?
field IS EMPTY (e.g. resolution IS EMPTY).

Intermediate core

Write a query for "my team's bugs opened in the last 14 days that are still unresolved, worst priority first".
type = Bug AND created >= -14d AND resolution = EMPTY AND assignee in membersOf("team-orion") ORDER BY priority DESC, created ASC. Notes: created >= -14d is relative to now; resolution = EMPTY is the reliable "unresolved" check (don't rely on status names); membersOf("group") expands a group, or use a "Team" custom field: "Team[Dropdown]" = "Orion". Add project in (WEB, API) to scope. If "my team" is defined by component: component in (checkout, payments).
You need a dashboard gadget for "issues that have been reopened this quarter". How?
"Reopened" = the status went from a done state back to an active one, or the resolution was cleared. Best expression: status CHANGED FROM "Done" TO "In Progress" AFTER startOfMonth("-3M") — but status names vary, so if your workflow has a dedicated Reopen transition or a "Reopened" status use that: status CHANGED TO "Reopened" AFTER -90d. A more workflow-agnostic version: resolution CHANGED FROM "Done" TO EMPTY AFTER startOfDay(-90d) (works if your Reopen transition clears Resolution, which it should). Save it as a filter, then point a Filter Results gadget or a Two Dimensional Filter Statistics gadget (e.g. project vs assignee) at it. Consider adding project in (...) and type != Sub-task.

Advanced deep

A JQL-heavy instance is slow: board loads, gadget refreshes, and automation JQL conditions all lag. Diagnose and remediate.
Where time goes: Jira JQL runs against a Lucene index; slowness comes from expensive query shapes, index size (driven by issue count and custom field count), and fan-out (many boards/gadgets/subscriptions/automation rules all re-running similar queries). Diagnose: (1) Identify the worst queries — slow-query logging (Data Center), the /rest/api/2/search timings, or an app; look for common offenders. (2) Check index health/size and reindex time; a bloated custom-field set (thousands of fields, unrestricted contexts) inflates every query. (3) Count active filter subscriptions and their cron alignment (everything at the top of the hour = a stampede) and the number of automation rules with JQL conditions/branches firing per event. (4) Look for dashboards with many heavy gadgets shared org-wide. Query-level fixes: avoid ~ free-text scans where a structured field would do; avoid negation-only queries (NOT IN, !=, IS NOT EMPTY with no positive anchor) — always include a selective positive clause (project, type, a date bound) so Lucene can narrow first; avoid ORDER BY on unindexed/large custom fields; replace WAS/CHANGED history queries (they hit the changelog, expensive) with a status/label the workflow sets, or run them less often; bound time ranges (created >= -90d) instead of "all time"; reference filters (filter = X) so the DB/index can reuse, and keep the base filter tight. System-level fixes: rationalize custom fields (fewer fields, restricted contexts) — often the biggest lever; stagger subscription cron times; consolidate duplicate boards/gadgets; cap automation rule fan-out (scope rules to fewer projects, add cheap conditions before expensive JQL branches, use scheduled rules with a JQL that's bounded); archive or split very large projects; ensure the instance is sized (memory, index on fast disk) and the index is not fragmented; on Cloud, lean on the platform but still fix query shapes and field bloat. Governance: a review for new custom fields, a limit on dashboard gadget count, and periodic cleanup of unused filters/subscriptions/rules.
Explain the difference between WAS/CHANGED and normal field operators, what data source they use, and their limitations for reporting.
Normal operators (=, IN, ~, IS EMPTY, >…) test the issue's current field values, served from the Lucene index — fast, and what boards/most filters use. WAS / WAS IN / WAS NOT test whether a field ever held a value (optionally within DURING (d1,d2), BEFORE, AFTER, ON, or BY user). CHANGED tests whether a field transitioned (with FROM, TO, AFTER, BEFORE, DURING, BY). Both read the issue change history (the changelog / change items), not just the current index — so they're more expensive and only work for fields Jira records history on (status, assignee, resolution, priority, fixVersion, sprint, custom fields with history — but not comment text, and historically not all custom field types). Reporting limitations: (1) They answer "did X happen" / "was it ever Y", not "how long was it in state Y" — you can't get cycle time, time-in-status, or age-in-column from JQL alone; that needs the Control Chart, a time-in-status app, or exporting the changelog. (2) You can't ORDER BY or aggregate on historical values — JQL returns a flat issue list, so "average time to resolve by month" isn't a JQL query. (3) DURING windows are inclusive/edge-case-sensitive and time-zone dependent. (4) History is only as good as the changelog — bulk edits, imports, and some automation/API writes may not create the change items you expect, so WAS/CHANGED can miss transitions that happened via those paths. (5) Deleted statuses/users still appear in history but by ID/name and can be awkward to match. (6) Performance: on large instances, unbounded WAS/CHANGED queries are slow — always add a positive selective clause and a date bound. For real flow metrics, use the built-in agile reports (Control Chart, CFD, cycle time), a marketplace time-in-status app, or pipe the changelog to a data warehouse; use WAS/CHANGED for targeted questions like "issues a specific person moved to Done last sprint".

Epics, Stories, Sub-tasks & Hierarchy

How Jira models "big thing → smaller things", and where the model runs out.

Notes

The default three levels

LevelTypeRole
Epic (level 1)EpicA body of work delivered over multiple sprints; groups stories.
Standard (level 0)Story / Task / BugA sprint-sized deliverable; the unit of estimation and board flow.
Sub-task (level −1)Sub-taskExecution breakdown of one story; can't stand alone.

How the links work

  • Sub-task → parent: a hard containment. The sub-task's parent is its story; it moves/clones with it; it shows nested on the board and issue view.
  • Story → Epic: historically the "Epic Link" custom field (company-managed classic); newer Jira (and team-managed, and the unified data model) uses "Parent" for this too. Cloud has largely unified on parent for both story→epic and sub-task→story.
  • Issue links (blocks, is blocked by, relates to, duplicates, clones) are peer relationships, not hierarchy — they don't roll up progress and can cross projects.

Above the epic

  • Base Jira stops at Epic. Advanced Roadmaps (Premium) adds configurable higher levels — commonly Initiative above Epic, and you can add more (e.g. Theme). These use parent links up the chain.
  • Without Premium, people fake higher levels with issue links or labels — which don't roll up and are fragile.

Rollup & progress

  • Epic progress on the board/roadmap = count (or estimate sum) of child issues by status category. Sub-task completion rolls into the story's progress bar.
  • Estimation lives at the story level. Epics aren't usually pointed (their size is the sum of their stories); sub-tasks aren't pointed (they'd double-count).
  • Cross-project epics: a story in project B can belong to an epic in project A (Cloud), but reporting and boards get messier — keep an epic's stories in one project where practical.

Practical guidance

  • Epic = a coherent outcome, 2–8 weeks, that you'd describe in one sentence to a stakeholder. If it never finishes, it's a label or a component, not an epic.
  • Story = independently valuable, fits in a sprint, testable. Use INVEST as a checklist.
  • Sub-task = "how", not "what". Use them for coordination within a story (design, backend, frontend, tests) — but don't over-decompose; many teams skip sub-tasks entirely.
  • Don't use sub-tasks to model separate deliverables (they can't be sprinted, ranked, or reported on independently, and moving the parent drags them along).
  • Keep hierarchy shallow: Initiative → Epic → Story → (maybe) Sub-task. Deeper "trees" via links become unmaintainable.
Cheat Sheet
  • Levels: Epic (1) → Story/Task/Bug (0) → Sub-task (−1). Premium adds Initiative+ above via Advanced Roadmaps.
  • Sub-task → parent = hard containment (moves/clones with parent, not on backlog alone). Story → Epic = "Epic Link" (classic) / parent (modern/Cloud).
  • Issue links (blocks / relates to / duplicates) = peer relationships, no rollup, can cross projects.
  • Estimate at the story level. Epic size = sum of stories; don't point epics or sub-tasks.
  • Epic progress = child issues by status category (count or estimate sum).
  • Epic = a finishable outcome (2–8 wks, one sentence). Never-ending → use a label/component. Story = INVEST. Sub-task = "how" not "what".
  • Don't model separate deliverables as sub-tasks (can't sprint/rank/report on them independently).
Q&A
What's the difference between a sub-task and an issue link?
A sub-task is a child in the hierarchy — it's owned by its parent story, contributes to its progress, moves and clones with it, and can't exist alone. An issue link (blocks, relates to, duplicates) is a peer relationship between two independent issues; it conveys dependency or relatedness but no ownership or rollup, and it can span projects.
How do you model something bigger than an epic?
With Jira Premium's Advanced Roadmaps, which adds configurable levels above Epic (typically "Initiative"), linked by the parent field. Without Premium there's no native level above Epic — teams approximate it with labels, components, or issue links, none of which roll up progress.
At which level do you put story points?
The story (standard issue) level. Epics are sized implicitly by the sum of their stories; sub-tasks aren't estimated because that would double-count the story's work. Some teams put remaining time on sub-tasks for a separate task-level burndown, but points stay on stories.
Why shouldn't you use sub-tasks to represent separate features?
Sub-tasks can't be added to a sprint independently, can't be ranked on the backlog, don't show as their own board cards in the normal flow, don't get their own epic link, and are dragged around whenever the parent moves or is cloned. Separate deliverables need to be standard issues (stories/tasks) so they can be planned, prioritised, and reported on individually.
What does an epic's progress bar actually measure?
The proportion of its child issues that are Done, either by count or by summed estimate depending on the view/config. Sub-task completion feeds into each story's own progress, which feeds the epic's. Issue-linked items are not counted.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are the three default hierarchy levels?
Epic → Story/Task/Bug → Sub-task.
Does a "blocks" link create hierarchy?
No — it's a peer relationship with no rollup.
What's needed to have a level above Epic?
Jira Premium / Advanced Roadmaps (adds Initiative and configurable levels).

Intermediate core

A team has "epics" that have been open for 8 months and keep growing. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
Those aren't epics — an epic should represent a finishable outcome delivered over a few weeks to a couple of months. An 8-month ever-growing container is really a theme / product area / component (e.g. "Search", "Billing"). Fixes: (1) Convert the long-lived container to a component or label (or a Premium Initiative if you need rollup and roadmap placement). (2) Carve the actual work into real epics with clear done criteria and target releases ("Search: add filters", "Search: relevance v2"), each closable in 2–8 weeks. (3) Re-parent the existing stories to the new epics; close the old mega-epic. (4) Going forward, add a definition-of-done and a target version to every epic at creation, and review epics that have been open > N sprints in backlog refinement. Never-closing epics break epic burn-up, roadmap forecasting, and "what did we ship" reporting.
How would you represent a cross-team feature where the frontend work is in project WEB and the backend in project API?
Options: (1) One epic, stories in both projects (Cloud allows a story's parent epic to be in another project). Put the epic in whichever project "owns" the feature; create WEB stories and API stories under it. Rollup works, but each team's board (filtered to its project) only shows its slice, and estimation/velocity stay per team. Watch that both projects' workflows/statuses are compatible enough for a shared epic view. (2) An epic per project, linked ("WEB epic" relates to "API epic", or an Initiative above both in Premium). Cleaner per-team ownership and reporting; the coordination point is the Initiative or the link, and you track combined progress at that level. (3) Use issue links ("WEB-123 is blocked by API-456") for the actual dependencies regardless of epic structure, so sequencing is visible on both boards. Recommendation: if you have Premium, an Initiative containing one epic per project is the cleanest; otherwise two linked epics plus dependency links between the stories, and a shared filter/dashboard to see the whole feature.

Advanced deep

Design an issue hierarchy and linking convention for a 200-engineer org doing quarterly planning, so roadmaps roll up and teams stay autonomous.
Levels (Advanced Roadmaps / Premium): Theme (optional, strategic, annual) → Initiative (a quarter-ish cross-team outcome, owned by a PM/lead) → Epic (a single team's 2–8 week deliverable, owned by that team) → Story/Task/Bug (sprint-sized, team's board unit) → Sub-task (optional, team's choice, execution only). Each level links up via parent. Ownership rule: an Epic and everything under it lives in one team's project; Initiatives live in a shared "Portfolio" project and have child epics across many team projects. This keeps team boards/velocity/workflows fully autonomous while the portfolio rolls up. Dependencies: use issue links ("is blocked by" / "blocks") between the specific stories/epics that actually depend on each other — not hierarchy. Advanced Roadmaps visualises these on the timeline and flags scheduling conflicts. A convention: dependencies are declared at the epic level for planning and refined to story level during execution. Estimation: points at story level only; team velocity forecasts the team's epics; Advanced Roadmaps rolls epic estimates/dates up to Initiatives with per-team capacity. Initiatives get a coarse T-shirt size and a target quarter, not points. Fields/labels: a "Team" field (or component) on every issue for cross-project slicing; a "Target Version"/"Fix Version" per team for release tracking; an "Initiative" is the parent, not a label. Quarterly planning: PMs define/adjust Initiatives in the Portfolio project; teams break them into Epics on their own projects and rank them; Advanced Roadmaps produces the combined timeline with dependencies and capacity, and scenario planning for trade-offs. Reporting: portfolio dashboards on Initiative status (child epic rollup), epic burn-up per team, dependency risk (open "blocked by" links crossing team boundaries), and a "no parent" hygiene filter. Governance: every Epic must have a parent Initiative (or an explicit "keep the lights on" bucket) and a done definition; every Initiative has an owner and target quarter; a monthly review closes stale epics and re-parents orphans. The result: teams run their own boards, workflows, and sprints untouched; the hierarchy plus links give leadership a rolled-up, dependency-aware roadmap without forcing process uniformity.
Cloud unified "Epic Link" and sub-task parent into a single parent field. What broke or changed, and what should teams watch for?
Historically, company-managed classic Jira had two distinct mechanisms: a custom field "Epic Link" connected a story to its epic, while "Parent" connected a sub-task to its story. Team-managed projects and the newer unified data model use one parent field for both story→epic and sub-task→story. Consequences and things to watch: (1) JQL — queries and filters written against "Epic Link" = KEY or the issuesInEpics() / parentEpic() functions may need to become parent = KEY (or use the newer parent in (...)); Atlassian kept some backward-compatible aliases but not everywhere, and third-party gadgets/apps that hard-coded "Epic Link" can break. (2) Automation rules referencing the Epic Link field or smart values like {{issue.epic.key}} vs {{issue.parent.key}} — audit and update. (3) CSV import mappings and REST API payloads — the API moved from the Epic Link custom field ID to fields.parent; integration code and scripts need updating. (4) Reports/dashboards and saved filters grouping by "Epic Link" — recheck. (5) Naming confusion — "Parent" now means different things depending on the issue's level, so UI and training need to be clear (a story's parent is an epic; a sub-task's parent is a story). (6) Advanced Roadmaps already used parent up the chain, so higher levels are consistent, but mixed old/new projects in one plan can behave inconsistently during transition. (7) Marketplace apps — some lagged the change; verify epic-related app features still populate. Practical steps for a team: inventory all filters/gadgets/automation/integrations mentioning "Epic Link" or epic, test them after the change, update to parent, and update any internal docs/runbooks. Data itself isn't lost — the relationships carry over — but anything that queried or wrote the old field needs attention.

Agile Reports & Metrics

Burndown, velocity, cumulative flow, control chart — what each shows and how to misread it.

Notes

Scrum reports

ReportShowsRead it for
Sprint BurndownRemaining work (points or issue count) vs time, with a guideline to zero and a scope-change lineAre we on track? Is scope creeping? Late-sprint cliff = stories only closed at the end
Sprint ReportCommitted vs completed vs incomplete vs added/removed; per-issue outcomeRetro facts: what we said, what we did, what changed
Velocity ChartCommitted vs completed points per sprint (last ~7)Forecasting (rolling average); consistency of estimation
Epic Burndown / Burnup & Release BurndownProgress toward an epic or version over sprints, incl. scope addedWill this epic/release land? How much is scope growth vs delivery?

Kanban / flow reports

ReportShows
Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD)Stacked count of issues in each status category over time. Band width = WIP in that stage; band widening = a bottleneck; vertical distance between top and bottom = total WIP; horizontal distance ≈ approximate lead time.
Control ChartCycle time (or lead time) per completed issue, with a rolling average and standard-deviation band. Outliers = investigate. Trend down = flow improving.
Cycle time report (newer boards)Distribution / scatter of cycle times, often with percentiles (e.g. "85% of issues finish within 6 days").

Definitions

  • Lead time: from request created (or committed) to delivered — the customer's wait.
  • Cycle time: from work started (entered In Progress) to done — the team's active time. Jira's Control Chart lets you pick the start/end statuses.
  • Throughput: issues completed per unit time.
  • WIP: items in progress at once. Little's Law: avg cycle time ≈ WIP / throughput — lower WIP → shorter cycle time.

Gotchas / how these mislead

  • Burndown by issue count hides that remaining issues are the big ones; by points hides that points were re-estimated mid-sprint.
  • Velocity only counts fully-done issues; a flat line at 0 for a sprint usually means "everything carried over", not "no work".
  • Control Chart cycle time depends on the chosen start/end columns and is skewed by items that sat in a status over a weekend/holiday, or were reopened (a second trip through).
  • CFD needs the board's columns to match real workflow stages; a giant "In Progress" column with everything in it tells you nothing.
