  • All of these break if the team games statuses (bulk-moving to Done at sprint end, skipping "In Review").
  • Comparing any of these across teams is invalid — different point scales, workflows, and DoD.

What to actually watch

Trend, not absolute: is cycle time stable or drifting? Is WIP creeping up? Is scope-change on the burndown consistently large? Is velocity predictable (variance low) rather than "high"? Predictability beats magnitude.

Cheat Sheet
  • Burndown: remaining work vs time + scope-change line. Late cliff = batch-closing at end.
  • Sprint Report: committed vs done vs incomplete vs added — retro facts.
  • Velocity: committed vs completed points/sprint; rolling avg to forecast; only fully-done counts.
  • CFD: band width = WIP per stage; widening band = bottleneck; top–bottom gap = total WIP; horizontal = ~lead time.
  • Control Chart: cycle time per issue + rolling avg ± stdev; pick start/end statuses; watch outliers & trend.
  • Lead time = created→done (customer wait). Cycle time = started→done (team active). Little's Law: cycle ≈ WIP / throughput.
  • Never compare metrics across teams. Value predictability (low variance) over big numbers.
Q&A
What does the scope-change line on a burndown tell you?
How much work was added to (or removed from) the sprint after it started. A burndown that isn't dropping might be fine if the flat part coincides with a jump in scope — the team is delivering but new work keeps arriving. Persistently large scope change means planning or interruption problems.
Lead time vs cycle time?
Lead time is the whole wait from when a request is created (or accepted) until it's delivered — what the requester experiences. Cycle time is the subset from when the team actually starts work (enters "In Progress") to done — the team's active handling time. Lead time includes backlog/queue time; cycle time doesn't.
How do you read a Cumulative Flow Diagram?
Each coloured band is a workflow stage; its vertical thickness at any date is how many issues are in that stage (WIP). A band that keeps widening over time is a bottleneck — work enters faster than it leaves. The vertical gap between the very top and bottom lines is total WIP; the horizontal gap between where a given quantity enters and exits approximates lead time. Parallel, roughly constant-width bands = healthy steady flow.
What does Little's Law imply for a team with long cycle times?
Cycle time ≈ WIP / throughput. If throughput (completion rate) is roughly fixed by capacity, the fastest lever to cut cycle time is to reduce WIP — start fewer things at once, enforce column limits, finish before starting. Adding more parallel work increases WIP and therefore cycle time.
Why can't you compare two teams' velocities?
Story points are calibrated to each team's own reference stories, skills, and codebase, and each team has its own workflow and definition of done. Team A's "20" and Team B's "20" represent different amounts of work, so the numbers aren't on the same scale. Compare a team only to its own history.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which report forecasts how much a team can take on next sprint?
The Velocity Chart (rolling average of completed points).
On a CFD, what does a widening band indicate?
A bottleneck at that stage — work is entering faster than it leaves.
Cycle time starts when an issue enters which status category?
In Progress (work actually started).

Intermediate core

A sprint burndown is flat for 8 days then drops straight to zero on the last day. What happened and what do you change?
Classic "big-bang" delivery: stories weren't being closed incrementally — either work was genuinely all finishing at once (stories too big / too interdependent), or the team wasn't updating statuses until the end, or everything piled up in "In Review" and got approved on the last day. Changes: (1) Slice stories smaller so several close every couple of days — target multiple items done by mid-sprint. (2) Enforce WIP limits and a "finish before you start" norm so work flows through Review instead of batching. (3) Make status updates a daily habit (or automate via PR/branch triggers) so the burndown reflects reality. (4) Watch the CFD — a fat "In Review" band confirms a review bottleneck; add reviewer capacity or a review SLA. (5) In the retro, check whether the sprint goal was actually met or just "everything got marked done". The flat-then-cliff shape means you have no early signal if the sprint is off track — that's the real risk to fix.
Leadership asks you to report "average cycle time" as a KPI and drive it down. What caveats do you raise and how do you set it up responsibly?
Caveats: (1) Cycle time depends entirely on the chosen start and end statuses — "In Progress→Done" vs "Committed→Released" give very different numbers; pick one and hold it constant. (2) The average is skewed by a few huge outliers; report the distribution and percentiles (median, 85th) instead — "85% of items finish within 6 days" is more honest and actionable. (3) It's gameable: split work into tiny issues, skip "In Review", or mark done early — so pair it with quality signals (reopen rate, escaped defects, review coverage). (4) Weekends/holidays and "waiting on customer" time inflate it — decide whether to use calendar or working days and whether to exclude explicit "blocked/waiting" statuses. (5) Reopened issues make two trips; decide how to count them. (6) Don't compare teams. Setup: define start = enters "In Progress", end = enters "Done", working days, exclude a "Blocked"/"Waiting" status if you have one; use the Control Chart / Cycle Time report per team; track the trend of the median and 85th percentile over rolling 4–8 weeks, not a single number; present alongside throughput and reopen rate so "faster" can't come at the cost of "worse". Frame it as a team-improvement signal in retros, not an individual or cross-team scorecard.

Advanced deep

Jira's built-in agile reports are limited (per-board, per-sprint, no cross-team roll-up, weak percentiles). Design a metrics pipeline that fixes this.
Source: extract issue data and, crucially, the changelog (status transitions with timestamps and author) via the Jira REST API (or Cloud's data connectors / a marketplace exporter) on a schedule. The changelog is what lets you compute time-in-status, cycle/lead time with any status boundaries, reopen counts, and flow efficiency — things JQL can't. Model: land it in a warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake/Postgres) as fact tables: issue, issue_status_history (issue, from_status, to_status, entered_at, duration), sprint_membership, plus dimensions (team, project, type, epic, initiative). Derive per-issue metrics: lead time (created→first Done), cycle time (first In Progress→Done), time in each status, number of Done→reopen transitions, whether it left/re-entered the sprint. Metrics layer: compute rolling percentiles (p50/p85/p95) of cycle & lead time per team per week; throughput (Done count/week); WIP over time (from history, count issues In Progress on each day) and flow efficiency (active time / total time); scope-change and say/do ratio per sprint; aging WIP (oldest unfinished item per stage); dependency/blocked time. Roll up epics→initiatives for delivery forecasts (Monte Carlo on historical throughput for "when will these N items be done, with confidence bands" — far better than velocity math). Presentation: dashboards (Looker/Grafana/Power BI) with team-level trend views, a portfolio view of initiative burn-up + forecast, and a "flow health" scorecard (cycle time trend, WIP trend, aging items, reopen rate). Explicitly no cross-team leaderboards. Governance: consistent status→category mapping across teams (or a per-team config table so boundaries are comparable), document each metric's definition, refresh daily, and validate against Jira's own Control Chart for a couple of teams as a sanity check. This gives cross-team roll-ups, proper percentiles, forecasting, and historical flexibility that the built-in per-board reports can't.
Explain flow efficiency and aging work-in-progress, why they often reveal more than cycle time or velocity, and how to surface them in Jira.
Flow efficiency = active (working) time ÷ total elapsed time for an item, as a percentage. Most teams discover it's shockingly low — often 15–40% — meaning items spend the majority of their life waiting (in queue columns, blocked, waiting for review, waiting on another team, waiting for deploy). This is more revealing than cycle time alone because it tells you where the time goes: if flow efficiency is 20%, hiring faster developers or working harder barely moves cycle time — you have to attack the queues and hand-offs. It's more revealing than velocity because velocity can look fine while every item still takes 3 weeks wall-clock due to waiting. Aging WIP = for every currently-unfinished item, how long has it been in progress (or in its current status). A simple chart of "days in progress" per open item, or the oldest item per column, surfaces stuck work now, while you can still act — unlike cycle time, which only tells you about items that already finished (a lagging indicator). An item aging well past the team's 85th-percentile cycle time is a live risk: escalate, unblock, split, or swarm it. Surfacing in Jira: (1) Flow efficiency needs the changelog — classify each status as "active" or "queue/wait", then compute active vs total from status history (a marketplace time-in-status app, or the warehouse pipeline). Add explicit "Waiting"/"Blocked" statuses so wait time is measurable rather than hidden inside "In Progress". (2) Aging WIP: a board quick filter or a dashboard filter gadget like statusCategory = "In Progress" AND status CHANGED TO "In Progress" BEFORE -5d ORDER BY updated; or use a board with card-age indicators / a marketplace "aging" gadget; or the newer Jira board's built-in "days in column" on cards. Review aging items daily at standup ("what's our oldest item and what does it need?"), and review flow efficiency + queue widths (from the CFD) in retros. The combination — where time is lost (flow efficiency / CFD) plus what's stuck right now (aging WIP) — drives concrete process fixes (review SLA, reduce hand-offs, WIP limits) in a way that a single cycle-time or velocity number never does.

Automation Rules

No-code "when this, if that, do this" rules — the modern replacement for most workflow scripting.

Notes

Rule structure

TRIGGER  (what starts the rule)
  → CONDITION(s)   (gate: stop if not met)
  → BRANCH        (optional: operate on related issues)
      → CONDITION
      → ACTION(s)
  → ACTION(s)     (do the thing)

Triggers

  • Issue events: created, updated, transitioned, assigned, commented, field value changed, linked.
  • Scheduled: cron or interval, optionally with a JQL to act on a set of issues each run.
  • Dev events: branch created, commit created, PR created/merged/declined, build/deployment status.
  • Incoming webhook: external system calls a rule URL (with a payload & optional issue list).
  • Manual: a button on the issue ("Run rule"), SLA threshold (JSM), form submitted, on a schedule.

Conditions & branches

  • Conditions: JQL condition, issue-fields condition, user condition, "related issues" condition (e.g. all sub-tasks are Done), advanced compare ({{smart value}} vs value).
  • Branches: re-scope the rest of the rule to related issues — sub-tasks, parent, epic, stories in epic, linked issues (by link type), or a JQL. Actions inside the branch run once per matched issue.
  • The "For current issue" vs branch distinction is the #1 source of bugs — forgetting a branch means you edit the trigger issue instead of the parent/children.

Actions

Edit issue / transition / assign / comment / add or remove label / create issue / create sub-tasks / clone / link issues / send email / send Slack or Teams message / send web request (outbound REST) / log action / set entity property / re-fetch issue data / lookup issues ({{lookupIssues}}) / create variable.

Smart values

{{issue.key}}  {{issue.summary}}  {{issue.assignee.displayName}}
{{issue.fields.customfield_10021}}   {{issue.Story Points}}
{{now}}  {{now.plusBusinessDays(3)}}
{{issue.fixVersions.name}}           {{#if}}  {{/}}  {{^}} (else)
{{fieldChange.fromString}}  {{fieldChange.toString}}
{{webhookData.some.path}}  {{triggerIssue.key}}
{{lookupIssues.size}}  {{#lookupIssues}}{{key}} {{/}}
{{sprint.name}}  {{comment.body}}

Smart values support text functions, math, list iteration ({{#list}}…{{/}}), conditionals, and date math — a small templating language.

Common recipes

  • When all sub-tasks → Done, transition the parent to Done (trigger: sub-task transitioned; branch: parent; condition: all sub-tasks Done).
  • When a story moves to In Progress, set the assignee, add it to the active sprint, comment on the epic.
  • Scheduled: find issues updated <= -5d AND status = "In Progress" → comment "@assignee still active?" and add a "stale" label.
  • On PR merged → transition to In Review; on deployment to prod → transition to Done and set Fix Version.
  • Sync a field from parent to all children on change (branch: children; edit issue).
  • Auto-triage: on create, if summary ~ "outage" set priority Highest, assign to on-call, notify Slack.

Scope, limits & gotchas

  • Rules are single-project, multi-project, or global (admin). Broad scope + broad trigger = lots of executions.
  • Execution limits (Cloud): monthly rule-run quotas by plan; heavy rules get throttled/queued. Watch the audit log for failures and "no actions performed".
  • Loop protection: by default a rule's own edits don't re-trigger it; "Allow rule trigger" on an action can create loops — use carefully. Rule chaining (rule A's action triggers rule B) is allowed but can cascade.
  • Actor: actions run as the "Automation for Jira" app user (or a chosen actor) — needs permission on the target project; shows as that user in history and notifications.
  • Prefer automation over workflow post-functions/scripts for maintainability — unless you need the change to be atomic with a transition.
Cheat Sheet
  • Rule = trigger → condition(s) → optional branch (related issues) → action(s).
  • Triggers: issue events, scheduled (+ JQL), dev events (PR/branch/deploy), incoming webhook, manual/SLA/form.
  • Branch re-scopes to sub-tasks / parent / epic / linked / JQL; actions run once per matched issue. Forgetting the branch = editing the wrong issue (the #1 bug).
  • Actions: edit/transition/assign/comment/label/create/clone/link/email/Slack/send web request/lookup issues.
  • Smart values: {{issue.key}}, {{issue.Story Points}}, {{now.plusBusinessDays(3)}}, {{fieldChange.toString}}, {{#lookupIssues}}…{{/}}, {{#if}}.
  • Scope: single / multi-project / global (admin). Cloud has monthly execution quotas; check the audit log.
  • Actions run as an actor (default "Automation for Jira") that needs permissions. Rule edits don't re-trigger unless you opt in (loop risk).
  • Prefer automation over post-functions/scripts unless the change must be atomic with a transition.
Q&A
What is a branch in an automation rule?
A step that changes which issue(s) the following conditions and actions apply to — from the trigger issue to related issues: its sub-tasks, its parent, its epic, stories in the epic, linked issues of a given type, or issues matching a JQL. Actions inside the branch execute once per matched related issue.
Why did my rule edit the wrong issue?
You almost certainly forgot a branch. Without one, every action operates on the issue that fired the trigger. To update the parent when a sub-task changes, you must add a "Branch: parent" step; to update children, "Branch: sub-tasks". This is the most common automation mistake.
How do you make a rule run over many issues on a schedule?
Use the Scheduled trigger with a cron/interval and tick "run a JQL search"; provide the JQL (e.g. stale issues). The rule then iterates the matching issues and runs the actions for each. Mind execution limits if the result set is large.
What are smart values?
A templating syntax ({{issue.key}}, {{now.plusDays(1)}}, {{fieldChange.toString}}…) for pulling data from the issue, the trigger, webhook payloads, and lookups into action fields — with text/date/math functions, list iteration, and conditionals. They're how you make actions dynamic.
Which user performs the actions, and why does it matter?
By default the "Automation for Jira" app account (you can override the actor per rule). That account must have permission on the target project or the action fails silently (check the audit log). It also appears as the author of comments, transitions, and notifications, which can confuse people or trip other rules that filter by user.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What are the three main parts of a rule?
Trigger, condition(s), action(s) — plus optional branches.
Where do you check why a rule didn't do anything?
The rule's audit log.
What smart value gives the current issue's key?
{{issue.key}}.

Intermediate core

Build the rule: when every sub-task of a story is Done, move the story to Done and comment on its epic.
Trigger: Issue transitioned — To status = Done, and restrict to issue type = Sub-task (add a "Issue fields condition: Issue Type is Sub-task" if the trigger can't). Branch: parent (the story). Condition inside the branch: "Related issues condition" → Sub-tasks → "all match" JQL statusCategory = Done (i.e. no sub-task is not-done). Also guard: parent's status is not already Done. Action (still in the parent branch): Transition issue to Done (choose the right transition; if none valid from current status, the rule logs an error — handle with a condition on the parent's current status). Then Branch: epic (parent of the story) → Action: Add comment — Story {{issue.parent.key}} completed: {{issue.parent.summary}} (or use a saved variable captured before the epic branch, since inside the epic branch {{issue}} is the epic). Edge cases: stories with zero sub-tasks (the "all done" condition is vacuously true — add "sub-tasks count > 0"); the transition not existing from certain statuses; and avoiding a loop if a Done transition itself fires other rules.
A global rule triggered on "issue updated" is hitting execution limits. How do you fix it?
"Issue updated" fires on every field change on every issue in every project — enormous volume. Fixes: (1) Use a more specific trigger — "Field value changed" for just the field you care about, or "Issue transitioned", or "Issue created". (2) Narrow the scope — make it a single- or multi-project rule instead of global, covering only projects that need it. (3) Add cheap early conditions — an issue-fields or JQL condition right after the trigger so the rule exits fast for non-matching issues (conditions are cheaper than actions but the run still counts; the bigger win is the specific trigger). (4) If it's really "react to any change of type X", consider a scheduled rule that batch-processes matching issues every N minutes instead of reacting in real time — far fewer executions. (5) Split into targeted per-project rules owned by those teams. (6) Check for rule chaining / loops inflating the count. (7) On Cloud, review the plan's monthly limit and the automation usage dashboard to see which rules dominate. General principle: the trigger should be as specific as possible; "issue updated" + global is an anti-pattern.

Advanced deep

An org has 400+ automation rules with lots of overlap, silent failures, and occasional loops. Design a cleanup and governance model.
Inventory: export all rules (REST API / the automation admin view). For each capture: scope (project/multi/global), trigger, actions, owner, last executed, success/failure counts, and monthly executions. Triage: (a) Dead — never executed in 90 days or always no-op → disable, then delete after a grace period. (b) Failing — audit log shows permission errors, invalid transitions, missing fields → fix or retire; the "Automation for Jira" actor needs project permissions everywhere it acts. (c) Overlapping — multiple rules reacting to the same trigger doing similar things (three rules all set assignee on create) → consolidate into one, or into a shared library rule. (d) Over-scoped — global rules that should be project rules; broad triggers ("issue updated") that should be specific → tighten. (e) Loop-prone — rules with "Allow rule trigger" on an edit action, or A→B→A chains → add guard conditions (only act if value differs), remove unnecessary re-trigger, document intended chains. Consolidate: define a small set of global rules for genuinely org-wide behaviour (SLA breach notifications, security-label handling), owned by the platform team; everything else is a project rule owned by that team. Use rule labels/naming conventions ([team] purpose) and put shared logic in fewer, well-documented rules. Governance going forward: (1) A request/review process for new global rules; project admins can create project rules freely but within guidance. (2) A monthly automation health dashboard: executions by rule, failure rate, quota usage, newly-failing rules → owners get alerted. (3) Naming + description standards; every rule states its purpose and owner. (4) A "no broad-trigger global rules" policy; prefer specific triggers and scheduled batch rules for bulk work. (5) Loop-safety checklist for reviewers. (6) Periodic (quarterly) prune of unused/failing rules. (7) Where a rule is really doing complex synchronous logic, evaluate whether it belongs as a workflow validator/post-function or an app instead. Execution: disable in waves with comms, keep an export to restore, and monitor the audit logs and quota after each wave.
Compare automation "send web request" + incoming webhooks against a real integration (app / middleware) for connecting Jira to other systems. When is each right?
Automation web request / webhook: a rule action POSTs JSON (built with smart values) to an external URL on some Jira event; an incoming-webhook trigger lets an external system push data into a rule (optionally with an issue list) which then edits issues. Pros: no code deployment, lives with your other rules, quick to build, good for simple one-directional notifications and light sync ("on transition to Done, notify our billing service"; "when CI calls this webhook, comment and transition"). Cons: (1) Reliability — limited ret/backoff on failed web requests, subject to automation execution quotas and throttling, and failures are only visible in the audit log (no alerting unless you build it). (2) Auth — you store a secret/token in the rule; limited to what headers/body you can template. (3) No state — can't easily do multi-step conversations, pagination, reconciliation, or dedupe; each run is stateless. (4) Payload limits and smart-value templating quirks for complex bodies. (5) Loose coupling to volume — a burst of events can hit quotas or rate-limit the target. (6) Hard to unit-test and version-control. Real integration (Marketplace app, or your own middleware / iPaaS like Workato/Zapier/n8n, or a service using the Jira REST API + registered webhooks): Pros: proper retries, dead-letter queues, backpressure, observability/alerting, secret management, stateful sync and reconciliation jobs, bidirectional field mapping with conflict handling, testing, and change management. Handles high volume and complex mappings. Cons: something to build/run/pay for; more moving parts; another deploy pipeline. When each: use automation web requests/webhooks for low-volume, low-stakes, mostly-notification or simple-trigger integrations where an occasional missed event is tolerable and you value speed and no-ops. Use a real integration when the sync is business-critical (billing, provisioning, compliance), high-volume, bidirectional, needs guaranteed delivery/reconciliation, involves complex mapping or many systems, or must be tested and audited. A common middle path: automation fires a webhook to your middleware, which owns the reliability, mapping, and state — keeping Jira-side config simple while getting production-grade delivery.

Projects, Schemes & Permissions

How Jira decides what a person can see and do — a stack of reusable schemes bolted onto each project.

Notes

Project styles

Company-managed (classic)Team-managed (next-gen)
ConfigShared schemes, changed by Jira adminsSelf-contained, changed by the project admin
ConsistencyHigh — many projects share one workflow/field/permission schemeLow — each project is its own island
Best forLarge orgs needing governance & cross-project reportingAutonomous teams wanting speed

The scheme stack (company-managed)

Each project is associated with one of each:

  • Permission scheme — who can do each permission (Browse, Create, Edit, Transition, Assign, Administer, Delete, Manage Sprints…). Grants are to: a project role, a group, a user, "Reporter", "Assignee", "Project Lead", a user custom field, or "Anyone".
  • Notification scheme — who gets emailed on each event.
  • Issue type scheme + issue type screen scheme — allowed types & their screens.
  • Workflow scheme — type → workflow.
  • Field configuration scheme — type → field configuration (required/hidden/default).
  • Screen scheme — operation → screen.
  • Issue security scheme (optional) — per-issue visibility levels.
  • Priority / component / version — some project-scoped, some via scheme.

Roles vs groups

  • Group = global membership list (e.g. jira-software-users), managed centrally; the same everywhere.
  • Project role = a named slot (Administrators, Developers, Users) whose members are set per project. Permission schemes grant to roles; each project decides who's in each role — so one shared permission scheme works for hundreds of projects.
  • Best practice: schemes grant to roles, not groups or users. Then onboarding a project = fill its role memberships; no scheme edits.

Global permissions & application access

  • Application access: which groups get a Jira Software / JSM / JWM license seat (controls who can log in at all).
  • Global permissions: Administer Jira, Browse Users, Create Shared Objects, Manage Group Filter Subscriptions, Bulk Change.
  • Project permissions (from the permission scheme) are per project; Project admin can manage roles, components, versions, and (limited) some config, but not global schemes.

Issue-level security

  • An issue security scheme defines security levels (e.g. "Reporter & Devs only", "Managers"). Setting a level on an issue hides it from everyone not in that level, even if they have Browse Project.
  • Used for sensitive work (HR, security incidents, embargoed features). Default level can be set per project.

Gotchas

  • Editing a shared scheme affects every project using it — check the "used by" list first. Copy the scheme if you need a variant.
  • "I can't see the issue" is usually: no Browse permission, an issue security level, or (for a board) an unshared filter.
  • Team-managed projects have their own simplified permission model (roles + "who can access") — not the scheme stack; migrating between styles remaps everything.
  • Granting via group in a scheme is a common source of "why does this contractor have edit rights everywhere".
Cheat Sheet
  • Company-managed: shared schemes, admin-governed, consistent. Team-managed: per-project config, autonomous, no scheme reuse.
  • Company-managed project = one each of: permission, notification, issue type (+ screen), workflow, field config, screen, optional issue security scheme.
  • Permission scheme grants each permission to: project role / group / user / Reporter / Assignee / Lead / user-field / Anyone.
  • Group = global list. Project role = per-project membership slot. Grant to roles, not groups/users — then onboarding = set role members, no scheme edits.
  • Application access = who gets a license/can log in. Global permissions = Administer Jira, Bulk Change, etc.
  • Issue security level hides an issue from anyone not in that level, overriding Browse Project.
  • Editing a shared scheme hits every project using it — check "used by", or copy first.
Q&A
Group vs project role — why prefer roles in permission schemes?
A group's membership is global and identical everywhere; a project role's membership is set per project. If a permission scheme grants "Edit Issues" to the Developers role, one scheme serves hundreds of projects and each project just populates its own Developers role. Granting to a group means every project sharing the scheme gives that whole group the same rights, and changing access requires scheme edits.
What does an issue security level do?
It restricts visibility of an individual issue to the users/roles/groups defined in that level. Someone with Browse Project permission still can't see an issue that has a security level they're not part of. It's for genuinely sensitive issues within an otherwise-visible project.
A user can log into Jira but sees none of a project's issues. Where do you look?
(1) The project's permission scheme — do they (via a role/group) have Browse Projects? (2) Issue security — are the issues at a level they're excluded from? (3) If it's via a board/filter, is the filter shared with them? (4) Application access — do they have a seat for the right product? Browse is the usual culprit.
What's the risk of editing a shared scheme?
Schemes are reused across many projects. Changing a workflow, permission, or field configuration in a shared scheme immediately changes behaviour for every project associated with it — possibly dozens you didn't intend. Always check the scheme's "used by" list; if only one project needs the change, copy the scheme and associate the copy.
What can a project administrator do vs a Jira administrator?
A project admin manages that project's role memberships, components, versions, and some project settings, and (with the right global setting) can do limited workflow/screen edits scoped to the project. A Jira admin manages the shared schemes, global permissions, application access, users/groups, and instance configuration.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which scheme controls who can transition issues?
The permission scheme (the "Transition Issues" permission).
Is a project role's membership global or per-project?
Per-project — each project sets who's in each role.
What overrides Browse Project permission to hide a single issue?
An issue security level.

Intermediate core

You're onboarding 30 new projects that should all behave identically. Design the config so it scales.
Build one set of shared schemes — a standard permission scheme, notification scheme, workflow scheme, issue type + screen schemes, field configuration scheme — with all permission grants made to project roles (Administrators, Developers, Users, plus any custom roles like "Product Owner", "Stakeholders"). Create a project template (or use "create with shared configuration" / a "Create project" automation) so each new project is associated with those schemes automatically. Then onboarding a project is purely: create it from the template, and populate its role memberships (add the team's group to Developers, PO user to Product Owner, etc.). No scheme edits, ever. Use groups synced from your IdP as the things you drop into roles, so access follows directory membership. Keep a naming convention for projects and roles. For any project that genuinely needs a variant, copy the relevant scheme and associate the copy — never edit the shared one. Document the standard so project admins don't reinvent it. Result: 30 (or 300) projects, one config to maintain, access changes = role/group membership only.
Security wants incident issues visible only to the security team and the reporter, in a project everyone can otherwise browse. How?
Use an issue security scheme. (1) Create a scheme with a security level, e.g. "Security Incident", whose members are: the security-team group (or a "Security" project role), plus "Reporter" (so the person who raised it keeps access), plus "Assignee" if handlers vary. (2) Associate the scheme with the project. (3) Set the default security level for the project's incident issue type to "Security Incident" — via a workflow post-function or an automation rule on create ("set security level" action), or the field configuration default — so new incidents are protected automatically; also add "Set Issue Security" permission to the security role so they can adjust it. (4) Ensure the "Set Issue Security Level" permission is granted appropriately and that automation's actor can set it. Now incident issues are invisible to the general population despite Browse Project, while normal issues in the project stay open. Test with a non-security user: they can see normal issues, not incidents; the reporter of an incident can still see their own.

Advanced deep

An instance has 150 permission schemes, 200 workflow schemes, and heavy use of direct user/group grants. Design a rationalization toward a governable model.
Assess: for each scheme, list projects using it and diff the schemes to find near-duplicates (they usually cluster into a handful of real patterns — "standard software", "service desk", "locked-down", "open/wiki-style"). Identify grants made to individual users or ad-hoc groups rather than roles — those are the governance debt. Target model: ~3–6 canonical permission schemes and a similar small number of workflow schemes, all granting to a fixed set of project roles (Admins, Developers, Users, Stakeholders/Viewers, plus maybe Approvers). All "who" decisions become role membership; all role members are IdP-synced groups, not individuals. Migrate: (1) Map each existing project to the closest canonical scheme; for genuine outliers, decide if the difference is essential (keep a 7th scheme) or can be absorbed (adjust and consolidate). (2) For each project, translate its current direct user/group grants into role memberships under the canonical scheme — e.g. everyone who had "Edit Issues" directly goes into that project's Developers role. Script this from the permission-scheme and role APIs. (3) Re-point the project to the canonical scheme, then verify with a permissions audit (pick sample users, compare effective permissions before/after). (4) Do the same for workflow schemes — consolidate to canonical workflows with consistent status categories (this also fixes cross-project reporting). (5) Delete the now-unused schemes after a soak period. Governance: (a) Remove the ability for project admins to request bespoke schemes without review; new projects use a template bound to canonical schemes. (b) Policy: schemes grant to roles only; roles contain groups only; groups come from the IdP. (c) A quarterly audit report: direct user grants (should be zero), schemes used by exactly one project (candidates to merge), and orphaned schemes. (d) Change control on canonical schemes (they affect many projects — PR-style review, staged rollout). (e) Document the canonical set and when to use each. Outcome: a handful of schemes, access = group-in-role, changes are auditable, and cross-project reporting works because workflows/statuses are consistent.
Explain how Jira computes whether a specific user may perform a specific action on a specific issue, covering application access, global, project, and issue-level checks.
The checks compose, roughly outermost to innermost: (1) Authentication & application access — is the user logged in and do they hold a license seat for the relevant product (Jira Software / JSM / JWM)? No seat → no access at all. Deactivated users fail here. (2) Global permissions — for instance-wide actions (Administer Jira, Bulk Change, Browse Users, Create Shared Objects) the user must be in a group granted that global permission. E.g. Bulk Change requires the global permission and the per-project permission for each affected project. (3) Project-level permission — the issue belongs to a project; that project is associated with a permission scheme. For the action's permission (Browse Projects, Create Issues, Edit Issues, Transition Issues, Assign Issues, Add Comments, Delete Issues, Administer Projects, Manage Sprints, …) Jira checks whether the user is covered by any grant for that permission: membership in a granted group, membership in a granted project role for this project, being the issue's Reporter or current Assignee or the Project Lead if those are granted, being named in a granted user custom field on the issue, or "Anyone" (for anonymous/public). Grants are additive — there is no explicit deny — so having the permission via one path is enough. Browse Projects is the gate for even seeing the issue; without it, nothing else matters. (4) Issue-level security — if the project has an issue security scheme and the issue has a security level set, the user must be a member of that level (via user, group, role, Reporter, Assignee, or user-field membership). If not, the issue is invisible regardless of Browse Project — this is a hard filter applied to search results, boards, links, and direct URL access. (5) Workflow constraints — for a transition specifically, the workflow's conditions on that transition can further restrict (e.g. "only the assignee", "only a user in role X", "only if sub-tasks are done"), and workflow status properties like jira.issue.editable = false can disable editing while in a status even for users with Edit permission. Validators then run on submit. (6) Field-level — the field must be on the relevant screen and not hidden by the field configuration; some apps ("behaviours") add per-field, per-context restrictions. (7) Comment visibility / property-level restrictions can hide specific comments by role/group. Net: the user may do the action iff (has a seat) AND (any needed global permission) AND (covered by a grant for the project permission) AND (passes issue security if set) AND (passes workflow condition/property for a transition) AND (the field/screen allows it for an edit). All permission grants are OR-ed within a permission; the layers are AND-ed. Team-managed projects collapse layers 2–3 into the project's own simplified access + role settings but the conceptual order (access → project permission → issue security → workflow) is the same.

Dev Tools, Releases & Integrations

Wiring Jira to source control, CI/CD, chat, and other systems — and shipping via versions.

Notes

The dev-tools integration

  • Connect GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket (and CI/CD, feature-flag, deployment tools) so Jira shows a Development panel on the issue: branches, commits, pull requests, builds, deployments.
  • The link is made by putting the issue key in the branch name, commit message, or PR title (PROJ-123 fix null check). Jira scans for keys and associates them.
  • Powers workflow triggers ("branch created" → In Progress), automation dev triggers, and the "Releases" / deployment views.

Smart commits

Commands in a commit message act on the referenced issue (if the author maps to a Jira user with permission):

PROJ-123 #comment Fixed the race condition
PROJ-123 #time 2h 30m Investigating and patching
PROJ-123 #transition "In Review"
PROJ-123 PROJ-124 #close #comment batched fix     (multiple issues, multiple commands)
  • Commands: #comment, #time (work log), and any transition by name/alias (#in-progress, #done).
  • Requires smart commits enabled and the committer's email to match a Jira account with the right permissions.

Versions & releases

  • A version is a project-scoped release marker with a name, optional start/release dates, and a state (unreleased / released / archived).
  • Issues get Fix Version/s = "planned for / delivered in". The Releases page shows each version's issues by status and a progress bar; you Release a version when it ships (optionally moving open issues to another version).
  • Release Burndown report forecasts which sprint a version completes in, accounting for scope added.
  • With the dev integration, a version can show associated commits, PRs, and deployments, and you can gate/track "is everything for 2.4 merged and deployed".

APIs & extensibility

  • REST API (v2/v3 on Cloud, plus the Agile and Service Management APIs): CRUD issues, search (JQL), transitions, worklogs, versions, comments, users, webhooks. Auth: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) / API tokens (Basic) on Cloud; PATs on Data Center.
  • Webhooks: register a URL to receive issue/version/sprint/project events as JSON (filtered by JQL). Automation's "send web request" + "incoming webhook" cover many cases without code.
  • Apps: Connect / Forge (Cloud) and P2 plugins (Data Center) extend the UI, add panels, workflow extensions (ScriptRunner), and integrations. The Marketplace is large; each app is a dependency, a cost, and a security review.
  • Built-in native integrations: Confluence (linked pages, requirements), Bitbucket/GitHub, Opsgenie, Slack/Teams, Jira Service Management, Assets/Insight.

Good practice

  • Standardize branch/PR naming to always include the issue key — it's what makes everything downstream work.
  • Use automation for status sync from dev events rather than asking devs to remember smart-commit transitions.
  • Keep integration credentials as service accounts with least privilege; rotate tokens.
  • Vet Marketplace apps for data residency, permissions requested, and vendor support before install; minimize the count.
  • For high-volume or bidirectional sync, use middleware/an integration platform, not raw automation web requests (delivery guarantees, mapping, reconciliation).
Cheat Sheet
  • Link code to issues by putting the issue key in branch name / commit / PR title → Development panel (branches, commits, PRs, builds, deploys) + dev triggers.
  • Smart commits: PROJ-123 #comment ..., #time 2h, #transition "In Review" (or #done). Needs enablement + committer email = Jira user with permission.
  • Version = project release marker (name, dates, unreleased/released/archived). Fix Version/s = planned/delivered in. Releases page + Release Burndown forecast.
  • REST API (v2/v3, Agile, JSM): issues, JQL search, transitions, worklogs, versions, webhooks. Auth: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) / API token (Cloud), PAT (DC).
  • Webhooks: URL gets JSON on events, JQL-filtered. Automation "send web request" / "incoming webhook" for no-code.
  • Apps: Forge/Connect (Cloud), P2 (DC). Each = dependency + cost + security review; minimize.
  • Standardize key-in-branch naming; sync status via automation not manual smart commits; least-privilege service accounts; middleware for heavy sync.
Q&A
How does Jira know a pull request belongs to an issue?
It scans branch names, commit messages, and PR titles/descriptions for text matching the issue-key pattern (PROJ-123) from a connected repo. Any it finds get linked, and the PR/branch/commit shows in that issue's Development panel. No key in the branch/PR = no link.
What are smart commits and their requirements?
Commands embedded in a commit message that act on referenced issues: #comment (add a comment), #time (log work), and #<transition> (move the issue). They require smart commits to be enabled for the repo connection and the committer's email to resolve to a Jira user who has permission to perform the action.
What's the difference between a version and Fix Version?
A version is the release object defined in the project (name, dates, released/unreleased state). Fix Version/s is the field on an issue that points at one or more versions, meaning "targeted for / shipped in". The Releases page and release reports are driven by which issues carry which Fix Version.
When should you use a webhook + middleware instead of an automation "send web request"?
When the integration is business-critical, high-volume, bidirectional, or needs guaranteed delivery, retries, dead-lettering, field mapping with conflict resolution, or reconciliation. Automation web requests are fine for low-volume notifications and simple triggers but have limited retry/observability and count against execution quotas.
What are the costs of installing a Marketplace app?
Licensing cost (usually per-user), a new external dependency that can lag Jira upgrades or break, the permissions and data access it requests (a security/compliance review — especially data residency for Cloud apps), added instance load, and operational ownership. Keep the installed set minimal and periodically review for unused apps.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What must be in a branch name for Jira to link it to an issue?
The issue key (e.g. PROJ-123).
Which field ties an issue to a release?
Fix Version/s.
Name a smart commit command.
#comment, #time, or a transition like #done.

Intermediate core

Design the flow so an issue moves through statuses automatically as code progresses, and Fix Version is set on deploy.
Connect the repo + CI/CD to Jira so dev events flow in. Then use automation rules (more reliable than relying on devs' smart commits): (1) Trigger "Branch created" (key in branch name) → if issue is in "To Do", transition to "In Progress" and set assignee to the branch author. (2) Trigger "Pull request created" → transition to "In Review"; add a comment linking the PR. (3) Trigger "Pull request merged" → transition to "Ready for Deploy" (or back to "In Progress" on decline). (4) Trigger "Deployment successful" with environment = production → transition to "Done", and set Fix Version to the current unreleased version (smart value {{issue.project.versions}} filtered to unreleased, or a fixed version per the deploy's tag passed via the deployment info / an incoming webhook from CI carrying the version name). (5) Optionally, when that version is fully deployed, an automation or a person Releases it on the Releases page. Guard each rule with a condition on the issue's current status so out-of-order events don't misfire, and handle the "no valid transition" case. Keep issue keys mandatory in branch names via a repo hook so nothing falls through.
A team wants "release notes" auto-generated from Jira for each version. How would you build it?
The data is already there: issues with fixVersion = "2.4.0". Options: (1) Automation: a rule triggered when a version is released (or a manual/scheduled rule) that runs a lookupIssues with JQL fixVersion = "{{version.name}}" AND statusCategory = Done, then builds a formatted string with {{#lookupIssues}}- {{key}} {{summary}} ({{issuetype.name}}){{/}} grouped by issue type or a "Release Note" custom field, and posts it to Confluence (via "send web request" to the Confluence API), Slack, or an email. (2) REST API script in CI: on tag/release, query the Jira search API for that fixVersion, filter to Done, group by type/label, render Markdown/HTML, and publish to the docs site / GitHub release / Confluence. (3) A Marketplace release-notes app if you want templating and history without building it. Refinements: add a "Release Notes" rich-text custom field so writers can craft a user-facing line per issue (fall back to summary); exclude internal/chore types via a label or type filter; include the version's release date and a link to the Jira Releases page. The automation route is quickest for a single destination; the CI-script route is best if release notes must live alongside the release artifact and be version-controlled.

Advanced deep

Design a two-way sync between Jira and an external system of record (e.g. a customer support tool or a hardware PLM), covering mapping, conflicts, delivery, and failure handling.
Don't do this with raw automation web requests — use a dedicated integration service (custom, or an iPaaS like Workato/Tray/n8n, or a purpose-built sync app like Exalate/Unito). Architecture: each side emits events (Jira webhooks filtered by JQL for the projects/types in scope; the other system's webhooks or a poll) into the integration service, which owns a mapping store (external ID ↔ Jira issue key) and a queue with retries and a dead-letter queue. Field mapping: an explicit, versioned config — which fields sync, in which direction (some bidirectional, some one-way: e.g. status bidirectional, "internal notes" Jira→only), and value transforms (status name ↔ external state enum, priority scales, user identity mapping by email, attachments, comments with author attribution). Decide the authoritative side per field to bound conflicts. Conflict handling: because both sides can change the same field between syncs, use one of: last-writer-wins with a timestamp/version check (simple, can lose data), authoritative-side-wins per field (clear, requires the mapping decision), or surface a conflict for a human (safest, more friction). Track a per-record sync version/hash so you only push real changes and can detect divergence; run a periodic reconciliation job that compares both sides for mapped records and repairs drift, reporting anomalies. Loop prevention: tag changes made by the sync (a marker field, a known actor account, or an idempotency key) so an inbound update the service just wrote doesn't bounce back; debounce rapid successive events. Delivery: at-least-once with idempotent apply (keyed by external event ID + target field state) so retries are safe; DLQ for poison messages with alerting; backpressure so a burst on one side doesn't overwhelm the other's rate limits (respect Jira's REST rate limits and 429s with backoff). Identity: map users by email; have a fallback "integration user" for unmapped authors, and don't leak internal usernames externally. Security: least-privilege service accounts/tokens on both sides, rotate them, restrict the webhook endpoints (shared secret / signature verification), and review data-residency for anything crossing boundaries. Observability: dashboards for sync lag, queue depth, error/DLQ rate, conflicts/day, and reconciliation diffs; alert on lag > threshold or DLQ > 0. Rollout: start one-directional and read-only to validate mapping, then enable write, then the second direction; keep the field-mapping config in version control with change review. Failure modes to plan for: one system down (queue and catch up; reconciliation heals gaps), schema change on either side (mapping config + tests catch it; alert on unmapped fields), rate limiting, duplicate creates (dedupe on mapping store before create), and deletes/merges (define behaviour — usually don't propagate deletes automatically).
Compare Forge, Connect, and Data Center P2 apps as extension models, and what that means for an org choosing where to run Jira.
P2 plugins (Data Center / Server): Java apps installed into the Jira process (OSGi), with deep API access — custom workflow functions, listeners, servlets, database access, scheduled jobs, UI via web-panels/velocity/React. Power: near-unlimited. Cost: they run in-process, so a bad app can destabilize Jira, they must be recompiled/tested against each Jira version (upgrade friction), and security is "trust the JAR". This is why Data Center instances often accrete ScriptRunner + a dozen plugins and upgrades become projects. Connect (Cloud): the app is a remote web service you host; Jira calls it via signed iframe/webhook and it calls back via REST with a JWT/OAuth. It can add UI panels, webhooks, workflow post-functions (as remote calls), and modules declared in a descriptor. Isolation is good (it's not in Jira's process), but it's your infrastructure to run, latency is a factor (every panel is a remote round trip), and capabilities are limited to what the Connect framework exposes. Forge (Cloud): Atlassian-hosted serverless platform — you write functions (Node) and UI (UI Kit or custom UI) that Atlassian runs, with a declared-permissions manifest, managed storage (Forge KV / SQL), and egress controls. Benefits: no infra to run, stronger security/data-residency story (runs in Atlassian's cloud, data governance built in), smoother install/marketplace, and it's Atlassian's strategic direction. Limits: young platform with evolving quotas/APIs, compute/runtime constraints, and some deep customizations still aren't possible that a P2 plugin could do. What it means for hosting choice: (1) If your value depends on heavy customization — complex scripted workflows, DB-level integrations, bespoke schedulers — Data Center + P2/ScriptRunner still offers the most power, at the price of upgrade toil and self-hosting. (2) If you want managed, secure, and lower-ops, Cloud with Forge apps (and Connect where needed) is the direction, but audit that the specific apps you rely on exist for Cloud and cover your use cases (the "can we migrate?" question is usually "are our critical apps Cloud-ready and do they preserve our config?"). (3) Automation rules now cover a large fraction of what people used post-functions/scripts for, reducing the need for code extensions on either platform — lean on automation first. (4) For new integrations prefer REST API + webhooks from an external service over an installed app when you can, so you're not coupled to a plugin's lifecycle. Net: Cloud/Forge for governance, security, and low ops with "good enough" extensibility that keeps improving; Data Center/P2 when you genuinely need in-process power and accept the operational and upgrade burden.

How a CDN Works: PoPs, Anycast & Edge

Push copies of content close to users, and route each user to the nearest copy.

Notes

The core idea

  • A CDN is a globally distributed set of caching servers (edge servers) in many Points of Presence (PoPs) near end users.
  • User requests are routed to a nearby PoP instead of your origin. If the edge has the response cached (HIT), it serves it immediately. On a MISS it fetches from origin (or a mid-tier), caches it, and serves it.
  • Wins: lower latency (RTT to a nearby PoP « RTT to origin), origin offload (fewer requests reach your servers), absorbs traffic spikes, terminates TLS close to the user, and provides a security perimeter (DDoS absorption, WAF).

How users reach the nearest PoP

MethodHow
AnycastThe same IP is announced from every PoP via BGP; the internet routes the packet to the topologically nearest one. Simple, fast failover, but "nearest by BGP" ≠ "lowest latency".
DNS-based (unicast) steeringThe CDN's authoritative DNS returns a different edge IP depending on the resolver's location/EDNS-client-subnet, load, and health. More control (geo, capacity, RUM-informed), but tied to DNS TTLs and resolver behaviour.
Often both: DNS picks a region/cluster, anycast within it.

Request flow (cache miss)

client --DNS--> nearest edge IP
client --TLS+HTTP--> edge PoP
  edge: cache lookup by cache key -> MISS
  edge --> (optional) regional mid-tier / origin shield  -> MISS
  shield --> origin (your server / object storage)
  origin --> response (+ Cache-Control)
  cached at shield and edge per TTL
  edge --> client   (X-Cache: MISS)
next client in that PoP --> HIT (served from edge, no origin hop)

Key terms & metrics

  • Cache HIT ratio = hits / total requests (by request count and by bytes). Origin offload = 1 − (origin requests / total).
  • TTFB (time to first byte) — dominated by cache state and distance.
  • Cache key — what identifies a cached object (see the Cache Keys topic).
  • Edge / mid-tier / shield / origin — cache layers; more layers → better offload, slightly higher miss latency.
  • PoP vs region; edge compute — run code at the PoP.

What CDNs are good/bad at

  • Great: static assets (JS/CSS/images/video, downloads), cacheable API responses, TLS termination, DDoS/WAF, global reach without global infra.
  • Harder: highly personalized/uncacheable dynamic content (mitigated by micro-caching, edge compute, or just using the CDN as a fast, secure transit + TLS layer — "dynamic acceleration" with keep-alive pooled connections and optimized routes to origin).
Cheat Sheet
  • CDN = edge caches in many PoPs near users; serve HIT locally, MISS → fetch from origin/shield, cache, serve.
  • Benefits: latency (near PoP), origin offload, spike absorption, TLS at edge, DDoS/WAF perimeter.
  • Routing to nearest PoP: anycast (same IP everywhere, BGP routes it) and/or DNS steering (geo/health/RUM-aware, TTL-bound). Often both.
  • Layers: client → edge → (mid-tier / origin shield) → origin. More layers = better offload, slightly slower miss.
  • Metrics: cache hit ratio (by requests & bytes), origin offload %, TTFB, X-Cache: HIT/MISS.
  • Best for static assets, cacheable API, TLS, security; dynamic/personalized needs micro-caching / edge compute / "dynamic acceleration".
Q&A
What's the difference between a cache HIT and a MISS?
On a HIT the edge server already has a fresh copy of the response for that cache key and serves it directly — no origin contact, minimal latency. On a MISS it has no fresh copy, so it fetches from the next layer (mid-tier/shield/origin), stores the result per its caching rules, and then serves it; that request pays the origin round trip.
Anycast vs DNS-based routing to the nearest edge?
Anycast announces one IP from all PoPs and lets BGP deliver the packet to the nearest one — simple and with instant failover, but "nearest" is by network topology, which isn't always lowest latency. DNS-based routing returns different edge IPs based on the client's location, PoP health, and capacity (and can use RUM data), giving finer control at the cost of being bound to DNS TTLs and resolver quirks. Many CDNs combine them.
What is origin offload and why does it matter?
The fraction of requests (or bytes) served from cache without touching your origin. High offload means your origin infrastructure can be far smaller and cheaper, survives traffic spikes and viral events, and is shielded from most attack traffic. It's the primary cost/reliability benefit of a CDN alongside latency.
Can a CDN help with uncacheable dynamic content?
Yes, though less dramatically. It still terminates TLS near the user, keeps warm pooled connections to origin, and routes over optimized backbone paths ("dynamic acceleration"), cutting connection-setup and transit latency. You can also micro-cache for a few seconds, cache fragments, or run logic at the edge to assemble/personalize responses.
Why put an origin shield between edge PoPs and the origin?
Without it, a miss at any of dozens of PoPs goes straight to origin, so a cold cache or a purge can hit the origin from many places at once. A shield is a single (or few) intermediate cache that all edges consult on a miss, so the origin sees at most one request per object and benefits from request collapsing across the whole CDN.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does a CDN edge server do on a cache HIT?
Serves the cached response directly, with no request to the origin.
What routing technique uses one IP announced from many locations?
Anycast.
What does "origin offload" measure?
The proportion of traffic served from cache without reaching the origin.

Intermediate core

Your CDN hit ratio is 60% but should be ~95% for a static site. List the likely causes.
(1) Missing/short cache headers — origin sends no Cache-Control, or no-store/private, or a tiny max-age; the CDN then doesn't cache or expires constantly. (2) Cache key fragmentation — the CDN is keying on the full query string (cache-buster params, analytics params, UTM tags) or on cookies or User-Agent, so each variation is a separate object with near-zero reuse. (3) Vary header on something high-cardinality (Vary: User-Agent). (4) Set-Cookie on responses (many CDNs won't cache a response that sets a cookie). (5) Purge/deploy storms — every deploy purges everything, so caches are perpetually cold. (6) Many small PoPs with low per-PoP traffic and short object lifetime — objects evicted before reuse; an origin shield / larger cache tier helps. (7) Cacheable methods only — lots of POST/authenticated traffic. (8) Response varies (different bytes each time, e.g. an embedded timestamp/nonce) so revalidation always misses. Fix: set long max-age/s-maxage + immutable on hashed assets, normalize the cache key (strip unknown query params, ignore cookies for static paths), remove Set-Cookie from static responses, use content-hashed filenames so deploys don't need purges, and add a shield tier.
A user in Sydney reports the site is slow; your CDN has a Sydney PoP. How do you investigate the routing?
(1) Confirm which PoP they hit — check response headers the CDN adds (X-Served-By, CF-Ray, X-Amz-Cf-Pop, Fastly-Debug, or a Server-Timing/PoP header); or have them load a debug endpoint. If it's not Sydney, routing is the issue. (2) DNS — what IP does their resolver get for your hostname? If they use a public resolver (8.8.8.8) far from them without EDNS Client Subnet, DNS-based CDNs may steer them to the resolver's location, not theirs. Check with dig from their network vs a Sydney resolver. (3) Anycast path — run mtr/traceroute from their machine to the edge IP; look for the traffic leaving Australia (backhauled to Singapore/US) due to their ISP's peering/transit choices — a known anycast pitfall. (4) Cache state — is it a MISS every time (cold PoP, low traffic, or bad cache key) so every request pays the origin RTT from Sydney? Check X-Cache and hit ratio for that PoP. (5) Origin distance — if content is uncacheable and origin is in the US, every request is a Sydney↔US round trip regardless of the PoP; consider a closer origin, edge compute, or micro-caching. (6) TLS/protocol — are they getting HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, session resumption, and 0-RTT? A renegotiation or downgrade adds RTTs. (7) Raise a ticket with the CDN including the trace and PoP headers — ISP peering issues often need the CDN to adjust announcements or add capacity/peering.

Advanced deep

Design the CDN layer for a global product: static assets, a cacheable read API, user-specific pages, video, and strict availability. Cover topology, cache tiers, and origin protection.
Topology: front everything with the CDN (anycast + DNS steering). One hostname strategy: static.example.com (assets), api.example.com (API), www.example.com (pages), video.example.com (streaming) — each mapped to a CDN config with its own caching policy. Static assets: content-hashed filenames, Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, no purge on deploy (new hash = new URL). Serve from object storage as origin. Aim >99% offload. Brotli/gzip at edge, HTTP/2+3. Cacheable read API: origin sends Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=86400 on the GET endpoints that tolerate it; normalize the cache key (whitelist query params, ignore auth cookies for public reads, Vary: Accept-Encoding only); use surrogate keys / cache tags per entity so a write can purge exactly the affected objects. Micro-caching (1–5s) even for "uncacheable" hot endpoints collapses stampedes. User-specific pages: don't full-page cache; cache the shell / static fragments; personalize at the edge (edge compute reads a session token, injects user bits, or does ESI-style composition) or client-side after a cached shell. Use the CDN for TLS termination + dynamic acceleration (pooled keep-alives, optimized routes) even when the response itself isn't cached. Video: HLS/DASH segments are highly cacheable (long TTL on segments, short on manifests); use a dedicated streaming config, large cache footprint, and possibly a separate video CDN. Signed URLs/tokens for entitlement. Cache tiers: edge → regional mid-tier → origin shield (one per origin region) so origin sees ~1 request per object even during global cold starts and purges; request collapsing at every tier. Origin protection: origin only accepts connections from the CDN (IP allowlist / mTLS / a shared secret header the CDN adds); WAF + rate limiting + bot management at the edge; L3/4 DDoS absorbed by the CDN's anycast capacity; stale-if-error and a static fallback page so an origin outage still serves cached/last-known content. Availability: multi-origin with health checks and automatic failover at the CDN; consider multi-CDN (two providers, DNS or RUM-based steering) for provider-level redundancy, with config parity enforced via IaC. Observability: per-config hit ratio, offload, edge/origin latency, 5xx by PoP, purge latency, WAF blocks; RUM for real user latency by geo; alerts on offload drop or origin error spike. Ops: all CDN config as code (Terraform), staged (dev/stage/prod configs), and a runbook for purge, failover, and a CDN-provider outage.
Explain request collapsing (a.k.a. coalescing) and the thundering-herd problem at a CDN, including how it interacts with cache tiers and stale content.
Thundering herd / cache stampede: when a popular object expires (or is purged, or was never cached), many concurrent client requests for it all miss at once. Without protection, each miss triggers its own fetch to the next layer, so the origin suddenly receives N identical requests — potentially overwhelming it exactly when the object is hot. Request collapsing: the cache detects that a fetch for a given cache key is already in flight and makes the other concurrent requests wait for that single fetch, then serves them all from the one response. So N concurrent misses become 1 origin request. This happens per cache node, so with many edge PoPs you still get up to (number of PoPs) requests to origin for a globally hot object at expiry — which is why you add a mid-tier / origin shield: all edges collapse locally, then send their one request each to the shield, which collapses again, so the origin sees exactly one. Collapsing across the whole CDN requires that shield layer. Interaction with stale content: stale-while-revalidate is the other half of the fix — on expiry the cache serves the slightly-stale copy immediately to everyone and does a single background revalidation, so no client waits and origin gets one request. stale-if-error serves stale if the revalidation fails, protecting against origin blips. Together: collapsing bounds concurrency to 1 per tier; SWR removes the latency penalty and further reduces synchronized load; the shield makes "1 per tier" mean "1 total". Edge cases: collapsing only helps for identical cache keys — if the key is fragmented (query params, cookies) the "same" content is many keys and none collapse; collapsing can add latency if the single origin fetch is slow and many requests block on it (some CDNs cap the wait or let a few through); and non-cacheable responses (the origin says no-store) can't be collapsed/served stale, so a hot uncacheable endpoint still herds — hence micro-caching (even 1s) plus SWR is a big win there. Purges should be "soft" (mark stale, revalidate on next request with SWR) rather than "hard" (evict, forcing blocking misses) precisely to avoid a self-inflicted herd.

Cache Keys, Variants & Normalization

Two requests share a cached object only if they produce the same cache key — get this wrong and your hit ratio collapses.

Notes

What forms the default cache key

  • Typically: scheme + host + path + (all or part of) the query string. Method is usually implicit (only GET/HEAD cached).
  • Some CDNs add things by default; most let you fully customize the key.
  • Everything in the key multiplies the number of stored objects for the "same" content. Fewer things in the key = higher reuse = higher hit ratio.

Query string handling

PolicyEffect
Include full query string (default on many)Every distinct URL is a separate object. Cache-busters, ?utm_*, ?fbclid, session tokens → fragmentation.
Ignore query string entirelyMax reuse, but dangerous if params actually change the response (?page=2, ?size=large).
Allowlist specific paramsBest practice: key on only the params that change the content (v, page, lang); drop the rest.
Denylist / sort paramsStrip known tracking params; sort remaining so ?a=1&b=2 == ?b=2&a=1.

Vary — response-driven variants

  • Vary: Accept-Encoding — store gzip / br / identity separately. Fine (low cardinality).
  • Vary: Accept-Language — acceptable if you serve a few languages and normalize.
  • Vary: User-Agent — disastrous: thousands of UA strings → near-zero reuse. Use device detection at the edge that maps UA to a small class (mobile/desktop/tablet) and key on that instead.
  • Vary: Cookie — usually means "don't cache"; if you must, normalize to the one cookie that matters.

Cookies

  • Many CDNs won't cache a response that contains Set-Cookie (it's assumed user-specific). Strip Set-Cookie from static/cacheable responses at the edge or origin.
  • By default request cookies often aren't in the key, but "cache by cookie X" is a common option for A/B tests or logged-in vs anonymous splits — keep the cookie value space tiny.

Deliberate cache splitting (good uses)

  • Device class: mobile vs desktop variants of an HTML page.
  • Country/region: currency, legal, language — key on a geo header the CDN injects.
  • A/B test bucket: key on a normalized bucket=A|B cookie/header, not a raw experiment ID.
  • Auth state: anon vs logged-in (cache the anon version aggressively; bypass or short-TTL the logged-in one).
  • Content negotiation: WebP/AVIF vs JPEG based on Accept, normalized to 2–3 buckets.

Normalization checklist

  • Lowercase host; strip default ports; collapse duplicate slashes; decide on trailing slash.
  • Query: allowlist meaningful params, drop tracking params, sort, lowercase keys if safe.
  • Fold header-based variance into small enumerated buckets (device, geo, encoding, language, auth).
  • Remove Set-Cookie from cacheable responses; don't Vary on high-cardinality headers.
  • Measure: objects per URL, hit ratio by path, and the top cache keys by count.
Cheat Sheet
  • Default key ≈ scheme + host + path + query (GET/HEAD only). Everything in the key multiplies stored objects → keep it minimal.
  • Query string: allowlist the params that change content; strip utm_*/fbclid/cache-busters; sort params.
  • Vary: Accept-Encoding ok; Accept-Language ok if few + normalized; never Vary: User-Agent — map UA to mobile/desktop at the edge and key on that.
  • Set-Cookie on a response usually blocks caching — strip it from static/cacheable responses.
  • Good deliberate splits: device class, country, A/B bucket (normalized), anon vs logged-in, image format bucket.
  • Normalize: host case, ports, slashes, trailing slash; fold header variance into small enums.
  • Measure objects-per-URL and hit ratio by path; inspect top cache keys.
Q&A
Why does keying on the full query string hurt hit ratio?
Marketing and analytics append parameters (utm_source, fbclid, gclid), apps add cache-busters and timestamps, and users share links with tracking params. Each unique query string becomes a separate cached object even though the response is identical, so reuse plummets and origin load rises. Allowlist only the params that actually change the content.
What's wrong with Vary: User-Agent?
There are effectively unlimited distinct User-Agent strings (browser, OS, minor version, bots), so the cache stores a separate copy per UA and almost never gets a hit. If you need device-specific responses, do UA parsing at the edge, reduce it to a handful of device classes, and vary the cache key on that small set instead.
Why might a CDN refuse to cache a response?
Common reasons: it contains Set-Cookie (assumed personalized), Cache-Control: no-store/private/max-age=0, no freshness information at all (and no heuristic caching configured), a non-cacheable method, a non-2xx status without explicit rules, or a Vary the CDN treats as uncacheable. Strip Set-Cookie and send explicit Cache-Control on things you want cached.
How do you serve mobile and desktop HTML from cache without fragmenting?
At the edge, classify the User-Agent into mobile/tablet/desktop (a small enum), add that as a header or cache-key component, and let origin return the right variant. The cache then holds ~3 copies per URL instead of thousands. Alternatively serve one responsive page and skip the split entirely.
What is cache-key normalization?
Transforming equivalent requests into one canonical key: lowercasing the host, removing default ports and duplicate slashes, deciding trailing-slash behaviour, allowlisting/sorting query params and dropping tracking ones, and folding header-based variance (encoding, language, device, geo, auth state) into a few enumerated buckets. It maximizes legitimate cache reuse.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Name three query params that fragment the cache and add no value.
utm_source/utm_*, fbclid, gclid (also random cache-busters, session tokens).
Which Vary header value is safe and low-cardinality?
Vary: Accept-Encoding.
What response header commonly prevents caching?
Set-Cookie (and Cache-Control: no-store/private).

Intermediate core

A product page needs to show local currency and language for ~30 countries and 8 languages, and stay cacheable. Design the cache key.
Don't Vary on raw Accept-Language or geo-IP directly. At the edge: (1) Resolve the visitor's country from the CDN's geo lookup and map the 200+ possible countries to your ~30 supported market buckets (plus a default). (2) Resolve language from an explicit preference (path prefix /de/, a lang cookie, or normalized Accept-Language) to one of your 8 supported languages (plus default). (3) Build the cache key as path + market + lang (e.g. via a custom cache key that appends normalized x-market and x-lang headers the edge sets). Result: at most ~31 × 9 ≈ 279 variants per URL — all highly reusable — instead of one-per-visitor. Set a sensible s-maxage and use surrogate keys so a price change purges just that product across all variants. Also emit Content-Language and a Vary that reflects the normalized inputs for correctness with downstream caches, and make the language choice available as a real URL (/de/product) so it's shareable and SEO-friendly.
After adding an A/B test, hit ratio dropped and origin load doubled. Why, and how do you fix it?
The test almost certainly introduced cache-key variance that's higher-cardinality than intended, or defeated caching entirely. Likely causes: (1) The experiment framework sets a unique per-user cookie/ID and the CDN is now keying (or the origin is Vary-ing) on that cookie — effectively one object per user. (2) The framework adds a query param (?exp=...&variant=...&_ab=timestamp) that's in the key. (3) Responses now include Set-Cookie (assignment cookie) so the CDN stops caching them. (4) The origin now sends Cache-Control: private/no-store for any request in an experiment. Fix: assign the bucket at the edge (edge compute) deterministically (hash a stable ID) into a small set like A/B, expose it as a normalized header/cookie value, and key the cache on that 2–3-value bucket only. Strip the raw experiment IDs and timestamps from the key. Move Set-Cookie for assignment to a separate lightweight endpoint or set it via an edge function that doesn't block caching of the main response. Keep Cache-Control: public with a normal TTL; the variance is captured by the bucket key. Now you have 2× the objects, not N×.

Advanced deep

Design a cache-key strategy for an org with 40 teams behind one CDN, so teams can customize keys without tanking global hit ratio or creating security bugs.
Central policy + guardrails: (1) A default, well-normalized cache key applied everywhere: scheme+host+path, query-string allowlist (empty by default — teams opt params in), tracking params stripped globally, params sorted, host lowercased, trailing-slash canonicalized, Vary limited to Accept-Encoding. (2) Teams customize via config as code (Terraform / the CDN's config repo) reviewed by a platform team, not ad-hoc dashboard clicks. (3) A linter / CI check on CDN config that rejects known-bad patterns: Vary: User-Agent or Cookie, keying on more than N query params, keying on a param matching *id*/token/session/utm, unbounded cookie-based keys, or "include all query string". (4) Provide sanctioned building blocks: a device-class function, a geo/market bucketer, an A/B bucketer, a language normalizer — teams compose these instead of inventing raw Vary. Security: the big risk is cache poisoning / cross-user leakage — caching a response keyed without a dimension that actually changed it (e.g. auth), or an unkeyed header that origin reflects into the response (classic web-cache-poisoning via X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, etc.). Mitigations: strip/normalize hop-by-hop and forwarding headers at the edge before they reach origin; never cache responses that carry Set-Cookie or Authorization-dependent content unless the auth state is explicitly in the key (anon vs a per-user bypass); a "no cache for authenticated requests" default with explicit opt-in; and a test suite that fuzzes header/param variations against cached endpoints to detect responses that change without a corresponding key change (cache-key auditing tools / Param Miner-style checks in CI). Observability: per-team dashboards of objects-per-URL, hit ratio by hostname/path, and top cache keys by count; alert when a team's objects-per-URL spikes (fragmentation) or when a new Vary/param appears. Governance: a short "cache key change" review checklist (does every keyed dimension actually change the bytes? is every dimension that changes the bytes keyed or is the response marked private? are forwarding headers sanitized?), and a quarterly audit. Teams get flexibility through the composable functions and an allowlist they own, while the platform prevents the two failure modes: cardinality blowups and poisoning.
Explain web cache poisoning via unkeyed inputs, with a concrete example, and the defenses at the CDN and application layers.
The vulnerability class: an "unkeyed input" is a request attribute that (a) influences the response the origin generates but (b) is not part of the cache key. An attacker sends a request with a malicious value for that input; the origin bakes it into the response; the CDN caches that poisoned response under the normal key; every subsequent victim requesting that key gets the attacker's payload — a stored XSS / redirect / denial-of-service affecting all users of that URL, with no per-victim interaction. Concrete example: the app builds absolute URLs (canonical link, script src, redirects, password-reset links) from the Host or a forwarding header like X-Forwarded-Host instead of a fixed configured domain. The CDN keys only on host+path, not on X-Forwarded-Host. Attacker requests GET / Host: example.com X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com. Origin emits <script src="//evil.com/app.js"> (or a Location: https://evil.com/...) into the HTML. The CDN caches it for example.com/. Now real visitors to example.com/ load the attacker's script. Variants use X-Forwarded-Scheme/X-Forwarded-Proto (force http → broken/mixed content, or an infinite redirect → DoS), X-Original-URL/X-Rewrite-URL (route confusion), oversized headers (400 cached → DoS), or a debug header the app reflects. CDN-layer defenses: (1) Strip or normalize all non-standard forwarding/debug headers at the edge before proxying to origin (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, X-Original-URL, X-Host, Forwarded, etc.) — allowlist only the ones you set yourself. (2) Set Host/forwarding headers to known values on the origin request. (3) Don't cache error responses (4xx/5xx) by default, or cache them very briefly. (4) Keep the cache key tight but ensure any header that can legitimately change the response is either keyed or stripped — never "influences response but unkeyed". (5) Limit header sizes; reject weird requests at the edge (WAF rule). (6) Run periodic cache-key auditing (send benign canary values in candidate unkeyed headers/params and diff the cached response). Application-layer defenses: (1) Build absolute URLs and redirects from a configured canonical domain, never from request headers. (2) Validate/allowlist any header you do consume. (3) Set Cache-Control: private/no-store on responses that legitimately depend on request-specific inputs.
