(4) Add a Vary for any header you genuinely must reflect (forces it into the key) — and reconsider whether you should reflect it at all. (5) Content-Security-Policy limits the blast radius of an injected script. Process: include cache poisoning in security testing (Burp's Param Miner or equivalent), review every place the app reads a header, and treat "unkeyed input that changes the response" as a bug regardless of exploitability.

Cache-Control, TTLs & Freshness

The headers that tell every cache how long to reuse a response and what to do when it goes stale.

Notes

Cache-Control response directives

DirectiveMeaning
max-age=NFresh for N seconds (for any cache).
s-maxage=NFresh for N seconds for shared caches (CDN/proxy); overrides max-age for them. Lets you cache long at the edge, short in the browser.
publicMay be stored by shared caches even if normally not (e.g. with Authorization).
privateBrowser may store; shared caches must not. For per-user responses.
no-cacheMay store, but must revalidate with origin before each reuse.
no-storeDon't store at all.
must-revalidate / proxy-revalidateOnce stale, must revalidate (can't serve stale on error).
immutableContent will never change for this URL — browser skips revalidation even on reload. Use with content-hashed asset names + long max-age.
stale-while-revalidate=NServe stale for up to N s after expiry while revalidating in the background — no user waits.
stale-if-error=NServe stale for up to N s if the origin errors/times out on revalidation.

Validators & conditional requests

  • ETag (opaque version id) + Last-Modified (timestamp) on the response.
  • On revalidation the cache sends If-None-Match: <etag> / If-Modified-Since; origin replies 304 Not Modified (cheap, no body) or 200 with the new body.
  • Strong vs weak ETag (W/"..."): weak = "semantically equivalent", used when byte-for-byte identity isn't guaranteed (e.g. gzip).

Freshness lifecycle

fetched -> FRESH (age < TTL): served instantly, no origin contact
         -> STALE (age >= TTL):
              with SWR: serve stale now, revalidate in background
              else: revalidate (If-None-Match) -> 304 (refresh age) or 200 (replace)
              on origin error + stale-if-error: keep serving stale
  • Age header tells you how long the object has been cached.
  • CDNs often let you set edge TTL independent of origin headers (override, or "respect origin", or "cache even without headers").
  • Heuristic caching: if no explicit freshness, some caches guess a TTL from Last-Modified (e.g. 10% of the age). Usually disable this — be explicit.

Patterns

ContentHeaders
Hashed static asset (app.3f9a.js)Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable — never purge, new hash on change
HTML page (may change)Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300, max-age=0, stale-while-revalidate=86400, stale-if-error=604800 + ETag
Cacheable JSON APICache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=60 + surrogate keys for purge
Per-user / sensitiveCache-Control: private, no-store
Frequently changing but hotMicro-cache: s-maxage=1..5 + SWR (collapses stampedes)

Gotchas

  • Expires (absolute date) is legacy; Cache-Control wins if both present.
  • no-cache ≠ no-store — the former stores-and-revalidates, the latter doesn't store.
  • Setting only max-age means the browser also caches it that long — you then can't "push" an update without changing the URL. Use s-maxage for edge + small/zero max-age for browser when you need fast invalidation.
  • A Vary mismatch or Set-Cookie can silently prevent caching regardless of Cache-Control.
Cheat Sheet
  • max-age = fresh seconds (all caches); s-maxage = fresh seconds for shared caches (overrides max-age there).
  • public/private (shared may/may-not store); no-cache = store but revalidate every time; no-store = don't store.
  • immutable = never revalidate (hashed assets + long max-age). stale-while-revalidate=N = serve stale, refresh in background. stale-if-error=N = serve stale if origin fails.
  • Validators: ETag + Last-Modified → conditional If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since → 304 or 200.
  • Hashed asset: public, max-age=31536000, immutable (never purge). HTML/API: short s-maxage + SWR + stale-if-error + ETag. Per-user: private, no-store. Hot+changing: micro-cache 1–5s + SWR.
  • Disable heuristic caching — always send explicit freshness. no-cache ≠ no-store.
Q&A
Difference between max-age and s-maxage?
max-age applies to every cache including the browser. s-maxage applies only to shared caches (CDN, proxies) and overrides max-age for them. Using both lets you cache aggressively at the edge (s-maxage=3600) while keeping the browser copy short-lived (max-age=0), so an edge purge propagates updates quickly.
no-cache vs no-store?
no-store means never write the response to any cache. no-cache means you may store it, but you must revalidate with the origin (conditional request) before serving it each time — useful for content that rarely changes but must always be verified.
What does stale-while-revalidate achieve?
When an object expires, the cache serves the stale copy immediately to the requesting user and revalidates with the origin in the background. No user pays the revalidation latency, and the origin gets one request instead of a stampede. The next request gets the refreshed copy.
When is immutable appropriate?
For URLs whose content will genuinely never change — typically build-output files with a content hash in the name (main.9f2c1a.js). immutable tells the browser not to send even a conditional request on reload, eliminating revalidation round trips. When the file changes, the build produces a new hash and thus a new URL.
How does a conditional revalidation work?
The cache stored an ETag (and/or Last-Modified). On revalidation it sends If-None-Match: "<etag>" (and/or If-Modified-Since). If the origin's current version matches, it returns 304 Not Modified with no body and the cache refreshes the object's freshness. If it changed, the origin returns 200 with the new body and headers, which replace the cached entry.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

Which directive lets only the browser cache, not the CDN?
private.
What status does an origin return when an ETag still matches?
304 Not Modified (no body).
Which directive serves stale content while fetching a fresh copy in the background?
stale-while-revalidate.

Intermediate core

You deployed a fix but users still see the old index.html for an hour. What went wrong and how should HTML be cached?
The old index.html was served with a long Cache-Control: max-age=3600 (or similar), so both the browser and the CDN hold it for an hour and a CDN purge can't reach the browser copies. HTML that can change should be: short or zero browser lifetime and short edge lifetime with graceful staleness — e.g. Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=86400, stale-if-error=604800, plus an ETag. Then the browser always revalidates (cheap 304s), the edge serves fast for up to 60s, SWR hides revalidation latency, and a deploy + edge purge propagates within seconds. The referenced assets (JS/CSS/images) get content-hashed names and max-age=31536000, immutable — so a new deploy changes the HTML (which is barely cached) which points at new hashed asset URLs, and no purge of assets is ever needed.
An API endpoint is cacheable for ~30s but the origin occasionally 500s under load. Design the caching so users rarely see errors.
Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=30, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=600 (tune the numbers). Effect: fresh for 30s (most requests are cheap edge hits); after 30s, SWR serves the slightly-stale response instantly while one background revalidation runs — users never wait and origin gets one request, not a herd; if that revalidation 500s or times out, stale-if-error keeps serving the last good response for up to 10 minutes instead of surfacing the error. Combine with request collapsing at the edge (usually automatic) and an origin shield so even the background revalidations from many PoPs collapse to one origin request. Add a short client max-age (or 0) so browsers don't hold stale data too long. Optionally have the edge serve a cached fallback or a graceful degraded response on repeated origin failure. Also fix the origin's overload behaviour (rate limits, autoscaling), but the caching alone turns transient origin 5xx into invisible-to-user staleness.

Advanced deep

Explain the full HTTP caching model a shared cache applies to a response: storability, freshness, revalidation, and the precedence of directives. Include the tricky interactions.
1. Is it storable? A shared cache may store a response only if: the method is cacheable (GET/HEAD, or others with explicit allowance); the status is cacheable by default (200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 404, 405, 410, 414, 501) or made cacheable by explicit freshness; there's no Cache-Control: no-store; it's not private (shared caches must not store private); if the request had Authorization, the response must have public, s-maxage, or must-revalidate to be shared-cacheable; and the CDN's own rules (e.g. won't cache with Set-Cookie, or a disallowed Vary) allow it. 2. How long is it fresh? Precedence: s-maxage (shared caches) > max-age > Expires (absolute date) > heuristic (if enabled: a fraction of now − Last-Modified). Freshness lifetime is compared against current age (roughly now − response_time + initial Age header, accounting for transit). While age < lifetime the cache serves without contacting origin. no-cache forces the effective fresh lifetime to zero (store, but always revalidate). 3. When stale, revalidate. The cache issues a conditional request with If-None-Match (ETag) and/or If-Modified-Since (Last-Modified). 304 → update stored headers and reset age, keep the body. 200 → replace. 5xx/timeout → if stale-if-error (or the CDN's config) permits, serve stale; else pass the error through (unless must-revalidate, which forbids serving stale on any error). 4. Serving stale proactively. stale-while-revalidate=N lets the cache return a stale response (up to N s past expiry) and revalidate asynchronously. must-revalidate/proxy-revalidate disable all stale-serving once expired. Tricky interactions: (a) no-cache is often confused with no-store — the former still stores and enables fast 304s, so it's cheaper than no-store. (b) max-age=0 alone ≈ no-cache (immediately stale, revalidate), but a cache may still serve stale on error unless must-revalidate. (c) s-maxage implies proxy-revalidate semantics in some readings — check your CDN. (d) Vary participates in matching: a stored entry only matches a request whose listed headers match the original; Vary: * means never reusable. (e) Age accumulates through cache tiers, so a multi-tier CDN can hand the browser an object already near its TTL. (f) The CDN's dashboard TTL settings can override or ignore origin Cache-Control entirely ("cache everything for 1h regardless"), which decouples edge behaviour from what downstream browsers see — you then rely on the response's own Cache-Control (or a separate one the CDN sends downstream) for browser behaviour. (g) immutable only affects revalidation-on-reload in browsers; shared caches still honour max-age. (h) A Content-Encoding/Accept-Encoding mismatch with a weak vs strong ETag can cause needless full 200s instead of 304s. The practical takeaway: be explicit (always send Cache-Control + an ETag), separate edge vs browser lifetimes with s-maxage vs max-age, and add stale-while-revalidate + stale-if-error for resilience.
Compare TTL-based expiry, ETag revalidation, and event-driven purge as freshness strategies. When do you use each, and how do you combine them?
TTL-based expiry (max-age/s-maxage): the cache just trusts the object for N seconds. Pros: zero origin traffic while fresh, simplest, predictable load. Cons: you accept up to N seconds of staleness; too-long TTL delays updates, too-short TTL kills offload. Best for content where bounded staleness is fine and you can't predict changes (news lists, catalog pages, aggregates) — pick the largest TTL your product tolerates. ETag / Last-Modified revalidation (no-cache, or TTL then conditional): after expiry the cache asks "still valid?" and usually gets a cheap 304. Pros: content is never more than one revalidation stale; bandwidth-cheap (no body on 304). Cons: still a round trip to origin per object per revalidation interval — latency on the critical path unless paired with SWR, and origin must compute the validator. Best when correctness matters and changes are unpredictable but the payload is large (so avoiding re-download is valuable), or as the browser-side strategy for HTML (max-age=0 + ETag). Event-driven purge (surrogate keys / cache tags, purge on write): the cache holds content ~indefinitely (s-maxage long) and the application actively purges the affected objects when data changes. Pros: near-100% offload and near-real-time freshness — the best of both. Cons: you must reliably enumerate what to purge (tag every response with the entity keys it depends on), the purge system must be fast and reliable across all PoPs, and a missed purge = indefinitely stale content. Best for content with clear write events and dependency mapping (product page → purge product-123 tag on product update; article → purge on publish). Combining: the standard production pattern is purge-driven with a TTL safety net and SWR: set a long s-maxage (hours/days) so offload is maximal, tag responses with surrogate keys, purge on every write for immediate correctness, but keep the TTL as a backstop so a missed purge self-heals within the TTL. Add stale-while-revalidate so the post-expiry (or post-soft-purge) refresh never blocks a user, and stale-if-error so origin problems don't cause errors. Use soft purge (mark stale, revalidate via SWR) rather than hard purge (evict, forcing blocking misses) to avoid a self-inflicted stampede. For truly static hashed assets, none of this applies — just immutable + a year, and change the URL. So: hashed assets → immutable URLs; HTML → short/zero browser TTL + ETag + short edge TTL + SWR; dynamic entity content → long edge TTL + surrogate-key purge + SWR + stale-if-error + a modest TTL backstop.

Purging & Invalidation

Getting new content out before the TTL expires — by URL, by tag, or by versioning the URL itself.

Notes

Ways to invalidate

MethodHowNotes
Purge by URLTell the CDN to drop /path?x=1Precise but you must know every variant (query params, device, geo, encoding).
Purge by prefix / path pattern/images/*, /blog/2024/*Coarse; handy for directory-scoped changes. Not all CDNs support wildcards natively.
Purge by tag / surrogate keyOrigin adds Surrogate-Key: product-123 category-shoes to responses; you purge the key and every object carrying it dropsThe scalable answer — decouples "what changed" from "which URLs".
Purge allWipe the whole propertyEmergency only — causes a global cold cache and origin load spike.
Versioned URLChange the URL so the old cache entry is simply never requested (app.9f2c.js, ?v=42)No purge needed; the cleanest approach for assets.

Soft vs hard purge

  • Hard purge: evict immediately. Next request is a blocking MISS → if many hit at once, a stampede to origin.
  • Soft purge: mark the object stale but keep it. Next request serves stale instantly and triggers a single background revalidation (needs stale-while-revalidate). Much gentler; preferred default.

Propagation

  • A purge must reach every PoP. Modern CDNs do this in ~100–500 ms to a few seconds globally via an internal pub/sub; older/edge cases can take longer.
  • The purge API has rate limits and sometimes a cost per purge — batch, and prefer tag purges over thousands of URL purges.
  • Multi-tier caches: a purge should invalidate edge and shield/mid-tier, or the edge just re-pulls the stale object from the shield.
  • Browser caches are not purgeable — only versioned URLs or short browser TTLs solve that.

Surrogate keys / cache tags in practice

Response for GET /product/123:
  Surrogate-Key: prod-123 brand-acme cat-shoes homepage-feature
Response for GET /category/shoes:
  Surrogate-Key: cat-shoes prod-123 prod-124 prod-125

On "product 123 price changed":
  PURGE key prod-123        -> drops /product/123 AND /category/shoes AND any page tagged prod-123
  • Tag each response with every entity it depends on. A write purges the entity's key(s).
  • Keep tags bounded and meaningful; a page tagged with 500 keys is a smell.
  • Header name varies: Surrogate-Key (Fastly), Cache-Tag (Cloudflare/Akamai), x-amz-... patterns, etc.

Common mistakes

  • Purging /page but not /page?utm=... or the mobile/geo variants — use tags or normalize the key.
  • Purge-all on every deploy → permanent cold cache. Use versioned asset URLs + targeted HTML/API purges.
  • Forgetting the shield tier → "I purged but it's still stale".
  • Relying on purge for correctness with no TTL backstop — a missed purge means indefinitely stale. Always keep a max TTL.
  • Hard-purging hot objects → origin stampede. Soft purge + SWR instead.
Cheat Sheet
  • Invalidate by: URL (precise, must cover all variants), prefix/wildcard (coarse), tag / surrogate key (scalable — purge "what changed"), purge-all (emergency), versioned URL (no purge needed).
  • Soft purge (mark stale, serve stale + background revalidate via SWR) > hard purge (evict → blocking misses → stampede).
  • Purge propagates to all PoPs in ~sub-second to seconds; APIs are rate-limited/cost-metered — batch, prefer tags.
  • Invalidate edge and shield/mid-tier, or the edge re-pulls stale.
  • Browser caches can't be purged — use versioned URLs / short browser TTL.
  • Tag each response with every entity it depends on (Surrogate-Key/Cache-Tag); write → purge the entity key.
  • Always keep a TTL backstop so a missed purge self-heals. Never purge-all per deploy.
Q&A
Why are surrogate keys / cache tags better than purging URLs?
They decouple "what data changed" from "which URLs contain it". You tag every response with the entities it depends on (prod-123, cat-shoes); when product 123 changes you purge the tag, and the CDN drops every page carrying it — the product page, category listings, the homepage feature, all query-string and device variants — without you enumerating URLs.
Soft purge vs hard purge?
Hard purge evicts the object, so the next request is a blocking miss to origin (and concurrent requests stampede). Soft purge marks the object stale but keeps it; with stale-while-revalidate the next request is served the stale copy instantly while one background revalidation refreshes it. Soft purge is gentler and should be the default for hot content.
You purged a URL but users still see old content. Causes?
(1) Their browser has it cached (not purgeable — needs a versioned URL or short browser TTL). (2) You purged the edge but not the shield/mid-tier, so the edge re-fetched the stale copy. (3) You purged /page but they're hitting a variant (?utm=, mobile, a different country) that's a different cache key. (4) Purge propagation hasn't reached their PoP yet (usually seconds). (5) You purged the wrong hostname/path.
Why is "purge everything on deploy" bad?
It empties every PoP's cache simultaneously, so every subsequent request is a miss and your origin gets hammered with the full request volume until caches refill — exactly when you're least sure the new deploy is stable. Instead, give assets content-hashed URLs (no purge needed) and purge only the specific HTML/API objects that changed.
Should you rely solely on purging for freshness?
No — keep a TTL as a backstop. Purge systems can drop events, lag, or be misconfigured; if an object has an effectively infinite TTL and its purge is missed, it stays stale forever. A finite max TTL (even hours or a day) means any missed purge self-corrects.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What invalidation method needs no purge at all?
Versioned URLs (content hash or ?v=) — the old URL is simply never requested again.
Which purge type risks an origin stampede?
Hard purge (evict), especially of hot objects.
Can you purge a user's browser cache?
No — only versioned URLs or short browser TTLs address that.

Intermediate core

An e-commerce site caches product and category pages for 24h at the edge. When a price changes it must reflect within seconds. Design the invalidation.
Use surrogate keys + soft purge + a TTL backstop. (1) Origin tags every response: the product page GET /p/123 gets Surrogate-Key: prod-123 brand-acme cat-shoes; each category listing GET /c/shoes gets Surrogate-Key: cat-shoes prod-123 prod-124 ... (every product it displays); the homepage gets keys for anything it features. (2) Keep s-maxage=86400 (long — maximizes offload) plus stale-while-revalidate=60 and stale-if-error=86400, and a short/zero browser max-age with an ETag. (3) On a price change for product 123, the app calls the CDN's soft purge by key for prod-123 (and any derived keys). Every object carrying that key — product page, all category pages listing it, homepage, all query/device/geo variants — is marked stale. (4) Next request to any of them serves the stale copy instantly (no user waits) and triggers one background revalidation; origin shield collapses those to one origin fetch per object. Within seconds globally, everyone sees the new price. (5) The 24h TTL is now just a safety net for missed purge events. (6) Rate-limit/batch purge calls (e.g. debounce bulk price updates into one key-set purge). This gives ~full offload and near-real-time correctness without enumerating URLs.
Your purge API is rate-limited to 1,000 ops/min and a bulk catalog import changes 50,000 products. How do you handle it?
Don't purge 50,000 URLs. Options in order of preference: (1) Purge by broader tags — if the import touches whole categories or a "catalog" scope, purge those few tags (cat-* or a single catalog-vN key that every product page carries) in a handful of calls. If you version the catalog (a catalog-2024-06-01 surrogate key bumped per import), one purge of the previous version handles everything. (2) Bump a global version token in the cache key (e.g. an edge-dictionary value or a key prefix) so all catalog objects become new keys at once — effectively an instant logical purge with zero purge ops, at the cost of a cold catalog cache (mitigate with SWR/shield). (3) If you must purge individual keys, batch them — most APIs accept many keys per call (hundreds to thousands), so 50,000 keys might be ~10–50 calls, within limits; add backoff on 429. (4) Soft purge so the refill is gradual (stale-served + background revalidation) rather than a synchronized stampede, and lean on the origin shield so the 50,000 revalidations collapse to at most one per object at the origin. (5) Spread the purge over a few minutes if the freshness SLA allows. The general lesson: design surrogate keys so that "a big change" maps to a small number of coarse keys or a version bump, not N per-URL purges.

Advanced deep

Design an end-to-end cache-invalidation system for a CMS-backed site: how content changes trigger purges, guarantee correctness, and stay resilient to failures.
Tagging: every rendered response is tagged (at the app/edge) with a surrogate key per content entity it reads — the article, its author, referenced media, the section/landing pages it appears on, navigation, and a site-wide layout-vN key. Keep the tag set per response bounded (dozens, not hundreds); if a page truly depends on hundreds of entities, tag it with a coarser aggregate key. Change capture: the CMS publishes a domain event on every content change (create/update/unpublish/reorder/media replace) — ideally via an outbox pattern or CDC so no event is lost even if the CMS crashes mid-transaction. A purge service consumes these events from a durable queue. Mapping: the purge service maps an event to the set of surrogate keys to purge (article id → article-123, author-9 if author metadata shown, section-news, home if featured, etc.), using the same dependency rules the renderer uses to tag. It issues soft purges by key to the CDN (edge + shield), batched, with retry/backoff on rate limits and a dead-letter queue for failures + alerting. Correctness guarantees: (1) TTL backstop — every cacheable response also has a finite s-maxage (e.g. 1–24h) so a missed/failed purge self-heals within that bound. (2) Idempotent, at-least-once purges — purging a key twice is harmless. (3) SWR + stale-if-error so purges never cause user-facing latency or errors. (4) Ordering — if rapid successive edits occur, the last purge wins; the revalidation always fetches current origin state, so out-of-order purges don't cause wrong content (they cause at most an extra revalidation). (5) Reconciliation job — periodically (or on demand) walk recently-changed content and re-purge its keys, catching anything the event pipeline dropped. (6) For structural changes (nav, layout, template deploy) bump the layout-vN key / a global version so everything refreshes without enumerating pages. Resilience: the purge service is stateless behind the queue; queue + DLQ absorb CDN API outages (purges retry when it recovers, and the TTL covers the gap); monitor purge lag (event time → purge acked), purge error rate, and "content age" (are pages older than expected?). Deploy: content-hashed assets need no purge; template/code deploys bump the layout version and optionally soft-purge HTML tags; never purge-all. Observability: dashboards for purge throughput, lag, failures, DLQ depth, hit ratio, and a canary that edits a test page and measures time-to-propagate globally, alerting if it exceeds the freshness SLA. Net: tag-based soft purges driven by durable events, a TTL safety net, SWR/stale-if-error for UX, and a reconciliation sweep for lost events.
Compare "invalidate the cache" vs "change the cache key / URL" as strategies. What are the failure modes and operational costs of each at scale?
Invalidate (purge): keep the URL stable, tell caches to drop/refresh the entry. Pros: URLs never change (good for SEO, bookmarks, shared links, HTML that references stable paths); works for content whose change events you can capture; fine-grained (purge one entity). Failure modes: (1) missed purge event → indefinitely stale (needs TTL backstop). (2) incomplete purge → some variants/tiers/PoPs still stale (needs tag-based purge covering all variants, and edge+shield purge, and propagation monitoring). (3) purge storms → origin stampede (needs soft purge + SWR + shield). (4) purge API outage or rate limit → delayed freshness (needs queue/retry/DLQ and TTL backstop). (5) browser caches unreachable (needs short browser TTL). (6) dependency-mapping bugs → you purge the wrong or too few keys (needs the renderer and purge service to share dependency logic, plus reconciliation). Operational cost: a durable event pipeline, a purge service, surrogate-key discipline in every response, monitoring of purge lag/errors, and often per-purge API cost. Change the URL / cache key (versioned assets, cache-key version tokens): the old entry is simply never requested again; the new content is a new object. Pros: no purge infrastructure; atomic (the moment the HTML references the new URL, everyone gets new content); browser caches handled for free (new URL = new fetch); immune to purge propagation and rate limits; enables immutable + 1-year TTL for maximum offload. Failure modes: (1) requires something that references the asset to change too — you must update the HTML/manifest/importmap, and that referencing document itself needs a fast-invalidation strategy (short TTL or its own versioning). (2) the old objects linger in cache/storage until evicted — storage bloat and origin-storage cleanup needed. (3) not applicable to canonical content URLs you can't change (/blog/my-post) — only to assets and internal/derived URLs, or via a query token you rotate. (4) a global cache-key version bump = instant cold cache for that whole class (mitigate with shield/SWR). (5) cache-busting query params can be stripped by misconfigured caches, defeating it — content-hash-in-filename is more robust than ?v=. Operational cost: build tooling to hash/version and rewrite references; storage lifecycle management for old versions; discipline that nothing references an unversioned path. At scale, use both: versioned URLs for everything you control the reference to (JS/CSS/images/fonts/generated data files) — zero purge, max TTL; and tag-based soft purge (with TTL backstop) for canonical content URLs (HTML pages, cacheable API responses) whose paths must stay stable. Reserve purge-all and global key bumps for emergencies and template-wide changes.

Origins, Shielding & Failover

Concentrating misses through a shield tier, and keeping the site up when an origin dies.

Notes

The origin

  • The origin is where the CDN fetches content on a miss: your app servers, a load balancer, an object store (S3/GCS), or another CDN.
  • Pull CDN (normal): origin holds the canonical copy; edges pull on demand. Push: you upload assets to CDN storage ahead of time (rare now; used for large media libraries).
  • Origin config: hostname(s), ports, TLS (verify cert, SNI, min version), host header to send, path rewrites, timeouts, retry policy, and which request headers to forward.

Origin shield / mid-tier

  • Without a shield: a miss at any of dozens/hundreds of PoPs goes straight to origin. A cold cache, a purge, or a new asset can hit origin from many PoPs at once.
  • A shield is a designated PoP (or small set) that all other edges route through on a miss. Origin then sees at most ~one request per object, and request collapsing works across the whole CDN, not just per-PoP.
  • Pick the shield PoP near your origin to minimize the miss round trip.
  • Trade-off: a miss now has an extra hop (edge → shield → origin), slightly higher miss latency, for much better offload and origin protection. Almost always worth it.
  • Some CDNs have multiple mid-tiers (regional) between edge and shield.

Origin protection

  • Lock the origin to the CDN: IP allowlist the CDN's egress ranges, require a shared secret header the CDN injects, or use mTLS / an authenticated origin pull cert. Otherwise attackers hit the origin directly and bypass the CDN's WAF/DDoS.
  • Don't expose the origin hostname/IP publicly (no DNS record, or a different name); watch for leaks via headers, error pages, certificates (SNI/SAN), and historical DNS.
  • Rate-limit and WAF at the edge so bad traffic never reaches origin.

Health checks & failover

  • The CDN periodically probes each origin (HTTP path, expected status/body, interval, unhealthy/healthy thresholds).
  • Origin groups: primary + backup origins; on primary failure (connection refused, timeout, 5xx per policy) the CDN retries the next origin. Configure which statuses count as failure and how many retries.
  • Failover scope: per-request retry (fast, transparent) vs marking an origin down for a cooldown (avoids hammering a sick origin).
  • Serve stale on origin failure: stale-if-error (and CDN "serve stale on error" settings) keep serving the last-good cached copy when all origins are unreachable — often the difference between "degraded" and "down".
  • Multi-region origins: geo-route edges to the nearest healthy origin; keep data replication in mind for write paths.

Failure modes to design for

  • Origin overloaded (slow, not down) — timeouts + circuit-breaking + serve-stale; don't let retries amplify load.
  • Origin returns wrong content (a bad deploy) — the CDN will happily cache it; have a fast purge + rollback, and don't cache non-2xx aggressively.
  • Shield PoP outage — CDN should fail the shield over to another PoP or bypass to origin.
  • DNS for the origin fails — pin origin by IP where possible, or use multiple resolvers.
Cheat Sheet
  • Origin = where the CDN pulls on a miss (app/LB/object store). Pull (default) vs push (pre-upload).
  • Origin shield = one PoP all edges route misses through → origin sees ~1 request/object, CDN-wide request collapsing, better offload. Place it near the origin. Cost: one extra hop on misses.
  • Lock origin to CDN: IP allowlist CDN egress, secret header, or mTLS/authenticated origin pull. Hide the origin hostname/IP.
  • Health checks + origin groups (primary/backup) → automatic failover; tune which statuses = failure, retry count, and down-cooldown.
  • Serve stale on error (stale-if-error + CDN setting) keeps the site up during an origin outage.
  • Design for: slow (not down) origin → timeouts + circuit-break + stale; bad deploy cached → fast purge + rollback; shield outage → failover/bypass.
Q&A
What problem does an origin shield solve?
It concentrates all cache misses from every edge PoP through one intermediate cache near the origin. Instead of the origin receiving a miss from each of many PoPs (especially after a purge or for a brand-new object), it receives about one request per object, and request collapsing works across the entire CDN. The cost is an extra hop on misses.
Where should the shield PoP be located?
As close to your origin as possible (same region/city). Misses traverse edge → shield → origin; putting the shield near the origin keeps the shield↔origin leg short, so the added latency is mostly just the edge↔shield leg.
How do you stop attackers from bypassing the CDN and hitting the origin directly?
Restrict the origin to only accept traffic from the CDN: allowlist the CDN's published egress IP ranges at your firewall/LB, and/or require a secret header that the CDN injects on every origin request (reject requests without it), and/or use mutual TLS with a CDN-provided client certificate. Also avoid publishing the origin's real hostname/IP.
What does "serve stale on error" do during an origin outage?
If all origins are unreachable or erroring, the CDN continues serving the last successfully cached copy of each object (governed by stale-if-error and CDN config) instead of returning 5xx. Users see slightly outdated but working content, turning a hard outage into a soft degradation for anything that was cached.
Why can retries make an overloaded origin worse?
If the origin is slow because it's saturated, each timed-out request that the CDN retries adds more load, pushing it further under — a retry storm. Mitigate with conservative retry counts, per-origin circuit breaking (mark it down after N failures and stop sending traffic for a cooldown), serving stale, and backoff, so the origin gets a chance to recover.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does the CDN do on a cache miss?
Fetches the object from the next tier (shield/mid-tier) or the origin, caches it per the rules, and serves it.
Where should an origin shield be placed relative to the origin?
As close to the origin as possible (same region).
Name one way to ensure only the CDN can reach your origin.
IP-allowlist the CDN's egress ranges (or require a secret header, or use mTLS).

Intermediate core

After enabling a purge-all on every deploy, your origin CPU spikes to 100% for 10 minutes post-deploy. Beyond fixing the purge-all, what architecture reduces this?
(1) Add an origin shield so that even a fully cold cache results in one request per object to the origin (from the shield) rather than one per object per PoP; the edges refill from the shield. (2) Soft purge + stale-while-revalidate so the refill is background revalidation serving stale meanwhile, not a wall of blocking misses. (3) Content-hashed asset URLs so deploys don't invalidate assets at all — only the small, barely-cached HTML changes. (4) Staggered / tag-scoped purge instead of purge-all — purge only what changed. (5) Request collapsing (usually on by default) at edge and shield so concurrent misses for the same object become one origin fetch. (6) Pre-warm critical objects after deploy (a script that requests the top URLs through the CDN) so the first real users get hits. (7) Give the origin some autoscaling headroom for the refill window. The shield + soft purge + hashed assets combination is what makes deploys a non-event for the origin.
Design origin failover for a site with an active origin in us-east and a warm standby in us-west, requiring < 30s of user-visible errors on a regional outage.
Configure an origin group on the CDN: primary = us-east LB, secondary = us-west LB. Health checks: probe a lightweight /healthz on each origin every ~5–10s, expecting 200; unhealthy after 2–3 consecutive failures (so ~15–30s to declare down), healthy after 2 successes. Per-request retry: on a connection failure, timeout, or configured failure status (e.g. 502/503/504) for a request, the CDN immediately retries the secondary origin — so individual users fail over in one request even before the health check flips, keeping user-visible errors near zero. Once the health check marks us-east down, all traffic routes to us-west for a cooldown. Serve stale: enable stale-if-error / "serve stale on origin error" so cached content keeps serving through the brief window. Data: us-west must have current data — async replication with acceptable lag for reads; for writes, either us-west accepts writes (multi-primary/conflict handling) or write endpoints return a clear degraded response until failback. DNS/latency routing: normally geo-route so nearby users use the closest healthy origin; on failover everyone uses us-west (accept the added latency). Failback: automatic when us-east passes health checks for a sustained period, or manual to avoid flapping. Test: game-day by blocking us-east at the firewall and measuring error rate and time-to-recover; confirm it's under 30s and mostly covered by per-request retry + stale.

Advanced deep

Your origin is object storage (S3) fronted by the CDN. Walk through the design: access control, shielding, cache behaviour, large files, and failure handling.
Access control: the bucket should not be public. Use the CDN's origin-access mechanism — an Origin Access Identity/Control (CloudFront OAC) or, for other CDNs, a bucket policy restricting s3:GetObject to the CDN's identity / a signed request / an allowlisted principal, plus optionally a secret header the CDN adds and a bucket policy that denies requests lacking it. Block all direct public access; enforce TLS. Shielding: enable an origin shield in the bucket's region so misses from all PoPs collapse to ~one GET per object against S3 — this also cuts S3 request costs (you pay per GET) substantially. Cache behaviour: set long edge TTLs (s-maxage days) since object-storage content is usually immutable or versioned; use content-hashed keys or S3 object versioning + versioned URLs so you never need to purge; normalize the cache key (drop query params S3 doesn't need, but keep any you use for signed URLs). Send Cache-Control as S3 object metadata (set at upload) so the CDN and browsers get correct freshness; add immutable for hashed objects. Enable Brotli/gzip at the edge (S3 stores raw). Large files: ensure the CDN supports and forwards Range requests to S3 (for video seeking, resumable downloads) and caches range/segment responses; enable partial-object caching / segmented caching so a huge file is cached in chunks and a range request doesn't fetch the whole object; set generous origin read timeouts. For very large media, consider push/pre-positioning or a dedicated media config. Failure handling: S3 is highly available but not infallible — enable stale-if-error / serve-stale so a transient S3 5xx/slowdown doesn't surface; consider a secondary origin (cross-region replica bucket) in an origin group with failover on 5xx/timeouts; handle S3 503 SlowDown with backoff (shield + collapsing already minimize request rate). Watch for 403 vs 404 semantics (S3 returns 403 for missing objects when the principal lacks ListBucket) — decide how the CDN should treat/caches those (short negative TTL). Observability: monitor hit ratio, S3 GET volume and cost (should be tiny relative to edge traffic — if not, cache-key or TTL problem), 4xx/5xx from origin, and range-request behaviour. Cost note: without a shield, a global purge or cold cache can generate millions of S3 GETs and data-transfer-to-CDN charges; the shield plus long TTLs plus versioned URLs keep origin cost near zero.
Explain request collapsing across a multi-tier CDN in detail, and the scenarios where it fails to protect the origin.
Mechanism: at each cache node, when a request misses and a fetch for that exact cache key is already in flight, subsequent concurrent requests for the same key are queued to wait on that single upstream fetch, then all served from its result. In a multi-tier CDN (edge → regional mid-tier → shield → origin), collapsing happens at every tier: N concurrent user requests at one edge → 1 request to the mid-tier; N mid-tiers → 1 request each to the shield, collapsed there → 1 request to origin. So a globally hot object that expires simultaneously everywhere results in exactly one origin fetch, provided the shield tier exists and all misses route through it. Where it fails to protect origin: (1) No shield — collapsing is only per-PoP, so you still get up to (number of edge PoPs or mid-tiers) simultaneous origin requests. (2) Cache-key fragmentation — if the "same" content has many keys (query params, cookies, Vary: User-Agent, device/geo variants not normalized), each key is a separate in-flight fetch and none collapse; a hot page with per-user cache-buster params herds fully. (3) Uncacheable responses — if origin returns no-store/private/Set-Cookie, the cache won't hold or collapse it; every request for a hot uncacheable endpoint hits origin (fix with micro-caching + SWR). (4) Range requests / segmented objects — different byte ranges are different sub-keys; a swarm of clients requesting different ranges of a new large file can each miss (mitigated by segment caching and collapsing per segment). (5) Collapsing timeouts / caps — some CDNs limit how long requests wait on the shared fetch or how many can queue; past the cap they're released to fetch independently, so a slow origin fetch under high concurrency can still leak multiple requests. (6) Non-collapsible upstream errors — if the single fetch returns a non-cacheable error, the waiters may each retry to origin. (7) Purge/expiry skew — if TTLs or purge propagation aren't synchronized, objects expire at slightly different times across nodes, spreading (but not eliminating) the load; conversely a synchronized purge-all maximizes the herd. (8) Different edges not sharing a mid-tier for the same object (routing/hashing quirks) — more than one path to the shield/origin. (9) First-ever request for a brand-new object across many regions before any tier has it. Defenses: always run an origin shield (single collapse point), aggressively normalize cache keys, micro-cache + SWR for hot uncacheable content, use soft purge instead of hard purge, stagger TTLs where possible, enable segment caching for large files, and pre-warm critical objects after deploys/purges.

Dynamic Content, ESI & Edge Compute

Making a CDN useful for content that isn't a static file — from micro-caching to running code at the PoP.

Notes

The spectrum, cheapest to richest

TechniqueWhat
Dynamic accelerationDon't cache the response, but still route through the CDN: TLS terminated near the user, warm pooled keep-alive connections to origin, optimized backbone paths. Cuts connection-setup and transit latency.
Micro-cachingCache "uncacheable" responses for a very short time (1–10s) + stale-while-revalidate. Even 1s collapses a stampede on a hot endpoint and hugely offloads origin, with bounded staleness.
Fragment / partial caching (ESI)Cache the static shell of a page with different TTLs per fragment; assemble at the edge.
Edge computeRun your code (JS/WASM) at the PoP on each request/response: rewrite, route, personalize, auth, A/B bucket, do small API calls, assemble responses, cache programmatically.
Edge rendering / SSR at edgeRender pages (often with a framework's edge runtime) close to users, pulling data from regional stores or origin APIs.

ESI (Edge Side Includes)

<esi:include src="/header" />
<esi:include src="/user-widget" />   <!-- short TTL / no cache -->
<esi:include src="/footer" />         <!-- long TTL -->
  • The page template is cached long; each esi:include is fetched/cached on its own TTL and stitched in at the edge.
  • Great for "mostly static page with one personalized box". Older tech; edge compute now covers the same need more flexibly (and ESI support/behaviour varies by CDN).

Edge compute — models & limits

  • Runtimes: V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers), lightweight containers/functions (Lambda@Edge, CloudFront Functions, Fastly Compute@Edge/WASM, Akamai EdgeWorkers, Vercel/Netlify Edge).
  • Two hook points: viewer request/response (runs on every request, tight CPU/time limits, no origin needed) vs origin request/response (runs only on cache miss).
  • Limits: small CPU-time budgets (sub-ms to tens of ms), limited memory, restricted APIs, cold-start considerations (isolates ~0, containers more), no local disk, careful with outbound fetches (each adds latency and can defeat the point).
  • State: edge KV stores (eventually consistent, read-optimized), durable objects / edge databases (stronger consistency, regional), config/secret stores. Don't assume a local cache persists.

Common edge-compute uses

  • Auth/token check and redirect before hitting origin; geo/device redirects; URL rewrites and A/B routing.
  • Inject personalized snippets into a cached shell (name, cart count) via a cheap KV lookup or a signed cookie — keeping the page itself cacheable.
  • Normalize the cache key (strip params, bucket device/geo) programmatically.
  • Assemble a response from multiple cached fragments or API calls; serve a fast JSON from edge KV.
  • Security: bot checks, request signing/verification, header sanitization, rate limiting.
  • Serve a maintenance/fallback page or synthetic response when origin is down.

Design guidance

  • Keep the expensive/personalized part small and the cacheable part large — cache the shell, personalize the crumbs.
  • Prefer micro-caching + SWR before reaching for edge compute — it's simpler and often enough.
  • Every outbound fetch from an edge function adds latency; minimize and parallelize; use edge KV for hot data.
  • Watch cold starts, CPU limits, and per-request cost at scale; test the p99, not just the average.
  • Edge code is still code — version it, test it, stage it, and be able to roll back fast (a bad edge function breaks every request).
Cheat Sheet
  • Spectrum: dynamic acceleration (route via CDN, TLS+keep-alive+optimized path, no cache) → micro-caching (1–10s + SWR, collapses stampedes) → fragment caching / ESI → edge compute → edge rendering.
  • ESI: cache the shell long, <esi:include> each fragment on its own TTL, stitch at edge. Older; edge compute is the flexible successor.
  • Edge compute hooks: viewer req/resp (every request, tiny CPU budget) vs origin req/resp (miss only).
  • Runtimes: V8 isolates (near-zero cold start) vs functions/containers. Limits: sub-ms–tens-of-ms CPU, small memory, restricted APIs, no disk; outbound fetches add latency.
  • Edge state: KV (eventually consistent, read-fast), durable objects / regional DB (stronger, regional), config/secret stores.
  • Uses: auth/redirect before origin, personalize a cached shell, normalize cache key, assemble fragments, bot/security, origin-down fallback.
  • Rule: cacheable part big, personalized part small. Try micro-caching first. Version/stage/rollback edge code — it runs on every request.
Q&A
What is micro-caching and why is it so effective?
Caching a normally-dynamic response for a very short time (often 1–10 seconds) plus stale-while-revalidate. On a hot endpoint, thousands of requests per second collapse into roughly one origin request per cache period, cutting origin load by orders of magnitude, while the maximum staleness is only a second or two. It's the highest-leverage, lowest-effort dynamic-content optimization.
How does ESI let you cache a personalized page?
You cache the page template (the shell) with a long TTL and mark the personalized regions as <esi:include src="...">. The CDN fetches and caches each include separately — the static ones long, the personalized one short or not at all — and assembles the final page at the edge. The bulk of the page is served from cache; only the small dynamic fragment involves fresh work.
Viewer-side vs origin-side edge functions?
Viewer (or "request/response") functions run on every request/response at the edge, before/after cache lookup, with very tight CPU limits — good for redirects, header rewrites, auth checks, cache-key normalization. Origin functions run only on a cache miss (around the origin fetch) — good for modifying the request to origin or transforming the origin response before caching. Putting heavy logic in a viewer function taxes every request including cache hits.
What's the risk of calling an external API from an edge function?
Each outbound fetch adds its own latency (DNS, TLS, round trip) on the request's critical path, and can be less reliable than the CDN itself — potentially negating the latency benefit of being at the edge. Minimize calls, parallelize them, cache their results in edge KV, and have a fallback for when they fail.
When should you reach for edge compute vs simpler caching?
Try TLS/dynamic acceleration and micro-caching + SWR first — they're config, not code, and often enough. Use edge compute when you genuinely need per-request logic close to the user: auth/routing decisions before origin, injecting personalization into an otherwise-cacheable page, assembling responses from multiple sources, or programmatic cache-key control. It's powerful but it's code running on every request, with cost, limits, and rollback concerns.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What does "dynamic acceleration" cache?
Nothing — it routes uncached requests through the CDN for TLS termination, keep-alive pooling, and optimized paths to origin.
How long is a typical micro-cache TTL?
About 1–10 seconds (plus stale-while-revalidate).
Which edge-function hook runs only on a cache miss?
The origin request/response function.

Intermediate core

A news homepage is personalized only by a small "for you" module and a logged-in header. Make it cacheable.
Split the page. (1) The shell (layout, top stories, sections) is identical for everyone — cache it hard at the edge (s-maxage minutes, SWR) with surrogate keys for purge on publish. (2) The logged-in header (name, avatar, notification count) — render a generic/anonymous header in the cached shell, then hydrate it client-side from a tiny authenticated /me call, or inject it at the edge via an edge function that reads a signed session cookie and does one edge-KV lookup for display fields (no origin round trip). (3) The "for you" module — load it client-side as a separate authenticated fetch after the shell paints (it's below the fold / non-critical), or edge-assemble it from a personalization service with a short cache. Net: one cached shell served to everyone at edge speed; personalization is a few crumbs added by the client or a cheap edge lookup. Avoid caching per-user full pages (cardinality) and avoid making the whole page uncacheable for the sake of two small regions. Use ESI or edge compose only if you can't do it client-side.
You move auth checks into a viewer-side edge function and p99 latency for cache hits gets worse. Why, and how do you fix it?
Viewer-side functions run on every request, including cache hits that previously never executed any code — so you've added compute (and possibly an outbound token-validation fetch or a KV lookup) to the fast path. If the function does a network call (introspect a token, hit an auth service), that call's latency and variance land on every request; cold starts (for container-based runtimes) add spikes. Fixes: (1) Make the check self-contained — verify a signed/JWT cookie locally (crypto verify, no network) instead of calling an auth service; keep the signing key in the edge config/secret store. (2) Use a V8-isolate runtime (near-zero cold start) rather than a container function for per-request logic. (3) If you must call out, cache the result in edge KV keyed by a token hash with a short TTL so most requests are local. (4) Scope the function to only the paths that need auth (don't run it for static assets / public pages). (5) Consider moving the check to the origin-request hook if it's only needed to protect origin content, so cache hits skip it entirely. (6) Keep the function's CPU tiny and measure p99, not mean. The principle: anything on the viewer path must be cheap, local, and deterministic.

Advanced deep

Design an edge-personalization architecture for a global storefront: cached catalog, per-user cart/pricing, geo/currency, A/B tests, and auth — with correctness and cost control.
Layering: (1) Catalog / content (product pages, listings, images) — cached hard at edge with a long s-maxage, surrogate keys per product/category, soft purge on merchandising changes. Cache key includes normalized market bucket (country→~N markets) and language only — not per user. Currency and legal text that depend only on market are baked into these market variants. (2) Per-user data (cart contents, loyalty pricing, saved items, "recently viewed") — never in the cached page. Delivered by a small authenticated API (/cart/summary, /pricing?skus=...) called client-side after the shell paints, or assembled by an edge function that verifies a signed session cookie and reads a regional edge store / calls a regional pricing service. Keep these responses private, no-store. (3) A/B tests — bucket deterministically at the edge (hash a stable anonymous ID) into a tiny enum (A/B); include the bucket in the cache key for pages whose content differs by variant, or apply the variant client-side for presentational tests so the page stays single-variant. Assignment cookie set via an edge function in a way that doesn't add Set-Cookie to the cached shell (set it on a separate beacon or via the function on the response without marking it uncacheable). (4) Auth — signed JWT/session cookie verified locally at the edge (no network); an edge-request function redirects unauthenticated users away from account pages before origin; logged-in state on shared pages is a client-side hydration, not a cache dimension. (5) Geo/currency — from the CDN's geo header, mapped to market at the edge; user can override (stored in a cookie that maps to the same market enum). Correctness: price shown on the cached product page is the market list price; the authoritative price (with user discounts, taxes for their address) is re-fetched and shown at cart/checkout from origin, and checkout re-validates server-side — the cache never determines money that's charged. Inventory/availability that changes fast is a small client-side or micro-cached (1–5s) call, not baked into the long-cached page. Cost control: minimize edge-function invocations (scope to the paths that need them; static assets bypass), avoid per-request outbound fetches (verify tokens locally, use edge KV for hot config/pricing tables), keep functions in an isolate runtime, and watch invocation count × CPU-ms × egress. The catalog's high hit ratio (few market×language variants) keeps origin and edge-compute cost low; personalization is a handful of small authenticated calls per session. Observability: hit ratio by page type, edge-function invocations/errors/CPU p99, personalization-API latency, and a correctness canary that checks cached list price vs authoritative price stays within policy. Ops: edge code and CDN config as versioned, staged IaC with instant rollback, because a bad edge function affects every request globally.
Compare ESI, client-side composition, and edge-compute composition for assembling a page from cacheable + personalized parts. Trade-offs and when each wins.
ESI (Edge Side Includes): the origin returns a template with <esi:include> markers; the CDN fetches each fragment (each with its own cache policy) and stitches server-side at the edge before responding. Pros: the client gets one fully-assembled HTML document (good for first paint, SEO, no client JS needed), each fragment cached independently, works with plain HTML. Cons: ESI support and feature coverage vary a lot by CDN (some don't support it, some only a subset); limited logic (includes, simple vars, basic conditionals — not arbitrary code); a slow/failing fragment can stall or break the whole assembled response unless you set onerror/timeouts carefully; debugging is opaque; personalization still requires the personalized fragment to be fetched per user (so it's an origin call unless itself edge-computed). Wins when: mostly-static pages with one or two low-logic personalized boxes, SEO/first-paint matters, and your CDN has solid ESI support. Client-side composition: serve a cached shell; the browser fetches personalized parts via JS after load. Pros: shell is trivially cacheable and identical for everyone (max hit ratio, min cardinality); personalization APIs are simple authenticated JSON; no special CDN features; easy to develop, test, and reason about; failures degrade gracefully (shell still renders). Cons: personalized content isn't in the initial HTML (SEO impact for those parts — usually fine since personalized bits aren't SEO-relevant), a flash of generic-then-personalized content, extra client round trips, requires JS. Wins when: personalized parts are non-critical / below the fold (cart count, "for you", recommendations), you want the simplest high-hit-ratio setup, and the app is already JS-driven. Edge-compute composition: an edge function fetches the cached shell + fragments (from cache, edge KV, or origin APIs) and assembles the response in code at the PoP. Pros: full programmability (arbitrary logic, auth, personalization from edge KV without origin, A/B, conditional assembly); returns a complete document like ESI but far more flexible; can cache the assembled result or parts programmatically; graceful fallback logic you control. Cons: it's code running on requests (CPU/time limits, cost, cold starts for some runtimes), each fragment fetch adds latency unless served from edge state, more to build/test/version/roll back, and doing it on the viewer path taxes cache hits (scope to miss path or specific routes). Wins when: you need real logic in assembly (personalize server-side into the HTML, combine multiple sources, auth-gated fragments), you have hot data you can put in edge KV to avoid origin calls, and first-paint/SEO of the composed result matters enough to justify the complexity. Rule of thumb: default to client-side composition for non-critical personalization (simplest, best hit ratio); use edge compute when the personalized content must be in the delivered HTML or needs logic; use ESI only if your CDN supports it well and your needs are simple includes — it's largely superseded by edge compute.

TLS, HTTP/2 & HTTP/3 at the Edge

The CDN terminates TLS close to the user and speaks modern protocols — that's a big chunk of the latency win.

Notes

TLS termination at the edge

  • The TLS handshake costs 1–2 round trips. Doing it against a nearby PoP instead of a distant origin removes those RTTs from every new connection.
  • The CDN holds your certificate (uploaded, or CDN-managed/ACME auto-issued, or via SNI for many customers). SNI lets one IP serve many hostnames' certs.
  • Edge ↔ origin is a separate TLS connection ("origin pull over HTTPS") — verify the origin cert, set min TLS version, and ideally use mTLS / authenticated origin pull so origin only trusts the CDN.
  • Session resumption: session IDs / session tickets / TLS 1.3 PSK let returning clients skip the full handshake (1-RTT or 0-RTT).
  • OCSP stapling: the edge attaches the cert's revocation proof so the client doesn't make its own OCSP call.
  • ALPN negotiates the protocol (h2, http/1.1) during the TLS handshake.

TLS 1.3

  • 1-RTT handshake (vs 2 for 1.2); 0-RTT resumption sends early data with the first packet — faster, but early data is replayable, so only use it for idempotent requests (GET), never for state-changing ones.
  • Removed weak ciphers/kex; forward secrecy is mandatory.

HTTP/2

  • Multiplexing: many concurrent streams over one TCP connection — no more 6-connections-per-origin limit, fixes HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.
  • Header compression (HPACK), stream prioritization, server push (now deprecated/removed in practice).
  • Remaining problem: TCP-level head-of-line blocking — one lost packet stalls all streams on that connection until retransmit.

HTTP/3 & QUIC

  • Runs over QUIC (UDP), with TLS 1.3 built in. Streams are independent at the transport level, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream — true fix for head-of-line blocking, big win on lossy/mobile networks.
  • Faster connection setup: crypto + transport handshake combined (1-RTT, or 0-RTT on resumption).
  • Connection migration: a connection ID survives the client's IP changing (Wi-Fi ↔ cellular) — no re-handshake.
  • Advertised via the Alt-Svc header (or HTTPS DNS record); the client upgrades on the next visit. UDP may be blocked on some networks → fall back to h2.

Edge ↔ origin efficiency

  • The CDN keeps a pool of warm keep-alive connections to origin, so a cache miss reuses an existing connection (no TCP+TLS setup per miss). This is a large part of "dynamic acceleration".
  • Often HTTP/1.1 or h2 to origin; connection reuse and pipelining matter more than the version here.
  • Tune origin keep-alive timeouts to match the CDN's, or you get churn.

Practical checklist

  • TLS 1.2 + 1.3 only; modern cipher suites; HSTS; OCSP stapling on.
  • Enable h2 and h3; verify with tooling that clients actually get h3 (Alt-Svc).
  • 0-RTT only for safe methods.
  • Automate cert issuance/renewal (ACME); monitor expiry.
  • mTLS / authenticated origin pull; verify origin certs; strong min version to origin.
Cheat Sheet
  • Edge TLS termination removes handshake RTTs (handshake vs a nearby PoP, not a distant origin). SNI = many certs per IP. Edge↔origin is a separate TLS connection — use mTLS / authenticated origin pull.
  • Speedups: session resumption (tickets / TLS 1.3 PSK), OCSP stapling, ALPN protocol negotiation.
  • TLS 1.3: 1-RTT handshake; 0-RTT resumption is replayable → idempotent (GET) only.
  • HTTP/2: multiplexed streams on one TCP conn, HPACK headers; still has TCP-level head-of-line blocking (one lost packet stalls all streams).
  • HTTP/3 / QUIC (UDP + TLS 1.3): independent streams (no transport HOL blocking), combined 1-RTT handshake, connection migration across IP changes. Advertised via Alt-Svc; falls back to h2 if UDP blocked.
  • Edge keeps warm keep-alive pools to origin so misses skip TCP+TLS setup.
  • Checklist: TLS 1.2/1.3 only, HSTS, OCSP stapling, h2+h3 on, ACME auto-renew + expiry alerts, mTLS to origin.
Q&A
Why does terminating TLS at the edge speed things up?
The TLS handshake takes one or two round trips before any application data flows. Performing it against a PoP a few milliseconds away instead of an origin hundreds of milliseconds away removes those RTTs from every new connection, and session resumption then makes subsequent connections even cheaper.
HTTP/2 solved head-of-line blocking — so why HTTP/3?
HTTP/2 removed HOL blocking at the HTTP layer (one connection, many multiplexed streams) but the streams still share one TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes in order — so a single lost packet blocks every stream until it's retransmitted. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, where each stream is independent at the transport level, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream. This matters most on lossy or mobile networks.
What is 0-RTT and its danger?
With TLS 1.3 session resumption, the client can send application data ("early data") in its very first flight, saving a round trip. The danger is that early data can be replayed by an attacker who captures it, because the server can't guarantee freshness before processing. So 0-RTT must be restricted to idempotent, non-state-changing requests (GETs), never things like "transfer money".
What is connection migration in QUIC?
QUIC identifies a connection by a connection ID rather than the 4-tuple of IPs and ports. If the client's network changes — phone switching from Wi-Fi to cellular, NAT rebinding — the connection continues under the same ID without a new handshake, avoiding the stall that TCP would incur.
What is authenticated origin pull / mTLS to origin?
The CDN presents a client certificate when connecting to your origin, and the origin is configured to accept connections only from clients presenting that CDN-issued cert. It ensures traffic to your origin genuinely comes from your CDN (not an attacker who found the origin IP), complementing IP allowlisting and secret headers.
Interview Questions

Basic warm-up

What transport does HTTP/3 run on?
QUIC (over UDP), with TLS 1.3 built in.
Which requests are safe to send as 0-RTT early data?
Idempotent ones (GET) — never state-changing requests, because early data can be replayed.
What header advertises HTTP/3 support?
Alt-Svc (or an HTTPS DNS record).

Intermediate core

Users on mobile networks report slow, janky page loads even though your CDN hit ratio is high. What protocol-level changes help?
Mobile networks have higher loss and variable latency, which punishes TCP+HTTP/2: one lost packet stalls all multiplexed streams (TCP head-of-line blocking), and every network change (Wi-Fi↔cell, cell handoff) forces a fresh TCP+TLS handshake. Enable HTTP/3 / QUIC: independent streams mean a lost packet only delays its own resource; the combined crypto+transport handshake is 1-RTT (0-RTT on resumption); and connection migration keeps the session alive across IP changes. Also ensure TLS 1.3 (fewer handshake RTTs), session resumption so repeat visits skip the handshake, and OCSP stapling so the client doesn't make a separate revocation call. Verify clients actually negotiate h3 (check Alt-Svc and real-world analytics — some carrier networks block UDP/443 and fall back to h2). Complement with smaller critical resources, Brotli, and prioritization so the first bytes that matter arrive first.
Your CDN shows high TLS handshake time to origin and origin CPU is spent on TLS. What's happening and how do you fix it?
The CDN is opening a new TLS connection to origin per request (or per miss) instead of reusing a pooled connection — so origin pays a full handshake (asymmetric crypto, cert chain) repeatedly, and the miss latency includes TCP+TLS setup each time. Causes: origin keepalive_timeout too low (or keep-alive disabled), so connections close between requests; the CDN's origin keep-alive pool set too small or disabled; a load balancer in front of origin not honoring keep-alive; mismatched idle timeouts causing churn; or HTTP/1.0-style Connection: close responses from origin. Fixes: (1) Enable and lengthen keep-alive on the origin and any LB, and raise max requests per connection. (2) Configure the CDN's origin connection pool (keep-alive enabled, adequate pool size, idle timeout slightly below origin's). (3) Ensure the origin isn't sending Connection: close. (4) Use TLS session resumption on the edge↔origin path and a modern cipher/curve (ECDSA cert, X25519) to cut handshake cost when one does happen. (5) Add an origin shield so far fewer connections/handshakes reach origin at all. (6) Offload TLS to a dedicated terminator or hardware if origin CPU is genuinely the bottleneck. The main lever is connection reuse — warm pooled keep-alives mean origin handshakes become rare.

Advanced deep

Walk through everything that happens, RTT by RTT, from a cold first visit to a CDN-fronted HTTPS site over HTTP/3, and contrast with HTTP/2 over TLS 1.2.
HTTP/2 over TLS 1.2 (cold): (1) DNS — resolve the hostname (0–1+ RTT depending on cache; may involve CNAME chains to the CDN). (2) TCP handshake — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK = 1 RTT to the edge before anything else. (3) TLS 1.2 handshake — ClientHello → ServerHello + certificate + key exchange → client key exchange + Finished → server Finished = ~2 RTT (ALPN negotiates h2 here; OCSP stapled inline). (4) HTTP request — client sends the GET; server responds = 1 RTT for first byte. Total before first byte ≈ 1 (TCP) + 2 (TLS) + 1 (request) = ~4 RTT after DNS. If the response is an HTML that references sub-resources on the same origin, those reuse the connection (h2 multiplexing) so no new handshakes, but a lost packet stalls all of them (TCP HOL). HTTP/3 over QUIC (cold): (1) DNS — same; an HTTPS/SVCB record can even hint h3 and the address, saving a step. Note the client typically must first learn h3 is available (via Alt-Svc on a prior h2 response, or the HTTPS DNS record) — a truly cold client with no hint may do the first request over h2 and upgrade afterward. (2) QUIC handshake — QUIC combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshake: the client's first flight carries the QUIC transport params and the TLS ClientHello; the server responds with its params + ServerHello + cert + Finished; client sends Finished and can send the request = 1 RTT to first byte (no separate TCP handshake — there is no TCP). (3) On a resumed visit, 0-RTT: the client sends the GET in its very first packet using a cached PSK = first byte in ~0 RTT (data in flight immediately), with the replay caveat (GET only). (4) Sub-resources multiplex over QUIC streams that are transport-independent, so a lost packet only delays its own resource. (5) If the network changes, the connection ID lets it migrate without re-handshaking. Contrast: h3 cuts the pre-first-byte cost from ~4 RTT (1 TCP + 2 TLS + 1 request, TLS 1.2) or ~3 RTT (TLS 1.3: 1 TCP + 1 TLS + 1 request) down to ~1 RTT cold / ~0 RTT resumed, removes transport HOL blocking, and survives IP changes — the gains are largest on high-latency, lossy, or mobile links and for connections that would otherwise be set up fresh. The catch: the client needs to know to use h3 (first visit often still starts on h2), and some networks block UDP so a fallback path must exist.
What are the security and operational considerations of the CDN holding your TLS private keys and terminating TLS, and what are the alternatives?
The concern: when the CDN terminates TLS, it has your certificate's private key (or one it issued for your domain) and sees your plaintext traffic at the edge. That means: the CDN (and anyone compromising it, or compelled via legal process) can read/modify requests and responses; a CDN breach could expose the key; and you're trusting the CDN's key storage, access controls, and personnel. For regulated data this needs due diligence (SOC 2 / ISO, key handling, data residency of PoPs). Mitigations / alternatives: (1) CDN-managed certificates — the CDN issues and holds a cert for your domain (via ACME) and you never upload your "real" key; a compromise is scoped to that CDN-issued cert, which you can revoke, and your primary key never leaves your control. This is the common modern default. (2) Keyless SSL / delegated credentials — the CDN terminates TLS but does not hold the private key; during each handshake it calls back to a key server you run to perform the single private-key signing/decryption operation, then proceeds. The key stays in your infrastructure (or an HSM). Adds a round trip to your key server on full handshakes (mitigated by session resumption) and you must run that key server highly available. Cloudflare "Keyless SSL", plus the IETF delegated credentials mechanism (short-lived credentials the CDN can hold, limiting blast radius without a callback per handshake). (3) Bring-your-own-cert with tight controls — upload your cert but use a dedicated, short-lived cert just for the CDN, separate from your origin's, with monitoring (Certificate Transparency logs) so mis-issuance or unexpected use is detected. (4) End-to-end encryption / pass-through — the CDN operates at L4 (TCP/SNI routing) and does not terminate TLS; the client's TLS session goes to your origin. You lose most CDN value (no caching of encrypted bodies, no WAF, no edge compute, limited DDoS L7 protection) — only sensible for specific TCP services, not web content. (5) Split trust — serve the most sensitive flows on a hostname that bypasses the CDN (direct to origin) and CDN-front only the cacheable/public content. Operational: automate issuance/renewal (ACME) and alert well before expiry; monitor CT logs for certs issued for your domain; use CAA records to constrain issuers; have a revocation + rotation runbook; verify the CDN's origin-pull uses a properly validated cert and ideally mTLS; and document in your threat model that the edge sees plaintext. For most sites, CDN-managed certs (or delegated credentials / keyless for higher assurance) give the CDN's benefits while limiting private-key exposure.

CDN Security: WAF, DDoS, Bots & Tokens

The edge is your outermost security perimeter — it absorbs volume and filters bad requests before origin.

Notes

DDoS absorption

  • L3/L4 (volumetric) — SYN floods, UDP/amplification, sheer bandwidth. The CDN's anycast network spreads the attack across many PoPs, each absorbing a slice with far more capacity than any single origin; scrubbing drops malformed/spoofed packets. Largely automatic.
  • L7 (application) — floods of "valid-looking" HTTP requests (GET floods, expensive endpoints, cache-busting queries). Defended with rate limiting, challenge/JS/CAPTCHA for suspicious clients, caching (so the flood hits the edge, not origin), anomaly detection, and blocking by fingerprint/ASN/geo.
  • Cache-busting attacks append random query strings to force misses → normalize the cache key (ignore unknown params) so the flood still hits cache.
  • Keep origin locked to the CDN, or attackers hit it directly and bypass all of this.

WAF (Web Application Firewall)

  • Inspects requests at the edge for attack patterns: SQLi, XSS, RCE, path traversal, known CVEs, protocol anomalies. OWASP Core Rule Set is the common managed baseline.
  • Modes: detect/log only → then enforce/block. Always run in log mode first and tune out false positives.
  • Custom rules: block/allow/challenge/rate-limit by URI, method, header, body, geo, IP/ASN, JA3/TLS fingerprint, or a scoring engine.
  • Positive vs negative security: negative = block known-bad signatures (CRS); positive = allow only known-good (schema/allowlist) — stronger, higher maintenance, used for APIs.
  • Virtual patching: a WAF rule to block exploitation of a specific vuln while you fix the code.

Bot management

  • Distinguish good bots (search crawlers, monitoring), bad bots (scrapers, credential stuffing, inventory hoarding, carding), and humans.
  • Signals: request rate/patterns, TLS/HTTP fingerprint (JA3/JA4), header order, browser challenges (JS execution, proof-of-work), behavioral analysis, known-bot IP lists, and device/browser attestation.
  • Actions: allow, challenge, throttle, serve alternate content, or block. Beware blocking legit crawlers or accessibility tools.

Access control & token auth

  • Signed URLs / signed cookies (token auth): the origin/app generates a URL with an HMAC signature over path + expiry (+ optional client IP, allowed referrers). The edge validates the signature and expiry before serving — used for paid downloads, video segments, private media. No origin call needed per request.
  • Geo/IP restrictions, referer checks (weak, spoofable), hotlink protection.
  • mTLS at the edge for API clients; API key / JWT validation in an edge function.
  • Basic auth / IP allowlist for staging environments.

Headers & hardening

  • Add/enforce security response headers at the edge: HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy.
  • Sanitize inbound: strip/normalize forwarding & debug headers (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL) to prevent cache poisoning and host-header attacks.
  • Strip response headers that leak origin details (server version, internal hostnames, stack traces).

Operational notes

  • Log to a SIEM: WAF events, rate-limit triggers, bot verdicts, blocked requests — with sampling for volume.
  • Have a break-glass plan: quickly tighten rules, enable "under attack" mode, or shed traffic during an incident.
  • Test WAF changes in staging; a bad rule can block all legit traffic.
  • The CDN protects inbound; you still need origin-side auth/validation (defense in depth — never trust the edge alone).
Cheat Sheet
  • L3/4 DDoS: anycast spreads volume across PoPs + packet scrubbing (mostly automatic). L7 DDoS: rate limiting, challenges/CAPTCHA, caching the flood, anomaly detection, geo/ASN blocks. Normalize cache key to defeat cache-busting floods.
  • WAF: edge inspection for SQLi/XSS/RCE/traversal/CVEs; OWASP CRS baseline. Run log-only first, tune, then block. Custom rules by URI/header/geo/IP/fingerprint. Negative (block bad) vs positive (allow good) security; virtual patching.
  • Bot management: rate/pattern + TLS/HTTP fingerprint (JA3/JA4) + JS challenge + behavior + known lists → allow/challenge/throttle/block. Don't block real crawlers.
  • Token auth: signed URLs / signed cookies = HMAC over path+expiry(+IP/referrer), validated at the edge — for paid/private content, no origin call.
  • Enforce security headers (HSTS/CSP/nosniff) at edge; sanitize inbound forwarding/debug headers; strip origin-leaking response headers.
  • Keep origin locked to the CDN; log to SIEM; have an "under attack" break-glass; test rules in staging; keep origin-side validation too (defense in depth).
Q&A
How does a CDN absorb a volumetric (L3/L4) DDoS?
Its anycast network announces the target IP from many PoPs, so the attack traffic is split across all of them by internet routing. Each PoP has far more capacity than a single origin and drops spoofed/malformed packets (scrubbing) close to the source. The origin, locked to only accept CDN traffic, never sees the flood.
Why run a WAF in log-only mode first?
Managed rulesets (like the OWASP CRS) generate false positives against real application traffic — legitimate requests that look like attacks. Running in detect/log mode lets you see what would be blocked, tune or disable the offending rules and add exceptions, and only switch to blocking once the false-positive rate is acceptable. Flipping straight to block risks taking the site down.
What is a cache-busting DDoS and how do you mitigate it?
Attackers request cacheable URLs with a random query string on each request (/page?x=93842), so every request is a cache MISS and goes to origin, defeating the CDN's protection. Mitigate by normalizing the cache key to ignore unknown/unexpected query parameters, so the randomized requests all map to the same cached object and the flood is absorbed at the edge.
How do signed URLs work?
The application generates a URL containing an expiry timestamp and an HMAC signature computed over the path, expiry, and a shared secret (optionally the client IP or allowed referrers). The CDN edge recomputes the HMAC and checks the expiry on each request; if it doesn't match or has expired, it returns 403 — all without contacting the origin. Used for paid downloads, private media, and video segments.
Does a CDN WAF mean you can skip origin-side input validation?
No. The edge is one layer; requests can reach origin by other paths (a leaked origin IP, an internal caller, a WAF bypass, an allowed-but-malicious request).
